h-rider-haggard: Henry Rider Haggard was born at Bradenham, Norfolk, the eighth of ten children of William Meybohm Rider Haggard, a barrister, and Ella Doveton, an author and poet. Unlike his elder brothers he attended Ipswich Grammar School, because his father could no longer afford expensive private schooling and perhaps doubted that he would amount to much. After he failed his army entrance examination he was sent to a London crammer to prepare for the Foreign Office examination, which he never sat. In London he met people interested in the study of psychic phenomena.

In 1875 his father sent him to South Africa as an unpaid assistant to the secretary to Sir Henry Bulwer, Lieutenant-Governor of Natal. In 1876 he joined the staff of Sir Theophilus Shepstone, Special Commissioner for the Transvaal, and in April 1877 he was in Pretoria for the announcement of the British annexation of the Transvaal. He raised the Union Flag and read much of the proclamation after the official chosen lost his voice. In 1878 he became Registrar of the High Court in the Transvaal. He married Marianna Louisa Margitson in 1880 and returned to England in 1882, settling at Ditchingham, Norfolk. He was called to the bar in 1884.

His legal practice was desultory, and after a book on the political situation in South Africa and a few unsuccessful novels he completed King Solomon's Mines, published in September. He accepted a 10 per cent royalty rather than £100 for the copyright. Allan Quatermain, She and its sequel Ayesha followed, with Nada the Lily, a tale of the Zulus, and the Viking romance Eric Brighteyes. Haggard also worked for agricultural reform and sat on commissions on land use. He stood unsuccessfully as a Conservative for East Norfolk in 1895, losing by 197 votes, and was knighted in 1912.

Haggard died on 14 May 1925 in Marylebone, London, aged 68, and his ashes were buried at St Mary's Church, Ditchingham. His novels carry many stereotypes of colonialism, yet they treat African characters with unusual sympathy; Africans often play heroic roles, such as the Zulu warrior Umslopogaas. Critics have also condemned his depiction of non-Europeans, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o names him among the canonical authors he calls geniuses of racism. Carl Jung read Ayesha as a manifestation of the anima, and the first chapter of People of the Mist is credited with inspiring the Royal Air Force motto Per ardua ad astra.
ha-giang-province: Hà Giang lay in the far north of Vietnam, with the country's northernmost point and a 270 km border with Yunnan province in China. It covered 7,927.55 square kilometres and was bordered by Cao Bằng, Tuyên Quang, Lào Cai and Yên Bái provinces. The terrain is mountainous, with limestone and granite peaks; the highest, Tây Côn Lĩnh, rises to 2,419 metres. The Lô River flows through the province, and the provincial capital, also called Hà Giang, stands on its left bank 320 km from Hanoi. Farming was limited by the mountains, and forests cover much of the land.

Excavations at Đồi Thông, near Hà Giang city, show that the region was inhabited about 30,000 years ago. In the Bronze Age, ceremonial bronze drums were made there, and the Lô Lô and Pu Péo peoples still use such drums today. The area was once part of bộ Tân Hưng in the ancient state of Văn Lang, and at the start of the 15th century, under Ming occupation, it was known as the district of Bình Nguyên before it was renamed châu Vị Xuyên.

The French occupied the region in 1886. Dao rebels rose against the French in 1901, and again in 1913 in the White Hat Revolt, which lasted until 1915 and was suppressed with the deportation of many and the hanging of at least 67. From the late 18th century the Hmong dominated the north of the province: the Vương family ruled at Đồng Văn and Mèo Vạc with the endorsement of the Nguyễn kings. Vương Chính Đức was recognised as king of the Hmong in 1900 and built a palace at Sà Phìn between 1902 and 1903. Hà Tuyên province was divided in 1991 into Tuyên Quang and Hà Giang provinces.

The Vietnamese government recognised 43 ethnic groups in the province, the largest being the Mông at about 34%, the Tày at about 23% and the Dao at about 15% of the population. Each has its own language and traditions, and the Khâu Vai love market is held once a year on the 27th day of the third lunar month. On 12 June 2025 Hà Giang province was merged with Tuyên Quang province to form a new Tuyên Quang province, and the former province was reorganised into two wards. The Vương family mansion at Sà Phìn was listed as an architectural heritage landmark in 1993.
ha-long-bay: Hạ Long Bay lies in northeastern Vietnam and is administered by the city of Quảng Ninh. The name Hạ Long means descending dragon. The bay covers about 1,553 km2 and holds 1,969 islets, most of them limestone, with a core area of 334 km2 that has 775 islets. Several of the islands are hollow, with large caves; Hang Dau Go is the largest grotto in the area.

Surveys show that people lived in the area tens of thousands of years ago. The Soi Nhụ culture, a people of the coast who caught fish and shellfish and gathered fruits and roots, was followed by the Cái Bèo culture, whose inhabitants had reached the level of exploiting the sea, and then by the Hạ Long culture. Before the 19th century the name Hạ Long Bay had not been recorded in the country's old books, and the bay was called other names such as An Bang, Lục Thủy and Vân Đồn. In the late 19th century the name appeared on a French maritime map. French tourists who visited the cave of Hang Dau Go at that time named it the Grotte des Merveilles.

The channels near the bay were the setting for naval battles against Vietnam's neighbours. On three occasions the Vietnamese army stopped Chinese invaders from landing among the channels of the Bạch Đằng River. In 1288 General Trần Hưng Đạo stopped Mongol ships from sailing up that river by setting steel-tipped wooden stakes that were covered at high tide, sinking the fleet of Kublai Khan.

On 5 June 1948 the Halong Bay Agreements were signed by High Commissioner Emile Bollaert and President Nguyễn Văn Xuân, and the new national flag of the Provisional Central Government of Vietnam was raised for the first time. During the Vietnam War many of the channels between the islands were heavily mined by the United States Navy, and some mines still threaten shipping routes.

In 1994 the core zone of the bay was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its aesthetic value, and in 2000 the World Heritage Committee also recognised its geological and geomorphological value. Tourism has led to the clearing of mangroves and seagrass beds, and the province of Quảng Ninh has banned coal and stone extraction in the heritage area and moved fishing households from floating villages to the mainland.
haakon-iv-of-norway: Haakon was born in the summer of 1204, probably in March or April, at Folkenborg to Inga of Varteig. His father was widely held to be King Haakon Sverresson, leader of the Birkebeiner faction in the civil war against the Baglers, though he had died before the birth. Born in Bagler territory, the child was in danger. In the winter of 1205/06 a group of Birkebeiners fled with him, and two skiers, Torstein Skevla and Skjervald Skrukka, carried him over the mountain from Lillehammer to Østerdalen. The Birkebeinerrennet ski race commemorates the journey.

After King Inge Bårdsson died in 1217 a succession dispute followed. Haakon had the backing of most Birkebeiners, and in June 1217 he was proclaimed king at Øyrating. Inge's half-brother Earl Skule Bårdsson settled on being his regent during his minority. In 1218 his mother proved his parentage by trial by ordeal in Bergen.

Haakon and Skule drifted apart, and a great meeting at Bergen in 1223 confirmed Haakon as king. He defeated the last Bagler pretender, Sigurd Ribbung, in 1227, and ended the civil war era in 1240 by having Skule killed, a year after Skule had proclaimed himself king. The pope withheld recognition because of Haakon's illegitimate birth; Innocent IV granted it in 1246, and Cardinal William of Sabina crowned him in 1247. He designated children of his marriage to Margrete Skulesdatter as heirs, bringing Catholic legitimacy into the order of succession.

At court he had European literature translated into Old Norse, beginning with the romance Tristan and Iseult in 1226, which helped begin the Norse chivalric sagas. He built a stone palace at Bergen, and his New Law of about 1260 advanced public justice over feud and revenge. Late in his reign Greenland and Iceland came under the Norwegian crown. He rejected Scottish attempts to buy the Hebrides, and when Alexander III attacked them he led an expedition.

Haakon fell ill and died on 16 December 1263 while wintering in Orkney, after engagements with Scotland, and was succeeded by his son Magnus VI. The Saga of Haakon Haakonsson, written soon after by the Icelandic writer and politician Sturla Þórðarson, is the chief source, and is considered the most detailed and reliable of the sagas of Norwegian kings, though written in support of the House of Sverre. Under him medieval Norway is considered to have reached its golden age, and the realm its largest extent. Historians have differed: P. A. Munch saw an almost flawless ruler, while Hans E. Kinck saw an insignificant king.
haakon-the-good: Haakon is not mentioned in any narrative source earlier than the late 12th century. According to the late saga tradition he was the youngest son of King Harald Fairhair and Thora Mosterstang and was born in Hordaland. Harald sent him to the court of King Æthelstan, who fostered him, which is why he was nicknamed Adalsteinfostre. The sagas say Æthelstan was tricked into this through the custom of knésetja, in which a child set on the knees of a foster-parent was formally adopted. Haakon appears in no contemporary Anglo-Saxon source. Norwegian royal biographies of the late 12th century say the English court introduced him to Christianity.

On news of Harald's death Æthelstan gave Haakon ships and men for an expedition against his half-brother Eric Bloodaxe, who had been proclaimed king. Back in Norway Haakon won the support of the landowners by promising to give up his father's rights of taxation over inherited property. Eric was soon deserted, fled to the Orkney Islands and later to the Kingdom of Jorvik, and died at Stainmore in 954.

Haakon fought Eric's sons at Avaldsnes in 953, at Rastarkalv near Frei in 955, where he placed ten standards along a ridge to make his army seem larger, and again in 957, when they returned with support from Gorm the Old of Denmark. Skaldic poems and the sagas link him with the introduction of the leiðangr naval system.

Haakon was noted for his attempts to introduce Christianity into Norway. The Historia Norwegiæ describes him as an apostate who observed both pagan and Christian rites. In 961 three of Eric's sons landed undetected in Hordaland and surprised him at Fitjar. After a final victory he was mortally wounded by an arrow and died later of the wound. He was buried in a mound at Seim, and his court poet Eyvindr skáldaspillir composed the Hákonarmál on his fall and reception into Valhalla. Harald Greycloak, Eric's eldest surviving son, succeeded him.
haakon-vi-of-norway: Haakon was the younger son of Magnus Eriksson, king of Sweden and Norway, and Blanche of Namur, and was born in 1340, most likely in Sweden. He belonged to the Swedish House of Bjälbo and, through his great-grandfather Haakon V, was considered an acceptable heir by the Norwegian nobility. He was raised in Norway to prepare him to rule there. On 15 August 1343 letters were issued stating that the king and the Council of the Realm had decided to place him on the Norwegian throne, and in the following year representatives of the cities and the public hailed him as king at Båhus Castle. Magnus abdicated the Norwegian throne in August 1355, though he kept control of parts of the kingdom.

Haakon's elder brother Eric rebelled against their father in Sweden, and when Eric died of the plague in 1359 the Swedish nobility deposed Magnus and elected Haakon king of Sweden at Uppsala on 15 February 1362. In 1363 Haakon married Margaret, daughter of Valdemar IV of Denmark, at Copenhagen Cathedral. That same year Swedish nobles led by Bo Jonsson Grip persuaded Duke Albert II of Mecklenburg to depose Magnus and Haakon in favour of his son Albert, who was crowned in 1364. Haakon and Magnus lost most of Sweden at the battle of Gataskogen, where Magnus was captured and held for six years.

In 1371 Haakon's campaign ended in the siege of Stockholm and a peace treaty signed on 14 August 1371, which freed Magnus for a ransom of 12,000 silver marks, more than the kingdom's ordinary tax income before the plague, so that a special tax was imposed.

Haakon allied with Valdemar, turning Norwegian policy eastwards. In 1367 the Hanseatic League formed the Confederation of Cologne against Denmark and Norway and raided the Norwegian coast, and the Treaty of Stralsund of 24 May 1370 ended the war and left the League with a virtual monopoly on trade. When Valdemar died on 24 October 1375, Haakon borrowed money for the League's neutrality, and on 3 May 1376 his son Olav was elected king of Denmark at Slagelse. In 1379 Haakon confirmed Henry Sinclair as Earl of Orkney. The Black Death had reached Bergen in 1349 and killed between 50 and 60 per cent of its population.

Haakon died on 11 September 1380 and was succeeded by Olav, with Margaret as regent. Olav died childless seven years later, and Margaret asserted authority over all three Scandinavian kingdoms as their first female monarch.
haakon-vii: Prince Carl was born on 3 August 1872 at Charlottenlund Palace north of Copenhagen, the second son of Crown Prince Frederik of Denmark, the future Frederick VIII, and Louise of Sweden. Through his mother he was a grandson of King Charles XV of Sweden and Norway, which linked him to both the Danish and Swedish royal houses. As a younger son he was third in line to the Danish throne, with little prospect of inheriting it. He was educated at the Royal Danish Naval Academy and served in the Royal Danish Navy. On 22 July 1896 he married his first cousin Princess Maud of Wales; their only child, the future Olav V, was born in 1903.

The union between Sweden and Norway, in existence since 1814, was dissolved unilaterally by the Storting on 7 June 1905, and the Norwegian people confirmed this in a referendum on 13 August. Sweden recognized it on 23 September in the Treaty of Karlstad. Carl was offered the Norwegian crown, accepted after a referendum on the monarchy and was elected by the Storting, taking the Old Norse name Haakon. He was the first independent Norwegian monarch since Olav IV in 1387. He arrived in Kristiania on 25 November 1905 and was crowned in Trondheim on 22 June 1906.

Although the Constitution vested him with considerable executive powers, parliamentary rule had existed in Norway since 1884, so nearly all decisions were made by the Council of State in his name. He confined himself to a representative role, a practice continued by his son and grandson, and his long rule gave him considerable moral authority as a symbol of unity.

Germany invaded Norway in the early hours of 9 April 1940. Oscarsborg Fortress sank the heavy cruiser Blücher, which delayed the occupation of Oslo and allowed the royal family, the cabinet and most Storting members to leave by special train. German bombers attacked Nybergsund on 11 April, but the king and his ministers escaped into the woods. Haakon rejected German demands to legitimise the Quisling regime, vowing to abdicate rather than do so, and he refused to abdicate in exile.

In Britain his wartime speeches were broadcast to Norway by the BBC, which established him as a national symbol of resistance. He returned to Norway in June 1945 and limited himself to constitutional duties. He died at the Royal Palace in Oslo on 21 September 1957 and was succeeded by Olav V.
haapsalu: Haapsalu lies on the west coast of Estonia and is the administrative centre of Lääne County. Its name derives from the Estonian words haab, aspen, and salu, used in an archaic sense for a forested island. Until the first half of the 20th century it was called Hapsal in Swedish and German. The town has six neighbourhoods: Holmi, Kesklinn, Männiku, Paralepa, Randsalu and Vanalinn.

The first written record of Haapsalu dates from 1279, when the town was chartered and became the capital of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek, which it remained for the following three centuries. The episcopal castle survives, and its church is the largest single-nave church in Estonia. From the 13th century Haapsalu and the surrounding area were the centre of the Estonian Swedes, until almost all ethnic Swedes were evacuated from Estonia in 1944, before the Soviet invasion.

In 1825 a military doctor, Carl Abraham Hunnius, founded the first mud cure resort there, because the sea mud was claimed to have a curative effect. News of the curative mud spread quickly among wealthy customers in Saint Petersburg and elsewhere in the Russian Empire, and the Romanov family frequented the mud spas. In 1867 Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote a suite of three piano pieces during his stay, titled Souvenir de Hapsal.

Haapsalu is a seaside resort town with a population of 9,375. For almost 200 years it has been a summer destination for people seeking medical treatment with the sea mud, and three mud cure establishments operate there. In the 19th century the town became known for the Haapsalu shawls, a delicate craft made by local women. It hosts summer festivals, among them the August Blues Festival and the White Lady Days. The Haapsalu Horror and Fantasy Film Festival has been held there annually since 2005.
haarlem: Haarlem lies on the river Spaarne, about 20 km west of Amsterdam and near the coastal dunes. It stands on a thin strip of land above sea level known as the strandwal, which connects Leiden to Alkmaar, where people struggled against the North Sea to the west and the waters of the IJ and the Haarlem Lake to the east. The city became wealthy from the tolls it collected from ships and travellers on this busy north–south route. For centuries it was the centre of the tulip bulb-growing district.

The oldest mention of Haarlem dates from the 10th century, and a Christian parish church has stood there since the 9th. The first city walls were built in 1270. Beer brewing was important from the 15th century, when there were 100 breweries in the city, and clean water from the dunes also served the bleaching trade.

After the Geuzen conquered Brielle, Haarlem began to support them, and King Philip II of Spain sent an army north under Don Fadrique. It besieged the city on 11 December 1572. The defences were commanded by the governor Wigbolt Ripperda, and a widow, Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer, helped defend the city with some three hundred other women. A great fire on the night of 22 to 23 October 1576 began in a brewery near the weighhouse. The Spanish left in 1577.

To restore the economy and attract workers, the council promoted the arts and showed tolerance for diversity of belief. Haarlem declined in the 18th century as trade gravitated to Amsterdam. On 19 January 1795 a bloodless revolution removed the city's administrators the night William V fled the country, and the Batavian Republic was proclaimed.

Haarlem is the capital of the province of North Holland. Teylers Museum, on the Spaarne, is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, and the Frans Hals Museum houses Dutch master paintings. The city is known for its hofjes, almshouses built around courtyards, of which 19 survive.
haber-process: During the 19th century the demand for nitrates and ammonia, for use as nitrogen fertilisers and as industrial feedstocks, grew rapidly. The main sources were mined niter deposits and guano from tropical islands, and at the beginning of the 20th century these reserves were thought insufficient for future demand. Atmospheric nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air but is exceptionally stable and does not readily react with other chemicals. The cyanamide process, its chief competitor at first, used large amounts of electrical power and was more labour-intensive.

Fritz Haber and his assistant Robert Le Rossignol developed the high-pressure devices and catalysts needed to demonstrate the process in the laboratory. In the summer of 1909 they made ammonia from the air, drop by drop, at about 125 millilitres an hour. The German company BASF bought the process and set Carl Bosch to scale up Haber's tabletop machine. Haber was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 and Bosch in 1931, for overcoming the chemical and engineering problems of large-scale, continuous-flow, high-pressure technology.

Nitrogen and hydrogen gas react on the surface of a solid catalyst, usually iron, to form ammonia. The two nitrogen atoms in each molecule are held by a very strong triple bond, which must be broken before they can react. This is the slowest step and controls the speed of the whole process. The reaction needs high pressure and high temperature, and the synthesis loop works at 300 to 500 °C. Only about 15 percent of the gases turn into ammonia on each pass, so the ammonia is cooled and removed as a liquid and the unused gases are recycled. Most of the hydrogen comes from natural gas. The first catalysts Haber used were based on osmium and uranium.

The first industrial plant opened in 1913 at Oppau. During the First World War Germany used the process to make nitric acid for explosives, which it could no longer import because of the Allied blockade. Most of the ammonia is used for nitrogen fertiliser, either directly or as ammonium nitrate and urea. Vaclav Smil writes that with average crop yields at the 1900 level the harvest of the year 2000 would have needed nearly four times more land. In 2018 the process produced about 230 million tonnes of ammonia, using 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy and contributing to the buildup of reactive nitrogen in the biosphere.
habib-bourguiba: Habib Bourguiba was born in Monastir, the youngest of eight children. His father had spent nineteen years campaigning in the army and later became a city councilman, which allowed him to pay for his son's modern education. Bourguiba attended Sadiki College and the Lycée Carnot in Tunis, took his baccalaureate in 1924 and graduated from the University of Paris and Sciences Po in 1927. He returned to Tunis in August 1927 to practise law, and in the early 1930s joined the Destour party.

After the riots of 9 April 1938 he was sent to Marseille, where he was held during the Second World War. Following his release in 1945 he went to Cairo to seek the support of the Arab League, and he returned to Tunisia in 1949. In 1950 he travelled to Paris and set out the nationalists' demands in seven points. When talks failed, unrest began in 1952, and he was imprisoned on La Galite Island for two years before being moved to France. There he negotiated with Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France, who recognised Tunisia's internal autonomy on 31 July 1954.

Bourguiba came back to Tunis on 1 June 1955 and then faced Salah Ben Youssef, who rejected his gradual policy and called for the independence of the whole Maghreb. The dispute set Bourguibists against Youssefists and ended in Bourguiba's favour at the Sfax Congress of 1955. Independence was proclaimed on 20 March 1956. Bourguiba became prime minister under the bey and proclaimed the Republic on 25 July 1957.

On 8 February 1958 the French army bombed the border village of Sakiet Sidi Youssef, killing 72 people, and Bourguiba responded by banning French warships from Tunisian waters. His government's reforms covered female emancipation, public education, family planning, state healthcare and the ending of religious endowments known as waqf, and the Code of Personal Status was the main one. He also built a presidential system. The Neo Destour was declared the only legal party in 1963, and in 1975 he proclaimed himself president for life.

The 1980s brought Bourguiba's declining health, a struggle over his succession and a political and social crisis. On 7 November 1987 his prime minister, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, removed him from power. He was kept in a house in Monastir until he died there on 6 April 2000, and he was buried in a mausoleum he had built earlier. His supporters called his pragmatic doctrine Bourguibism. He is remembered for leading Tunisia to independence and for founding its republic.
habibullah-kalakani: Habibullah Kalakani was born Habibullah Khan on 19 January 1891 in the village of Kalakan, north of Kabul, and was an ethnic Tajik. His father was a water carrier for Afghan soldiers in Kabul during the Second Anglo-Afghan War. At fourteen he rode to Kabul with two friends. He later joined King Amanullah Khan's army and fought in the Third Anglo-Afghan War and the Khost rebellion of 1924, serving with distinction as an officer of the Model Battalion. He deserted at some unspecified time, worked in Peshawar, and was arrested at Parachinar and sentenced by the British to eleven months in prison.

In 1928, while the Afghan army was engaged with Pashtun tribes in Laghman and Nangarhar in the east, the Saqqawists led by Kalakani attacked the unprotected capital from the north. The revolt grew into the Afghan Civil War of 1928 and 1929. On the night of 14 January 1929 Amanullah handed the kingdom to his brother Inayatullah Khan and left Kabul for Kandahar. Two days later Kalakani demanded that Inayatullah surrender or fight, and Inayatullah agreed to abdicate. Kalakani was Emir of Afghanistan from 17 January to 13 October 1929, a period known in Afghan historiography as the Saqqawist period. No country recognized him as ruler.

The Pashtun tribes, including the Ghilzai, chafed under a non-Pashtun ruler. Nadir Shah, who had been Amanullah's minister of war, and his Musahiban brothers raised a force mostly from the British side of the Durand Line. Anti-Soviet Basmachi rebels, who had taken refuge in Afghanistan, also launched raids into the Soviet Union and were expelled from Afghanistan after his fall.

Nadir's force took Kabul on 13 October 1929. Nadir considered pardoning Kalakani, even swearing on the Quran according to some accounts, but pressure from loyal tribes led him to execute Kalakani and some of his closest followers on 1 November 1929. His reported last words were that he had nothing to ask of God, who had made him king. His remains lay at an undisclosed location for 87 years. After a campaign in 2016 by some Tajiks and scholars, he was buried on the Shahrara hill on 2 September 2016, after clashes between his supporters and soldiers loyal to Abdul Rashid Dostum in which one person died and four were injured.
habsburg-castle: Habsburg Castle stands in the canton of Aargau, near the Aar River, the largest tributary of the High Rhine, and at the time of its building the site lay in the Duchy of Swabia. It was built around 1020 by Count Radbot of the nearby county of Klettgau and Werner, Bishop of Strasbourg, on the Aar 35 kilometres southwest of Klettgau. It is believed that it was named after a hawk, in German Habicht, seen sitting on its walls.

Some historians and linguists think the name may come from the Middle High German hab or hap, meaning ford, as the castle is near a ford of the Aar. The name Habsburg was not added to the noble title until Radbot's grandson Otto II added von Habsburg to his title, which began the House of Habsburg.

The castle lost importance when Radbot's descendant in the seventh generation, Rudolph, moved the family's power base to Austria in 1276. In 1415 Duke Frederick IV of Austria lost the canton of Aargau to the Swiss Confederacy. The original coat of arms flown over the castle, a red lion on a golden field, remained part of the Austrian arms to the end of the imperial period, and the modern arms of the municipality of Habsburg show the castle. The forests around it were cleared only around 1500, nearly half a millennium after the castle was first built. The Canton of Aargau has owned it since 1804, and it became part of Museum Aargau in 2009.

The large and small towers of the original castle survive, attached to a residential building of the 13th century, while large parts of the complex lie in ruins, and the extent of the eastern part can be made out only from foundation walls. The palatial residence houses a restaurant and a small exhibition. The castle is listed as a Swiss heritage site of national significance.
haci-i-giray: Haji I Giray was born in 1397, probably at Trakai in Lithuania. His grandfather Tash-Timur minted coins in Crimea in 1394 and 1395, which may imply some independence, but was driven out during one of Tamerlane's wars, and Haji's father Gyyas-ed-Din and uncle Devlet-Berdi fled to Lithuania. They supported Tokhtamysh against Edigu, and Gyyas-ed-Din was killed in one of the battles. Tradition says that a servant hid the boy for six years. According to a story told by Milner, a shepherd protected him as a boy, and when he grew powerful he took the shepherd's name, Giray. His early ancestor was Togay Timur, a younger son of Jochi.

After Edigu died in 1419, Devlet-Berdi and his nephew Haji established themselves in Crimea. In 1428 Haji took Crimea with the support of Vytautas of Lithuania and the Shirin mirzas, but he was driven out when Ulugh Muhammad invaded and the Shirin nobles changed sides. He returned in 1431 with troops raised in Lithuania. In 1433 he allied with Alexios I of the Principality of Theodoro, and he defeated the Genoese near Stary Krym, after which the Genoese recognised him as khan. In 1434 Ulugh Muhammad invaded again, and Haji fled to Lithuania, where Sigismund Kęstutaitis held him hostage in a castle at Lida.

Around 1440 the Crimean nobles asked Casimir IV Jagiellon to release him, and he returned with a large army and drove out the governor of Sayid Ahmad I. Genoese sources name him khan in March 1441, and he minted coins at Chufut-Kale that year, so 1441 is often taken as the start of his reign and of the Crimean Khanate. Other dates are 1428 and 1449. He then fought Sayid Ahmad, whom he defeated in 1452 and who spent the rest of his life in Lithuania. When a Turkish fleet approached Kaffa the year after the fall of Constantinople, he negotiated with its commander and the fleet withdrew. He moved his capital to the rock fort of Chufut-Kale.

Haji I Giray died in August 1466 and was buried at Salachik, now on the edge of Bakhchysarai. A contemporary chronicle, that of Dlugosz, described him as a man of outstanding personal values and an effective governor. He is said to have introduced the trident of the Girays as the state symbol. His sons Nur Devlet and Meñli I Giray fought over the throne from 1466 to 1478, and in 1478 the Turks made Meñli khan as a vassal and ally, an arrangement that lasted until 1774. In 1502 Meñli destroyed the remnant of the Golden Horde.
hacienda: Haciendas originated during the Reconquista of Andalusia, when the sudden acquisition of conquered land allowed kings to grant large holdings to nobles, mercenaries and religious military orders as a reward for service. Andalusian haciendas produced wine, grain, oil and livestock and were more purely agricultural than what followed in Spanish America.

The word comes from Spanish hacer, to make, and refers to productive enterprises. The term is imprecise, but it usually means landed estates of significant size, while smaller holdings were called estancias or ranchos. In the Americas the model was exported with colonisation, and the crown gave conquistadores large land grants that became haciendas. The system in Mexico is considered to have started in 1529, when the crown granted Hernán Cortés the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca.

Haciendas were profit-making enterprises linked to regional or international markets. They grew sugar, wheat, fruit and vegetables and produced meat, wool, leather and tallow. Land distribution ran parallel to the allotment of indigenous people to servitude under the encomienda. As the crown moved to end encomienda labour, Spaniards consolidated private landholdings and recruited labour on a permanent or casual basis. The owner, called the hacendado or patrón, often lived in a city, while a paid administrator managed the estate. Near indigenous communities, as in central Mexico, a small permanent workforce was supplemented at planting and harvest.

Cattle, horses, sheep and goats came from Spain, and sheep in particular did great environmental damage by overgrazing. Caribbean haciendas were mainly sugar plantations worked by enslaved people brought from Africa, and in Puerto Rico that system ended with abolition on 22 March 1873. The Church, especially the Jesuits, held vast hacienda lands or lent money to hacendados.

After independence in the early 19th century the hacienda remained in much of South America. In Bolivia haciendas were prevalent until the Agrarian Reform that followed the 1952 Revolution of Víctor Paz Estenssoro. In Peru they lasted until the Agrarian Reform of 1969 under Juan Velasco Alvarado, who expropriated the land and redistributed it to peasants. In Chile the institution was eliminated by the land reform of 1962 to 1973. In the Philippines it survived efforts at land reform, and in Puerto Rico the last haciendas had ended by the 1990s. Today the word also names an architectural style in the United States, and in Spain and Mexico it names the finance ministry.
hadad: Hadad was introduced from the Levant to Mesopotamia by the Amorites, where he became the Akkadian god Adad. The same logogram, dIM, writes Adad, the Sumerian Iškur and the Hurrian god Teshub. Adad's worship became widespread in Mesopotamia after the First Babylonian dynasty. Iškur appears in the god list from Shuruppak but was of far less importance, perhaps because storms and rain were scarce in Sumer, where agriculture depended on irrigation. The gods Enlil and Ninurta also had storm-god features. His consort was the grain goddess Shala, and his Babylonian cult centre was Karkara.

Hymns, incantations and votive inscriptions show two aspects of Adad. He brings rain in due season to fertilise the land, and he sends storms that wreak destruction; in hymns the sombre aspect predominates. In Assyria he was developed as a warrior god, and from the reign of Tiglath-Pileser I he shared a double sanctuary with Anu in Assur. With the sun-god Shamash he presided over oracles and divination, and the two were addressed as lords of divination.

At Ugarit the Baal Cycle, composed between 1400 and 1200 BCE, presents Ba'al, also called Hadad, as lord of the sky who governs rain and crops. With two clubs made by the craftsman Kothar-wa-Khasis he strikes down Yamm (Sea) and is supreme. A palace of silver, gold and cedar is built for him, but Mot (Death) overcomes him, until his sister 'Anat cleaves Mot and the sun goddess Shapash fetches Ba'al back.

In Egypt, during the Hyksos period and the New Kingdom, Baal was strongly identified with Set, the god of storms and foreign lands, and the Hyksos worshipped him at Avaris as Set of Avaris. Pharaohs of the 19th Dynasty such as Ramesses II described their armies as like Baal in battle. In Aram the name Hadad appears in royal names: Hadadezer was the Aramean king defeated by David, and later kings of Damascus took the title Ben-Hadad, son of Hadad. A king of Yamhad, in the second millennium BCE, called himself beloved of Hadad, and the god's temple stood in the citadel of Halab, modern Aleppo.
hadamar: Hadamar is a small town in the Limburg-Weilburg district of Hesse, Germany. It lies 7 kilometres north of Limburg, between Cologne and Frankfurt am Main, on the southern edge of the Westerwald, at elevations from 120 to 390 metres above sea level. The town consists of eight formerly autonomous communities, among them Niederhadamar, Niederzeuzheim, Oberzeuzheim and Steinbach. A Wartberg culture cist grave about 5,000 years old, at Niederzeuzheim, is among the oldest signs of settlement.

Oberweyer and Niederweyer were the first of the communities named in documents, in 772; Hadamar itself first appears in a Carolingian exchange document of 832. Cistercian monks of Eberbach Abbey ran a model farm on the site of the palace in the 13th century. Count Emich of Nassau-Hadamar bought it in 1320 and made it a moated castle, and in 1324 Emperor Ludwig IV granted him Frankfurt town rights for his residence.

After a fire in the 16th century the town was rebuilt in the 17th under Count, later Prince, Johann Ludwig of Nassau-Hadamar (1590-1653), who enlarged the castle into a palace, laid out the baroque new town in a grid and invited the Franciscans and, in 1630, the Jesuits. The emperor named him commissioner-general at the negotiations for the Peace of Westphalia, and he was the first to sign the treaty. In 1650 he became a prince, and Hadamar a residence town. Altar sculptors of the so-called Hadamar Baroque, among them Martin Volk and Johann Valentin Neudecker, worked in the region.

The Corrigendenanstalt, a workhouse for vagrants, was built in 1883 on the Mönchberg and became a care facility for the mentally ill in 1906. In Nazi Germany, from 1941, at least 14,494 disabled or mentally ill people, along with those classed as Half-Jews under the Nuremberg Laws and Ostarbeiter, were murdered in the killing facility there. In 1942 alone, 19 Jewish inhabitants were deported and murdered.

A memorial at the site recalls those crimes, and a clinic for forensic psychiatry stands on the grounds. After the Second World War refugees from the Sudetenland brought glass crafts, which led to the founding of the Erwin-Stein-Glasfachschule, a vocational school for glass craftsmen. The old town keeps many timber-frame buildings, the town hall of 1639, the princely palace on the Elbbach with its stone bridge, the Gothic Liebfrauenkirche built before 1376 and a synagogue that houses an exhibition on Jewish life.
hadith: The Arabic word hadith means a report or an account of an event. It refers to the oral tradition of anecdotes containing the purported words, actions and silent approvals of Muhammad or his immediate circle, the companions in Sunni Islam and the Ahl al-Bayt in Shia Islam. The traditions first circulated in early discussions after Muhammad's death, often without formal attribution. They were not promptly written down in his lifetime or immediately after his death, and the majority were documented several centuries later, some 200 to 300 years afterwards in Sunni sources and 400 to 500 in Shia books. From the 7th to the 10th centuries scholars called muhaddiths compiled them, organising them first by the primary authority and then by subject.

Each hadith has two parts: the text of the report, the matn, and the chain of narrators, the isnad, a chronological list of those who heard and repeated it. Scholars from the eighth century onward have repeated that the isnad is part of the religion. Biographical analysis examines each narrator's dates, teachers, religiosity and travels to judge reliability, and a report carried by many independent chains is called mutawatir. Reports are graded as sahih (authentic), hasan (good) or daif (weak), and fabricated reports are classed as mawdu.

Different branches of Islam refer to different collections. For Sunnis the canonical collections are six books, of which Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim generally have the highest status. Twelver Shia use the Four Books, beginning with Kitab al-Kafi, the Ismaili Shia use the Da'a'im al-Islam, and the Ibadi branch uses the Tartib al-Musnad. Shia collections give preference to hadith attributed to Muhammad's family and close companions. Hadith are part of the Sunnah, the body of traditions and practices, and a significant portion of Sharia rules is derived from them rather than the Quran.

Hadith gained their standing as the second authority after the Quran over centuries. Some groups have questioned or rejected them, among them the Kharijites, the Mu'tazila and certain early jurists, and Quranists regard the collections as historical sources to be assessed critically rather than as binding teaching. Western critical scholarship rejects the authenticity of hadith as an accurate record of the historical Muhammad, and some scholars argue that the corpus does not reflect the seventh century but projects back the legal, theological and political conflicts of the 8th to 10th centuries.
hadrians-villa: Several Republican-era villas, one or more possibly inherited by Hadrian's wife Vibia Sabina, already stood on artificial terraces at the site. Hadrian began construction early in his reign, a few months after he arrived in Rome.

His first documented presence at the villa came in 125, after the return from his first journey, and he started using it as his official residence around 128. Most brick stamps date to 123, and building continued during his absences on later journeys, so that he could enjoy finished buildings on his return in about 130. He had at most six years of residence there, yet a large court lived at the villa permanently. He is believed to have retired there towards the end of his life, and some work may have been unfinished at his death.

The buildings are of travertine, brick, lime, pozzolana and tufa. Water for the fountains, pools and gardens came from aqueducts that fed Rome, including the Aqua Anio Vetus, Aqua Anio Novus, Aqua Marcia and Aqua Claudia, which required the villa to lie on land lower than the aqueducts. The Historia Augusta, the only ancient written evidence, says that Hadrian named rooms after places in the empire, such as the Lyceum, the Academy and Hades. The Poecile was modelled on the Stoa Poikile in the agora of Athens, a pool of 232 by 97 m within colonnaded walls.

The Maritime Theatre is a miniature house built on an islet in a circular moat, with a ring-shaped pool and a symmetrical plan that is rare in Roman architecture; it may have been Hadrian's first temporary residence on the site. The Piazza d'Oro had a peristyle of 61 by 51 m with a central canal and a vestibule under an umbrella dome. Portraits of Sabina, Marcus Aurelius and Caracalla found there show that it was used after Hadrian's time.

The Piazza d'Oro was plundered several times in treasure hunts from the 16th century, and many marble sculptures entered foreign collections. They include the Diana of Versailles, now in the Louvre, and the Discobolus. In 1998 scholars rediscovered the Antinoeion, where a concrete foundation has been used as evidence for the original site of the Antinous Obelisk; some argue that Antinous was buried there, others that the area was a highly Egyptianised nympheum. UNESCO designated the villa a World Heritage Site in 1999, citing its brought-together material culture of the Mediterranean world and its influence on Renaissance and baroque architecture. Much of the site remains unexcavated.
hadrians-wall: Hadrian's Wall was probably planned before the emperor's visit to Britain in 122. Hadrian ended the expansionist policy of his predecessor Trajan and concentrated on defending the existing borders. Britain had no natural boundary, such as the Euphrates, Rhine or Danube, to divide the Roman province from the peoples of the north.

Building began in 122, and most of the work took about six years. It was done by soldiers of three legions, the Legio II Augusta, Legio VI Victrix and Legio XX Valeria Victrix, some 15,000 men in all, together with some members of the Roman fleet. The wall ran for 80 Roman miles, equivalent to 73 modern miles, from Segedunum at Wallsend on the Tyne to the shore of the Solway Firth near Bowness-on-Solway. Its planned thickness of 10 feet was soon reduced to about 8 feet. West of Milecastle 49 it was first built of turf and later replaced in stone.

The wall was built with an alternating series of forts, each housing 600 men, and milecastles manned by between 12 and 20 men, with a turret every third of a mile. After construction almost 10,000 soldiers were probably stationed along it, drawn not from the legions that built it but from regiments of auxiliary infantry and cavalry raised in the provinces. Troops in the forts had the primary duty of defence, while those in the milecastles and turrets were responsible for frontier control.

Roman coins and pottery generally did not cross the wall, which seems to have been an effective barrier to trade. After Hadrian died in 138 his successor Antoninus Pius began the turf Antonine Wall about 160 km to the north, leaving Hadrian's Wall occupied in a support role. Marcus Aurelius abandoned the Antonine Wall and reoccupied Hadrian's Wall in 164.

Almost all the standing masonry was removed in early modern times for local roads and farmhouses, and long sections were used in the 18th century to build General Wade's military road. The antiquarian John Clayton, town clerk of Newcastle in the 1830s, saved much of what remains by buying land along the wall. Hadrian's Wall became a World Heritage Site in 1987. It lies wholly in England and has never formed the Anglo-Scottish border.
haeinsa: Haeinsa lies in Gayasan National Park, South Gyeongsang Province, and is the head temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Seon Buddhism. According to legend, two monks of royal Daegaya descent, Suneung and Ijeong, returned from Tang China and healed the wife of Aejang of Silla, and the king ordered the temple built in gratitude. Another account, by Choe Chi-won in 900, says that the two won the support of a queen dowager who converted to Buddhism and helped to finance the building. The complex was renovated in the 10th century and again in 1488, 1622 and 1644, and a fire in 1817 burned down most of it before it was rebuilt in 1818.

The main hall, the Daejeokgwangjeon, or Hall of Great Silence and Light, is dedicated to Vairocana, unlike the main halls of most Korean temples, which house images of Gautama Buddha. The Janggyeong Panjeon, the storage halls for the Tripitaka Koreana, is the oldest part of the temple. Its construction date is uncertain, but Sejo of Joseon is believed to have expanded and renovated it in 1457. Four plain halls stand around a rectangle, and the two main ones, the Beopbojeon and the Sudara-jang, are 60.44 metres long.

The halls stand at the highest point of the temple, 655 metres above sea level, facing south-west to avoid damp winds from the valley and sheltered from the cold north wind by mountain peaks. Windows of different sizes on the north and south sides ventilate them, and clay floors filled with charcoal, lime, salt and sand absorb moisture when it rains and release it in the dry winter.

The halls were untouched during the Japanese invasions of Korea that began in 1592 and have survived seven serious fires. In September 1951, during a bombing campaign against guerrillas in the Korean War, Colonel Kim Young-hwan was ordered to destroy the temple, refused, and led his fighter jets over it without dropping a bomb. The Korean government designated the halls National Treasure No. 32 in 1962, and UNESCO made them a World Heritage Site in 1995, noting that no other historical structure was dedicated specifically to preserving such artefacts.
hafez: Khajeh Shams-od-Din Mohammad Hafez Shirazi was born in Shiraz and identified as a Sufi Muslim. Few details of his life are known, and accounts of his early years rely on traditional anecdotes; the early tazkiras, or biographical sketches, that mention him are generally considered unreliable. He is said to have memorized the Quran at an early age, and the title Hafez, which he later used as his pen name, was given to him for this.

He was supported by the patronage of several successive local regimes, among them Shah Abu Ishaq, who came to power while Hafez was in his teens, and the strict Mubariz ud-Din Muhammad. His work flourished most under the 27-year rule of Jalal ud-Din Shah Shuja. Hafez also exchanged letters and poetry with Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, the Sultan of Bengal, who invited him to Sonargaon; he could not go.

Hafez wrote chiefly lyric poetry in the form of the ghazal. His Divan, probably compiled after his death, deals with the beloved, faith, wine and taverns, and the exposure of hypocrisy. Whether the poems are to be read literally, mystically or both has been disputed. William Jones saw a conventional lyricist like Petrarch, Henry Wilberforce Clarke a poet of ecstatic mysticism like Rumi, and Ralph Waldo Emerson rejected the Sufi reading of wine. The argument arises because early Persian poetic vocabulary was taken over by mystics, so that no 14th-century lyric could avoid a mystical flavour; Hafez embraced the fusion.

According to an account by Jami, Hafez died in 1390. Twenty years later a tomb was raised for him in the Musalla Gardens in Shiraz; the present mausoleum was designed by André Godard in the late 1930s. There is no definitive version of the Divan: editions run from 573 to 994 poems. Hafez was acclaimed across the Islamic world in his lifetime, and William Jones first translated him into English in 1771. In Iran families open the Divan at random on Nowruz and Yalda Night and read the poem as a sign of what will come.
hafez-al-assad: Hafez al-Assad was born on 6 October 1930 in Qardaha, a town in northwest Syria, into a poor Alawite peasant family of the Kalbiyya tribe. He was the ninth son of his father Ali al-Assad, who had eleven children. He became the first in his family to attend high school, in Sunni-dominated Latakia, where he faced anti-Alawite bias, and he joined the Ba'ath Party in 1946. He wanted to study medicine, but his father could not pay, so in 1950 he entered the Homs Military Academy and then the flying school in Aleppo. He graduated in 1955 as a lieutenant in the Syrian Air Force.

Assad, Salah Jadid, Muhammad Umran and others established the Ba'ath Military Committee, and he was a key participant in the 1963 coup that brought the party to power. He was appointed commander of the Syrian Arab Air Force. After a second coup in February 1966 he became Minister of Defense under Jadid, who gave him de facto control of the army. Four years later Assad initiated a third coup, ousting the quasi-Marxist Jadid, and became prime minister in 1970. A referendum approved him as president on 12 March 1971.

In power he dropped Jadid's policy of exporting socialist revolution and allied Syria with the Soviet Union while keeping ties with some Western European and Gulf states. Syria fought Israel in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and in 1976 it invaded Lebanon with 30,000 troops. Syria remained a one-party system, with decision-making placed under the president's control. From 1973 to 1976 an Arabization campaign known as the Arab Belt deported around 140,000 Kurds from 332 villages in the north-east. His regime crushed an Islamist uprising led by the Syrian Muslim Brotherhood through crackdowns that culminated in the Hama massacre, in which two thirds of the city was destroyed.

Assad's eldest son Bassel, his chosen heir, died in a car crash in 1994, and he turned to his younger son Bashar, then a medical student abroad. He demoted officials who opposed the succession. Assad died in office in June 2000 and Bashar succeeded him. Hafez al-Assad exerted considerable influence on the politics of the region; the New York Times wrote that no lasting peace could hold without him, but none could be negotiated with him either.
hafizullah-amin: Hafizullah Amin was born on 1 August 1929 in Paghman, into a Kharoti Ghilzai Pashtun family. His father, a civil servant, died in 1937, and his brother Abdullah, a primary school teacher, helped him to attend school and then Kabul University, where he studied mathematics. He became a teacher, vice-principal of the Darul Mualimeen teachers' college and principal of Avesina High School.

In 1957 he went to Columbia University in New York, where he took a master's degree in education and, in 1958, joined the Socialist Progressive Club. He later returned to Afghanistan to teach at Kabul University and met the communist Nur Muhammad Taraki. In 1969 he was the only Khalqist elected to parliament, and from 1973 until the unification of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan in 1977 he was second only to Taraki in its Khalq faction.

On 18 April 1978 the Parchamite ideologue Mir Akbar Khyber was killed, and his funeral became a large demonstration. President Mohammad Daoud Khan arrested party members, and Amin, the main organiser, was one of the last Central Committee members taken, and was held under house arrest. When Taraki's arrest, the agreed signal, became known, Amin ordered the revolution to begin at 9 am on 27 April. With the overwhelming support of the military, the Saur Revolution succeeded, and Daoud, his family and high-ranking loyalists were killed.

Taraki headed the new government, with Amin as foreign minister and a deputy prime minister, and Amin soon became its strongman. Land reforms and other socialist measures provoked armed resistance, and by early 1979 25 of Afghanistan's 28 provinces were unsafe. The Herat uprising began on 29 March 1979. Amin's rivalry with Taraki grew, and on 16 September 1979 he took the posts of head of government, head of state and general secretary of the party. Taraki was later killed.

Amin's government failed to end the revolt, and army desertions continued. He tried to reassure Afghans that the regime was not anti-Islamic by rebuilding mosques and promising freedom of religion, but many Afghans, especially in rural areas, held him responsible for the regime's harshest measures, including thousands of executions. Thousands disappeared. The Soviet Union under Leonid Brezhnev mistrusted him after purges of the Parcham and feared he might turn towards the United States.

On 25 December 1979 Soviet forces crossed the frontier, and on 27 December Soviet operatives killed Amin at the Tajbeg Palace in Operation Storm-333. Babrak Karmal was installed as leader, and the Soviet intervention lasted nine years. The men of Amin's family were executed, and the women, including his daughter, were held in Pul-e-Charkhi prison until released in 1992.
hafsid-dynasty: The Hafsids were a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Berber descent, who also claimed Arab ancestry from the caliph Omar to legitimise their rule. Their name comes from Abu Hafs Umar ibn Yahya al-Hintati, a Berber of the Hintata confederation, a member of the Almohad Council of Ten and a close companion of Ibn Tumart, the founder of the Almohad movement. His son Abu Muhammad Abd al-Wahid governed Ifriqiya from Tunis from 1207 to 1221 for the Almohad caliph, with a considerable degree of autonomy.

As Almohad authority weakened, another Hafsid, Abu Zakariya Yahya, was placed in charge of Ifriqiya in 1228. A year later the caliph al-Ma'mun renounced Almohad doctrine, and Abu Zakariya used this as a pretext to declare his independence. He took the caliphal title Amir al-Mu'minin in 1236 or 1237, annexed Constantine and Béjaïa in 1230, took Algiers in 1235 and welcomed refugees from al-Andalus, some of whom he made officials and soldiers.

Under Abu Zakariya and his successor al-Mustansir, who reigned from 1249 to 1277, the Hafsids prospered from trade with Europe and the Sudan region. Louis IX of France died of dysentery at Carthage in 1270 during the Eighth Crusade. After 1277 internal conflict, aggravated by Aragon, divided the dynasty into an eastern branch at Tunis and a western branch at Béjaïa and Constantine. Abu Yahya Abu Bakr II reunited them from 1318. After his death in 1346 the Marinid ruler Abu al-Hasan conquered Tunis in 1347, and the plague epidemics of the mid-14th century reduced the population further.

Abu al-Abbas Ahmad II took Tunis in 1370 and centralised power, which began the dynasty's height under Abu Faris Abd al-Aziz II, who reigned from 1394 to 1434, and Abu 'Amr 'Uthman, who reigned from 1435 to 1488 and for a time made the whole Maghreb accept Hafsid suzerainty. In the 16th century the Hafsids were caught between Spain and the Ottomans. The Ottomans took Tunis in 1534, Charles V restored the Hafsid ruler as his tributary a year later, and the Ottoman reconquest of Tunis in 1574 ended the dynasty; its last caliph, Muhammad VI, was taken to Constantinople and executed.

The Hafsids encouraged learning and were the first to introduce madrasas to the Maghreb, beginning with the Madrasa al-Shamma῾iyya in Tunis in 1238 or 1249. The Great Mosque of al-Zaytuna became the country's leading centre of learning, and the historian Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in this period. By the mid-14th century Tunis had about 100,000 people. Nearly all of Ifriqiya became fully Arabized. Jews, whose communities had nearly disappeared under the Almohads, recovered under Hafsid tolerance, and Christian merchants and Catalonian mercenaries lived under treaties with European states.
hagakure: Hagakure, also called Hagakure Kikigaki, The Book of the Samurai or the Analects of Nabeshima, is a practical and spiritual guide for a warrior. It is drawn from the commentaries of the clerk Yamamoto Tsunetomo, a former retainer of Nabeshima Mitsushige, the third lord of Saga Domain. Tashiro Tsuramoto compiled the text from his conversations with Tsunetomo between 1709 and 1716, but it was not published until many years afterwards.

The book belongs to a time of peace. After the Tokugawa shogunate suppressed the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638, Japan saw no warfare for about two centuries, and private feuding and dueling between samurai were also suppressed. Tsunetomo was born in 1659, had no combat experience and worked as a scribe. The book reflects the problem samurai faced of keeping a warrior class in the absence of war, and the nostalgia of an old man for a vanished world.

The book records Tsunetomo's views on bushido, the warrior code of the samurai. It is sometimes said to hold that bushido is really the Way of Dying, or living as though one were already dead, so that a samurai must be ready to die at any moment in order to be true to his lord. Some readers take this to mean that bushido is a code of death, but others hold that its true meaning is that by keeping death constantly in mind a person can reach a state of freedom in which it is possible to fulfil perfectly one's calling as a warrior.

Hagakure was largely forgotten for two centuries. The first modern edition appeared in 1900 and drew little attention in the early decades of the century. It came to be seen as a definitive book of the samurai for the armed forces of the Empire of Japan only during the Pacific War. Mark Ravina has written that it serves less as an account of samurai tradition than as an example of what the Japanese army thought soldiers should believe about samurai practice. After the war the nationalist author Yukio Mishima, inspired by the work, wrote a book in praise of it.
haghpat-monastery: Haghpat Monastery, also called Haghpatavank, was built between the 10th and 13th centuries. It stands on a fertile promontory in the Javakheti Range, partway up a hillside overlooking the Debed River in the Lori region. The site was chosen to give protection and concealment while remaining inconspicuous, and the monastery is surrounded by many hamlets. Sanahin Monastery nearby was built around the same time.

The largest church, the Cathedral of Surb Nshan, was probably begun in 967-976 by Queen Khosrovanuysh and was completed in 991 by King Smbat II. It is a typical example of tenth-century Armenian architecture: its central dome rests on four large pillars of the lateral walls, and the outer walls are dotted with triangular recesses.

A fresco in the apse shows Christ Pantocrator. Its donor, the Armenian Prince Khutulukhaga, is depicted in the south transept, and the founder's sons, Princes Smbat and Kurike, appear with Queen Khosravanuysh in a bas-relief on the east gable.

Further buildings followed over the centuries. The small domed Church of Sourb Grigor dates from 1005. Two side chapels were added to the original church, the larger at the beginning of the 13th century and the smaller, known as the Hamazasp House, in 1257. A three-storey free-standing belltower was built in 1245. Other additions of the 13th century include the chapel of Sourb Astvatsatsin, a library and scriptorium, later converted into a storeroom, and a large refectory outside the monastery limits. Khachkars, or cross-stones, of the 11th to 13th centuries stand in the grounds; the best known is the Amenaprkich, or All-Savior, khachkar, which has stood since 1273.

In 1260 Prosh Khaghbakian led Georgian and Armenian forces with his Zakarid suzerains Avag and Shahnshah to support the smaller Mongol force of Hulegu at the siege of Mayyafariqin. When the city was captured after a siege of two years, the Muslims were massacred and the Christians spared. Christian relics were brought back to Armenia, many to Haghpat, which received the hand of the Apostle Bartholomew.

The monastery has been damaged many times. An earthquake around 1130 destroyed parts of it, and it was not restored for fifty years. It was attacked by armed forces over the centuries and damaged by another earthquake in 1988, yet much of the complex stands without substantial alteration. In 1996 UNESCO placed Haghpat and Sanahin on the World Heritage List, describing them as a masterpiece of religious architecture and a major centre of learning in the Middle Ages, the highest flowering of Armenian religious architecture, which blended Byzantine ecclesiastical and Caucasian vernacular styles.
hagia-sophia: Justinian's building was the third church on the site. The first, known as the Magna Ecclesia, or Great Church, because of its size, was consecrated on 15 February 360 under the emperor Constantius II. A second church, ordered by Theodosius II, was inaugurated on 10 October 415. It was destroyed, and on 23 February 532, only a few weeks later, Justinian began a third and entirely different basilica, larger and more majestic than its predecessors. He appointed two architects to design it, the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer and engineer Isidore of Miletus.

The dome is carried on four spherical triangular pendentives, making the building one of the first large-scale uses of that element. It was the largest pendentive dome in the world until St Peter's Basilica, and its height is much lower than that of any other dome of such a diameter. After the vault first collapsed, the dome was rebuilt in 558. The church stayed the largest in the world for more than five hundred years, until the abbey church at Cluny was completed in the 12th century. The horseshoe-shaped upper gallery was reserved for the empress and her court. The Imperial Gate was originally used only by the emperor.

Under Justinian the interior had abstract designs on marble slabs and mosaics on the vaults, with a few figurative decorations. Figurative mosaics added later were destroyed during the iconoclastic controversy of 726–843, and the surviving mosaics are post-iconoclastic. The minarets are Ottoman additions, and the two western ones, by Selim II and designed by Mimar Sinan, are 60 metres high. Sinan also directed the building of buttresses, and 24 were added in all.

For nearly a thousand years Hagia Sophia was the religious centre of the Eastern Orthodox Church. In 1054 the envoy of Pope Leo IX, Humbert of Silva Candida, delivered the excommunication of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius there, an act considered the start of the East–West Schism. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, it became a Catholic cathedral under the Latin Empire, and it was restored to the Orthodox Church in 1261. Enrico Dandolo, the doge of Venice who led the Crusade, was buried in the church.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453, Mehmed II performed the Friday prayer there and ordered its conversion to a mosque. It was the principal mosque of Istanbul until the Sultan Ahmed Mosque was built in 1616. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk made it a museum in 1935, and in 2020 it was reclassified as a mosque. Its style became the model for Eastern Orthodox church architecture and was emulated by Ottoman mosques, including the Şehzade Mosque and the Süleymaniye Mosque.
haifa: Haifa lies on the Israeli Mediterranean coastal plain, at the mouth of the Kishon River and on the northern slopes of Mount Carmel around Haifa Bay. The city is split over three tiers: the lowest holds commerce, industry and the port, the middle level the older residential districts, and the upper level modern neighbourhoods. It is about 90 km north of Tel Aviv. The origin of its name is unclear; proposals include the high priest Caiaphas, a Hebrew root meaning to cover or shield, and the Hebrew words for 'beautiful shore'.

The earliest known settlement nearby was Tell Abu Hawam, a port and fishing village founded in the Late Bronze Age, in the fourteenth century BCE. Haifa is first mentioned in Talmudic literature about the third century CE, as a Jewish fishing village whose fishermen caught murex snails for purple dye. After the Arab conquest of the Levant it was overshadowed by the port of Akka.

Shortly after the First Crusade the crusaders took Haifa after a fierce battle with its Jewish inhabitants and Fatimid garrison, and it became a small fortified stronghold in the Principality of Galilee. Saladin's army captured it in July 1187 after the Battle of Hattin, and the crusaders under Richard the Lionheart retook it in 1191. In the 1760s the old settlement was moved 2.5 km east as a fortified town, today the Old City.

British forces captured Haifa in September 1918. Its population was 98 percent Arab in 1872, and Jewish immigration from 1881 changed the balance, so that by 1945 it was 55 percent Jewish and 45 percent Arab. During and after the Battle of Haifa in the 1948 war most of the Arab population fled or was expelled, and the Old City was later demolished.

Haifa is the third-largest city in Israel, with 297,082 inhabitants in 2024. The Baháʼí World Centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a destination for Baháʼí pilgrimage, stands there. The city has a major seaport, the Technion and the University of Haifa, and the Carmelit underground railway. About ten percent of the population is Arab.
haigerloch: Haigerloch lies in the north-western part of the Swabian Alb, at between 430 and 550 metres above sea level, in the valley of the Eyach. The river forms two loops in a steep limestone valley, and the town is therefore also called the Felsenstädtchen, the rocky small town. It has nine districts, among them Bad Imnau, Gruol, Owingen and Weildorf. Around 1700 the physician Samuel Caspar discovered several small pools of mineral water in the valley, and in 1733 the Prince's Spring was uncovered and named after Prince Josef Friedrich of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen.

Haigerloch is first documented in 1095, on the occasion of a gift of the local castle, probably in the area of the Upper Town. By 1200 the Counts of Hohenberg appeared as local lords and built a new castle on the Schlossberg, and the lower town developed into a market town. Rudolf I awarded it a town charter before 1231. A battle between Zollern and Hohenberg was fought just outside the town in 1268, and Count Eberhard I of Württemberg besieged it in 1291 and again in 1347.

From 1356 the upper and lower towns were administered separately, until the lordship of Haigerloch was sold to Austria in 1381; the Habsburgs pawned it on several occasions. Under the Hohenzollern it later became the independent territory of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch within the Holy Roman Empire. The present castle was built on the Schlossberg as the residence of its counts, replacing the high-medieval structure. Haigerloch was the residence of the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line between 1737 and 1769.

In the last months of the Second World War the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Physics, part of the German nuclear programme, was at Haigerloch. Its research reactor was built in a beer cellar beneath the palace church. The pastor's negotiations spared the facility from demolition by an American command on 24 April 1945.

The cellar is now the Atomkeller-Museum, which holds a replica of the reactor. Other sights include the Roman tower of the castle and the former synagogue. Salt has been extracted from the rock salt mine in the Stetten district since 1854.
haiku: Haiku grew out of the opening verse of renga, a long collaborative form of linked poetry, and of its later derivative renku. That opening verse was called hokku, and its position made it the most important, since it set the tone for the whole composition. By the time of Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) the hokku had begun to appear as an independent poem, and it was also used in haibun, a combination of prose and hokku, and in haiga, a combination of painting with hokku. Bashō raised haikai from a playful game of wit to serious poetry. Yosa Buson (1716–1784) was also a master of haiga, and Kobayashi Issa (1763–1827) made the genre accessible to wider audiences. Masaoka Shiki (1867–1902) gave the form its present name.

A traditional Japanese haiku has three phrases of five, seven and five on, the sound units called morae. A word such as haibun counts as four on in Japanese though two syllables in English, so a poem of 17 on may hold only 15 syllables. A kireji, or cutting word, usually ends one of the phrases and acts like a caesura or a sonnet's volta. A kigo, a word implying the season, is drawn from a list called a saijiki. These rules were not absolute: Bashō himself wrote a haiku of 18 on in a 6-7-5 pattern, and some verses lack a kireji. Free-form haiku, advocated by Ogiwara Seisensui and his disciples, give up the 17-on pattern.

Several women learned haiku from Bashō or his disciples in the early 18th century, among them Chiyo-ni. Hendrik Doeff, a Dutch commissioner at Dejima, wrote haiku in the early 19th century, and Paul-Louis Couchoud introduced haiku in France around 1906. They influenced the Imagists, notably Ezra Pound's poem of 1913, In a Station of the Metro. R. H. Blyth's four volumes of 1949–52 introduced haiku to the English-speaking world after the war. The carving of haiku on stone, as monuments called kuhi, has been a custom for many centuries.
haile-selassie: Haile Selassie was born Tafari Makonnen on 23 July 1892 in the village of Ejersa Goro in the province of Hararghe. His father was Ras Makonnen Wolde Mikael, and his mother, Yeshimebet Ali Abba Jifar, was of Oromo and Silte descent. His royal line descended through his paternal grandmother from the Shewan king Sahle Selassie. He became titular governor of Selale in 1906 and was appointed governor of part of Sidamo in 1907. On 3 August 1911 he married Menen Asfaw, and the marriage lasted fifty years.

He rose to power as regent of Empress Zewditu from 1916, after Lij Iyasu, the designated but uncrowned emperor, was deposed on 27 September 1916. In 1924 he toured Europe and the Middle East, chiefly hoping to win Ethiopia access to the sea, which the French Foreign Ministry told him would not be granted.

Tafari became Negus in 1928 and emperor in 1930, taking the name Haile Selassie, which he had received at baptism. He introduced a constitution in 1931 and abolished slavery in 1942. Fascist Italy invaded in 1935, partly to avenge its defeat at Adwa, and the League of Nations failed to protect Ethiopia. He went into exile in the United Kingdom, later travelled to Sudan, and returned after British forces, including Colonel Orde Wingate's Gideon Force, and Ethiopian resistance liberated the country.

After the war Ethiopia became a charter member of the United Nations. On 2 December 1950 the General Assembly's Resolution 390 (V) ceded Eritrea to Ethiopia, and the emperor later dissolved the federation and annexed it as a province. In November 1955 he introduced a revised constitution that made the lower house of parliament elected while he kept effective power. In 1963 he presided over the formation of the Organisation of African Unity and was its first chairman. Critics, among them Human Rights Watch, called his administration autocratic, and some sources say the Oromo language was in practice kept out of education and administration.

In February 1974 riots against inflation in Addis Ababa left five dead, the army mutinied, and strikes and protests followed. The Derg, a military junta, deposed him in 1974. It was revealed in 1994 that the Derg had killed him at the Jubilee Palace on 27 August 1975. His bones were found in 1992 under a concrete slab on the palace grounds, and he was buried on 5 November 2000 at the Holy Trinity Cathedral in Addis Ababa. He belonged to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Among followers of Rastafari, a movement that arose in Jamaica in the 1930s, he is viewed as a messiah, which he did not affirm.
hainan: Hainan consists of Hainan Island and more than 200 smaller islands in the South China Sea. Its name literally means South of the Sea, after its position south of the Qiongzhou Strait, a channel 20 kilometres wide that separates it from the Leizhou Peninsula of Guangdong. The province has a land area of 33,920 square kilometres, almost all of it the island, which is slightly smaller than Taiwan. Wuzhi Mountain, at 1,840 metres, is the highest peak. The climate is mostly tropical, and the island holds over 1,500 square kilometres of tropical forest. Earlier names for the island include Zhuya, Qiongya and Qiongzhou.

Hainan Island was recorded by Chinese officials in 110 BCE, when the Western Han dynasty established a military garrison there after the arrival of General Lu Bode. Over many centuries imperial authorities exiled people condemned as criminals or political dissidents to Hainan and northern Vietnam, where banished people were put to harsh labour in the tropical climate. The Hlai, a Kra-Dai-speaking people, are native to the island.

After 1912 Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit within Guangdong, and in 1920 Sun Yat-sen proposed a Qiongya Special District. The Hainan Special Administrative District was formally established in 1949. On 1 May 1950, under the People's Republic of China, it became an Administrative Region Office, a branch of the Guangdong provincial government. On 13 April 1988 the National People's Congress decided to establish Hainan Province, and Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up programme made it a special economic zone.

The capital is Haikou on the northern coast, and Sanya on the southern coast is a well-known tourist destination. Han Chinese make up 82% of the population and the Hlai 15%. Most people speak Hainanese, a variety of Min Chinese, and most practise Chinese folk religion and Chinese Buddhism.
haiphong: Haiphong lies at the mouth of the Cấm River in the north-eastern coastal area of Vietnam. Its territory covers 3,194.72 square kilometres and includes the islands of Bạch Long Vĩ and Cát Bà and the Long Châu islands in the Gulf of Tonkin. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, humid summers and warm, dry winters, with most rain between April and October.

Haiphong was the home of Lê Chân, one of the women generals who served the Trưng Sisters in their rising against Chinese rule in 40 CE. The rising lasted until 43 CE. Lê Chân is said to have established the Hải tần Phòng thủ, the Defense of the Coast, in the war against the Han general Ma Yuan.

Under French rule Haiphong ranked as a first-level city equal to Saigon and Hanoi, and in the last years of the nineteenth century the French proposed to make it the economic capital of Indochina. After the defeat of Japan in World War II, Vietnamese nationalists pressed for independence against the French return. French forces landed at Haiphong and met resistance in which three French soldiers died. In retaliation French ships, among them the cruiser Suffren, shelled the city and set it ablaze, an event that precipitated the First Indochina War. French infantry under Jean-Étienne Valluy then entered, fighting house to house with armour and aircraft in support.

In the Vietnam War the city was bombed by United States Navy and Air Force aircraft. Admiral Thomas H. Moorer ordered the mining of the harbour on 8 May 1972, effectively sealing the port. The mining caused no casualties, and the city's buildings were largely unaffected, as the United States had set a prohibited zone around the city. After the war Haiphong recovered its role as an industrial centre.

Haiphong is a major port, the Port of Haiphong standing on the Cấm River, and a centre of shipbuilding, steel and plastic pipes, textiles, cement and food processing. It is the first city in Vietnam and in mainland Southeast Asia to have been electrified. Route 5 leads west to Hanoi and Route 10 south towards Nam Định. A railway built by the French links the city with Hanoi and with Lao Cai on the Chinese border.
haiti: Haiti forms the western three-eighths of Hispaniola, the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and shares a border of 360 km with the Dominican Republic. It is the most mountainous country in the Caribbean, with plains covering only 22% of its territory, and the highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,680 m. The name comes from the Taino language and means land of high mountains. It was the native name for the whole island, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines restored it as the official name of independent Saint-Domingue, in tribute to the Amerindian predecessors.

Indigenous peoples have lived on Hispaniola for about 6,000 years. Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taino arrived during the 1st millennium BCE, and at the time of European contact the island was divided among five caciquedoms led by chiefs. Christopher Columbus landed on 6 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. The 39 men he left behind founded La Navidad but were later killed by the Taino.

European diseases caused epidemics among the native people, the first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas breaking out on Hispaniola in 1507, and the encomienda system, which forced natives to work in gold mines and plantations, reduced their numbers further. Spain held the island until 1697, when the western part was ceded to France as Saint-Domingue, a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans.

The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean and the first country in the Americas to abolish slavery officially. The independent state began as an empire, later split into two and reunited in 1820, and a second empire under Faustin Soulouque ended with the return of the republic in 1859. The 19th century brought instability, international isolation and a crippling debt to France. United States forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986.

Haiti is a republic with Port-au-Prince as its capital and largest city, and about 11 million people, the most in the Caribbean. Its culture blends French and African customs with Spanish and Indigenous influences. The Citadelle Laferrière, built between 1805 and 1820, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
haitian-creole: Haitian Creole took shape in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, where French colonists lived beside enslaved Africans who spoke various Niger-Congo languages.
