Its vocabulary comes largely from the French of the eighteenth century, but its grammar follows West African patterns, particularly those of Fongbe and Igbo. Words from Wolof, Fon, Kongo, Spanish, Taino and others also entered it. Often the French definite article stayed attached to the noun: la lune, the moon, became lalin.

In Saint-Domingue people of all classes spoke a Creole French, with lower and higher registers according to education and class, and it served as a lingua franca through the West Indies. The first written text in the French-lexicon creole is said to be a poem, Lisette quitté la plaine, composed in 1757 by Duvivier de la Mahautière, a white Creole planter.

Haitian Creole is not mutually intelligible with standard French. Its grammar is analytical: verbs are not conjugated, tense, mood and aspect are shown by markers placed before the verb, and there is no grammatical gender.  The definite article follows the noun. Many words that look like French have shifted in sense: frekan, from fréquent, means insolent or rude.

Spelling is phonemic and highly regular. The official system, set out by the Institut Pédagogique National, uses 32 symbols and keeps only the grave accent, on è and ò. It built on an orthography devised in 1940 by the Irish Methodist missionaries H. Ormonde McConnell and Primrose McConnell and revised with Frank Laubach. The three main dialects are the Northern, Central and Southern, centred on Cap-Haïtien, Port-au-Prince and Les Cayes.

Its place in schools and public life has been contested since at least the nineteenth century. Some Haitians see French as bound up with colonialism, while Francophones have dismissed Creole as the French of the uneducated. Until the late twentieth century Haitian presidents addressed their fellow citizens only in standard French, and until the twenty-first century elementary teaching was in French, a second language for most pupils. Even so, literary works in Creole existed by the end of the nineteenth century, among them Oswald Durand's Choucoune and Georges Sylvain's Cric? Crac!

The 1987 constitution named Creole and French the official languages and recognised Creole as the only language all Haitians share. It is spoken by more than 13 million people, including large communities in the United States, Canada, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas, and it is the most widely spoken creole language in the world.
haitian-revolution: In 1789 Saint-Domingue produced 60 percent of the world's coffee and 40 percent of the sugar imported by France and Britain, and its largest sugar plantations and concentrations of enslaved people lay in the north. Enslaved people were kept in check by whipping and worse punishments. The Code Noir of 1685, issued to regulate the treatment of the enslaved, was openly and consistently broken. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 26 August 1789 was ambiguous about slaves and colonial citizens. After the revolt of Vincent Ogé in 1790, France granted citizenship to free people of colour in May 1791. White planters refused to comply, fighting between the groups broke out, and on 21 August 1791 the enslaved rose.

When France declared war on Britain in 1793, the grands blancs asked British help, and Britain invaded Saint-Domingue, as did Spain. The French commissioners Sonthonax and Étienne Polverel offered freedom to enslaved people who would fight for them and in 1793 proclaimed abolition in the colony's provinces. On 6 May 1794 Toussaint Louverture turned from the Spanish to the French. The British sent about 30,000 men in 1795 but suffered heavily from disease, and at least three of every five British troops sent between 1791 and 1797 died of it. The British left Port-au-Prince on 18 May 1798, and Toussaint defeated the forces of Rigaud in the War of the South, taking Jacmel on 11 March 1800.

A French expedition arrived at Le Cap on 2 February 1802. Dessalines held the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot for about twenty days before slipping out on 24 March. Toussaint agreed to terms on 6 May 1802, was later seized and shipped to France, and died in prison at Fort-de-Joux. French plans to restore slavery brought a new revolt in the summer of 1802, while yellow fever killed about 10,000 French by mid-July and the commander Leclerc in November. After war between France and Britain resumed on 18 May 1803, the Royal Navy blockaded the colony. On 30 November 1803, 8,000 French soldiers boarded British ships under terms agreed with Dessalines.

On 1 January 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti a free republic. From February until 22 April 1804, on his order, the remaining white colonists were massacred. France recognised independence in 1825 only on condition that Haiti pay an indemnity of 150 million francs to former slaveholders. Estimates of the dead vary: Robert Scheina gave 350,000 Haitians and 50,000 European troops, and the Encyclopedia of African American Politics nearly 200,000 Black people and as many as 100,000 French and British soldiers, with yellow fever the largest cause. Historians such as David Geggus judge the effect on slavery limited, while W. E. B. Du Bois held that it made British abolition easier.
hajar-mountains: The Hajar Mountains, also called the Oman Mountains, separate the low coastal plain of Oman from the high desert plateau and lie 50 to 100 km inland from the Gulf of Oman. They run for 700 kilometres and are about 100 km wide, on the north-eastern corner of the Arabian Plate, from the Musandam Peninsula to the east coast of Oman.

Jabal Shams, at 3,009 metres, is the highest peak, in the central section, which is the highest and wildest terrain in Oman. East of the Samail Valley the Eastern Hajar run to the port of Sur. The Western Hajar include the mountains of Musandam, known as Ru'us al-Jibal, Heads of the Mountains, and those of the United Arab Emirates.

The range is the product of several phases of mountain building. In the late Cretaceous the Semail Ophiolite, a slab of oceanic crust, was thrust over the continental rocks of the Arabian margin. A second phase of deformation began in the Eocene, about 45 to 40 million years ago, and the present topography formed after the late Eocene; geologists dispute exactly when, and whether the collision of the Zagros Mountains drove it.

The Semail ophiolite is regarded as the most complete on Earth, with pillow basalt and exposures of the boundary between crust and mantle, and the Wadi Mayh sheath fold is one of the best exposed ever found. Eclogite at As Sifah records rocks carried about 80 km into the mantle and brought back to the surface.

The mountains are rich in plant life compared with most of Arabia and have a number of endemic species. Shrubland at lower elevations gives way to woodland, with wild olive and fig trees, and junipers higher still; pomegranates and apricots are grown in the cooler valleys. Mountain gazelles, the Arabian tahr and several species of gecko and lizard live there.

Domestic goats, camels and donkeys graze extensively, and clearing for towns and mining has damaged vegetation and water supplies. Oman has created the Wadi Sareen Reserve and an area of Jebel Qahwan to protect the Arabian tahr and the mountain gazelle.
hajj: The word ḥajj is similar to the Hebrew ḥag, 'festival', from the same Semitic root; the Hebrew term referred to the three pilgrimage festivals Israelites made to the Temple in Jerusalem each year. The present pattern of Hajj was established by Muhammad, but according to the Quran, elements of it trace back to Abraham. In Islamic tradition Abraham left his wife Hajar and his son Ishmael in the desert of ancient Mecca. Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah looking for water, and a spring then rose beneath Ishmael's foot. Abraham was later commanded to build the Kaaba with Ishmael's help and to invite people to make pilgrimage there. The Quran refers to these events in verses 2:124–127 and 22:27–30.

Hajj is an annual pilgrimage to Mecca and one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is a once-in-a-lifetime duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able to make the journey and to support their family during their absence. Its rites are carried out over five to six days, from the 8th to the 12th or 13th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Because that calendar is lunar, the Gregorian date moves each year, and the season falls twice in one Gregorian year about every 33 years.

The pilgrim enters the sacred state of ihram, wearing unstitched white clothing, and walks seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, an act called tawaf, then walks seven times between Safa and Marwah. On 9 Dhu'l-Hijja, the Day of Arafah, pilgrims stand in vigil on the plain of Arafat, about 20 km east of Mecca, from noon until sunset; a pilgrim's Hajj is considered invalid without this. They spend a night at Muzdalifah, and on 10 Dhu'l-Hijja at Mina they throw seven stones at the largest of three pillars representing Satan.

After the sacrifice of an animal, pilgrims shave or trim their hair, and the festival of Eid al-Adha follows. The shorter pilgrimage to Mecca, Umrah, can be made at other times of the year but does not replace the Hajj.
hakka-people: The Hakka are a Han Chinese sub-ethnic group whose settlements are widely dispersed across southern China, and whose language is closely related to Gan, spoken in Jiangxi. Their name, written 客家, means guest families. They are distinguished from other southern Han by their dispersal and their tendency to occupy marginal, hilly land. They are commonly held to have come from the Central Plain in the north and to have arrived in the south much later than other southern Han. Earlier settlers had taken the fertile lowlands, assimilated local peoples and driven others, such as the Tanka, to the coasts and rivers, so the Hakka had to settle poorer territory.

The Hakka identify as Han, and a 2009 genetic study found them principally of Han descent, with a slight skew towards northern Han compared with other southern groups, despite recorded intermarriage with the Yao and the She. The word Hakka is sometimes also used for other southern Han groups on their southward migration, which complicates the historical record.

People of Hakka ancestry formed the mainstay of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, which began at the Hakka village of Jintian in Guiping, Guangxi, under Hong Xiuquan, whose first followers were Hakka peasants. The Cantonese regarded the Hakka as opportunists intruding on their territory, and friction between the groups sometimes turned violent. The Red Turban rebels, mostly of Cantonese ancestry, carried out a genocidal campaign against the Hakka during their revolt of 1854–1856, killing 13 village chiefs and 7,630 others on the way to Heshan and another 1,320 after taking it. The Xiang Army under Zeng Guofan massacred tens of thousands of Hakka in Guanghai, a region of Taishan.

Hakka went overseas in large numbers, chiefly to Malaysia, Taiwan, Singapore, Indonesia and Vietnam, and also to the Americas, the Caribbean, Mauritius and India. The first Hakka reached Australia in the 1880s and Tahiti in 1865. In Taiwan they are the second-largest ethnic group, descended largely from migrants from Guangdong and western Fujian who were the island's first agriculturalists.

Poor hill land shaped Hakka culture, and many men turned to military or public careers. Hakka women did not bind their feet and are known for taking on hard work that other groups reserved for men, perhaps from necessity. The Hakka hold Confucian values such as respect for family, ancestor veneration and learning. They built tulou, fortified earth buildings, in Fujian, Jiangxi and Guangdong, and a representative sample of ten Fujian tulou was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. Their cuisine uses preserved meats and tofu and stewed and braised dishes, and their hill songs carry across valleys.
hakodate: Hakodate stands at the centre of the Kameda Peninsula in southern Hokkaido and is overlooked by Mount Hakodate. The region was originally populated by the Ainu, and the name Hakodate may derive from an Ainu word, hak-casi, meaning shallow fort.

Hakodate was founded in 1454, when Kono Kaganokami Masamichi built a large manor house in the fishing village of Usukeshi. His son Kono Suemichi was driven out into Kameda during an Ainu rebellion in 1512. In 1741 the Matsumae clan moved its Kameda magistracy to Masamichi's house in Hakodate. The Tokugawa shogunate took direct control of the town in 1779, which brought rapid development under the merchant Takadaya Kahei, honoured as the founder of its port. The Matsumae clan was restored to full power in 1821.

Under the Convention of Kanagawa, negotiated by Commodore Matthew C. Perry, Hakodate became in 1854 the first Japanese port opened to foreign trade, and it was fully opened on 2 June 1859 as one of five open ports of the 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce signed with the United States. From the Russian consulate Nicholas of Japan is credited with introducing Eastern Orthodox Christianity to Japan in 1861.

Hakodate was central to the Boshin War. The shogunate rebel Enomoto Takeaki fled there in the winter of 1868 with the remnants of his navy and a handful of French advisers, and they proclaimed the Republic of Ezo on 25 December. It failed to win international recognition. The rebels held the European-style Goryōkaku fort, and the naval Battle of Hakodate, fought from 4 to 10 May 1869, was a decisive victory for the Imperial Japanese Navy. Government forces defeated the secessionists and the fort and city were surrendered.

Hakodate is a port city in Oshima Subprefecture, Hokkaido, and the third largest in the island. It was the biggest city in Hokkaido until a fire on 21 March 1934 destroyed about two thirds of its buildings. The former Goryōkaku fort is now a public park, popular for cherry blossom viewing, and the foreign settlement, Orthodox church and other missionary churches are legacies of the port's opening.
hakon-sigurdsson: Haakon Sigurdsson was the son of Sigurd Haakonsson, Jarl of Lade and ruler of Trøndelag and Hålogaland, and of Bergljot Toresdatter, daughter of Thorir Rögnvaldarson, Jarl of Møre. Adam of Bremen wrote that he was of the stock of Ivar and descended from a race of giants, while in the sagas Haakon claimed descent from Sæming, a son of Odin. He became jarl after his father was killed in 961 by the men of King Harald Greycloak. Haakon warred with Harald for some time, until he was forced to flee to Denmark, where he conspired with Harald Bluetooth against Harald Greycloak.

Harald Bluetooth and Haakon arranged the death of Harald Greycloak around 971, after which Harald Bluetooth invited his foster-son to be invested with new Danish fiefs. A civil war followed between Haakon and the surviving brothers of Harald Greycloak, and Haakon won it. He recognised the overlordship of Harald Bluetooth and around 973 to 974 went to Denmark to help him defend against the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II. Otto's forces successfully opposed Harald's attempt to throw off German rule, and after that Haakon paid no taxes to Denmark.

Haakon was a strong believer in the old Norse gods, even after Harald Bluetooth forced him to accept baptism around 975 and gave him clergymen to take to Norway. When a favourable wind came, Haakon ordered the clergymen back ashore and broke his allegiance to Denmark. In 977 Vladimir of Novgorod fled to him and gathered Viking warriors, and on his return the next year marched against Yaropolk I of Kiev. In 986 a Danish invasion fleet led by the Jomsvikings was defeated at the Battle of Hjörungavágr.

In 995 a quarrel broke out between Haakon and the Trønders just as Olaf Tryggvason, a descendant of Harald Fairhair, arrived. Haakon quickly lost all support and was killed by his slave and friend Tormod Kark while hiding in a pigsty at the farm Rimul in Melhus. His sons Eirik and Sveinn fled to the Swedish king Olof Skötkonung. The Skáldatal names poets at his court, among them Eyvindr Finnsson and Einarr skálaglamm. Snorri Sturluson tells his story in Heimskringla, and Adam Oehlenschläger's tragedy Hakon Jarl of 1805, on the conflict between paganism and Christianity, later inspired Smetana's symphonic poem of the same name.
hakor: Hakor, also called Hagar and known in Greek as Achoris or Hakoris, was a pharaoh of the 29th Dynasty. His accession and his relationship with his predecessor Nepherites I were long debated. After Nepherites died a dynastic struggle seems to have followed, in which Hakor, Psammuthes and possibly a figure called Muthis, mentioned only in Eusebius' epitome of Manetho, claimed the throne. In 1986 John D. Ray suggested that Hakor was Nepherites' heir, deposed in his second year by Psammuthes and restored a year later, and that he dated his reign from his first coronation as though the gap had never occurred. Alan B. Lloyd and Toby Wilkinson accept this view.

Once re-established, Hakor made considerable efforts to affirm his legitimacy, stressing his real or fictional descent from Nepherites. His building was extensive and he restored many monuments of earlier kings. At Karnak he finished the chapel for the sacred barque of Amun-Ra near the first pylon, begun by Psammuthes or possibly Nepherites I, and he possibly began a temple complex in northern Saqqara that was later developed under Nectanebo II. His building is attested at Luxor, Medinet Habu, El-Kab, El-Tod, Medamud and Elephantine, in the Temple of Hibis in Kharga Oasis and in Middle Egypt.

Hakor continued Nepherites' foreign policy and was allied with Evagoras I of Cyprus against the Achaemenids. After the peace of Antalcidas in 387 BCE, Egypt and Cyprus remained the only opponents of Artaxerxes II. It seems the Persians first attacked Egypt in 385 BCE and, after three years of war, the Egyptians defeated them. In 381 BCE Hakor sent Evagoras aid, money and 50 triremes, but when Evagoras came to Egypt in 380 BCE to beg for more he was sent back with only some money. Hakor then joined a short-lived alliance with Sparta and with Glos, and took the Athenian general Chabrias into his service.

Hakor was succeeded by his son Nepherites II, who kept the throne for only four months before an army general from Sebennytos, Nectanebo I, overthrew him. Nectanebo I called Hakor an usurper shortly after his death, though it has been suggested that the two were relatives, possibly both related to Nepherites I but rivals. Hakor's tomb has not been found. Only one funerary object can be linked to him, an ushabti inscribed with his name found at Mendes, which may indicate that his tomb was looted in antiquity, though this is unproven.
halabja-massacre: Northern Iraq was unsettled during the early stage of the Iran–Iraq War, and the militias of the Kurdistan Democratic Party and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan joined forces with Iranian support in 1982 and 1983. From 1985 the Ba'athist government under Saddam Hussein decided to eradicate pockets of Kurdish insurgents and to strike down the peshmerga by all means possible, including large-scale punishment of civilians and the use of chemical weapons. The attack on Halabja took place during the Anfal campaign, led by the Iraqi officer Ali Hassan al-Majid. Two days earlier Iran had captured the town as part of Operation Zafar 7.

The attack began on 16 March 1988 and lasted five hours. After a series of indiscriminate conventional attacks with rockets and napalm, Iraqi MiG and Mirage aircraft dropped chemical bombs on Halabja's residential areas. According to regional Kurdish commanders, aircraft coordinated by helicopters made up to 14 bombings in sorties of seven to eight planes each.

Eyewitnesses described clouds of white, black and then yellow smoke rising in a column. The United Nations later concluded that mustard gas and unidentified nerve agents had been used, and the BBC reported a mixture of mustard, tabun, sarin and VX. The attack killed between 3,200 and 5,000 people and injured 7,000 to 10,000 more.

The first pictures were taken by Iranian journalists, among them the photographer Kaveh Golestan, and a British ITN crew was airlifted in by the Iranians. Iraq did not comment publicly on the use of chemical weapons at Halabja until 23 March, and it ultimately denied responsibility and blamed Iran. The US Defense Intelligence Agency initially blamed Iran, but the majority of later evidence showed that Iraq had used the weapons.

Survivors, helped by peshmerga and Iranians, hastily buried most of the dead in makeshift mass graves. After Iraqi forces retook the town, troops in protective suits came to study the effects of their weapons, and the town was then razed with bulldozers and explosives. Surveys in the years afterwards found raised rates of cancer, miscarriage and birth defects. The Security Council condemned Iraq's use of chemical weapons against Iran in Resolutions 612 and 620 but did not mention their use against its own citizens.

Al-Majid was found guilty of ordering the attack and sentenced to death in June 2007, and he was hanged in January 2010. That year the Supreme Iraqi Criminal Tribunal defined the attack as a genocidal massacre against the Kurdish people, and the Parliament of Canada formally condemned it as a crime against humanity. Foreign firms had supplied precursor chemicals for Iraq's chemical weapons.
halberstadt: Halberstadt received market rights from King Otto III in 989 and became the administrative centre of the Saxon Harzgau. Its bishops had the Church of Our Lady built from about 1005. In 1179 the forces of Henry the Lion devastated the town in his conflict with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, and after Henry's fall the diocese became a prince-bishopric about 1180. The cathedral was rebuilt from 1236 and consecrated in 1491. Halberstadt joined a league of towns with Quedlinburg and Aschersleben in 1326, and from 1387 it was a member of the Hanse.

The citizens turned Protestant around 1540, and in 1566 the cathedral chapter elected the first Lutheran bishop, Prince Henry Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Wallenstein's troops occupied the town in 1629. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the prince-bishopric into the Principality of Halberstadt, held by Brandenburg-Prussia, and the town became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. From 1747 the official and poet Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim made his house an intellectual centre of the German Enlightenment. It is now the Gleimhaus museum.

Halberstadt's Jewish community is recorded from the 13th century. Berend Lehmann founded a beth midrash, the Klaus, in 1703 and financed a Baroque synagogue completed in 1712, and the town had one of the largest Jewish communities in central Europe. The synagogue was burned in the pogrom of 9 November 1938. After local Nazi leaders refused to surrender, 218 American bombers dropped 595 tons of bombs on the centre on 8 April 1945. About 2,500 people were killed and most of the old town was reduced to rubble.

Halberstadt is now a town in Saxony-Anhalt and the capital of Harz district. Its cathedral is notable among those of northern Europe for keeping its medieval treasury almost complete, including the oldest surviving tapestries in Europe, from the 12th century. About 450 timber-framed houses stand in the centre, and the Klaus houses the Moses Mendelssohn Academy. A performance of John Cage's organ piece As Slow As Possible began in the Burchardikirche in 2001 and is scheduled to last 639 years.
haleakala: Haleakalā, also called the East Maui Volcano, is an active shield volcano that forms more than 75 per cent of Maui. The western quarter of the island is formed by another volcano, Mauna Kahalawai, also called the West Maui Mountains. Its tallest peak is Puʻu ʻUlaʻula, or Red Hill, at 3,055 metres. From the summit one looks down into a depression about 18 km across, 5 km wide and nearly 800 metres deep, with steep walls and a scattering of volcanic cones. Early Hawaiians used the name Haleakalā, house of the sun, for the whole mountain.

In Hawaiian folklore the depression at the summit was home to the grandmother of the demigod Māui, who helped him capture the sun and force it to slow its journey across the sky so that the day would be longer. Geologically Haleakalā began forming about 2 million years ago, building a shield along three rift zones. It has produced numerous eruptions in the last 30,000 years, including ten in the past 1,000 years, and is the only active volcano on Maui.

The summit basin is not a volcanic crater. Water and wind erosion, and possibly glaciers, carved two large valleys out of the rim, and their headwalls merged at the summit to form the depression, with the gaps of Koʻolau on the north and Kaupō on the south. The last eruption was long thought to have been about 1790, from a comparison of maps by La Perouse and Vancouver, but radiocarbon dating published in 1999 placed it between 1480 and 1600. The lava deposits of the Ahihi Kina'u and La Perouse Bay area belong to this last flow.

The crater and its surroundings lie within Haleakalā National Park, of 30,183 acres, which includes the summit depression, Kipahulu Valley and ʻOheʻo Gulch, with two main trails into the crater, Sliding Sands and Halemauʻu. Visitors come to watch the sunrise. Haleakalā Highway, completed in 1935, climbs to the summit. Because of the clarity and dryness of the air the summit is a site for ground-based telescopes, in an astrophysical complex known as Science City. The park shelters the endemic Haleakalā silversword and the nēnē.
halfdan-ragnarsson: Halfdan Ragnarsson, in Old English Halfdene or Healfdene and in Old Irish Albann, was one of six sons of Ragnar Lodbrok named in the Norse sagas. His brothers and half-brothers included Björn Ironside, Ivar the Boneless, Sigurd Snake-in-the-Eye, Ubba and Hvitserk. Because Halfdan appears in no source that mentions Hvitserk, some scholars suggest they were one man, Hvitserk, 'white shirt', being a nickname that set him apart from other men called Halfdan. Asser and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle name Halfdan and Ivar as brothers.

Halfdan led the Great Heathen Army that landed in East Anglia in the autumn of 865. According to the sagas, the sons of Ragnar organised it to avenge him on Ælla of Northumbria, who had supposedly had him thrown into a snake pit. The army invaded Northumbria, then in civil war between Ælla and Osberht, and conquered York late in 866. Ælla and Osberht both fell in a failed attempt to retake it, and the Danes installed a puppet king, Ecgberht.

The army then took Nottingham in Mercia and withdrew to York under a truce. After the conquest of East Anglia, where Ivar and Ubba are named as commanders, Halfdan became the main commander and led an invasion of Wessex in 870. The Danes fought the West Saxons nine times, including at Ashdown on 8 January 871, and Halfdan accepted a truce from Alfred. Coins minted in London in the following winter bear his name.

The army conquered Mercia in 874, deposing King Burghred and installing the puppet regent Ceolwulf. It then split, Guthrum going south against Wessex and Halfdan north against the Picts and the Britons of Strathclyde. He is generally agreed to be the Albann who, according to the Annals of Ulster, killed Eystein Olafsson, King of Dublin, in 875. Halfdan then sailed up the River Tyne, sacked the monasteries at Tynemouth and Jarrow, and camped at Gateshead. His men settled an area largely coextensive with the old Kingdom of Deira, and sources sometimes title him King of Jórvík.

Halfdan was deposed in Dublin while away in York. In 877 he returned to Ireland to recapture the city but met an army of Fair Heathens, usually taken to be the Viking population longest in Ireland, and was killed at the Battle of Strangford Lough. His surviving men returned to Northumbria through Scotland, fighting a battle in which Constantine I, King of the Picts, was killed. The Vikings of Northumbria had no king until Guthred was made king in 883.
haliacmon: The Haliacmon, in Greek Aliákmonas, flows entirely on Greek soil in the region of Macedonia and is 297 km long, with a drainage basin of 8,813 square kilometres. Three Greek rivers are longer overall, but each reaches Greece from another country. It rises in the Gramos mountains of Western Macedonia, near the border with Albania, flows east and then south-east near Kastoria, curves round the Vourinos mountains and turns north-east. Past Veria it enters the central Macedonian plains, an area of great importance to agriculture, and reaches the Thermaic Gulf west of the delta of the Axios.

The Latin name comes from the Ancient Greek, a compound of words for salt or sea and for anvil. In mythology Haliacmon was a river god, a son of Oceanus and Tethys. Pliny the Elder recorded a tradition that sheep which drank from the river turned white, while those that drank from the Axios turned black. The Ottoman Turks called it Ince-Karasu.

In antiquity the river marked a boundary. According to Julius Caesar it formed the dividing line between Macedon and Thessaly. In its upper course it watered Elimiotis, and further downstream it separated Pieria from Eordaea and Imathia. In the time of Herodotus it was apparently joined by the Loudias, the outflow of the lake of Pella, which has since changed course and flows directly into the Aegean.

Before a diversion dam was built near Aghia Varvara in the mid-1950s, the lowland river had no permanent bed and often flooded, forming extensive marshes. The dam at Polyfyto created a large artificial lake. The river passes Veria and Alexandreia, and at its mouth it has built an extended delta, part of the Axios-Loudias-Haliacmon Delta National Park, where about 90 per cent of Greece's mussels are produced and 215 kinds of birds have been observed.
halifax-nova-scotia: The area was called Chebucto until Halifax was established in 1749 by Governor Edward Cornwallis, who named it in honour of George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax. The Mi'kmaq name for the harbour is K'jipuktuk or Chebookt, meaning Chief Harbour or Great Harbour. They called the Halifax Peninsula, with the downtown area and Point Pleasant Park, Amntu'kati, and the hillside where the town was established was known, according to Thomas Raddall, as Goo-ow-ak-a-de, place of many pines.

Before 1749 the Colony of Nova Scotia had been administered from Annapolis Royal, near the western opening of the Bay of Fundy. In 1749 King George II ordered Cornwallis to establish Halifax as a new capital. Equipped with 13 transports and a sloop of war, Cornwallis founded the Town of Halifax on what is now the Halifax Peninsula on 21 June 1749. The original grid plan devised at the founding included a central military parade square, the Grand Parade, which has City Hall at one end and hosts the annual Remembrance Day ceremony at its cenotaph. The fortress of Citadel Hill overlooks the downtown.

Halifax is the capital and most populous municipality of Nova Scotia, and the most populous in Atlantic Canada. The Halifax Regional Municipality consists of four former municipalities amalgamated in 1996: Halifax, Dartmouth, Bedford and Halifax County. In the 2021 census 348,634 people lived in its urban area, which surrounds Halifax Harbour. The Port of Halifax and Dalhousie University are among its major employers, and the Royal Canadian Navy has major installations along the harbour. The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21, an immigrant entry point prominent through the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s, opened as a National Historic Site in 1999.
hall-heroult-process: Aluminium is the most abundant metallic element in the Earth's crust but is rarely found in its elemental state. Before the process, the metal was made by heating ore with elemental sodium or potassium in a vacuum, a complicated method that consumed expensive materials. Bars of aluminium were exhibited alongside the French crown jewels at the Exposition Universelle of 1855, and Napoleon III was said to have reserved his few aluminium dinner sets for his most honoured guests. When aluminium was chosen for the cap and lightning rod of the Washington Monument, completed in 1884, it still cost more than silver.

Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult devised the process independently and almost simultaneously in 1886. Some authors claim that Hall was assisted by his sister Julia Brainerd Hall, though the extent of her involvement has been disputed. In 1888 Hall opened the first large-scale aluminium plant in Pittsburgh, which became the Alcoa corporation.

Aluminium cannot be made by electrolysis of an aqueous salt, because hydronium ions readily oxidise the metal, and alumina melts at 2072 °C, which makes electrolysing it directly impractical. In the process alumina is dissolved in molten synthetic cryolite, which lowers the melting point. Cryolite also dissolves alumina well, conducts electricity and is less dense than liquid aluminium. Aluminium fluoride is usually added.

A direct current of under 5 V and 100 to 300 kA passes through the mixture. Liquid aluminium collects at the cathode, while oxygen from the alumina combines with carbon from the anode to form mostly carbon dioxide. The molten metal sinks to the bottom of the cell and is siphoned off every one to three days, and the cells run around the clock so that their contents never solidify. The theoretical minimum energy requirement is 6.23 kWh per kilogram of aluminium, but 15.37 kWh is commonly needed.

With cheaper electric power the process helped turn aluminium from a precious metal into an inexpensive commodity, which made it possible for Hugo Junkers to build metal aircraft by the thousands. Because smelting needs large amounts of cheap electricity, plants have often been sited where it is available, as at Kitimat in British Columbia, built by Alcan and powered by the Kenney Dam. In 1997 the American Chemical Society designated the process a National Historic Chemical Landmark.
hall-of-mirrors: The Hall of Mirrors was built between 1678 and 1684, in the third building stage of the Palace of Versailles under Louis XIV. It replaced a large terrace and several smaller salons facing the gardens. The terrace had been judged a misplaced element, exposed to the weather, and was demolished. The architect Jules Hardouin-Mansart designed and built the gallery, and Charles Le Brun created its interior decoration.

The hall is flanked by the Salon of War at the north end and the Salon of Peace at the south, which were joined to the king's and the queen's apartments. It is 73 m long, 10.50 m deep and 12.30 m high. No fireplaces were planned, since the room was too large to heat.

Seventeen windows open towards the park, and on the opposite wall are seventeen mirrors of the same size, each made up of many separate pieces of glass, more than 350 in all. The mirrors reflected the garden and the candlelight in the evening. Mirror glass was an expensive product, and the order was the first major one for the Manufacture royale de glaces de miroirs, a glass factory founded by Jean-Baptiste Colbert, which broke the Venetian monopoly on mirror making in Europe.

The ceiling paintings, directed by Le Brun, glorify Louis XIV as the Sun King and the successes of the first two decades of his personal rule. The central scene is titled The King rules by Himself. Most of the larger panels concern the Franco-Dutch War of 1672 to 1678, and others show episodes of the War of Devolution of 1667 to 1668. The original silver furniture was soon lost: the silver tables were melted down and coined on Louis XIV's order in 1689 to pay for the War of the League of Augsburg.

In the 17th century the hall served as a covered promenade for the king's visit to the chapel, and courtiers gathered there to meet him. It also housed court weddings, audiences for foreign embassies and balls, among them the Yew Tree Ball of 25 February 1745, at which Louis XV met the future Madame de Pompadour. Over 3,000 candles lit it in its prime.

On 18 January 1871, after the siege of Paris in the Franco-Prussian War, the German princes proclaimed William I emperor in the hall, in a ceremony led by Otto von Bismarck. Versailles was the headquarters of the German armies, and the hall was chosen because its ceiling paintings glorified French conquests of German territory. Georges Clemenceau chose the same room for the signing of the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919. It remains reserved for official ceremonies of the French Republic.
halland: Halland is one of the traditional provinces of Sweden, on the western coast of Götaland, bordering Västergötland, Småland, Scania and the Kattegat. Its name means Land of Rocky Slabs, from the Swedish hällar, referring to the coastal cliffs of the northern part. The rivers Viskan, Ätran, Nissan and Lagan flow through it to the Kattegat, and it is well known for its fertile soil and as an agricultural district. The Swedish provinces serve no administrative function; that is done by the counties, and Halland County is almost coextensive with the province.

The Bronze Age was probably a period of relative prosperity in Halland, with over 1,100 tumuli and grave mounds found. Around 200 CE villages began to form larger communities and small kingdoms, and during the 5th and 6th centuries large free-standing farms were created, as at Slöinge. The account of Ohthere of Hålogaland, who travelled to Hedeby in the 870s, shows Halland to have been Danish then, and it stayed so for most of recorded history. As part of the Scanian lands it came under the Scanian Law and took part in the Scanian Thing, one of the three Things that elected the Danish king.

From the 13th century Halland was the scene of considerable military action as Sweden, Denmark and to some degree Norway fought for supremacy in Scandinavia, and the wars made the province poor. It was invaded by Haakon IV of Norway in 1256, by Magnus III of Sweden in 1277 and by Eric VI of Denmark in 1294. It was split in two along the river Ätran for the next century. The Count's Feud, the Northern Seven Years' War and the Kalmar War all affected it, and one of the major battles of the Northern Seven Years' War was fought at Axtorna.

Under the Second Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645 Halland was transferred to Sweden for a period of thirty years, and the transfer was made permanent by the cession in the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658. The last battle in Halland was fought at Fyllebro on 17 August 1676, during the Scanian War. Under Danish rule the province had no coat of arms; when Charles X Gustav died in 1660, one with a lion had to be created for the newly acquired province, since each province was to be represented by its arms at the royal funeral. Calmer conditions after the wars let the province develop, and farming became one of the more efficient in Sweden by the end of the 19th century.
halle-saale: Halle lies in the south of Saxony-Anhalt, in the Leipzig Bay, the southernmost part of the North German Plain, on the River Saale, a tributary of the Elbe. Leipzig is 35 kilometres away, and the two cities form the centres of the Central German Metropolitan Region.

Halle's early history is bound up with salt. The name of the river contains the Germanic root for salt, and salt has been harvested there since at least the Bronze Age. The salters, who wore a uniform with eighteen silver buttons, were known as Halloren, and the name was later given to chocolates shaped like those buttons.

The earliest documented mention of the town dates from 806. It became part of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg in the 10th century and remained so until 1680, when the Margraviate of Brandenburg annexed it together with Magdeburg. It was a member of the Hanseatic League at least as early as 1281, and an important location for Martin Luther's Reformation. The Moritzburg, built between 1484 and 1503 as the archbishops' residence, was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War. In 1840 Ludwig Wucherer opened the Magdeburg-Halle-Leipzig railway line, making Halle a rail hub. After the Second World War Halle was the capital of Saxony-Anhalt until 1952, and then of the district of Halle. When Saxony-Anhalt was re-established in 1990, Magdeburg became the capital.

Halle is the second largest city of Saxony-Anhalt, with around 226,000 inhabitants. Giebichenstein Castle, first mentioned in 961, stands above the Saale. Georg Friedrich Händel, later George Frideric Handel, was born in Halle in 1685 and spent his first 17 years there; his house is a museum, and the city has held a Handel Festival since 1922. The Francke Foundations are home to the Stadtsingechor zu Halle, one of the oldest boys' choirs in the world. The Nebra sky disc is exhibited in the State Museum of Prehistory.
hallein: Hallein is the capital of Hallein district in the Tennengau region. The town stretches along the Salzach river in the shadow of the Untersberg massif, close to the German border on the west. The municipal area includes the cadastral communities of Adnet II, Au, Burgfried, Dürrnberg, Gamp, Gries, Hallein proper, Oberalm II and Taxach. It is linked to the city of Salzburg by the suburban S-Bahn railway and by the A 10 Tauern Autobahn.

The area is known for the Hallein Salt Mine on the Dürrnberg plateau, and settlement has been traced back 4,000 years. A Celtic community lived there from 600 BCE until the Romans took over its Noricum kingdom in 15 BCE. In the middle of the 8th century Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria granted the estates to the Salzburg diocese, and from 987 they were held by St Peter's Abbey. Salt became crucial to the wealth of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, competing with the production of Reichenhall in Bavaria. Salt mining is first mentioned in a deed of 1198, and the name Hallein is documented from the early 13th century.

Beer brewing became common from the 15th century, and in 1489 Prince-Archbishop Leonhard von Keutschach acquired a large brewery whose Hofbräu Kaltenhausen beers became another main source of revenue. At the end of the 17th century Prince-Archbishop Kuenburg had the Protestant miners expelled, and several hundred of them emigrated to Walcheren and Zeelandic Flanders. Hallein became part of the Austrian Empire by 1816. In World War II the town had a work camp annex to the Dachau concentration camp, and afterwards a camp for displaced persons, Beth Israel, which closed in 1954.

Hallein is a historic town with about 21,150 inhabitants and the second largest in the state of Salzburg. The Keltenmuseum shows the Hallstatt and La Tène Celtic cultures and the development of salt mining through the Middle Ages and Renaissance. The Silent Night Museum documents the life of the composer Franz Xaver Gruber, who lived locally, and holds the guitar used by the lyricist Joseph Mohr.
hallstatt-culture: The Hallstatt culture developed out of the Urnfield culture and was followed in much of its area by the La Tène culture. Paul Reinecke's scheme of 1902, based on finds from the south of Germany, divided the end of the Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age into four periods, Hallstatt A to D. Hallstatt A and B are regarded as Late Bronze Age, while Hallstatt C and D, dated roughly 800 to 620 BCE and 620 to 450 BCE, make up the Early Iron Age phase. Radiocarbon dating is hard to use here because of the so-called Hallstatt Plateau, so dating rests mainly on dendrochronology and on the changing fashions of brooches.

The community at Hallstatt itself was untypical of the wider, mainly agricultural, culture, since its economy exploited rich salt mines. These were extensively mined, with a peak from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE, and the salt preserved textiles, wood, leather, shoes and miners' backpacks. Some 1,300 burials are known from the cemetery.

The culture fell into two zones. The western zone covered parts of north-eastern France, northern Switzerland, southern Germany, Bohemia and western Austria, and its elite were buried with a sword or dagger and sometimes a chariot. In the eastern zone, which included eastern Austria, Moravia, Slovenia and parts of Hungary and Serbia, warriors were buried with an axe, helmet and breastplate, and art more often told stories.

After about 600 BCE the founding of Marseille and the arrival of Greek and Etruscan goods led to long-range trade up the Rhône valley. Powerful local chiefdoms emerged that controlled the redistribution of luxury goods, among them the Greek Vix krater and the Greek cauldron from Hochdorf. At the end of the period many major centres were abandoned, and towns did not re-emerge across temperate Europe until the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE.

Farming was the base of the economy, but metalworking was advanced and iron became more common after about 800 BCE. Settlements were mostly small, though the largest, known as princely seats, were fortified hilltop sites with workshops, elite residences and rich burials. Heuneburg on the upper Danube and Mont Lassois in eastern France are typical, and some have been called the first cities north of the Alps.

Rulers lay under large tumuli in timber-lined chambers with wagons and bronze vessels. Ancient DNA has been taken to show matrilineal elites linked by marriage over distances of more than 100 km, and the archaeologist Dirk Krausse has suggested that some rulers may have been sacral kings. Later Hallstatt art in the west is generally agreed to be the early period of Celtic art, and the culture is commonly associated with speakers of Proto-Celtic.
halmahera: Halmahera, formerly known as Jilolo, Gilolo or Jailolo, has a land area of 17,780 square kilometres and is the seventh largest island of Indonesia. It is a volcanic island on an island arc that includes the Raja Ampat Islands, all uplifted by the northward movement of Australia and the subduction of the Pacific Plate. Dukono is an active volcano at the northern end of the island and Mount Ibu another on its northwest coast. Ultramafic rocks and ophiolites form the bedrock over large areas of the eastern peninsula. The flightless invisible rail and the palm Jailoloa halmaherensis are found only on the island.

Sparsely populated Halmahera has long had its fortunes tied to those of the smaller islands of Ternate and Tidore off its west coast. It was the site of the Sultanate of Jailolo, one of the four kingdoms of Maluku, the Maloko Kië Raha, with Ternate, Tidore and Bacan, in the era before the Dutch East India Company colonized the whole archipelago. The north of the island was the base of the Loloda Kingdom, one of the earlier Moluccan kingdoms of the 13th century, though it was not counted among the four prominent ones.

The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace visited Halmahera, as he described in his book The Malay Archipelago (1869). In February 1858, on Ternate or perhaps on Halmahera itself, between bouts of fever, he arrived at the idea of natural selection, wrote it down over the next couple of days and sent the letter to Darwin.

During World War II the island was the site of a Japanese naval base at Kao Bay. In 1999 and 2000 a dispute between the mainly Christian district of Kao and the wholly Muslim district of Malifut grew into religious fighting that spread through much of the North Moluccas, and thousands of people on Halmahera were killed.

Sofifi, the capital of North Maluku province, stands on the west coast of Halmahera, opposite Tidore; the provincial government moved there from Ternate in 2010. In that year the island itself had a population of 449,938, and about half of its inhabitants are Muslim and half Christian. Tobelo is the largest town. The coast is inhabited by the Tobelo people, while the Togutil, a small semi-nomadic related people of the interior, are estimated at 1,500 to 3,000 people.
ham-nghi: Hàm Nghi was born Nguyễn Phúc Ưng Lịch in Huế, the fifth son of Prince Nguyễn Phúc Hồng Cai and brother of Emperor Kiến Phúc. After Emperor Tự Đức died in July 1883, the regents Nguyễn Văn Tường and Tôn Thất Thuyết held power over the choice of emperors. Three emperors had already been removed or had died. The regents wanted a young ruler who shared their anti-French stance, and they chose Ưng Lịch, who had lived in poverty and simplicity with his mother rather than being educated in the palace. He was enthroned in the Thái Hòa Hall on 2 August 1884 with the reign title Hàm Nghi.

The Resident Superior, Pierre Paul Rheinart, sent troops into Huế to force the court to ask France's permission after the fact. The court's request, written in chữ Nôm, was refused until it was rewritten in Chinese characters. At the investiture on 17 August 1884 Tôn Thất Thuyết allowed only three French envoys through the Noon Gate, which was traditionally reserved for the emperor.

On 4 July 1885 an insurrection against the French broke out in the emperor's name, and after the French stormed the palace Tôn Thất Thuyết took Hàm Nghi into hiding. The French replaced him with his brother Đồng Khánh. Hàm Nghi withdrew into the hills around Laos with Tôn Thất Thuyết's force, and the Cần Vương edict called scholars and patriots to resist French rule.

In 1888 Hàm Nghi was betrayed by Trương Quang Ngọc, the head of his Muong guards, and captured while hiding near the Nai river. He was exiled to French Algeria, arriving on 13 January 1889, and was deposed and titled Duke Ưng Lịch. In Algiers he studied under the painter Marius Reynaud, and his painting moved from Orientalism towards Impressionism and Post-Impressionism. He signed his works Tử Xuân. The art historian Amandine Dabat, his descendant, argues that he was the first modern Vietnamese painter. He died on 14 January 1944 and lies in a simple grave at Thonac in the Dordogne. Under French pressure the Nguyễn dynasty gave him no temple name. Vietnamese history counts him among three patriotic emperors of the colonial period.
hama: The ancient settlement of Hamath was occupied from the early Neolithic to the Iron Age. After the fall of the Hittite Empire it was the capital of a Syro-Hittite kingdom known from the Hebrew Bible, which traded with Israel and Judah. In 853 BCE its king Irhuleni and Hadadezer of Aram-Damascus led a coalition against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III at the Battle of Qarqar, a battle that seems to have been closer to a draw. Around 720 BCE Sargon II razed the city after a failed revolt, resettled it with 6,300 Assyrians and had its king flayed alive in Assyria.

Under the Seleucids the city was renamed Epiphaneia after Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and the Romans annexed Syria in 64 BCE. Five hundred Hamian archers were stationed on Hadrian's Wall from 120 CE. Muslim forces under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah took the city in 638 or 639, and it regained its old name. The Crusader Tancred took it in 1108, but the Seljuks recovered it in 1114. Two earthquakes in 1157 shattered it, and Nur al-Din rebuilt its walls and, in 1172, its Great Mosque.

Saladin took Hama in 1175 and gave it four years later to his nephew al-Muzaffar Umar, beginning Ayyubid rule that lasted almost continuously until 1342. The Mongols sacked it in 1260. The historian and geographer Abu al-Fida governed the city from 1310 to 1332. Ibn Battuta visited in 1335. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516. It became part of the French Mandate of Syria after 1918, and a rising took place in the city in 1925 during the Great Syrian Revolt.

Hama lies on the Orontes 213 kilometres north of Damascus and is the capital of the Hama Governorate. Its seventeen norias, water wheels up to 20 metres across, were used for irrigation and now serve as a symbol of the city. In February 1982 government forces under the president's brother Rifaat al-Assad put down an Islamist revolt in the city, shelling quarters held by the insurgents and razing part of the old city. Government forces are alleged to have executed thousands of prisoners and civilians afterwards.
hamadan: Hamadan lies in the foothills of Alvand Mountain in midwestern Iran, at about 1,850 metres above sea level and some 360 kilometres south-west of Tehran. It is the capital of Hamadan province and is believed to be among the oldest Iranian cities. Classical sources call it Ecbatana, from Old Persian Hamgmatāna. The Ganj Nameh inscription and the monuments to Avicenna and Baba Taher are its main sights.

The city may conceivably, though improbably, be mentioned in cuneiform texts of about 1100 BCE from the time of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I, according to Clifford Edmund Bosworth. It is certainly mentioned by Herodotus, who says that the king of Media, Diokes, built Ecbatana in the 7th century BCE. It later became one of several capitals of the Achaemenid dynasty. The book of Ezra says that at Ecbatana a scroll was found that gave the Jews permission from King Darius to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

Under the Parthians, whose capital was Ctesiphon, Hamadan was the summer capital, and the Sasanians built summer palaces there. After the Battle of Nahavand in 642 it fell to the Arabs. In 931 Mardavij, founder of the Al-Ziyar dynasty, plundered it after its people killed his nephew. The Seljuks took the last Kakuyid fortress in 1047 and later moved their capital from Baghdad to Hamadan. The Mongols destroyed it in 1220, and the Timurid invasions destroyed it again, but it thrived in the Safavid era. Benjamin of Tudela reported 30,000 Jews there in 1170.

In the 18th century the city was surrendered to the Ottomans and returned to Iran through the work of Nader Shah. During the First World War Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over it and occupied it in turn. Avicenna entered the city when it was the capital of the Buyid dynasty, taught at its great school and completed many of his writings there.
hamamatsu: Hamamatsu lies in western Shizuoka Prefecture, 260 kilometres south-west of Tokyo, between Lake Hamana to the west, the Tenryū River to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the south. It has a flat plain and the Mikatahara Plateau in the south and mountains in the north. The area has been settled since prehistoric times, and the Shijimizuka shell mound and the Akamonue Kofun tomb survive from the Jōmon and Kofun periods.

In the Nara period it became the capital of Tōtōmi Province. In the Sengoku period Hamamatsu Castle was the home of the future shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu. The city flourished in the Edo period under a succession of daimyō as a castle town and a post town on the Tōkaidō highway between Edo and Kyoto. The Hamamatsu Kite Festival, held each May, is said to have begun about 430 years ago, when the lord of the castle marked the birth of his first son by flying kites.

After the Meiji Restoration Hamamatsu was a prefecture from 1871 to 1876 before it was united with Shizuoka Prefecture. The station opened on the Tōkaidō Main Line in 1889, the same year it became a town, and it became a city on 1 July 1911. An Army air base opened in 1926 and a flight school in 1933. The Tonankai earthquake of 7 December 1944 caused much damage, and US air raids largely destroyed the city in June 1945.

Hamamatsu is the largest city in Shizuoka Prefecture, with an estimated 780,128 inhabitants in 2023,. It is known as an industrial city, above all for musical instruments and motorcycles. Honda was founded there, and Yamaha, Suzuki, Kawai and Roland have headquarters in the city. A 1990 change in Japanese immigration law drew a large Brazilian Nikkei population to work in its factories. The Hamamatsu International Piano Competition has been held every three years since 1991, and the Museum of Musical Instruments opened in 1995.
hamani-diori: Hamani Diori was born on 6 June 1916 at Soudouré, near Niamey, the son of a public health officer in the French colonial administration. He attended the William Ponty Teachers' Training College in Dakar and worked as a teacher in Niger from 1936 to 1938, then became a Hausa and Djerma instructor at the Institute of Study Abroad in Paris.

In 1946, as headmaster of a school in Niamey, he helped to found the Nigerien Progressive Party (PPN), a regional branch of the African Democratic Rally. That year he was elected to the French National Assembly. He lost his seat in 1951 to his cousin and rival Djibo Bakary, regained it in 1956 and became its deputy-speaker.

After a referendum in 1958 granted Niger self-government, Diori became president of the provisional government, and in 1959 prime minister. Niger became independent on 3 August 1960, and the National Assembly elected him president in November. A coalition of Hausa, Fula and, most prominently, Djerma leaders, including chiefs and traditionalists, had supported him and gained him French favour.

Soon after independence he made the PPN the only legal party. His government favoured traditional social structures and close economic ties with France. He ruled through a small group of pre-independence figures on the PPN Politburo and often bypassed the cabinet, leading several ministries himself. Boubou Hama, President of the National Assembly, was among his most powerful advisers. As sole candidate he was re-elected unopposed in 1965 and 1970.

Diori was respected abroad as a spokesman for African affairs and an arbitrator in conflicts, but at home his administration was accused of corruption and could not relieve the famine of the Sahelian drought of the early 1970s. He put down a coup in December 1963 and narrowly escaped assassination in 1965, using French advisers and troops against his opponents; students and unions protested against what they called French neocolonialism. In 1972 his government voiced dissatisfaction with investment in uranium production during Georges Pompidou's visit.

Disorder followed allegations that ministers were misappropriating food aid, and critics said he was consolidating power by limiting cabinet posts to fellow Djerma, relatives and friends. On 15 April 1974 Lieutenant Colonel Seyni Kountché led a military coup that ended his rule. Diori was imprisoned for six years, and after his release in 1980 he remained under house arrest until 1987. He then moved to Morocco and died there on 23 April 1989, aged 72.
hamburg: Hamburg lies at a sheltered natural harbour on the southern fanning-out of the Jutland Peninsula, between continental Europe to the south and Scandinavia to the north, with the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the northeast. It stands on the River Elbe at its confluence with the Alster and Bille, where the 110 km Elbe estuary begins. The city centre is around the Binnenalster and Außenalster, both lakes formed by damming the Alster. The Altes Land, part of the city, is the largest contiguous fruit-producing region in Central Europe.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, reported the first name for the vicinity as Treva. The name Hamburg comes from the first permanent building on the site, a castle which Charlemagne ordered built in 808. It rose on rocky terrain in a marsh between the Alster and the Elbe as a defence against Slavic incursion and acquired the name Hammaburg, burg meaning castle or fort.

In 834 Hamburg became the seat of a bishopric, whose first bishop, Ansgar, later known as the Apostle of the North, founded the city's early Christian institutions. Two years later it was linked with Bremen to form the Bishopric of Hamburg-Bremen. The town was destroyed repeatedly in its early centuries. In 845 a fleet of 600 Viking ships sailed up the Elbe and destroyed it, when it had about 500 inhabitants. King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland burned it in 1030, and Valdemar II of Denmark raided and occupied it in 1201 and 1214. The Black Death reached Hamburg in 1350 and killed at least 60 per cent of its population, and the city suffered several major fires in the medieval period.

Hamburg was a member of the Hanseatic League and a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. Before the unification of Germany in 1871 it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 it was a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten. Later disasters included the Great Fire of 1842, the Allied fire-bombing of 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962.

Officially the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, it is the second-largest city in Germany after Berlin and one of the country's three city-states, with Berlin and Bremen. Its population is over 1.9 million. The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest. The Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2015.
hamdanid-dynasty: The Hamdanids ruled Upper Mesopotamia and Syria. They were a Shia Muslim Arab dynasty descended from Adi ibn Usama al-Taghlibi and the ancient Banu Taghlib tribe of Mesopotamia and Arabia, and historical sources sometimes call them Adawis or Taghlibis. The dynasty was founded by Hamdan ibn Hamdun. By 892 to 893 he held Mardin, after fighting the Kharijites of the Jazira. In 895 Caliph al-Mutadid invaded and Hamdan fled; he later surrendered and was imprisoned.

Hamdan's sons held office under the caliphs. Abdallah became governor of Mosul in 905 to 906, campaigned against the Kurds and was dismissed and reinstated. His brother Husayn was made governor of Diyar Rabi'a, revolted in 916 after a disagreement with the vizier Ali ibn Isa, and was captured and executed in 918. During their rule the Hamdanids intermarried with Kurdish dignitaries. Nasir al-Dawla, governor of Mosul and Diyar Bakr from 929, ruled so harshly that his own family deposed him. His lineage still ruled in Mosul, despite a heavy defeat by the Buyids in 979, until 990, after which northern Iraq was divided between the Uqaylids and the Marwanids.

Ali Sayf al-Dawla, the Sword of the Dynasty, ruled northern Syria from Aleppo between 945 and 967 and became the most important opponent of the re-expansion of the Christian Byzantine Empire. His court was a centre of culture and fostered Arabic literature, but it lost that standing after the Byzantine sacking of Aleppo. To stop the Byzantine advance Aleppo was put under the suzerainty of the Fatimids of Egypt, and in 1003 the Fatimids deposed the Hamdanids.

The Aleppo line was ruled in turn by Sayf al-Dawla, Sa'd al-Dawla from 967 to 991 and Sa'id al-Dawla from 991 to 1002, who was deposed by the ghulam Lu'lu' al-Kabir. In the Jazira the rulers after Nasir al-Dawla were Abu Taghlib from 967 to 978, then direct administration as part of the Buyid-controlled Abbasid Caliphate from 979 to 981, and two sons of Nasir al-Dawla in 989 to 990, who were deposed by the Uqaylid chieftain Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab.
hami: Hami, in Uyghur Kumul, lies in eastern Xinjiang on the border with Gansu. The city stands in a fault depression about 759 metres above sea level, under mountain ranges that rise to about 4,900 metres. Its climate is a dry continental desert one. The Tang pilgrim Xuanzang described it as the first of a string of oases supplied by the Tian Shan, whose water had been kept in underground wells and channels since time immemorial.

Its oldest known native name is Cumuḍa, given by the people Han sources call the Xiao Yuezhi in the 1st millennium BCE. In Chinese it was Yiwu under the Han and Yizhou under the Tang, and the Mongols called it Qamil. Marco Polo wrote of Camul, and from the Ming dynasty Chinese sources used the name Hami.

The Han set up military agricultural colonies at the oasis and struggled with the Xiongnu for control of it. It was noted for melons, raisins and wine. The Northern Wei occupied the region in 456 and raided the Rouran Khaganate from it, and the First Turkic Khaganate took control after the 6th century. The Tang asserted control in the 7th century, and the Tibetan Empire and the Tang vied for the region until the Chinese were repelled in 851. After the collapse of the Uyghur Khaganate a group of Uyghurs settled in the Hami region and brought linguistic and cultural change.

The Mongols conquered it under the Yuan dynasty. Gunashiri, a descendant of Chagatai Khan, founded the small state of Qara Del there, which accepted Ming supremacy, and the Ming established Kumul Hami in 1404. Oirat Mongols later controlled it, and it was conquered and converted to Islam in 1513. From the 18th century Kumul was the centre of the Kumul Khanate, a semi-autonomous vassal state within the Qing Empire and then the Republic of China as part of Xinjiang. Its last ruler was Maqsud Shah.

Hami is a prefecture-level city, formed in 2016 when the former county-level city merged with Hami Prefecture and became Yizhou District. It is still known for its sweet melons, and the Lanzhou–Xinjiang Railway and China National Highway 312 pass through it.
hamilcar-barca: Little is known of the Barca family before the Punic Wars. One suggestion is that it came from Cyrene; another is that it belonged to the landed aristocracy of Carthage. The epithet Barca, in Punic brq, means thunderbolt or shining. Hamilcar was the father of Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Mago and the father-in-law of Hasdrubal the Fair. He was 28 when he received the command in Sicily in 247 BCE, and he already had three daughters.

Hamilcar commanded the Carthaginian land forces in Sicily from 247 to 241 BCE with a small mercenary army and little money. Carthage invested few men in the island, and his aim was probably to keep a stalemate. He fought a guerrilla war against the Romans, moved his army by night to the slopes of Mount Eryx in 244 BCE and held it for about three years, supplied by road from Drepana. When the Romans in 241 BCE demanded that he surrender his army's arms and Roman deserters, he refused, and the army left Sicily under arms.

The army then rebelled over unpaid wages in the Mercenary War. After Hanno the Great failed to defeat the rebels, Carthage gave Hamilcar command of 10,000 men and 70 elephants. He won at the Bagradas, and when the rebels led by Spendius trapped him in a valley he was saved by the defection of the Numidian chieftain Naravas with 2,000 horsemen, who later married his third daughter. He then crushed the rebel army and crucified Spendius and other hostages outside Tunis. Hamilcar allied with Hasdrubal the Fair against Hanno's aristocratic party and avoided trial for having caused the war with unrealistic promises to his soldiers.

In 237 BCE Hamilcar led an expedition to Iberia, with Hasdrubal the Fair and the nine-year-old Hannibal. Before he left Hannibal is said to have sworn never to be a friend of Rome; some modern historians read this as lifelong enmity, others call that a distortion.

Hamilcar secured the gold and silver mines of the Sierra Morena, defeated the Turdetani and a 50,000-strong army under Indortes, whom he crucified, and in four years of campaigns subdued the country between Gades and Cape Nao. He probably founded Akra Leuke, now Alicante, in 235 BCE, and built a professional army of Iberians, Africans and Numidians that Hasdrubal inherited and Hannibal later led. When a Roman embassy came in 231 BCE he answered that he was gathering booty to pay Carthage's war indemnity.

He died in 228 BCE while besieging a town. Appian says he was thrown from his horse and drowned in a river; Polybius says he fell in battle against an unnamed tribe. A third version has the Oretani chieftain Orissus attack him as he retreated across the Júcar.
hammer-deroburt: Hammer DeRoburt was born on Nauru on 25 September 1922. His maternal grandfather Daimon was head chief of the island from 1920 to 1930. After school on Nauru he attended the Gordon Institute of Technology in Geelong, Australia, and worked as a teacher. During the Second World War the Japanese deported him to Truk with most of the Nauruan population, and he returned in 1946 to work in the Department of Education. In 1953 he led the Nauru Workers' Organisation in a four-month strike that won higher wages and more training from the Australian administration. He was elected to the Local Government Council in 1955 and became Head Chief of Nauru in 1956.

As head chief he lobbied the United Nations Trusteeship Council directly. In 1957 he protested the British Phosphate Commission's continued exploitation of the island's phosphate. In 1962 he and two colleagues called for independence. When the Australian government offered resettlement on Curtis Island in Queensland, he insisted on full sovereignty over it, which was refused, so the council rejected resettlement altogether. He signed the Nauru Island Phosphate Industry Agreement in June 1967, which provided for Nauruan ownership of the phosphate reserves, and the Nauru Independence Act 1967 gave independence from 31 January 1968.

DeRoburt was elected the first president on 17 May 1968, when the constitution was adopted, and held the external affairs, internal affairs and island development portfolios. His government created the Nauru Phosphate Corporation, Air Nauru and Nauru Pacific Shipping Lines. In December 1976 Bernard Dowiyogo defeated him by nine votes to seven, and he returned to the presidency in 1978. His terms ran 1968 to 1976, 1978 to 1986, 1986 and 1986 to 1989, with a short interval under Kennan Adeang. In his last term Nauru brought a case against Australia in the International Court of Justice over the rehabilitation of mined land. He died in Melbourne on 15 July 1992.
hammurabi: Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon and the son of Sin-muballit. His reign came after the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur in 2004 BCE, when Mesopotamia was divided among several kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties, of which Isin and then Larsa were the strongest in the south. Babylon had been a secondary city until an Amorite dynasty took root there around 1880 BCE with Sumu-la-El. Babylonian sources give Hammurabi a reign of 43 years. The first two decades are poorly documented, and the names of the years of that time refer chiefly to public works and offerings to the gods.

Elam, whose heartland lay in the south-west of present-day Iran, expanded into the Mesopotamian plain and subjugated Eshnunna. This led to war with a coalition of kingdoms that included Babylon and Mari, and the Elamites were eventually repelled with great difficulty with the help of troops from Mari and other northern kingdoms. Strengthened by this success, Hammurabi went on to conquer the kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Almost all of Mesopotamia came under Babylonian rule, so that it is possible to speak of an empire. His conquests seem to have come mainly from opportunities as they arose, not from a prepared imperial plan.

Hammurabi is best known for his law code, which is said to have been inspired by Shamash, the Babylonian god of justice. It was written towards the end of his reign and is known mainly from a large stele, which shows the king facing Shamash. It has a prologue, a set of provisions and an epilogue. It is not the only Mesopotamian legislative collection, nor the oldest, but it is the longest known. Its status is debated, and in its prologue and epilogue it presents itself as a commemorative inscription that celebrates his sense of justice. The prologue names the gods who bestow sovereignty, Enlil, Marduk and Ishtar, and his descent from the founder of his dynasty.

Hammurabi also carried out public works. The 33rd year of his reign commemorates a canal named in his honour, which gave perennial water to Nippur, Eridu, Ur, Larsa, Uruk and Isin. He rebuilt sanctuaries, including the ziggurat of Zababa at Kish. Letters found at Mari and at Larsa, more than 200 of the latter addressed to his subordinates, make his the best documented of the Mesopotamian reigns. His son Samsu-iluna failed to maintain the empire. Hammurabi was later revered as a great conqueror, then chiefly as the ideal lawgiver, and archaeologists rediscovered him in the late 19th century. He is seen as an important figure in the history of law.
hampshire: Hampshire is bordered by Berkshire to the north, Surrey and West Sussex to the east, the Solent to the south, Dorset to the west and Wiltshire to the north-west. Undulating hills characterise much of it, with a belt of chalk running from the Hampshire Downs in the north-west to the South Downs in the south-east. The Loddon and Wey drain north into the Thames, while the Itchen and Test flow south into Southampton Water. The south-west holds the New Forest, one of the largest expanses of ancient woodland remaining in England. The county historically contained Bournemouth, Christchurch and the Isle of Wight.

The region is believed to have been continuously occupied since the end of the last Ice Age, its first inhabitants being Mesolithic hunter-gatherers concentrated around the river valleys. Hampshire was incorporated into the Roman province of Britannia soon after the invasion of 43 CE, and its political leaders are generally believed to have accepted this peacefully. Its chief town, Venta Belgarum, now Winchester, became capital of the Belgae. A fortification near Southampton, Clausentum, belonged to the Saxon Shore forts, and a New Forest pottery industry exported widely across southern Britain. The West Saxons moved south in the late seventh century and incorporated Hampshire into their kingdom. The name is attested as Hamtunscir in 755, from the Saxon settlement of Hamtun, now Southampton.

After the Norman Conquest London became the capital, but Winchester remained important, and the New Forest was a prized royal hunting forest, where King William Rufus was killed while hunting in 1100. The Domesday Book of 1086 records 44 hundreds. From the 12th century the ports grew with trade, wool and cloth, fishing and shipbuilding, and by 1523 at the latest Southampton had outstripped Winchester in population. In the two world wars the county played a crucial military role through the Royal Navy base at Portsmouth, the army camp at Aldershot and Netley Hospital. Supermarine, designer of the Spitfire, was based in Southampton, which led to severe bombing of the city in the Second World War.

Hampshire is a ceremonial county in South East England with an area of 3,769 square kilometres and Southampton as its largest settlement. Portsmouth lies in the south-east, Winchester in the centre, and Basingstoke and Andover in the north. Hampshire County Council sits at Castle Hill in Winchester. Its county day is 15 July, St Swithun's Day. The Hambledon Club, formed about 1750, created many of cricket's early laws, and the Battle of Cheriton was fought near Winchester in 1644.
han-chinese: Han Chinese trace their ancestry and culture to the Huaxia, a confederation of agricultural tribes of the late Neolithic and early Bronze Age that lived along the Guanzhong and Yellow River basins in northern China. Early Chinese history is largely mythical: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian records successive overlords, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, for whom little reliable archaeological evidence exists. The name Han people first appeared during the Northern and Southern period and was inspired by the Han dynasty, and the Chinese language and script came to be called the Han language and Han characters.

Qin and Han rule sent settlers south. Qin Shi Huang is said to have sent several hundred thousand men and fifteen thousand women to settle Lingnan under a general named Zhao Tuo, and the Han emperor Wu later ordered a further two hundred thousand men to build ships to attack and colonize the region. Successive migrations southward fused the newcomers with the peoples south of the Yangtze, while the centres of Han wealth and culture moved from the Yellow River basin to Jiangnan. By the Tang and Song dynasties the Han were the main inhabitants of the fertile lowlands and cities of the south.

Han Chinese have often held the dominant positions of governance, but dynastic rule was in notable periods held by others, among them the Liao (916–1125), the Jin (1115–1234), the Yuan (1271–1368) and the Qing (1644–1912). Sun Yat-sen made the restoration of Han rule a tenet of the 1911 Revolution, which overthrew the Manchu-led Qing and established the Han-dominated Republic of China.

Scholars such as Kevin Carrico and Dru Gladney argue that a single Han identity, set against Manchu rulers, is a modern development promoted by nationalists near the end of the Qing. Liang Qichao coined the term Zhonghua minzu between 1902 and 1905 to refer to the Han; it later became a wider concept for all the peoples of China. Han Chinese make up about 91 percent of the population of China. Their literary heritage includes the Analects, the Tao Te Ching and the Four Great Classical Novels.
han-dynasty: The Han dynasty was established by Liu Bang after the short-lived Qin dynasty collapsed within four years of the death of Qin Shi Huang. Two former rebel leaders, Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han, fought for hegemony, and Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE. He took the title of emperor and is known after death as Emperor Gaozu. Chang'an, modern Xi'an, became the capital. The dynasty took its name from Hanzhong, the small fief on the Han River that Xiang Yu had given Liu Bang. The Western Han lasted until 9 CE, and the Eastern Han formally began on 5 August 25 CE, when Liu Xiu became Emperor Guangwu.

The Xiongnu defeated the Han in 200 BCE, and the court responded with marriage alliances and payments of tribute. Emperor Wu changed this policy in 133 BCE with a series of campaigns that took the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, helping to establish the Silk Road. He also annexed Nanyue in 111 BCE and Dian in 109 BCE, and in 108 BCE Han forces conquered Gojoseon and set up the Xuantu and Lelang commanderies in Korea. From his reign onward the court sponsored Confucianism, and in 124 BCE he established the Imperial University. To finance his campaigns he nationalised the salt and iron industries in 117 BCE, monopolies repealed under the Eastern Han.

Wang Mang, regent after the death of Emperor Ai, interrupted the dynasty with his Xin dynasty from 9 to 23 CE. After 92 CE palace eunuchs became involved in violent power struggles with the consort clans of the empresses. The Yellow Turban and Five Pecks of Rice rebellions, led by Taoist religious societies, challenged imperial authority in 184. After the death of Emperor Ling in 189 the eunuchs were massacred by military officers, and governors became warlords who divided the empire. The dynasty ended in 220 when Cao Pi, king of Wei, usurped the throne from Emperor Xian.

The emperor stood at the apex of society and was in theory unlimited in power, but ministers pressed him through institutions such as the court conference, and emperors were often minors ruled over by a regent. Below him came the kings of the Liu clan, and the empire was divided into provinces, commanderies and counties, plus semi-autonomous kingdoms that lost autonomy after the Rebellion of the Seven States. Taxes were paid in coin, and the poll tax stimulated a money economy. Han technology included papermaking, which the Han tradition credits to Cai Lun in 105, rudders, raised-relief maps and seismometers. Today the majority ethnic group of China calls itself the Han people.
han-fei: Han Fei was born into the ruling family of the State of Han in the last phase of the Warring States period, which made him unlike most philosophers of his age, who came from outside the aristocracy. Scholars place his birth at about 280 BCE, though the exact year is unknown. Some have read his writings as addressed to his cousin, the King of Han.
