In the 17th century Ali ibn Da'ud founded the Emirate of Harar, a dynasty that ruled for the next two centuries. His successor Abdullah improved relations with the Oromo by marrying five of his sons to Oromo women, and the emirate extended its economic influence from Shewa to Zeila and began to mint its own coins. In 1887 the army of Menelik II conquered Harar and appointed his nephew Ras Makonnen as governor. Makonnen had the main mosque torn down and replaced it with an Orthodox church.

Harar is the capital of the Harari Region, and Harar Jugol was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006. UNESCO describes it as considered the fourth holiest city of Islam, with 82 mosques, three of which date from the 10th century, and 102 shrines. Harari houses, called gey gar, form a distinct type whose layout dates back to 1754. They stand in walled compounds arranged around a courtyard. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud settled in Harar as a merchant between 1880 and 1891, and his house is one of its landmarks.
harare: Harare lies in north-eastern Zimbabwe, in the Mashonaland region, on one of the higher parts of the Highveld plateau at an elevation of 1,483 metres. Its climate is subtropical highland, cooler and drier than a tropical or subtropical climate because of the altitude and a cool south-easterly airflow. The original landscape could be described as parkland, and Harare Kopje, at 1,540 metres, is the highest point in the city. The name comes from the village near Harare Kopje of the Shona chief Neharawa, whose nickname was he who does not sleep.

The Pioneer Column, a military volunteer force of settlers organised by Cecil Rhodes for the British South Africa Company, founded the city as a fort on 12 September 1890. It was named Fort Salisbury after the British prime minister, the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, and became known simply as Salisbury. Company administrators demarcated the city and ran it until Southern Rhodesia achieved responsible government in 1923. Salisbury was declared a municipality in 1897 and became a city in 1935.

After the Second World War the city expanded rapidly with its designation as capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963, with significant immigration from Great Britain, Southern Africa and, to a lesser extent, Southern Europe. Suburbs such as Alexandra Park and Mount Pleasant sprawled outwards as motor vehicle ownership grew, while mostly black suburbs like Highfield suffered from overcrowding. The Federation was dissolved in 1963. Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front government declared Rhodesia independent of the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 and kept Salisbury as the capital, and the country was internationally recognised as independent under the name Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980.

The city was renamed Harare on 18 April 1982, the second anniversary of independence. Before the change the black residential area now called Mbare was known as Harari. Investment in education and healthcare produced a growing middle class, and the Eastgate Centre and the New Reserve Bank Tower became landmarks of the period.

Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe, with 1,849,600 inhabitants in the 2022 census and an estimated 2,487,209 in its metropolitan province, which also includes Chitungwiza, Epworth and Ruwa. It is the country's financial, commercial and communications centre and a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus fruits. About 90 percent of its people are Shona-speaking. The University of Zimbabwe, founded in 1952, is in the city, and the National Gallery, the National Archives and the Harare Gardens stand in its central district. The city hosted the 1995 All-Africa Games and the 2003 Cricket World Cup.
harbin: Harbin lies in southern Heilongjiang on the south bank of the middle Songhua River, at the south-eastern edge of the Songnen Plain. The terrain is generally flat and low. It is the northernmost of China's major cities and has long, dry and freezing winters, which have earned it the nickname Ice City. The city government says the name means 'swan' in Jurchen, while other sources derive it from a Manchu word meaning 'a place for drying fishing nets'.

Human settlement in the area dates from at least 2200 BCE. Wanyan Aguda, founder of the Jin dynasty, who reigned from 1115 to 1123, came from the Jurchen Wanyan tribes living near the Ashi River. In 1115 he established the Jin capital, Shangjing Huiningfu, in what is now Acheng District of Harbin. Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing, now Beijing, in 1153, and Wanyan Yong restored the city as a secondary capital in 1173.

The modern city dates from 1898, when the Russian Empire built the Chinese Eastern Railway. The Polish engineer Adam Szydłowski drew plans for the city, and the Russians made it the base of their administration of the railway. The settlement grew into a city within five years, with settlers from across the Russian Empire, including Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Georgians and Tatars. In the 1920s it was considered China's fashion capital.

Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden Incident of September 1931, and Japanese forces occupied Harbin within hours. From 1932 until 1945 it was the largest city of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army took the city on 20 August 1945 and handed it to the People's Liberation Army in April 1946. Most of the European community left in the early 1950s, so that by 1964 the Russian population was reduced to 450.

Harbin is the capital and largest city of Heilongjiang, with a metropolitan population of 10,009,854 at the 2020 census. Its Russian and European legacy survives in Central Street and in Saint Sophia Cathedral. UNESCO named Harbin a City of Music in 2010, and the city is known for its winter ice sculpture festival.
harda-district: Harda district is a district of Madhya Pradesh in central India, with its headquarters at the town of Harda, which is also known as Hridaynagari. It was organised in 1998 and is part of the Narmadapuram Division. It covers 2,644 square kilometres. The district lies in the valley of the Narmada River, which forms its northern boundary, and the land rises toward the Satpura Range to the south. Its neighbours are the districts of Sehore to the north, Narmadapuram to the northeast and Betul to the southeast. It is divided into three Janpad Panchayat areas, Harda, Timarni and Khirkiya, and six tehsils: Harda, Timarni, Khirkiya, Sirali, Rahatgaon and Handia.

The 2011 census counted 570,465 people, an increase of 20.25 per cent over 2001, with a density of 171 inhabitants per square kilometre. Hindus made up 92.46 per cent of the population and Muslims 6.77 per cent. At the census 89.88 per cent spoke Hindi as a first language, 6.52 per cent Korku and 1.76 per cent Gondi. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes made up 16.28 and 27.99 per cent. About 20.92 per cent of the population lived in towns. The district has four municipalities, Harda, Timarni, Khirkiya and Sirali, and two seats in the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly.

Joga Fort stands on an island in the middle of the Narmada at Joga village, 45 kilometres from Harda. Handia has the Riddheshwar Mandir and a ghat on the Narmada, and Makrai has a historic fort. The district was also the setting for the film Ammaa Ki Boli, Matrubhoomi, shot at Ranhai Kala, which deals with the consequences of female infanticide.
hargeisa: Hargeisa lies in a valley in the Galgodon, or Ogo, highlands at an elevation of 1,334 metres. The Laas Geel complex on its outskirts holds Neolithic cave paintings in an excellent state of preservation, in ten rock alcoves. They show human figures with raised hands facing long-horned, humpless cattle, and a French team found them in 2002, though local people had known of them for centuries. The climate is hot and semi-arid but tempered by the altitude, with most of the roughly 400 millimetres of annual rain falling between April and September.

Oral poetic accounts say Hargeisa began as a watering and trading stop for nomads and caravans, and the modern settlement grew from the Big Commune founded around 1860 by Sheikh Madar Shirwa, a Qadiriyya scholar born in Berbera who had studied at Harar. He and his companions founded a religious commune, introducing farming on large sorghum plantations in place of pastoral wandering, caring for the sick and elderly and promoting a common religious identity above tribe. One account derives the name from Harar as-sagir, little Harar, another from a Somali phrase for a place to sell hides and skins.

In 1888 the British established a protectorate in British Somaliland with Berbera as its capital. The capital was later moved to Hargeisa, which was granted capital status in 1941. The protectorate became independent on 26 June 1960 and united days later with the former Italian Somaliland to form the Somali Republic. On 31 May 1988 the Somali National Movement attacked Hargeisa, and the government of Siad Barre answered with shelling and aerial bombardment of the city. Up to 90 percent of it was destroyed in what is described as the Isaaq genocide. After the collapse of the central government and the declaration of independence of the Republic of Somaliland, reconstruction began, financed largely by local entrepreneurs and by remittances from relatives abroad.

Hargeisa is the capital and largest city of Somaliland, a partially recognised state that is still considered internationally part of Somalia. It hosts the parliament, the presidential palace and the government ministries. Its population was estimated at about 30,000 in 1958. It is a commercial centre for retail, trading, construction and stone-cutting, and the University of Hargeisa is one of several colleges and universities there.
hari-singh: Hari Singh was born in September 1895 at the Amar Mahal Palace in Jammu, into the Dogra Rajput royal family. He was the only surviving son of Raja Amar Singh, brother of Maharaja Pratap Singh, who had no child, so that Hari Singh was heir presumptive. At the age of 13 he was sent to Mayo College in Ajmer, and when his father died in 1909 the British appointed Major H. K. Barr as his guardian. Pratap Singh appointed him commander-in-chief of the State Forces in 1915, and in 1918 he was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire. In 1919 he sailed from Bombay for Britain, and spent a year studying government, transport, industry, education and sanitation.

After Pratap Singh died on 23 September 1925, the British overruled his choice of an adopted heir, Raja Jagat Dev Singh of Poonch, and Hari Singh's coronation took place from 22 to 28 February 1926. On the recommendation of the Glancy Commission, a Praja Sabha was set up in April 1932, with 75 members: 12 officials, 16 state councillors, 14 nominated and 33 elected. A written constitution for the state followed on 7 September 1939. He made primary education compulsory, prohibited child marriage and opened places of worship to low-caste subjects. He also faced an agitation in Kashmir in 1931.

In 1947 Jammu and Kashmir could join India or Pakistan or remain independent. Hari Singh wished to stay independent for the time being, since both dominions were in the grip of partition violence and the state had a Muslim-majority population. He signed a standstill agreement with Pakistan on 14 August 1947. An uprising began in Poonch on 6 October, and a Pakistan-backed Pashtun tribal invasion reached Muzaffarabad on 22 October. He appealed to India for help, Lord Mountbatten advised accession first, and Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947. Indian troops repelled the invaders in what became the first Indo-Pakistan War.

Under pressure from Jawaharlal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel, Hari Singh made his son Karan Singh Prince Regent in June 1949 and left for Bombay, where he lived for the rest of his life. He remained titular Maharaja until the monarchy was abolished in 1952. He died on 26 April 1961, and his ashes were scattered over Jammu and Kashmir and immersed in the Tawi River at Jammu. Singh remained a controversial ruler. The Amar Mahal Museum in Jammu, inaugurated in 1975, displays the gold throne on which he sat.
harihara: Harihara is the dual representation of the Hindu deities Vishnu (Hari) and Shiva (Hara), and is also known as Shankaranarayana. The name is sometimes used as a philosophical term for the unity of Vishnu and Shiva as different aspects of the same Ultimate Reality, Brahman. This idea is discussed in texts of Advaita Vedanta and in some schools of Shaivism, such as Virashaiva. Hinduism includes large traditions focused on Vishnu, with his avatars such as Rama and Krishna, and on Shiva. The Puranas and various traditions treat both as aspects of the one Brahman, and Harihara is a symbolic representation of that view.

Some of the earliest sculptures of Harihara are found in the surviving cave temples of India, such as caves 1 and 3 of the 6th-century Badami cave temples. The earliest mention of the being is probably in the Vishnu Parva of the Harivamsha, where Markandeya discusses it. In one legend, Vishnu appeared as the enchantress Mohini, and Shiva, besotted, tried to embrace her; she reverted to Vishnu's true form, and the two deities fused into Harihara. According to the Skanda Purana, the devotees of Shiva and Vishnu disputed which god was supreme, and to end the quarrel the two merged into one being.

In art Harihara is split down the middle, one half Shiva and the other Vishnu. The Shiva half has the matted locks of a yogic master piled high on the head and sometimes wears a tiger skin, reserved for the most revered ascetics. The Vishnu half wears a tall crown and other jewellery, representing his responsibility for maintaining world order, and his black skin represents holiness. These distinctions broadly express the duality of humble religious influence in the ascetic and authoritative secular power in the king or householder. Harihara has been part of temple iconography throughout South Asia and Southeast Asia.
harjedalen: Härjedalen is a historical province, or landskap, in the centre of Sweden. It borders the Norwegian county of Trøndelag and the provinces of Dalarna, Hälsingland, Medelpad and Jämtland. Four-fifths of it lies above 500 metres, as part of the Scandinavian mountain range, and Högvålen, at 835 metres, is the highest village in Sweden. The name comes from Old West Norse Herjárdalr, the valley of the Härje river, though one explanation holds that her or har means a mound of stones, referring to stones in the river Härjån.

The first people are estimated to have arrived around 7,000 BCE, living by hunting and fishing close to the inland ice, which had begun to melt. At Ruändan in the Flatruet mountains there is a large site of rock paintings, some twenty figures of people, bears, moose and reindeer, first reported in 1896 and estimated to be over 4,000 years old.

A legend says the province is named after a Norseman who fled east from the court of King Halfdan Svarte after killing one of the king's men with a horn, and so became known as Härjulf the Hornbreaker. He served the Svea king Anund, eloped with the king's sister Helga, and settled with her in the remote valley. A statue of them stands in Lillhärdal. The same legend makes them forebears of the Icelander Bjarni Herjólfsson, who first sighted the New World when blown off course on a voyage to Greenland.

Härjedalen came under the Norwegian king in the Middle Ages, around 1100, and Christianization followed the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030. It remained with Jämtland a province of Denmark-Norway until the Second Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645 ceded both to Sweden. Agriculture was the main industry for a long time, with ironmaking and trade mainly to Røros. Forestry brought industrialization from the mid-1850s, and many residents emigrated to America, chiefly to north-western Minnesota, in the late 1800s.

Härjedalen has no cities. Sveg, the only village of modest size, was once the administrative centre of the province. The traditional provinces of Sweden serve no administrative purpose today, and Härjedalen Municipality, in the south of Jämtland County, is larger than the province. Sånfjället National Park extends through the municipality, and mountain resorts at Funäsdalen, Vemdalen and Lofsdalen draw visitors. The provincial arms were granted in 1660, and the provincial flower is the Arctic violet.
harju-county: Harju County lies on the southern coast of the Gulf of Finland and borders Lääne-Viru, Järva, Rapla and Lääne counties. The county has several islands, the largest of which is Naissaar, and Lahemaa National Park, created in 1971, was the first national park in the Soviet Union.

The modern county was formed from two ancient Estonian counties, Revala, around what is now Tallinn, and Harjumaa, which lay south of Revala. They were merged into one in 1266. Lindanise, a small trading post on the Gulf of Finland, was the capital of Revala and grew into the Hanseatic town of Reval and later Tallinn.

In 1219 King Valdemar II of Denmark landed at Lindanise and conquered Revala and Harju, and the inhabitants were forced into Christianity. During the Livonian Crusade the Order of the Sword Brothers took both counties, and they were given back to Denmark by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238.

The Danes built Toompea Castle in Tallinn, which in 1248 was the first settlement in Estonia to receive town rights, and in 1285 Tallinn became the northernmost member of the Hanseatic League. German dominance led to the St George's Night Uprising of 1343, which began with the burning of Padise Abbey, and Denmark then sold its possessions in northern Estonia to the Livonian Order. In 1561 the nobility of North Estonia and the Tallinn Town Council declared loyalty to Sweden.

During the Great Northern War the plague of 1710 to 1713 killed more than eighty percent of the county's population, and Russian forces took Tallinn in 1710 after a month's siege. Russian rule was secured by the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. The railway between Paldiski, Tallinn and Saint Petersburg opened in 1870.

The Republic of Estonia was proclaimed in Tallinn on 24 February 1918. The Soviet Union annexed Estonia on 6 August 1940, and a German occupation followed from 1941 to 1944, during which concentration camps were set up in northern Estonia. After the Soviet reoccupation Paldiski became a nuclear submarine training centre in 1962, a closed town until 1994. Harju County was replaced by raions in 1950 and re-formed in 1990, and Tallinn rejoined it in 1993.

Harju County is one of the fifteen counties of Estonia and contains the capital and largest city, Tallinn. It has 16 municipalities, and 614,567 people live there, which is almost half of the population of Estonia.
harmonia: The name Harmonia derives from the Greek noun harmoníā, meaning means of joining, frame, covenant or agreement, which in turn comes from an adjective preserved only as the personal name Harmōn. In myth she is the goddess of harmony and concord. Her parentage varies between accounts. Most often she is the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, which makes her the sister of Aeneas, Phobos and Eros.

In other accounts she was born on Samothrace to Zeus and the Pleiad Electra, and was the sister of Dardanus and Iasion, who under the instruction of Zeus founded the mystic rites of that island. She was also closely associated with Aphrodite Pandemos, an aspect of Aphrodite that personified order and civic unity.

Almost every account marries Harmonia to Cadmus, the mythical hero and founder of Thebes. In the version set on Samothrace she was given to Cadmus, or carried off by him, after he was initiated into the island's mysteries. In the other version Zeus gave her to him when he founded Thebes and finished eight years of servitude to Ares for killing a dragon sacred to the god. All the gods attended the wedding and gave gifts, most notably a peplos and a necklace wrought by Hephaestus.

Common versions say Hephaestus made the necklace in anger at his wife Aphrodite's affair with Ares, and vowed to curse any children of that union. Other traditions credit Athena, Aphrodite or Cadmus's sister Europa with the gifts. Ancient passages describe the Necklace of Harmonia as beautifully wrought gold inlaid with jewels, typically emeralds. Hyginus blames not a necklace but a peplos dipped in crime, given by Hephaestus and Hera. Harmonia and Cadmus had Ino, Polydorus, Autonoë, Agave and Semele, and in some accounts Illyrius. Through Semele she was the grandmother of Dionysus.

The necklace brought misfortune on all who wore it, chiefly the queens and princesses of Thebes. It passed through Pentheus to Jocasta, who killed herself on learning Oedipus's identity, and then to her son Polynices, who used it to bribe Eriphyle into urging her husband Amphiaraus to join the Seven against Thebes. After Amphiaraus died, Alcmaeon killed Eriphyle and took the necklace, and he in turn was killed. His sons dedicated it at the temple of Athena at Delphi, from where the Phocian general Phayllus stole it. His mistress wore it until her youngest son, seized by madness, burned down the house with her inside.

When Cadmus was expelled from Thebes, Harmonia went with him to Illyria, where he became king of the Illyrians. He was turned into a serpent, and Harmonia begged the gods to share his fate. They took pity and changed her too, and the couple were sent to Elysium.
harold-godwinson: Harold was a son of Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and of Gytha Thorkelsdóttir, who was related to King Cnut. Around the time Edward the Confessor married Harold's sister Edith in January 1045, Harold became Earl of East Anglia. About then he began a relationship with Edith the Fair, a union in the Danish manner, more danico, which was not blessed by the Church but was accepted by most laypeople and counted as legitimate.

In 1051 the Godwins were driven into exile, but they raised an army that forced the king to restore them. Godwin died in 1053 and Harold succeeded him as Earl of Wessex, becoming the most powerful lay figure in England after the king.

In 1064 Harold was apparently shipwrecked at Ponthieu and taken to Duke William II of Normandy. Norman sources say he swore an oath on relics to support William's claim to the throne, and scholars disagree about the reliability of this story. In 1065 Harold supported Northumbrian rebels against his brother Tostig, who then allied with King Harald Hardrada of Norway.

Edward died on 5 January 1066, and the Witenagemot chose Harold the next day. He was crowned on 6 January, probably in Westminster Abbey. William began building about 700 ships and transports at Dives-sur-Mer.

Harold assembled troops on the Isle of Wight but disbanded them on 8 September when provisions ran out. Hardrada and Tostig landed the same day and defeated the earls Edwin and Morcar at Fulford on 20 September. Harold marched north from London, reached Yorkshire in four days and defeated them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, where both were killed.

William's fleet set sail on 27 September and landed at Pevensey the next day. Harold marched about 390 kilometres south to meet him and set his army in earthworks near Hastings. On 14 October, after nine hours of fighting at Senlac Hill, Harold was killed and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine with him. The sources for his death contradict each other.

A Norman poem says four knights lanced and dismembered him, twelfth-century histories say an arrow struck his head, and the Bayeux Tapestry shows a figure with an arrow in the eye, though that detail may be a later restoration. William of Poitiers says William gave the body to William Malet for burial by the sea. His sons Godwine and Edmund invaded England in 1068 and 1069 and were defeated at Northam in Devon.
harold-harefoot: Harold was the son of Cnut the Great and Ælfgifu of Northampton. His nickname, first recorded in the twelfth century in the history of Ely Abbey as Harefoh or Harefah, was read by some late medieval chroniclers as meaning fleet of foot. His paternity was questioned: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that he claimed to be Cnut's son, although it was not true, and Florence of Worcester says that Ælfgifu passed off adopted children as her own, Harold being the son of a cobbler. The historian Harriet O'Brien doubts that Cnut could have been deceived so, and suggests the tale was a popular myth or hostile propaganda tied to Emma of Normandy, Ælfgifu's rival.

Cnut died on 12 November 1035. His son Harthacnut, by Emma, had a strong claim to Denmark and England but could not leave Denmark, which was threatened by Magnus I of Norway and Anund Jacob of Sweden. The magnates of England favoured Harold as regent or joint ruler, against the opposition of Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and Queen Emma. According to the Encomium Emmae Reginae, Archbishop Æthelnoth refused to crown him. For a time the kingdom was divided: Harold held the lands north of the Thames, with the support of Leofric, Earl of Mercia, while the south under Godwin and Emma was ruled in Harthacnut's name. Godwin later changed sides, Emma was driven into exile in Flanders, and in 1037 Harold was accepted as king.

Ælfred Ætheling, Emma's son by Æthelred, came from Normandy with an armed escort. Earl Godwin seized him and delivered him to men loyal to Harold, who blinded him on board a ship bound for Ely, and he died soon afterwards. Few documents survive for the reign. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle mostly records the deaths and appointments of bishops, a skirmish with the Welsh in 1039 and a great gale that year. The historian Frank Stenton thought it probable that Ælfgifu was the real ruler of England for part or all of the reign.

Harold died at Oxford on 17 March 1040, as Harthacnut prepared an invasion, and was buried at Westminster Abbey. When Harthacnut took the throne in June 1040 the body was exhumed and thrown into a fen beside the Thames. Fishermen reportedly recovered it, and Danes of London buried it again. The cause of death is uncertain; one charter describes him lying ill and in despair at Oxford. The Prose Brut judged him unflatteringly, saying he cared nothing for knighthood, courtesy or honour. He may have had a son, Ælfwine, who became a monk on the continent.
harold-innis: Harold Adams Innis was born on 5 November 1894 on a small livestock and dairy farm near Otterville in Oxford County, Ontario. His mother, Mary Adams Innis, named him Herald, hoping he would become a minister in the strict evangelical Baptist faith that she and her husband William shared. He became an agnostic in later life. He began studying at McMaster University in 1913.

After graduating he enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force and was sent to France in the autumn of 1916. As an artillery signaller he took part in the Canadian attack on Vimy Ridge, and on 7 July 1917 a shrapnel wound in the right thigh required eight months of hospital treatment. His biographer John Watson notes that the wound took seven years to heal while the psychological damage lasted a lifetime. Innis took a master's degree at McMaster in 1918 and a doctorate at the University of Chicago in August 1920, with a dissertation on the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

In 1920 Innis joined the department of political economy at the University of Toronto, where he later became its head. He worked to build a body of Canadian scholars so that universities would not rely so heavily on professors trained abroad, and he helped to establish sources of funding for Canadian research, among them the Canadian Social Science Research Council in 1940 and the Humanities Research Council of Canada in 1944. After 1947 he warned repeatedly that Canada was becoming a subservient colony of the United States. He died on 8 November 1952.

Innis is regarded as the leading founder of the staples theory, which holds that the exploitation and export of staples such as fur, fish, wood, wheat, mined metals and fossil fuels shaped Canada's culture, politics and economy. He argued that dependence on exporting natural resources made Canada reliant on more industrialised countries and exposed it to disruption as demand for a staple fell, as the staple became scarce or as technology shifted trade to another.

In his later years he turned to communication, in Empire and Communications (1950) and The Bias of Communication (1951). He argued that a medium is biased: printed media favour control over space and secular power, while engraved media such as stone or clay tablets favour continuity in time and religious knowledge. He held that a balance of oral and written communication contributed to the flourishing of Greek civilization in the 5th century BCE. His ideas passed to his colleague Marshall McLuhan, who called his own book The Gutenberg Galaxy a footnote to Innis.
harold-macmillan: Maurice Harold Macmillan was born on 10 February 1894 in Belgravia, London, the son of the publisher Maurice Crawford Macmillan and Helen Belles, an American from Spencer, Indiana. His grandfather Daniel MacMillan, who founded Macmillan Publishers, was the son of a Scottish crofter from the Isle of Arran. He was educated at Eton and Oxford. In the First World War he served in the Grenadier Guards and was wounded three times. At the Battle of Flers-Courcelette in September 1916 he lay for over twelve hours in a shell hole, reading Aeschylus in Greek, and he suffered pain and partial immobility for the rest of his life. He married Lady Dorothy Cavendish on 21 April 1920.

Macmillan won Stockton-on-Tees in 1924, lost it in 1929 and regained it in 1931 as a supporter of economic planning. He opposed the appeasement of Nazi Germany and first held office in 1940 at the Ministry of Supply. Late in 1942 he became British Minister Resident at Algiers. Under Churchill he became Minister of Housing in 1951, charged with building 300,000 houses a year, then Minister of Defence in 1954. Under Anthony Eden he was Foreign Secretary in 1955 and Chancellor of the Exchequer from December 1955.

When Eden resigned in 1957 after the Suez Crisis, Macmillan succeeded him as prime minister. In July 1957 he told the nation it had never had it so good, but warned of inflation, and he led the Conservatives to success in 1959 with an increased majority. He worked to rebuild the Special Relationship with the United States and presided over much of the decolonisation of Africa, beginning with the Gold Coast in 1957, citing the wind of change blowing across the continent. He ended National Service, acquired Polaris and pioneered the Nuclear Test Ban with the United States and the Soviet Union. A French veto blocked the United Kingdom's entry into the European Economic Community.

The Vassall affair, in which an Admiralty clerk was convicted in October 1962 of passing secrets to the Soviet Union, and the Profumo affair damaged his government. After a controversial Cabinet reshuffle he resigned the premiership in October 1963, citing ill health, and was succeeded by Lord Home. He stood down from the Commons at the 1964 election, after 37 years of service. He was Chancellor of the University of Oxford from 1960 until his death and chaired Macmillan Publishers from 1964 to 1974, publishing a multi-volume autobiography. He received the Order of Merit in 1976 and died on 29 December 1986, aged 92.
harold-wilson: Harold Wilson was born on 11 March 1916 in Huddersfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, into a politically active family. His father, a works chemist, had been active in the Liberal Party before joining Labour. Wilson won a scholarship to Royds Hall Grammar School, studied philosophy, politics and economics at Jesus College, Oxford, and became a lecturer and research fellow there. In the Second World War he worked in the civil service, as research assistant to William Beveridge and then as Director of Economics and Statistics at the Ministry of Fuel and Power. He entered Parliament in 1945, and on 29 September 1947 became President of the Board of Trade, at 31 the youngest member of a British Cabinet in the 20th century.

When Hugh Gaitskell died in January 1963, Wilson won the Labour leadership. Labour won the 1964 general election with a majority of four seats, and he became prime minister at 48, the youngest holder of the office since Lord Rosebery 70 years earlier. In March 1966 he won a majority of 96. His government abolished capital punishment and theatre censorship, partially decriminalised male homosexuality in England and Wales, relaxed the divorce laws and outlawed racial discrimination. A persistent balance of payments deficit forced him to devalue the pound in 1967. In 1969 he sent troops to Northern Ireland to contain sectarian violence.

He lost the 1970 election to Edward Heath but stayed on as leader. The February 1974 election produced a hung parliament, and Wilson became prime minister again on 4 March 1974. His second government held the referendum of June 1975, in which a near two-to-one majority voted for Britain to remain in the European Community. Inflation peaked at 26 per cent in 1975. He announced his resignation on 16 March 1976, effective 5 April, citing exhaustion, and James Callaghan succeeded him.

After leaving office Wilson chaired a committee on financial institutions, which reported in June 1980, and he sat in the Commons until 1983, when he became Lord Wilson of Rievaulx. He died on 23 May 1995, aged 79. His reputation was low when he left office and remains disputed: some scholars praise his electoral success for a Labour prime minister, while others criticise his political style and handling of the economy.
harpagus: According to Herodotus, Harpagus belonged to the Median royal house and served Astyages, the last king of Media. Herodotus tells that Astyages dreamed that his daughter Mandane would bear a king who would overthrow him, and ordered Harpagus to expose the child at birth. Harpagus, reluctant to spill royal blood, gave the infant Cyrus to a shepherd named Mitradates, who raised him as his own son.

When Cyrus was discovered alive ten years later, Astyages punished Harpagus cruelly by killing Harpagus' only son and serving him to his father at a banquet. Herodotus reports that Harpagus showed no reaction, but gathered the remains of his son and took them away for burial. The Magi advised Astyages that the boy, who had been playing at being king with other children, had fulfilled the prophecy in play, and Astyages sent Cyrus to his parents Cambyses I and Mandane.

Harpagus kept in touch with Cyrus through gifts while he worked to turn the Median nobles against Astyages, and he sent Cyrus a message hidden in the belly of a hare. When Astyages sent him to lead the army against Cyrus, he changed sides on the battlefield, and Astyages was defeated, which led to the formation of the Persian Empire. The Chronicle of Nabonidus gives a shorter account in which the army of Astyages revolted and delivered him to Cyrus in fetters.

After 550 BCE Harpagus served Cyrus. Herodotus says it was Harpagus who suggested putting camels in front of the army against the Lydian cavalry, whose horses panicked at their smell. When the Lydians revolted and the commander Mazares died, Cyrus gave Harpagus charge of the conquest of Asia Minor. He took the Ionian cities by building earthwork mounds against their walls, and he attacked the Carians, the Caunians and the Lycians, forcing the Ionians and Aeolians to serve in his army. Miletus was spared because Thales had advised it to stay neutral. The people of Xanthos in Lycia chose to die rather than surrender, saying that they had never been conquered.

After his conquests Harpagus was appointed satrap of Asia Minor, and his descendants became the royal family of Lycia in what is now south-western Turkey. His use of siege mounds and of mountain climbers to scale walls is noted as a technique that Alexander the Great later employed at the siege of Tyre. Most of what is known of him comes from Herodotus, whose version of his change of loyalty is told in the manner of the feast of Thyestes.
harper-liberia: Harper stands on Cape Palmas, between the Atlantic Ocean and the Hoffman River, and is the capital of Maryland County. The sea there is warm all year and rich in fish, with whales, dolphins and large oysters. Fanti canoes sail from Harper to Monrovia by way of Greenville, a trip that takes from three to six days depending on wind and weather. From the Ivory Coast the town can be reached from Tabou.

Harper was the capital of the Republic of Maryland, an independent country from 1834 to 1857 and the last component of modern Liberia. The town is named after Robert Goodloe Harper, a prominent American politician and member of the American Colonization Society, who proposed the name Liberia for the society's settlement in Africa. Cape Palmas is one of the traditional hometowns of the Americo-Liberians, the descendants of free people of colour and freed slaves from the United States who settled in Liberia and declared it independent in 1847. The abolitionist John Brown Russwurm, governor of Monrovia, was buried in Harper after his death, and a statue marks his grave.

Before the Liberian civil wars the town was based on the plantation architecture of the southern United States, from which many Americo-Liberians came, and its oldest neighbourhoods have been compared to New Orleans. President William Tubman, born in Harper in 1895, built a mansion and the Morning Star Masonic Lodge there, and both now lie in ruins. Before the First Liberian Civil War Harper was an important administrative centre. In the 1970s the town was terrorised by the Maryland ritual killings, regarded as Liberia's most notorious ritual killing case because of the number of murders, the involvement of high-ranking government officials and their later public executions.

Harper is the seat of Tubman University, one of only two public universities in Liberia, and of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Cape Palmas, one of the three dioceses of the Catholic Church in Liberia. A ship sails fortnightly between Harper and Monrovia.
harran: Harran lies about 40 kilometres south-east of Urfa in south-eastern Turkey, at a crossroads between the Euphrates and the Tigris and on the border between the ancient Mesopotamian and Anatolian cultures. Its name goes back to the earliest documents that mention it, where it is written Ḫarrānu, meaning journey, caravan or crossroad. The Assyrians also called it Huzirina, the Greeks Kárrhai and the Romans Carrhae.

The earliest written records suggest that Harran was founded between about 2500 and 2000 BCE, possibly as a merchant outpost of traders from Ur. Tablets from Ebla of the 24th century BCE name a queen Zugalum as its ruler. Its place on trade routes made it a target for raids. Harran passed to Mitanni in the 16th century BCE and was conquered by the Assyrian king Adad-nirari I. It became a fortified provincial capital second only to Assur, and its temple of the moon god Sin, the Eḫulḫul, was consulted and renovated by many Mesopotamian rulers. Harran was the last capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 612 to 609 BCE.

It then came under the Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, Macedonian and Seleucid empires, and many Greeks settled there. In 53 BCE the Battle of Carrhae, one of the worst defeats in Roman history, was fought there. The moon cult lasted long into the Middle Ages, and the city was sometimes called Hellenopolis, city of the pagan Greeks. In the winter of 639-640 the pagans of Harran negotiated its surrender to the Rashidun general Iyad ibn Ghanm, who gave them a new moon temple. Harran was briefly the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 744 to 750 and again of the Numayrid Emirate from 990 to 1081. The Mongols conquered it in 1260 and largely destroyed it in 1271.

Harran is a district of Şanlıurfa Province. Its old town is largely surrounded by ancient walls about 4.5 kilometres long, which once had 187 bastions. The Harran Castle is a large brick fortress of unknown date. The town is known for its beehive houses, which resemble domed buildings shown in Assyrian reliefs of the 7th century BCE.
harriet-tubman: Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross, called Minty, to enslaved parents, Harriet Green, known as Rit, and Ben Ross. The exact year and place of her birth are unknown. She gave 1825, her death certificate lists 1815 and her gravestone 1820, but the biographer Kate Larson, working from a midwife's payment and other documents, recorded 1822, and recent biographies accept March 1822 as most likely.

As a child she was hired out as a nursemaid and whipped when the baby cried. Early in life an overseer threw a heavy metal weight at another enslaved person and struck her on the head. The injury caused dizziness, pain and spells of sleep for the rest of her life, and she ascribed the visions that followed to God. Around 1844 she married John Tubman, a free Black man.

In 1849 Tubman fell ill, which lowered her value to slave traders, and Edward Brodess tried to sell her. After his death his widow began selling the people the family enslaved, and Tubman escaped to Philadelphia. She then returned to Maryland to bring out her family, one group at a time, and guided dozens of others, travelling by night and usually in winter. Called Moses, she later said she never lost a passenger. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 she guided escapees on to Southern Ontario. In April 1858 she met John Brown and helped him plan his raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859.

In January 1862 she volunteered to help refugees at Port Royal, South Carolina. In early 1863 she led scouts there under orders of Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, and later that year she guided three steamboats with Black soldiers under Colonel James Montgomery up the Combahee River. Enslaved people warned by her network understood from the steamboat whistles that they were being liberated. She received a total of $200 for over three years of service. In her later years she spoke for women's suffrage and worked with Susan B. Anthony.

Tubman died on 10 March 1913, after being admitted to a home for elderly African Americans that she had helped establish. Her unofficial status as a scout, spy and nurse made her service hard to document, and she lived in poverty, since she kept using her money for her family and for formerly enslaved people. She is commonly viewed as an icon of courage and freedom.
harry-s-truman: Harry S. Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on 8 May 1884, the oldest child of John Anderson Truman and Martha Ellen Young Truman. His middle initial honours both his grandfathers and is not an abbreviation of one name. His father was a farmer and livestock dealer, and the family settled in Independence, Missouri, when Harry was six. He was refused an appointment to West Point because of poor eyesight and served in the Missouri National Guard from 1905 to 1911.

When the United States entered World War I on 6 April 1917, Truman rejoined his battery and fought in France as a captain in the Field Artillery. In 1919 he married Bess Wallace. He and Edward Jacobson opened a haberdashery in Kansas City, which went bankrupt in the recession of 1921.

Truman was elected a judge of Jackson County in 1922 and a senator for Missouri in 1934. From 1940 to 1944 he gained national prominence as chairman of the Truman Committee, which aimed to reduce waste and inefficiency in wartime contracts. He was nominated as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate, though reluctant, and was sworn in as vice president on 20 January 1945. He became president on Roosevelt's death in April. Only then was he told about the Manhattan Project and the atomic bomb.

As president Truman authorized the use of nuclear weapons against the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan and established the Truman Doctrine. He supported the founding of NATO and presided over the onset of the Cold War in 1947 and the Berlin Airlift in 1948. When Congress refused his proposal for comprehensive civil rights legislation, he issued orders that prohibited discrimination in federal agencies and desegregated the armed forces. He won the 1948 election against Thomas E. Dewey. The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953. Corruption in parts of his administration, which did not implicate Truman himself, became a campaign issue in 1952, and he chose not to run again.

In retirement Truman founded his presidential library and published his memoirs. He was admitted to hospital in Kansas City with pneumonia on 5 December 1972, developed multiple organ failure and died on 26 December, aged 88. When he left office in 1953 his administration was heavily criticised, but public feeling towards him grew warmer over the following decades.
harsha: Much of what is known of Harsha's youth comes from the account of the poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa. He was the second son of Prabhakaravardhana, king of Thanesar, the first monarch of the Vardhana dynasty with his capital at Sthanvesvara. After the downfall of the Gupta Empire in the middle of the 6th century, northern India had split into several independent kingdoms, and Prabhakaravardhana extended his control over neighbouring states. When he died in 605 his eldest son, Rajyavardhana, took the throne.

Harsha's sister Rajyashri had married the Maukhari king Grahavarman, who was defeated and killed by King Devagupta of Malwa, after which she was imprisoned. Rajyavardhana marched against Devagupta and defeated him, but Shashanka, king of Gauda in eastern Bengal, who had entered Magadha as his friend while in a secret alliance with Malwa, murdered him. Harsha ascended the throne at the age of 16, rescued his sister as she was about to immolate herself.

Representatives of the small republics from Punjab to central India crowned Harsha emperor at an assembly in April 606, with the title Maharajadhiraja. At the height of his power his realm covered much of northern and north-western India, with the Narmada River as its southern boundary, and he made Kanyakubja his capital. Harsha was the most powerful emperor of northern India without ruling all of it.

In the winter of 618 to 619 Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty repelled an invasion led by Harsha on the banks of the Narmada, and made a treaty fixing the river as the border. The court became a centre of cosmopolitanism, drawing scholars, artists and religious visitors. Xuanzang wrote a favourable account of Harsha, praising his justice and generosity.

Harsha was eclectic in religion. His seals call his ancestors worshippers of the sun god Surya, his brother a Buddhist and himself a Shaivite, and his land grants style him a supreme devotee of Shiva. Xuanzang portrays him as a devout Buddhist who banned animal slaughter for food and built monasteries and stupas, but historians such as S. R. Goyal and S. V. Sohoni hold that he was personally a Shaivite whose patronage of Buddhists misled the traveller. He is widely believed to be the author of three Sanskrit plays, Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarsika. Wendy Doniger is persuaded that the king wrote them himself.
harsha-of-kashmir: Harsha, also called Harshadeva, was born in 1059, the son of King Kalasha of Kashmir. Almost everything known of him comes from the Rajatarangini of Kalhana, whose father Champaka had been one of Harsha's ministers and who wrote in the time of Jayasimha, between 1127 and 1159. According to Kalhana he was built like a god and extremely handsome. He is said to have begun as a capable and noble king before his spending brought him into financial trouble.

Extravagant outlay on his troops and on pleasures left the king in grave difficulties. The historian Prithvi Nath Kaul Bamzai notes Kalhana's statement that even night soil was taxed. An accidental discovery of hoarded treasure at the Bhimasahi temple led him to despoil other temples and to melt down gold and silver images. Kalhana writes that not one temple kept its images, and that only two chief divine images were respected, Ranaswamin in the city and Martanda. Two colossal statues of the Buddha were saved by requests made one at Parihasapura by the singer Kanaka and one in the city by the monk Kusalsri.

Kalhana calls him that Turushka, and he bore the epithet raja-Turushka, Turk king. Turkish troops served him as mercenaries, and the chronicle says he continually supported Turushka captains-of-hundreds with money, while adding that he ate domesticated pigs until his death. According to the historian André Wink, Harsha in all likelihood took up the Muslim tradition of iconoclasm, as the epithet indicates. Kalhana also charges him with credulity towards parasites at court, who passed off slave girls as goddesses, and with incest with his sisters and violence against Naga, his father's sister's daughter.

Harsha died on 31 August 1101, the last ruler of the First Lohara dynasty. His conduct has remained a subject of discussion. The great Buddha of the capital outlived him: Kalhana records that when a fire reduced the city to a heap of earth in the reign of Sussala, the statue alone stood visible, blackened by smoke. The statue at Parihasapura had been made by Lalitaditya Muktapida, and Abul-Fazl states that the temples of that place were finally destroyed by Sikandar Butshikan, who ruled from 1389 to 1413.
hartford-connecticut: Hartford lies on the west bank of the Connecticut River, which forms the boundary between Hartford and East Hartford. The city covers about 47 square kilometres, of which about 1.8 square kilometres is water. It is bordered by the towns of West Hartford, Newington, Wethersfield, East Hartford, Bloomfield, South Windsor, Glastonbury and Windsor. Several Algonquian peoples lived in or around the area, including the Podunks east of the river, the Poquonocks, the Massacoes, the Tunxis, the Wangunks, and the Saukiog in Hartford itself.

The first Europeans known to have explored the area were the Dutch under Adriaen Block, who sailed up the Connecticut River in 1614. Dutch fur traders from New Amsterdam returned in 1623 to establish a trading post for the Dutch West India Company, partly to control the flow of wampum, the de facto currency of New Netherland and parts of New England. Their fort, Fort Hoop or the House of Hope, stood on the south bank of the Park River. In 1633 Jacob Van Curler formally bought the land around it from the Pequot chief. The fort was abandoned by 1654, and the area is still called Dutch Point.

Hartford alternated with New Haven as dual capital of Connecticut from 1664 and has been the sole capital since 1875. On 15 December 1814 delegates from the five New England states met at the Hartford Convention to discuss New England's possible secession from the United States. In the early nineteenth century the area was a centre of abolitionist activity, notably through the Beecher family: the minister Lyman Beecher, his daughter Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, and Isabella Beecher Hooker, a leading figure in the women's rights movement. The American School for the Deaf, founded by Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet in 1817, was the first school for deaf children in the country.

After the American Civil War Hartford was the richest city in the United States for several decades. The Connecticut River reached a record flood stage in April 1909. On 6 July 1944 a fire at a performance of the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey Circus, known as the Hartford Circus Fire, killed 168 people, mostly children and their mothers.

Hartford is the capital of Connecticut and the core of the Greater Hartford metropolitan area, which has about 1.17 million residents. The city itself had a population of 121,054 at the 2020 census. It is nicknamed the Insurance Capital of the World, and the industry remains the region's largest. The city holds the Wadsworth Atheneum, the oldest continuously operating public art museum in the country, Bushnell Park, and the Mark Twain House, where Mark Twain wrote his best-known works. The Hartford Courant, founded in 1764, is the oldest continuously published newspaper in the United States.
harthacnut: Harthacnut was born shortly after the marriage of Cnut the Great and Emma of Normandy in 1017. Cnut had set aside his first wife, Ælfgifu of Northampton, and according to the Encomium Emmae Reginae, which Emma later commissioned, agreed that sons of the new marriage would take precedence. In 1026, when Denmark was threatened from Norway and Sweden, Cnut sent his eight-year-old son there under a council headed by Earl Ulf. In 1027 Cnut arrived with a fleet, forgave his son's insubordination, but had Ulf murdered. When Magnus I of Norway invaded Norway in 1035, Harthacnut's half-brother Svein fled to his court, and they learned that their father had died.

Harthacnut succeeded in Denmark in 1035 but could not come to England because his position at home was under threat. Magnates north of the Thames backed Harold Harefoot, Cnut's son by Ælfgifu, who acted as regent, while Emma held Wessex. In late 1037 Harold was generally accepted as king and Emma went into exile at Bruges. Harthacnut and Magnus agreed that if either died without an heir his kingdom would pass to the other.

Harold died on 17 March 1040 and envoys offered Harthacnut the throne. He landed at Sandwich on 17 June with 62 warships and levied a geld of over 21,000 pounds, which made him unpopular. At Emma's urging he had Harold's body dug up and beheaded. He doubled the English fleet to thirty-two ships and raised taxes sharply during a poor harvest. In 1041 two tax collectors were killed at Worcester, and he ordered the town burned, though most people had fled.

In 1041 Harthacnut invited his half-brother Edward the Confessor back from exile in Normandy; some historians see Edward as heir, since Harthacnut had neither wife nor children and was said to suffer from frequent illness. On 8 June 1042 he attended a wedding in Lambeth where, according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, he died as he stood at his drink, falling to the ground in a convulsion.

Medieval sources are mostly hostile, but some modern historians note that he kept peace across his lands. Magnus claimed England after his death, a claim later pursued by Harald Hardrada, but Edward held the throne. Harthacnut was the last Dane to rule England.
harun-al-rashid: Harun was born in Rey, the son of the third Abbasid caliph, al-Mahdi, and his wife al-Khayzuran, a woman of strong character who greatly influenced affairs of state under her husband and sons. His birth date is debated, with sources giving dates from 763 to 766. He devoted most of his time to hadith and the Quran and trained in swordplay and archery. In 780 and again in 782 he nominally led campaigns against the Byzantine Empire under Empress Irene; the second reached the Asian suburbs of Constantinople. His raids raised his standing and earned him the title al-Rashid, the Rightly-Guided One. He was made crown prince and given the western territories from Syria to Azerbaijan.

Harun became caliph in September 786, in his early twenties, when his brother al-Hadi died. On his accession he led Friday prayers in Baghdad's Great Mosque. His mother kept a strong hand in government until her death in 789. His vizier Yahya ibn Khalid and Yahya's sons, especially Ja'far, of the Iranian family of the Barmakids, generally controlled the administration, and the position of Persians at court peaked in his reign. Their fall is more likely due to behaviour Harun found disrespectful, such as entering his court unannounced and deciding matters of state without consulting him; al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi succeeded Yahya as chief minister. In 796 he moved his court and government to Raqqa.

Envoys travelled between his court and that of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, discussing Christian access to holy sites and exchanging gifts. In 802 Harun sent silks, ivory chessmen, a large tent, an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock whose mechanical knights emerged one for each hour. Both rulers had common interests: Charlemagne's conflict with Cordoba and the Byzantine opposition to his claim to the imperial title. In 805 Harun defeated Emperor Nikephoros I at the Battle of Krasos, and in 807 his forces occupied Cyprus.

A major revolt led by Rafi ibn al-Layth in Samarqand drew Harun east to Khorasan in 808. He became ill and died in March 809 at Sanabad in Tus, and was buried in the summer palace of the governor, Humayd ibn Qahtaba. His son al-Amin succeeded him. The place later became known as Mashhad. Anecdotes gathered round him for centuries, and Saadi of Shiraz put several into his Gulistan, while parts of One Thousand and One Nights are set in his court. Al-Masudi wrote that the splendour and riches of his reign were such that the period was called the Honeymoon.
harvard-university: Harvard was founded and authorised by the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Its first headmaster, Nathaniel Eaton, took office the following year, and in 1638 the college acquired English North America's first known printing press. In the same year John Harvard, a Puritan clergyman who had emigrated from England, bequeathed it £780 and his library of some 320 volumes, and the college was named in his honour. Its earliest known official seal, of 1650, bears the motto In Christi Gloriam, To the glory of Christ. Although never formally affiliated with any Protestant denomination, Harvard trained Congregational clergy until its curriculum and student body were gradually secularised in the 18th century.

Harvard faculty and students largely supported the Patriot cause in the American Revolution. The Constitution of Massachusetts recognised the college as a university in 1780. In the 19th century Enlightenment ideas of reason and free will, widespread among Congregational ministers, set liberals against more traditional Calvinist pastors. The election of Henry Ware as Hollis professor of divinity in 1805 and the appointment of the liberal Samuel Webber as president in 1807 marked a shift to more liberal and Arminian ideas.

Under President Charles William Eliot, who served from 1869 to 1909, Harvard developed several professional schools and became a modern research university. Eliot, a chemist who had studied two years in Germany, used the German model: a graduate department formed in 1872 granted its first PhD degrees in 1873. Harvard Law School was established in 1817 through a bequest of 1779 by Isaac Royall Jr., and Harvard Business School in 1908. In 1900 Harvard became a founding member of the Association of American Universities, and James B. Conant led it through the Great Depression and the Second World War.

Harvard Yard in Cambridge, Massachusetts, holds Massachusetts Hall, built between 1718 and 1720 and the oldest building still standing. The university has three campuses, in Cambridge, in Allston and in Boston's Longwood Medical Area. Harvard Library, centred on Widener Library, holds more than 20 million volumes. The Harvard Crimson student newspaper, founded in 1873, counts among its alumni the presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy.
haryana: Haryana is a landlocked state in north-western India. It is bordered by Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to the north, Rajasthan to the west and south and Delhi to the south-east, while the Yamuna forms its eastern boundary with Uttar Pradesh. Most of it lies on the fertile Ghaggar Plain, part of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, and its highest point is Karoh Peak, 1,467 metres, in the Sivalik Hills. Some anthropologists believe the name comes from the period after the Mahabharata, when the Abhiras are thought to have settled there and developed advanced agricultural techniques.

The villages of Rakhigarhi in Hisar district and Bhirrana in Fatehabad district hold ancient sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with evidence of paved roads, drainage, terracotta brick and skilled metalworking. In the seventh century the Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled parts of northern India from Thanesar, and Harsha was its prominent king. The Tomara dynasty ruled the south of the region in the tenth century. In the British period the area was part of the province of Punjab, with princely states such as Jind, Kalsia, Loharu and Pataudi.

At the Partition of India, Punjab was divided between India and Pakistan, and Haryana became part of East Punjab. A significant number of Muslims left for Pakistan, and a huge number of Hindu and Sikh refugees arrived from West Punjab. The modern state was formed on 1 November 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act. The Shah Commission, set up in April 1966, fixed the boundaries by the languages people spoke. Haryana took the predominantly Hindi-speaking south of the former Punjab, while Punjab kept the area where Punjabi speakers formed the majority.

The capital is Chandigarh, shared with Punjab. Gurgaon is among India's large financial and technology centres, and Faridabad is the most populous city. The state surrounds Delhi on three sides, so a large part of it lies within the National Capital Region. Hindi is the official language, and Punjabi has been a second official language since 2010. The 2011 census counted 25,351,462 people.
harz: The Harz, also called the Harz Mountains, is a highland in northern Germany that extends across parts of Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. It is 110 kilometres long, from Seesen in the north-west to Eisleben in the east, and 35 kilometres wide, with an area of 2,226 square kilometres. It is divided into the Upper Harz in the north-west, up to 800 metres high apart from the Brocken massif, and the Lower Harz in the east, up to around 400 metres, whose plateaus can support arable farming. The Brocken, at 1,141.1 metres, is its highest summit. The name comes from the Middle High German Hardt or Hart, meaning hill forest.

Homo erectus hunted in and around the Harz some 700,000 to 350,000 years ago, and Neanderthals later left tools in caves such as the Einhorn Cave. In ancient times dense forests made the region almost inaccessible. The Harz was first mentioned as Hartingowe in an 814 deed of the Carolingian king Louis the Pious. Settlement names ending in -rode, meaning cleared woodland, appear from the mid-ninth century.

Mining in the Harz has its origins about 3,000 years ago, in the Bronze Age. The seven Upper Harz mining towns, among them Clausthal and Zellerfeld, and some thirty other villages owed their boom to mining and smelting, and the imperial town of Goslar mined silver-bearing lead ore from the Rammelsberg for centuries. Miners built the Upper Harz Water Regale, a system of ditches and ponds whose hydropower made silver mining possible; about 70 kilometres of ditch and 68 ponds are still used. In 1588 the Nordhausen doctor Johannes Thal published Silva hercynia, the first book on regional flora in the world, describing the flowers of the Harz.

During the Nazi era the Harz was an important site of the armaments industry, and in the last stage of the war its factories were increasingly staffed with slave labour. Several hundred forced labour and concentration camps stood there. The camp of Dora near Nordhausen, a subcamp of Buchenwald, supplied prisoners for the tunnels of the Mittelwerk, where the V-2 and V-1 weapons were produced, and more than 20,000 prisoners died there. Until 1990 the Inner German border ran through the western third of the Harz, and the Brocken and other peaks near the border lay in a military restricted area. Today the Harz National Park and the Brocken draw many visitors, and Goethe, Heinrich Heine and Hans Christian Andersen walked in these mountains.
harzgerode: Harzgerode lies in the lower eastern part of the Harz mountain range on the Selke River, south of Quedlinburg, and is linked to Gernrode and Quedlinburg by the narrow gauge Selke Valley Railway. The surrounding mountains were for centuries a significant mining area, mainly for fluorite and silver, as at the preserved Glasebach Pit near Straßberg. The Lower Harz Pond and Ditch System is a historic example of mining water management.

The settlement was first mentioned in connection with the Benedictine abbey of Hagenenrod in the Selke valley, founded in 975. King Otto III granted the abbey market, minting and customs rights in 993. Around 1000 the counts of Ballenstedt, forebears of the House of Ascania, served as its protectors. It lost its minting rights in 1035, when Emperor Conrad II had the mint moved to Nienburg. After the German Peasants' War of 1525 the abbey's local possessions fell to the Ascanian princes of Anhalt and its buildings decayed.

After a division of the Principality of Anhalt in 1252, Harzgerode became part of Anhalt-Bernburg, and its town privileges were renewed in 1338. Its sheltered position spared it many military conflicts, but fire repeatedly destroyed it: every building but seven was razed on Midsummer's Day 1635, 42 houses burned on 30 June 1722 and 52 on 23 October 1817. The Anhalt princes took the rule back from the Counts of Stolberg in 1535, and in 1635 Prince Frederick made Harzgerode Castle the residence of his principality of Anhalt-Harzgerode.

Harzgerode is a town in the district of Harz in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. In 2009 the towns of Güntersberge and Harzgerode and several neighbouring municipalities joined to form the present town, and Neudorf was added in 2010. Nearby stand the ruins of Anhalt Castle, which gave its name to the whole state of Anhalt.
hasan-i-sabbah: Very little is known of Hasan's early life. The main source is Sargozasht-i Seyyednā, possibly his autobiography, according to which he was born in Qom in Persia to a Twelver Shia family. The family soon moved to Rayy, where he studied languages, philosophy, astronomy and mathematics, especially geometry. Rayy was also a home of Ismaili missionaries, whose mission was directed from the Fatimid caliphate in Cairo.

At the age of 17 he converted to Ismailism and swore allegiance to the Fatimid caliph. The chief missionary of the region, 'Abdu l-Malik ibn Attash, made him a deputy missionary and advised him to study in Cairo. Hasan left Rayy in 1076 and reached Egypt on 30 August 1078 after a roundabout journey. He stayed about three years and supported Nizar, the caliph's elder son, as the next imam. After he displeased the army chief Badr al-Jamali, he was briefly imprisoned and deported, and he reached Isfahan in 1081.

Hasan then toured Persia on behalf of the mission. When the vizier Nizam al-Mulk sent soldiers to capture him, he withdrew into the Alborz Mountains. In 1088 he found the castle of Alamut in the Rudbar area, which guarded a valley about fifty kilometres long and five wide. His followers took it, according to the account without significant bloodshed, by first winning over the villages of the valley and then infiltrating the fort, in 1090.

Alamut became the headquarters of the Nizari mission. Hasan lived there austerely, studying, writing and directing the mission, and he declared Persian the language of Nizari holy literature, so that Nizari writing from Persia, Syria, Afghanistan and Central Asia was set down in Persian for centuries. Legend says he never left his quarters except twice to climb to the roof, but this is considered highly doubtful, given his work in organising the movement.

Hasan died on 12 June 1124. His Nizari followers called him Sayyidna, Our Master, and visited his mausoleum in Rudbar until the Mongols demolished it. Although the movement came to be associated with assassination, Hasan did not introduce it as a religious duty, since other sects had used it, and it is not clear that he advocated it himself. A Nizari assassin is called a fida'i, a devotee. Western tradition, through Marco Polo, called the leaders of the movement the Old Man of the Mountain. The Mongols captured and destroyed Alamut in the 13th century.
hasan-ibn-ali: Hasan ibn Ali was born in Medina in about 625, the firstborn of Muhammad's daughter Fatima and Muhammad's cousin Ali. Hasan was raised in Muhammad's household until the prophet's death, when he was about seven, and early sources widely report Muhammad's love for him and his brother Husayn. He is part of the ahl al-bayt, Muhammad's family, and of the ahl al-kisa, which comprises Muhammad, Ali, Fatima and their two sons.

Hasan did not play a major role under the first three caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. After Ali became caliph he were sent to Kufa, where they raised an army of some 6,000 men, and Hasan fought in the Battle of the Camel in 656 against Aisha, Talha and Zubayr.

After Ali was assassinated by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam in January 661, Hasan was acknowledged caliph in Kufa. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria, did not recognise him and marched an army of sixty thousand men to Maskin, north of present-day Baghdad, while urging Hasan in letters to give up his claim.

Hasan sent a vanguard under Ubayd Allah ibn al-Abbas, but he was severely wounded in an attempted assassination by a Kharijite, which demoralised his army and led to widespread desertion. Ubayd Allah and most of his troops also defected after Mu'awiya bribed him. In August 661 Hasan signed a peace treaty with Mu'awiya on the condition that Mu'awiya should rule in accordance with the Quran and the Sunnah, that a council should name his successor and that Hasan's supporters should receive an amnesty. He ruled as caliph from January until August 661, then withdrew to Medina and did not engage in politics.

Hasan most likely died on 2 April 670. The early sources are nearly unanimous that he was poisoned, and Mu'awiya is usually identified as the instigator. His death removed an obstacle to the succession of Mu'awiya's son Yazid I.

Critics have called the treaty with Mu'awiya a sign of weakness. His supporters hold that abdication was inevitable after his soldiers mutinied and that he sought unity and peace among Muslims, which a Sunni hadith says Muhammad had foretold. In Shia Islam Hasan is the second Imam, who succeeded Ali and was followed by his brother Husayn, and the imamate and the caliphate are viewed as separate institutions.
hasankeyf: Hasankeyf is a town on the Tigris in the Hasankeyf District of Batman Province, Turkey. It has been an ancient settlement under many names: possibly Ilanṣurā in the Mari Tablets of 1800-1750 BCE, Cephe, Cepha or Ciphas in Roman times from a Syriac word for rock, and, after the Arab conquest of 640, Hiṣn Kayfa, meaning rock fortress. The surrounding cliffs hold thousands of caves, many of them multi-storied and with their own water supply, and churches and mosques were also carved into the rock.

In the Bronze Age the area was probably part of the Hurrian kingdoms and by the 14th century BCE of Mitanni; between the 9th and 7th centuries BCE it belonged to the Neo-Assyrian Empire. In Roman times Hasankeyf was a legionary base on the frontier with the Sasanian Empire and for a time capital of the province of Arzanene. Muslim forces most likely took it in 640.

The Seljuk sultan Barkiyāruq granted it to the Artuqids in 1101 or 1102, and in 1104 Joscelin I of Edessa was held prisoner there after the Battle of Harran. Control of the Diyarbakır to Mosul road along the Tigris brought the Artuqids prosperity, and the Artuqids and their successors the Ayyubids built the Small Palace and the Great Palace and a bridge across the Tigris. The period made the town a staging post on the Silk Road. Ayyubid rule began in 1232 and was insecure from the start.

Ayyubid emirs still governed in the 15th century under the Aq Qoyunlu, whose ruler Uzun Hassan took the town in 1462 after a six-month siege. The Safavids held it briefly from 1504, and the Ottoman Empire took it in 1514 or 1517.

Until the 1980s Armenian, Aramean and Arab Christian families lived in cave houses by the river, and Arabic is still spoken in the town. Turkey declared it a natural conservation area in 1981. The Ilısu Dam project flooded the town despite local and international objections, and by 1 April 2020 the water had reached an elevation of 498.2 metres, covering it. Only some monuments were moved. The town had a population of 4,329 in 2021.
hasdrubal-barca: Hasdrubal Barca was the son of Hamilcar Barca and brother of Hannibal and Mago Barca; little is known of his early life. He was present, with Hannibal, when their father died in battle against the Iberians. When Hannibal marched for Italy in 218 BCE he left Hasdrubal in Iberia with 13,000 infantry, 2,550 cavalry and 21 war elephants, with orders to follow to Italy in 217 BCE. Instead he spent six years against the brothers Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, who had caught the Carthaginians by surprise and won the Battle of Cissa.

In 217 BCE the Roman fleet under Gnaeus Scipio crushed the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of Ebro River, and the dismissal of poor Iberian crews led to a rebellion of the Turdetani, which occupied Hasdrubal through 216 BCE. In 215 BCE he offered battle at Ibera.

He used his cavalry superiority and tried to envelop the enemy, but the Romans broke through his thinned centre and defeated each wing separately. The Scipios' victory kept him from reinforcing Hannibal; the classicist Howard Scullard thought it may have prevented the Romans being expelled from Iberia. Mago and Hasdrubal Gisco then joined him, ending the Barcid family's undisputed command.

In late 212 BCE Hasdrubal, with Mago Barca and Hasdrubal Gisco, routed the Roman armies at the Battle of the Upper Baetis and killed both Scipios, giving the Carthaginians Iberia up to the Ebro. In 209 BCE Scipio Africanus captured Carthago Nova while the Carthaginian armies were dispersed, and defeated Hasdrubal at the Battle of Baecula, though Hasdrubal retreated with two thirds of his army. Summoned to join Hannibal in 208 BCE, he crossed the Pyrenees to avoid Scipio, wintered in Gaul and crossed the Alps in spring 207 BCE, helped by roads Hannibal had left and by Gallic recruits.

Hasdrubal's messengers to Hannibal were captured, and he was checked by two Roman armies and forced to give battle at the Metaurus, where he was decisively defeated. As his army broke up he charged into the fray and died, and his head was thrown into Hannibal's camp. Edward Shepherd Creasy included the battle in The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, because it left Hannibal stranded in Italy.
hasdrubal-the-fair: Hasdrubal the Fair, in Punic ʿAzrobaʿl, was a Carthaginian military leader and politician. Livy's History of Rome records him as the son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca and the brother-in-law of Hannibal. He followed Hamilcar in his campaign against the governing aristocracy at Carthage at the close of the First Punic War, and in the career of conquest in Hispania that came after. In 237 BCE the two set out for the peninsula.

Around 231-230 BCE Hasdrubal allegedly acted in Hamilcar's name to make the Numidian tribes of northern Africa submit to the Barcid family, and Numidia soon fell within Carthage's sphere of influence. After Hamilcar died in 228 BCE, while fighting Iberian tribes, Hasdrubal succeeded him in command and followed orders from Carthage, because Hamilcar's sons were too young. Hannibal, the elder, was then 19.

Unlike his predecessor, Hasdrubal largely preferred diplomacy to military campaigns. In keeping with the customs of the time, he demanded hostages from the realms that submitted to Carthage, to deter them from breaking their treaties. He extended the territory by this diplomacy and consolidated it by founding the city and naval base of Qart Hadasht, which the Romans later called Carthago Nova, as the capital of the new province. Modern Cartagena descends from it.

He also made a treaty with the Roman Republic that fixed the River Ebro, the classical Iberus, as the boundary between the two powers. The treaty followed appeals to Rome from the Greek colony of Emporion and from Iberian Saguntum, both fearful of the growth of Punic power. Hasdrubal accepted it reluctantly, since Punic dominion in Iberia was not yet secure enough to risk a premature conflict.

Seven years after Hamilcar's death, Hasdrubal was assassinated in 221 BCE by a slave of the Celtic king Tagus, who thus avenged the death of his own master. His successor was his brother-in-law Hannibal Barca, the son of Hamilcar.
hasekura-tsunenaga: Hasekura Rokuemon Tsunenaga was born in 1571 in Okitama district, in what is now Yonezawa in Yamagata Prefecture. His father was Yamaguchi Tsuneshige, and the family claimed ancestral ties with Emperor Kanmu. A mid-level noble samurai of the Sendai Domain, he served the daimyō Date Masamune directly and received an annual stipend of 1200 koku. He was of roughly the same age as Masamune, who entrusted him with several important missions as his representative. In 1597 he served for six months as a samurai in the Japanese invasion of Korea under Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

The Franciscan friar Luis Sotelo persuaded Tokugawa Ieyasu and his son Tokugawa Hidetada to send a representative to New Spain, and a Japanese embassy was planned to accompany the explorer Sebastián Vizcaíno back there. A galleon, the San Juan Bautista, was built in 45 days, and Date Masamune, in charge of the project, named Hasekura to lead the mission. It left on 28 October 1613 with around 180 people, including samurai, merchants, sailors and some 40 Spaniards and Portuguese. It reached Acapulco on 25 January 1614 after three months at sea, and Mexico City in March. In July the embassy changed ships in Havana, and on 5 October 1614 it arrived at Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

Hasekura entered Seville on 23 October 1614 and met King Philip III in Madrid on 30 January 1615, delivering Masamune's letter and an offer of a treaty. Bad weather held the embassy at Saint-Tropez on the way to Italy. It reached Rome on 20 September 1615, and on 3 November Hasekura gave Pope Paul V two gilded letters, requesting a trade treaty between Japan and Mexico and missionaries for Japan. In April 1616 the king declined a trade agreement, since the embassy did not appear to be an official one from the ruler of Japan, who had ordered missionaries expelled in January 1614.

Hasekura left Seville in June 1616, crossed Mexico again in 1619, and sailed from Acapulco to Manila and then to Japan, reaching Nagasaki in August 1620. Japan had changed: persecution of Christians had begun in 1614, Ieyasu had died in 1616, and the country was moving towards isolation. Two days after his return to Sendai, an edict ordered Christians there to abandon their faith. What became of Hasekura is unknown; rumours said that he abandoned Christianity, was martyred, or practised in secret. His son Tsuneyori was beheaded in 1640 for failing to denounce Christians in his household.

His journey was forgotten in Japan until the Iwakura mission was shown documents in Venice in 1873. Statues of him stand in Acapulco, Havana, Coria del Río and several places in Japan. About 700 inhabitants of Coria del Río bear the surname Japón, identifying them as descendants of members of his delegation.
hashim-al-atassi: Hashim al-Atassi was born in Homs in 1875 into the large, landowning and politically active Atassi family. He studied public administration in Istanbul and graduated in 1893. Up to 1918 he served as governor of Homs, Hama, Baalbek, Anatolia and Jaffa. In 1919 he was elected chairman of the Syrian National Congress.

On 8 March 1920 the Congress declared independence as a constitutional monarchy under King Faisal I, and Atassi became prime minister.
