In Germany he supported Otto IV against Philip of Swabia, then changed sides in 1204. He fought alongside Otto IV at Bouvines in 1214 and was defeated. In 1213 he suffered a heavy defeat against the Bishopric of Liège at the Battle of Steppes, and he joined the Fifth Crusade in 1217–1218.

Under Henry there was town policy and town planning. He used the creation of new towns as an instrument in the political organisation of regions, and gave city rights and trade privileges to 's-Hertogenbosch and Eindhoven.

In 1235 Emperor Frederick II appointed Henry to bring his fiancée Isabella, daughter of King John of England, to Germany. Henry fell ill on the way back and died at Cologne on 5 September 1235. He was buried in Saint Peter's Church at Leuven. His tomb there is the oldest of its kind to survive, showing him as an idealised smiling young man in a long robe and the duke's cloak, holding a sceptre. It was damaged during the French occupation in the eighteenth century and restored in the mid-19th century. His bones were dug up in 1929 and returned to the tomb in 1998.
henry-ii-duke-of-austria: Henry, called Jasomirgott, was the second son of Margrave Leopold III of Austria and Agnes of Waiblingen, a sister of the last Salian emperor Henry V. His younger brothers included Bishop Otto of Freising and Archbishop Conrad II of Salzburg. The nickname is first documented in the 13th century as Jochsamergott and its meaning is unclear; popular etymology derives it from an oath, joch sam mir got helfe, "yes, so help me God". When Leopold III died in 1136 he was succeeded by his third-born son Leopold IV, probably because Henry already administered the Rhenish possessions of the extinct Salian dynasty. In April 1140 King Conrad III enfeoffed Henry with the County Palatine of the Rhine.

Henry became Duke of Bavaria and margrave of Austria in 1141, when Leopold IV died unexpectedly in October, and took his residence at Regensburg. In May 1142 he married Gertrude, daughter of Emperor Lothair and widow of Henry the Proud; she died within a year, giving birth to their only child. He remained loyal to the Hohenstaufens and in May 1147 accompanied Conrad III on the Second Crusade. After the defeat at the Battle of Dorylaeum against the Seljuk Turks he narrowly escaped with the young Frederick Barbarossa, and he attended the Council of Acre and the Siege of Damascus. In late 1148, at the court of the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos, he married the emperor's niece Theodora.

After Frederick Barbarossa was elected king in 1152 he sought a compromise with the Welfs and in 1156 endowed Henry the Lion with Bavaria. As a replacement, the Privilegium Minus raised Henry's margraviate of Austria to a duchy with complete independence from Bavaria. In 1145 Henry had moved his Austrian residence from Klosterneuburg, where his father had mostly lived, to Vienna, which could thereby surpass Krems, Melk and Klosterneuburg, and it has remained the capital. The first St. Stephen's Church was completed in 1147, and in 1155 he founded the Schottenstift monastery in Vienna.

In November 1176, while forces of Duke Soběslav II of Bohemia campaigned in his Austrian lands, Henry fell with his horse from a rotten bridge near Melk and suffered a femoral neck fracture. He died of his injuries in Vienna on 13 January 1177 and, as he had willed, was buried in the Schottenstift. His son Leopold V became Duke of Austria, his daughter Agnes married King Stephen III of Hungary and later Duke Herman of Carinthia, and his son Henry I became Duke of Mödling.
henry-ii-duke-of-bavaria: Henry, called the Wrangler or the Quarrelsome, was the son of Duke Henry I of Bavaria, a younger brother of Emperor Otto the Great. He succeeded his father at the age of four under his mother's guardianship. His sister Hadwig married Duke Burchard III of Swabia in 954, and in 972 Henry married Gisela of Burgundy, a niece of Empress Adelaide. After Otto's death in 973 he could rely on ties to Swabia and Bavaria and to the neighbouring Kingdom of Burgundy. He installed his cousin Henry as Bishop of Augsburg, denying the investiture rights of Otto II, who, not wanting civil war, invested the nominee on 22 September 973.

When Burchard III died without heirs, Henry claimed Swabia, but Otto II gave it to his own nephew Otto of Swabia against Hadwig's opposition. In 974 Henry resolved to oust Otto II, allying with Bavarian and Saxon nobles, Duke Boleslaus II of Bohemia and Duke Mieszko I of Poland; Otto took him captive at Ingelheim. Henry escaped in 976 and raised a revolt in Bavaria, but Otto II occupied Regensburg and stripped him of the duchy, making the Duchy of Carinthia and the Margraviate of Austria from Bavarian lands. After the War of the Three Henries the deposed duke was placed in the custody of Bishop Folcmar of Utrecht.

When Otto II died of malaria in Rome in 983, Henry was released. He abducted the infant Otto III and, according to the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg, had himself proclaimed King of the Romans at the graves of Otto I and Henry the Fowler in Magdeburg and Quedlinburg. He had lost the support of the German dukes, however, and could not oust Duke Henry the Younger from Bavaria. Through the agency of Archbishop Willigis of Mainz, Henry submitted in 985 to Empress Theophanu and Adelaide at an assembly in Rohr. He regained Bavaria and in 989 also received Carinthia.

Henry died on 28 August 995. His children with Gisela included Henry IV of Bavaria, who succeeded him in 995 and fulfilled his father's ambitions when he was elected King of the Romans as Henry II in 1002 and crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 1014; Bruno, Bishop of Augsburg from 1006; and Gisela, who married King Stephen I of Hungary.
henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born in May 973, son of Duke Henry II of Bavaria and Gisela of Burgundy, and was a great-grandson of King Henry I of Germany. Because his father rebelled against two emperors, he spent long periods in exile, where he turned to Christianity at an early age, first finding refuge with Bishop Abraham of Freising and later studying at the cathedral school in Hildesheim. He succeeded his father as Duke of Bavaria in 995.

When Emperor Otto III died childless in January 1002, Henry's right to succeed him was contested by rivals including Count Ezzo of Lotharingia, Margrave Eckard I of Meissen and Duke Herman II of Swabia. Henry was crowned king on 9 July 1002 and spent the following years consolidating his power. In Italy, Margrave Arduin of Ivrea proclaimed himself king, but Henry was anointed King of Italy on 15 May 1004, and he was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict VIII on 14 February 1014, after Benedict had fled to Germany and appealed to him for protection.

Where Otto III had pursued a renewal of the Roman Empire, Henry's seal spoke of a renewal of the Frankish kingdom, and he spent most of his reign on the territories north of the Alps. He made only three journeys south of the Alps. His long conflict with Duke Bolesław I of Poland, who had once been a loyal ally of Otto III, filled over sixteen years, with peace treaties made and broken in 1012 and 1013. Henry also relied on bishops and abbots, whom he made princes of the empire, as a counterweight to the secular nobles, and in 1004 he ordered the diocese of Merseburg re-established, appointing the chronicler Thietmar as its bishop.

In 1007 Henry announced a new diocese at Bamberg, a place he was fond of, where he had given estates to his wife Cunigunde of Luxembourg. He died on 13 July 1024 at Göttingen and was buried at Bamberg Cathedral. As the marriage was childless, the Ottonian line ended with him, and the nobles elected Conrad II, the first of the Salian emperors. Henry was canonised by Pope Eugene III in the twelfth century and Cunigunde in 1200. He is the only medieval German monarch honoured as a saint, and the patron saint of the city of Basel.
henry-ii-of-castile: Henry was the fourth of ten illegitimate children of King Alfonso XI of Castile and Eleanor de Guzmán, and the first of their sons to survive to adulthood. He was born a twin to Fadrique Alfonso, Lord of Haro. His father made him Count of Trastámara and lord of Lemos and Sarria in Galicia, a large inheritance that made him head of the new Trastámara line. When Alfonso XI died of a fever during the siege of Gibraltar in March 1350, the queen, Maria of Portugal, and her son Peter pushed Eleanor and her sons aside. In 1351 Peter had Eleanor executed at Talavera de la Reina, and Henry and his brothers rebelled repeatedly.

After a long, intermittent war Henry fled to France and served King John II of France, then fought in the army of Peter IV of Aragon against Castile. In the Castilian Civil War he led Castilian allies, Aragonese and mercenaries under Bertrand du Guesclin, expelled Peter and was proclaimed king at Burgos in 1366. Peter returned with an Anglo-Gascon army led by Edward, the Black Prince, and John of Gaunt, and defeated Henry at Nájera in 1367. Henry escaped to France, regrouped and defeated Peter at Montiel on 14 March 1369, killing his captive half-brother with his own hand.

As king he fought two of the three Fernandine Wars against Ferdinand I of Portugal and resisted John of Gaunt's claim to the throne through Constance of Castile. He favoured France over England, and Castilian ships under Ambrosio Boccanegra defeated an English fleet at La Rochelle. At home he began rebuilding the royal administration and held numerous courts. His generous rewards to his allies earned him the name el de las mercedes.

Henry was hostile to the Jews, in contrast to Peter's friendliness. He imposed a war contribution of twenty thousand gold doubloons on the community of Toledo, ordered that Jews wear a badge, and shortly before his death barred them from public office, although financial need led him to employ Jewish tax collectors. He died on 29 May 1379 at Santo Domingo de la Calzada and was succeeded by his son John I. He was buried in the Capilla de los Reyes Nuevos in Toledo.
henry-ii-of-england: Henry was born at Le Mans on 5 March 1133, the eldest child of the Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry I of England, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou. By the age of 14 he was involved in his mother's effort to claim the English throne, then held by her cousin Stephen of Blois. In 1150 his father made him Duke of Normandy, and in 1151 Henry inherited Anjou, Maine and Touraine. His marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine brought him that duchy. After a military expedition to England in 1153, Stephen agreed by the Treaty of Wallingford to leave the kingdom to Henry, who inherited it a year later.

Henry was crowned with Eleanor at Westminster Abbey on 19 December 1154. He inherited a country damaged by civil war, with unauthorised castles and a depleted royal income, and in the early years he restored royal administration. His invasion of Wales in 1157 met defeat at the Battle of Ewloe, where he was nearly killed. His desire to control the English Church brought conflict with Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, a controversy that lasted much of the 1160s and ended in Becket's murder in 1170. He also fought Louis VII of France for decades, in a struggle the historian Jean Dunbabin likened to a cold war.

His domains, later called the Angevin Empire, were a loose network of family connections and lands, each with its own customs. Henry travelled constantly, producing what the historian John Edward Austin Jolliffe describes as a government of the roads and roadsides. His court was probably the largest in Europe. He expanded royal justice in England, and the Treatise of Glanvill summarised the system at the end of his reign.

Henry and Eleanor had eight children, three of them kings: Henry the Young King, Richard I and John. Tensions over the inheritance, encouraged by Louis VII and his son Philip II, led in 1173 to a rebellion by Young Henry, joined by Richard, Geoffrey and Eleanor. Young Henry died during a second failed revolt in 1183, and Geoffrey died in 1186. By 1189 Philip had won Richard to his side, and Henry, weakened by a bleeding ulcer, was decisively defeated. He died soon afterwards, on 6 July 1189, and was succeeded by Richard. His empire collapsed quickly under John, but his legal reforms are generally considered to have laid the basis for the English Common Law.
henry-ii-of-france: Henry was born on 31 March 1519 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the second son of Francis I and Claude, Duchess of Brittany. After Francis I was captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525, Henry and his elder brother were sent to Spain as hostages and stayed there for over four years. On 28 October 1533 he married Catherine de' Medici, both being fourteen.

He formed a close attachment to Diane de Poitiers, more than twenty years older than he, whose colours he wore at a tournament in 1531. He became heir in August 1536 when his brother died after falling ill following a game of tennis; an autopsy report gave no sign of poison. Catherine bore their first son in 1544, and Henry's loyalty to Diane caused a breach with his father until 1545.

Francis I died on 31 March 1547, and Henry was crowned at Reims on 25 July 1547. He intensified the repression of Protestants. An edict of 5 April 1547 reaffirmed punishments for blasphemy, and in October a new chamber of the Parlement of Paris, called the chambre ardente, was set up to hear heresy cases. The Edict of Châteaubriant followed in 1551.

In foreign policy he declared war on Charles V in the Italian War of 1551–1559, allied himself with German Protestant princes at the Treaty of Chambord in 1552 and continued his father's Franco-Ottoman alliance. He occupied the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Verdun and Metz, and secured them at Renty in 1554. After Philip II's victory at St Quentin, French forces took Calais.

Henry raised Mary, Queen of Scots at his court, and she married the Dauphin Francis on 24 April 1558. Under the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis of April 1559, France gave up its claims in Italy and restored Piedmont and Savoy but kept Saluzzo, Calais and the Three Bishoprics. During his reign Henry also introduced the idea of publishing a description of an invention in exchange for monopoly rights, the beginning of the patent specification.

On 30 June 1559, at a tournament held to celebrate the peace, Henry was wounded in the eye by a splinter of the lance of Gabriel Montgomery, captain of his Scottish Guard. Surgeons including Ambroise Paré and Andreas Vesalius could not save him, and he died ten days later. Modern analysis points to an infection from a retained wooden fragment.

His death played a part in the decline of jousting in France. He left four young sons and a widow, Catherine de' Medici. Three of the sons became king, but their youth and Catherine's regency led to challenges from powerful nobles and helped to spark the French Wars of Religion, and in time the Valois dynasty ended.
henry-ii-the-pious: Henry was the second son of High Duke Henry the Bearded and Hedwig of Silesia. His elder brother Bolesław died in 1206, and in 1213 his younger brother Konrad the Curly died during a hunt, leaving Henry as sole heir of Lower Silesia. His father arranged his marriage to Anne, daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia. From 1222 he countersigned his father's documents, and when Henry the Bearded was captured in 1229 he acted as interim duke. When his father died on 19 March 1238 he became duke of Silesia, Kraków and Greater Poland.

Henry II was regent of the duchies of Opole and Racibórz and of Sandomierz while their rulers were minors, but he resigned the regency in 1239. The death of Władysław Odonic on 5 June 1239 let him take most of his lands, including Gniezno. He abandoned his family's alliance with the Hohenstaufen emperors and supported Pope Gregory IX, which settled his dispute with the Church. He ended the conflict with Konrad of Masovia by marrying two of his daughters to two of Konrad's sons, and in 1239 he won the Battle of Lubusz and recovered the fortress of Santok.

In February 1241 a Mongol army of about 10,000 men under Orda invaded Poland and destroyed much of the Kraków and Sandomierz nobility at Tursko and Chmielnik. Henry gathered troops at Legnica. Many European rulers, busy with the quarrel between the Holy Roman Empire and the papacy, did not answer his appeals; only a contingent sent by King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia and some Knights Templar joined him.

Henry was defeated and killed at the Battle of Legnica on 9 April 1241. His wife identified his decapitated body by the six toes on his left foot, a detail confirmed when his tomb was opened in 1832. The Mongols did not try to occupy Silesia and moved on to Hungary. His death split the Silesian Piast line into many ducal branches, and later traditions portrayed him as an ideal Christian knight and martyr. In October 2015 the Roman Catholic Diocese of Legnica opened his cause for beatification, giving him the title Servant of God.
henry-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was the eldest son of Conrad II and Gisela of Swabia. Conrad, a Franconian aristocrat with lands along the Rhine, was illiterate, but Gisela, who was descended from Charlemagne, saw to her son's education and Henry learnt to read. His father made him Duke of Bavaria in 1026 and had him elected co-ruler in 1028, when Pilgrim, Archbishop of Cologne, crowned him king at Aachen on Easter. In 1038 he received the duchy of Swabia and the Kingdom of Burgundy. His succession on his father's death was unusually smooth, and he also took the duchy of Carinthia and the Kingdom of Italy.

Henry began with a tour of his domains and made Goslar a future imperial residence. His first campaign, into Bohemia in 1040, ended in an ambush at the Battle of Brůdek and a heavy retreat, but a second campaign a year later brought a peace with Duke Bretislav I of Bohemia at Regensburg. In 1044 he entered Hungary and restored Peter Orseolo to the throne after Samuel Aba had overthrown him. In 1043 he married Agnes of Poitou, despite clerical objections to their kinship. He treated the duchies as royal offices to be filled at his discretion, which led to long conflict in Lorraine with Godfrey, the son of Duke Gothelo I.

In 1046 he went to Italy to deal with three men who claimed the papacy: Benedict IX, Sylvester III and Gregory VI. At Sutri, on 20 December 1046, he deposed all three. He had Suidger of Bamberg acclaimed as Pope Clement II, and on Christmas Day 1046 Clement crowned Henry and Agnes emperor and empress. The Roman citizenry gave Henry the Golden Chain of the Patriciate and the rank of patricius.

Henry's last years brought setbacks. In 1051 he suffered a major defeat at the Battle of Vértes in a third Hungarian campaign, and in 1052 he failed to take Pressburg, after which he never tried again. A Swabian army sent to help Pope Leo in southern Italy was cut to pieces by the Normans at the Battle of Civitate on 18 June 1053. Revolt in Bavaria followed the deposition of Duke Cuno.

His son Henry, born in 1050, was elected king of Germany at Tribur on 26 June 1053 and crowned at Aachen on 17 July 1054. In 1055 the heir was engaged to Bertha of Turin. Henry III died on 5 October 1056, aged only 39. Modern historians see the last years of his reign as the beginning of a crisis in the Salian monarchy, and the dispute over investiture overshadowed the reigns of his son and grandson.
henry-iii-of-england: Henry was born at Winchester Castle on 1 October 1207, the eldest son of King John and Isabella of Angoulême. When John died, Henry was at Corfe Castle in Dorset. John's deathbed wishes placed him under the guardianship of William Marshal, who knighted him, and Cardinal Guala Bicchieri, the papal legate, oversaw his coronation at Gloucester Cathedral on 28 October 1216, in the middle of the First Barons' War.

Guala declared the war against the rebels a crusade, and Henry's forces under William Marshal defeated them at Lincoln and Sandwich in 1217. The government reissued a version of Magna Carta, and Henry promised to abide by the Great Charter of 1225.

Hubert de Burgh, made Earl of Kent, dominated the government after William Marshal's death in 1219 until his fall in 1232. A failed invasion of France in 1230 and a revolt led by Richard Marshal in 1232 marked the early years. Henry then ruled in person. He left the post of justiciar vacant, made the chancellor a junior figure and took decisions with a small circle of advisers, which made it harder for outsiders to press grievances.

In 1236 he married Eleanor of Provence, then twelve years old. He was known for piety, attended mass at least once a day and took Edward the Confessor as his patron saint. His expeditions to Poitou in 1242 ended in the Battle of Taillebourg, and he spent large sums in a failed attempt to put his son Edmund Crouchback on the throne of Sicily.

By 1258 his foreign policy, his Poitevin half-brothers and his officials' tax collecting had made him unpopular, and a coalition of barons seized power and imposed the Provisions of Oxford. In 1259, under the Treaty of Paris, Henry gave up his claims in France except Gascony, which Louis IX recognised as his. In 1263 Simon de Montfort seized power, beginning the Second Barons' War. Henry was defeated and captured at Lewes in 1264, and his son Edward beat Simon at Evesham the following year. The Dictum of Kenilworth softened the revenge on the rebels.

Henry also took a heavy toll from the Jews of England, whose position as a source of royal loans he used until it crippled their ability to do business, and he later introduced the Statute of Jewry to separate them from the rest of the population. He died on 16 November 1272, leaving Edward as his successor.

He was buried in Westminster Abbey, which he had rebuilt in the second half of his reign, and his body was moved to its present tomb in 1290. His reign of 56 years was the longest in medieval England and was not exceeded by an English or British monarch until George III.
henry-iv-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was born on 11 November 1050, most likely at his father's palace at Goslar, the son of Emperor Henry III and Agnes of Poitou. He belonged to the Salian dynasty, which governed Germany from 1024 to 1125. His father named him successor at Christmas 1050, and at the age of six he became sole ruler while his mother acted as regent. In April 1062 Archbishop Anno II of Cologne and other nobles removed her in the Coup of Kaiserswerth, luring Henry onto a ship on the Rhine; he leapt into the river and was rescued by Egbert I of Brunswick. Henry was girded with a sword at Worms on 29 March 1065.

Around 1069 Henry set out to recover royal estates lost during his minority, most of them in Saxony. He used Swabian ministeriales as officials and built royal castles garrisoned by Swabian troops, which angered the Saxons, and he put down revolts there in 1069 and 1071. His insistence on appointing bishops and abbots brought conflict with Pope Alexander II, who excommunicated some of his advisers in 1073.

After crushing a new Saxon rebellion in 1075 he turned to Italy and appointed Tedald archbishop of Milan against the wishes of Pope Gregory VII, who threatened excommunication. At Worms on 24 January 1076 two archbishops and twenty-six bishops declared Gregory's election invalid. Gregory excommunicated Henry, and in 1077 Henry sought absolution in his penitential walk to Canossa. German opponents then elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden king on 14 March 1077. Excommunicated again in 1080, Henry was supported by an antipope, Clement III, who crowned him emperor in Rome in 1084.

From 1089 to 1096 he campaigned in Italy against Matilda of Tuscany and Welf I of Bavaria; his son Conrad turned against him in 1093. In 1103 he proclaimed the first imperial peace covering all Germany. His diplomas protected the Jews of Speyer and Worms from violence and forced baptism.

In December 1104 his younger son Henry deserted him, and in 1105 forced his abdication. Henry fled to Cologne in February 1106, where the townspeople received him, and he sought allies to regain the throne. He fell ill and died in 1106 without absolution. His conflicts with the popes, his sons and his subjects produced a rich polemical literature in his lifetime. The Song of the Saxon War praised him as pious, while Lampert of Hersfeld said he had inherited a peaceful realm and rendered it bloodstained and a prey to internal conflicts.
henry-iv-of-castile: Henry was born on 5 January 1425 in Valladolid, the son of John II of Castile and Maria of Aragon. He displaced his older sister Eleanor as heir apparent and became Prince of Asturias. In his youth Castile was controlled by Álvaro de Luna, who chose his companions and directed his education. One of them, Juan Pacheco, became his closest confidant. In 1440, at fifteen, he married Blanche II of Navarre. In 1445 he won the First Battle of Olmedo against the Infantes of Aragon, after which Luna's power waned.

John II died on 20 July 1454, and Henry was proclaimed king the next day. In 1455 he married Joan of Portugal, sister of Afonso V, to secure an alliance with Portugal. He convened the Cuéllar Courts to launch an offensive against the Emirate of Granada, but the campaigns of 1455 and 1458 became a war of attrition and were unpopular. Pacheco, by then Marquis of Villena, and his brother Pedro Girón handled much of the government, and Henry took other advisers, among them Beltrán de la Cueva, to balance them.

Nobles formed a League of Nobles in March 1460. On 11 August 1462 Catalonia elected Henry Count of Barcelona, but his intervention failed and he agreed to the Judgment of Bayonne, abandoning the Catalans. Queen Joan gave birth to a daughter, Joanna, in 1462, and rebels doubted her paternity and called her la Beltraneja. Under pressure from the league, Henry at Burgos in 1464 disowned Joanna and named his half-brother Alfonso heir. He later went back on this, and at the Farce of Ávila the nobles deposed him in effigy and crowned Alfonso as a rival king.

Alfonso died in 1468, and his sister Isabella took his place as the rebels' champion. At Toros de Guisando Henry agreed to exclude Joanna from the succession and recognise Isabella as heir. He died on 11 December 1474 and was buried at Santa María de Guadalupe. A war between Joanna, supported by Portugal, and Isabella, supported by Aragon, followed, and Isabella won.

Henry was nicknamed the Impotent, and contemporaries thought him impotent or homosexual. Historians note that the royal chronicles were written or revised under Isabella, who had a strong interest in proving Joanna illegitimate, so Joanna's paternity cannot be settled. During his reign the nobles grew more powerful and the nation less centralised.
henry-iv-of-england: Henry was born at Bolingbroke Castle in Lincolnshire in about April 1367, the son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and Blanche of Lancaster, and a grandson of King Edward III. He took the name Bolingbroke from his birthplace. As a youth he rode, hunted and jousted, and was besieged with Richard II in the Tower of London during the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

He joined the Lords Appellant's rebellion against his cousin in 1387, though Richard later made him Duke of Hereford. He went on crusading expeditions with the Teutonic Order to Lithuania in 1390 and 1392, and in 1392–93 made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

In 1398 a remark attributed to Thomas de Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, led to a planned duel, which Richard halted by exiling Henry, and Mowbray for life. When Gaunt died in February 1399, Richard cancelled the documents allowing Henry to inherit automatically. Henry returned from exile with Thomas Arundel, the former archbishop of Canterbury, while Richard was campaigning in Ireland, and gathered enough support to have himself declared king, imprison Richard and bypass Richard's heir-presumptive, Edmund de Mortimer, Earl of March. Richard died in prison in February 1400, probably of starvation, whether self-imposed or forced being a matter of historical speculation.

He put down the Epiphany Rising in January 1400, and invaded Scotland in August 1400, a campaign that accomplished little. Owain Glyndŵr declared himself Prince of Wales in 1400. The Percy rebellions followed, and in 1403 the royal army defeated them at the Battle of Shrewsbury, where Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, was killed and the king's eldest son, Henry of Monmouth, was wounded by an arrow in the face. In 1401 the statute De heretico comburendo prescribed burning for heretics, to suppress the Lollards.

From 1405 Henry suffered a disfiguring skin disease and acute attacks of a grave illness, whose nature medical historians still debate. His son Henry of Monmouth took over much of the government in 1410. Henry died on 20 March 1413 in the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster Abbey, during a meeting of Parliament.

He was buried not at Westminster but at Canterbury Cathedral beside the shrine of Thomas Becket, with his second wife, Joan of Navarre. Historians connect the choice with his wish to legitimise his dynasty. His son succeeded as Henry V, and the usurpation later contributed to the dynastic disputes of the Wars of the Roses.
henry-iv-of-france: Henry was born at the Château de Pau, the capital of Navarre and Béarn, the son of Jeanne III of Navarre and Antoine de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme. He was baptised a Catholic but raised as a Huguenot by his mother. Under the Huguenot leader Gaspard II de Coligny he witnessed the battles of Jarnac, La Roche-l'Abeille and Moncontour, and he saw combat for the first time in 1570 at Arnay-le-Duc.

On 9 June 1572 his mother died and Henry became King of Navarre. He married Margaret of Valois in Paris on 18 August 1572, and within days the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre killed several thousand Protestants who had come for the wedding. Henry survived by promising to convert, lived at court until early 1576, then escaped and returned to the Protestant side. When Henry III of France died in 1589 he nominally became king, but the Catholic League, backed by Spain, refused to accept him and Pope Sixtus V excommunicated him. He won at Arques and Ivry but failed to take Paris in 1590.

On 25 July 1593 he converted to Catholicism, which secured the allegiance of most of his subjects and earned the resentment of the Huguenots and of Elizabeth I of England. He was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594, since the League still held Reims, and Pope Clement VIII lifted the excommunication on 17 September 1595. After his victory at Amiens in September 1597 the Peace of Vervins ended the war with Spain in 1598, the year of the Edict of Nantes. Working through his minister Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, he regularised finance, promoted agriculture and built roads, bridges and canals.

Henry was the target of at least twelve assassination attempts. On 14 May 1610 François Ravaillac, a Catholic zealot, stabbed him in Paris while his coach was halted on the Rue de la Ferronnerie. Ravaillac was seized and executed days later. Henry was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis, and his widow Marie de' Medici acted as regent for their nine-year-old son Louis XIII until 1617. His statue was set up on the Pont Neuf in 1614, torn down in the Revolution and rebuilt in 1818.
henry-iv-probus: Henry Probus was the only son of Duke Henry III the White of Silesia-Wrocław and Judith of Masovia. His father died in 1266, leaving him a minor, and his uncle Archbishop Władysław of Salzburg became his guardian. In 1267 Władysław sent him to Prague to be raised at the court of King Ottokar II of Bohemia. After Władysław died in 1270 Henry returned to Wrocław and received a careful education, which may explain his later interest in culture and poetry. He was formally proclaimed an adult in 1273 and began a policy more independent of Bohemia.

In 1277 Duke Bolesław II the Bald of Legnica seized him at Jelcz and imprisoned him. He was freed at the end of the year after giving up a third of his duchy and pledging Krosno Odrzańskie for his ransom. Between 1282 and 1287 he fought Bishop Thomas II Zaremba of Wrocław over land and jurisdiction; he was excommunicated in March 1284, but the bishop submitted in 1287. In 1280 he went to King Rudolph I in Vienna, where he tried to obtain the Polish royal crown. He granted towns privileges under Magdeburg Law and encouraged the settlement of artisans and merchants, and two poems are recorded under his name in the Codex Manesse.

After Leszek II the Black died on 30 September 1288, Henry contested Kraków against Władysław I the Elbow-high. His allies were defeated at the Battle of Siewierz on 26 February 1289. In August 1289, helped by the townspeople and the Franciscans, he took Kraków and was recognised as High Duke. He died suddenly in 1290, aged no more than thirty-two.

Ottokar of Styria told that he was poisoned after a quarrel with the pope over money sent to Rome, though only some elements are confirmed by other sources. His will left Wrocław to Henry III of Głogów and Kraków to Przemysł II. In the event Henry V the Fat took Wrocław, and Wenceslaus II of Bohemia gained the Kraków lands, while Przemysł II kept the title of High Duke.
henry-king-of-portugal: Henry was born in Lisbon, the fifth son of King Manuel I of Portugal and Maria of Aragon. As a younger brother of King John III of Portugal he was not expected to succeed to the throne. Early in life he took Holy Orders to promote Portuguese interests within the Catholic Church, then dominated by Spain. In 1523, at the age of eleven, he received his first ecclesiastical benefice.

Henry rose rapidly through the Church, becoming in quick succession Archbishop of Braga, Archbishop of Évora and Grand Inquisitor. He was made a cardinal on 16 December 1545, with the titular church of Santi Quattro Coronati, and from 1564 to 1570 he was Archbishop of Lisbon. He worked, more than anyone, to bring the Jesuits to Portugal to encourage their activity in the colonial empire. In 1562 he replaced Queen dowager Catherine, his sister-in-law, as regent for his great-nephew King Sebastian.

King Sebastian died without an heir at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, and the elderly cardinal was proclaimed king soon afterwards. As a clergyman he was bound to celibacy and had no children. He sought release from his vows so that he could marry and continue the House of Aviz, but Pope Gregory XIII, unwilling to antagonize Philip II of Spain, did not grant it. He is the only cardinal known to have served as a monarch.

Henry died in the Royal Palace of Almeirim on his 68th birthday without naming a successor, leaving only a regency to govern. In June 1580 Philip II, one of the closest claimants, sent the Duke of Alba to take Portugal by force. Lisbon soon fell, and the Cortes of Tomar elected Philip king in 1581 on condition that the kingdom and its overseas territories keep their autonomy. The Iberian Union lasted sixty years, until John IV restored an independent throne.
henry-morgan: Morgan was born about 1635 in Monmouthshire, in Llanrumney or Pencarn, in an area now part of Cardiff or near it. Attempts to identify his parents have proved unsatisfactory, though several sources name his father as Robert Morgan, a farmer. It is not known how he reached the Caribbean. He was probably a member of the raiders led by Sir Christopher Myngs in the early 1660s, and in 1666 he married his cousin Mary Morgan at Port Royal.

Sir Thomas Modyford, governor of Jamaica, depended on the revenue that about 1,500 privateers brought to the island. In 1667, as relations between England and Spain worsened, he gave Morgan a letter of marque and the rank of admiral. His commission allowed attacks on Spanish ships at sea, not on land. He took Puerto del Príncipe, and in July 1668 captured the three castles and town of Porto Bello, losing 18 men. Exquemelin wrote that he used monks and nuns as a shield for scaling ladders, an account Morgan later won a libel suit against in England.

In January 1669 the flagship Oxford blew up during a council of war, killing over 200 crew, and the flotilla was too small for Cartagena. Morgan attacked Maracaibo and Gibraltar on Lake Maracaibo instead. In December 1670 he took Old Providence and Chagres, and in January 1671 he led his men up the Chagres River towards Panama City, much of the way on foot through rainforest. The destruction of Panama came after England and Spain had signed the Treaty of Madrid, and Morgan was sent to London in April 1672. He was received there as a hero, and was knighted in November 1674.

Back in Jamaica, Morgan served as lieutenant governor and on the Assembly until 1683 and acted as governor on three occasions. In 1678 and 1680 he declared martial law against a French threat and strengthened Port Royal. He owned three large plantations and led three campaigns against the Maroons of Juan de Serras, without capturing him. At his death he held 131 Africans as slaves. He died on 25 August 1688 and was given a state funeral, with a 22-gun salute. The earthquake of 1692 sent his grave into the sea.

His reputation was shaped by Exquemelin's memoir, written, Cordingly argues, with a grudge over the Panama plunder. Spanish reports of Porto Bello and Gibraltar do not mention torture, though torture at Panama is reliably reported. The Spanish regarded Morgan as a pirate, which he rejected, since he always held a commission from the governor of Jamaica.
henry-morton-stanley: Henry Morton Stanley was born John Rowlands in Denbigh, Wales, to the unmarried Elizabeth Parry, who was 18. She abandoned him as a baby, and his father died within weeks of his birth. The stigma of illegitimacy weighed on him all his life. He spent ten years of his childhood in the workhouse at St Asaph, and emigrated to the United States in 1859 at the age of 18. By his own account he took the name of a trader he met at New Orleans, Henry Hope Stanley, though discrepancies in the story have led some biographers to doubt it.

Stanley went to Zanzibar in March 1871 on an expedition funded by James Gordon Bennett Jr., publisher of the New York Herald, and found David Livingstone. In 1874 the New York Herald and the Daily Telegraph financed a second expedition to map the Central African Great Lakes and rivers and to locate the source of the Nile.

In 1878 King Leopold II of the Belgians received him, since the Foreign Office and the Prince of Wales would not, and signed a five-year contract with him. Stanley reached Stanley Pool on 3 December 1882 after almost two years of moving 50 tonnes of equipment past rapids, and began Léopoldville, now Kinshasa. In 1886 he led the Emin Pasha Relief Expedition, mapped the Ruwenzori Range and Lake Edward, and came out of the interior at the end of 1890. He then married the artist Dorothy Tennant, took British citizenship and sat as Liberal Unionist member for Lambeth North from 1895 to 1900.

Stanley's books, among them How I Found Livingstone (1872) and Through the Dark Continent, fostered a public reputation as a hard and cruel leader. In 1871 a House of Commons committee investigated missionary reports of his violence, and John Kirk's unpublished report accused him of reckless use of modern weapons against people who had never heard a gun fired. Tim Jeal holds that Stanley, unlike Richard Burton and Samuel Baker, was not a racist, and Stanley praised the Zanzibari Wangwana who formed the backbone of his expeditions. He also wrote that Africans must submit to Europeans.
His reputation suffered further in the 20th century from his part in founding the Congo Free State for Leopold. He was knighted as a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath in 1899.
henry-of-flanders: Henry was born in Valenciennes, the son of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut and Countess Margaret I of Flanders. He married Agnes of Montferrat, daughter of Boniface of Montferrat, in 1204; their only child died in childbirth with her mother. He also had a daughter by an unnamed mistress, who probably married Alexius Slav, the founder of a state in the Rhodope mountains and later a despot. Some contemporary historians say that Henry made peace with the Bulgarians after the death of Kaloyan and that a marriage was arranged in 1213 with Maria, Kaloyan's daughter and stepdaughter of Tsar Boril of Bulgaria.

Henry joined the Fourth Crusade in about 1201 and distinguished himself at the siege of Constantinople of 1203. He was one of eight division generals in July 1203, with Boniface of Montferrat, Doge Enrico Dandolo, Louis of Blois and his brother Baldwin IX of Flanders, who controlled the largest division. During the siege of 1204 he led a foraging expedition and raided a castle at Philia, near the Black Sea, with about 30 knights according to Robert de Clari. Emperor Alexius V Ducas laid an ambush for him, but Henry's force routed the Greeks and captured a revered icon said to contain relics of Christ. He became prominent among the princes of the new Latin Empire.

When the Bulgarians captured his brother Emperor Baldwin at the Battle of Adrianople in April, Henry was chosen regent, and he succeeded to the throne when news of Baldwin's death arrived. He was crowned on 20 August. The Lombard nobles of the Kingdom of Thessalonica refused him allegiance, and after a two-year war Henry defeated them and confiscated the Templar castles of Ravennika and Zetouni. His reign was spent largely in struggles with Tsar Kaloyan, whom he later followed with Boril, defeated at the Battle of Philippopolis, and with Theodore I Lascaris of Nicaea. He campaigned in Asia Minor at Nicomedia in 1207 and in 1211 to 1212, winning the Battle of the Rhyndacus, and in 1214 agreed a truce with Theodore.

The Greek historian George Akropolites wrote that Henry, though a Frank, behaved graciously to the Romans of Constantinople and made many of them his magnates and soldiers. In 1213 he countermanded the orders of the papal legate Pelagio Galvani, who had begun to imprison Orthodox clergy and close churches. Henry died on 11 June 1216, poisoned, it is said, by Oberto II of Biandrate; Gardner suggests this was at the instigation of his wife Maria of Bulgaria. His brother-in-law Peter was crowned emperor but never reached Constantinople, and his sister Yolanda ruled alone in 1217 to 1219.
henry-purcell: Henry Purcell was born in Westminster in 1659, in St Ann's Lane, and the family lived a few hundred yards from Westminster Abbey. His father, also named Henry, died in 1664, and the child was placed under the guardianship of his uncle Thomas, a gentleman of the Chapel Royal. Thomas arranged for him to become a chorister, and he studied under Captain Henry Cooke and then Pelham Humfrey, a pupil of Lully. The composer Matthew Locke was a family friend.

When his voice broke in 1673 he left the Chapel Royal and became assistant to the organ-builder John Hingston. The earliest work identified as his with certainty is an ode for the King's birthday written in 1670, when he was eleven. After Humfrey's death he studied under John Blow, was a pupil at Westminster School, and in 1676 was appointed copyist at Westminster Abbey.

In 1679 Blow resigned the post of organist of Westminster Abbey in Purcell's favour, and he devoted himself almost entirely to sacred music for six years. Soon after his marriage in 1682 he became organist of the Chapel Royal as well. In 1685 he wrote the anthems I was glad and My heart is inditing for the coronation of King James II, and in 1694 he composed Come Ye Sons of Art, one of his most elaborate works, to a birthday ode by Nahum Tate for Queen Mary.

He returned to the theatre in 1687 with music for John Dryden's Tyrannick Love. His later stage works included Dioclesian in 1690, King Arthur in 1691 and The Fairy-Queen in 1692, an adaptation of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream whose score was rediscovered in 1901. His chamber opera Dido and Aeneas, to a libretto by Nahum Tate, was written for private performance. In his last six years he wrote music for forty-two plays. His Te Deum and Jubilate Deo of 1694 was the first English Te Deum with orchestral accompaniment.

Purcell died on 21 November 1695 at his home in Marsham Street, at the height of his career, aged about 35 or 36. The cause is unclear: one theory is that he caught a chill, another that he died of tuberculosis. He was buried in the north aisle of Westminster Abbey beside the organ, and the music he had written for the funeral of Queen Mary was performed at his own. His widow Frances published many of his works, including the collection Orpheus Britannicus.

John Blow wrote an ode on his death, and later composers admired him. His setting of Thou knowest Lord has been sung at every British state funeral since William Croft preserved it in 1724. Benjamin Britten arranged many of his vocal works. A Purcell Society, founded in 1876, published new editions of his music.
henry-raspe: Henry Raspe was born about 1204, the son of Hermann I, Landgrave of Thuringia, and Sophia of Wittelsbach. In 1226 his brother Louis IV, Landgrave of Thuringia, died on the way to the Sixth Crusade, and Henry became regent for his under-age nephew Hermann II. He managed to remove his nephew and the boy's young mother, Elisabeth of Hungary, from the line of succession, and around 1231 he formally succeeded his brother as landgrave.

He married three times and had no children from any of the marriages. His wives were Elisabeth, daughter of Margrave Albert II of Brandenburg, whom he married in 1228; Gertrude, daughter of Duke Leopold VI of Austria; and Beatrice, daughter of Duke Henry II of Brabant.

In 1242 Emperor Frederick II chose Henry, together with King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia, as administrator of Germany for Frederick's under-age son Conrad. After Pope Innocent IV placed a ban on Frederick in 1245, Henry changed sides. On 22 May 1246, with the support of the papacy, he was elected anti-king in opposition to Conrad. The strong papal pressure behind his election earned him the derogatory nickname Pfaffenkönig, the priests' king, and the papal legate in Germany was Filippo da Pistoia.

In August 1246 Henry defeated Conrad in the Battle on the Nidda in southern Hesse and besieged Ulm and Reutlingen. He suffered a mortal wound and died on 16 February 1247 at Wartburg Castle near Eisenach in Thuringia, so that his contested reign as king lasted only about nine months. After his death the emperor granted Thuringia as a fief to Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, the son of Henry Raspe's sister Jutta.
henry-the-bearded: Henry was the fourth son of Duke Bolesław I the Tall of Silesia and his second wife Christina, probably a German. He was born in Głogów in Lower Silesia. His three older brothers died, and he became his father's sole heir. He married Hedwig of Andechs, later canonized as Saint Hedwig of Silesia. Bolesław died on 8 December 1201, and early in 1202 Henry's uncle, Mieszko IV Tanglefoot, took the Duchy of Opole, which had passed to Henry.

Henry spent much of his rule contesting Lubusz Land and Kraków. After the margrave Konrad II of Lusatia died on 6 May 1210 he took Lubusz and held it until 1218. On 23 November 1227, at an assembly of Piast dukes at Gąsawa, Henry and the High Duke Leszek I the White were ambushed; Leszek was killed and Henry badly wounded. In 1229 Duke Konrad I of Masovia had him seized at Spytkowice during mass and imprisoned at Płock, and he was freed only after Hedwig went to Płock and he renounced his rights to Kraków, a promise the Pope later released him from.

Władysław III of Greater Poland died in 1231 without a son, leaving Henry his heir. In 1232 Henry entered Kraków and was proclaimed High Duke, recovering for the Silesian Piasts the title lost by his grandfather Władysław II the Exile in 1146. A treaty with Konrad at Chełm in 1233 confirmed his rule at Kraków. In 1234 he named his son Henry II the Pious heir, as duke of Silesia and Greater Poland, and sought a royal crown for him, but conflict with the Church and his death ended the effort.

Henry supported mining, carried out a monetary reform and encouraged German settlers, mainly from Franconia and Bavaria. Złotoryja received the first town charter in Poland, in 1211, and he founded the Cistercian church at Trzebnica in 1202 at his wife's request. He died in 1238 at Krosno Odrzańskie and was buried there. Historians agree that without the disaster at Legnica in 1241 Poland might have been united by the middle of the 13th century. A contemporary chronicler called him an honest man who thought only of being useful to his people.
henry-the-fowler: Henry was born in Memleben, in what is now Saxony-Anhalt, into the Liudolfing line of Saxon dukes, the son of Otto the Illustrious, Duke of Saxony. His mother, Hedwiga, was probably a great-granddaughter of Charlemagne through her mother. In 906 he married Hatheburg of Merseburg, a former nun; the church annulled the marriage in 909. In the same year he married Matilda, daughter of Dietrich of Ringelheim, who was later canonised. He succeeded his father as duke in 912 and rebelled against King Conrad I over lands in Thuringia before they reconciled in 915.

Conrad I died on 23 December 918 after recommending Henry as king, since only he could hold the kingdom together against revolts and Magyar raids. At the Diet of Fritzlar in 919 Franconian and Saxon nobles elected him, the first non-Frank on the throne. Archbishop Heriger of Mainz offered to anoint him, but he refused, the only king of his time to do so, allegedly because he wished to be king by acclamation of the people and not by the church's. He then had to subdue the other dukes. Arnulf of Bavaria, who had crowned himself king of Bavaria in 919, submitted only in 921, keeping substantial autonomy.

Henry did not seek a centralised monarchy and ruled through autonomous stem duchies. In 925, after Duke Gilbert of Lotharingia rebelled, he invaded and besieged Gilbert at Zülpich, then in 928 married his daughter Gerberga to Gilbert, bringing Lotharingia back as the fifth stem duchy. He agreed a ten-year truce with the Magyars in 924 in return for annual tribute, and used it to build fortified towns and train a cavalry force. In 932 he refused the tribute, and in 933 he crushed the Magyars at the Battle of Riade.

During the truce he marched on the Hevelli in the winter of 928 and seized their capital, Brandenburg. In 929 he forced Duke Wenceslaus I of Bohemia to resume tribute, and in 934 he conquered Schleswig.

Henry planned a journey to Rome to be crowned emperor, but died on 2 July 936 and was buried at Quedlinburg Abbey, founded by Matilda. He had prevented a collapse of royal power such as occurred in West Francia and left a stronger kingdom to his son Otto I, the first of the Ottonian rulers who held East Francia and later the Holy Roman Empire from 919 until 1024. Richard Wagner made him a character in his opera Lohengrin in 1850.
henry-the-lion: Henry came from the Welf dynasty, whose rise came largely through advantageous marriages. His grandfather, Duke Henry the Black of Bavaria, married Wulfhild, daughter of the Saxon Duke Magnus Billung, which brought large lands around Lüneburg to the Welfs. His father, Henry the Proud, married Gertrude, the only daughter of the Saxon Duke Lothar III, and ruled the duchies of Bavaria and Saxony. In 1138 and 1139 King Conrad III, whose rival for the crown Henry the Proud had been, took the duchies from him and gave Saxony to Albert the Bear and Bavaria to Leopold of Austria. Henry the Proud died in 1139, when his son was still a child.

Henry did not give up his claim, and Conrad returned Saxony to him in 1142. He took part in the Wendish Crusade of 1147. In 1156 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, his cousin, restored Bavaria to him, though the East Mark was not returned and became the Duchy of Austria. Henry is associated with the founding of Munich in 1157 and Lübeck in 1159, and he developed other towns such as Brunswick, Schwerin and Lüneburg. In 1166 he had a bronze lion, his heraldic animal, set up at his castle Dankwarderode in Brunswick, the first bronze statue north of the Alps, and later built Brunswick Cathedral near it.

He married Clementia of Zähringen in 1147 and divorced her in 1162, apparently under pressure from Barbarossa, and in 1168 married Matilda, daughter of Henry II of England. Henry supported Barbarossa in his wars with the cities of Lombardy and the popes, and took part in the sieges of Crema and Milan. In 1172 he made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and spent Easter in Constantinople. He later refused to aid a renewed invasion of Lombardy, being occupied with his eastern borders and wanting the imperial city of Goslar as the price, which Barbarossa refused. Barbarossa's expedition failed, and he resented Henry.

Other German princes were hostile to Henry's power. In 1180 a court of bishops and princes tried him in absentia for insubordination, stripped him of his lands and declared him an outlaw. Barbarossa invaded Saxony, Henry's allies deserted him, and he submitted in November 1181 at an Imperial Diet in Erfurt. He was exiled in 1182 for three years and stayed with his father-in-law in Normandy, and was exiled again in 1188. In 1194 he made peace with Emperor Henry VI and returned to his diminished lands around Brunswick, where he sponsored art and architecture. His son became Otto IV, Holy Roman Emperor.
henry-the-proud: Henry was the second son of Duke Henry IX of Bavaria and Wulfhilde, daughter of Duke Magnus of Saxony, so that he belonged to the Welf family and was also senior heir of the Saxon House of Billung. He came of age in 1123, and in 1126 his father retired to Weingarten Abbey; as Henry's elder brother Conrad entered the Cistercian Order, Henry was enfeoffed with Bavaria. In 1127 he married Gertrude, the only child of King Lothair III, who had been promised to Henry's father as a reward for supporting Lothair in the royal election of 1125 against Duke Frederick II of Swabia. She was heir to the properties of three Saxon dynasties, and the couple had a son, Henry the Lion.

Henry supported Lothair in the warfare against the Hohenstaufen brothers Frederick II and Conrad, the anti-king of Germany, and put down a rising in Bavaria led by Count Frederick of Bogen, who submitted in 1133. In 1136 he accompanied Lothair to Italy and led a Bavarian division into the Kingdom of Sicily as far as Bari. He was appointed margrave of Tuscany and Lothair's successor in Saxony, and Pope Innocent II gave him the private properties of Margravine Matilda of Tuscany. According to the chronicler Otto of Freising, he boasted of a realm stretching from sea to sea, from Denmark to Sicily.

When Lothair died in December 1137, Henry's wealth and position made him a formidable candidate for the crown. The qualities that earned him his epithet, however, aroused the jealousy of the princes. The new king, Conrad III, demanded the imperial regalia and refused to invest Henry with Saxony, on the pretext that two duchies could not be in one hand. In July 1138 Henry refused to take the oath of allegiance and was banned and deprived of both duchies. Bavaria was given to the Babenberg margrave Leopold IV of Austria and Saxony to the Ascanian count Albert the Bear.

In 1139 Henry expelled his enemies from Saxony and was preparing to attack Bavaria when he died suddenly at Quedlinburg. He is buried in the Imperial Cathedral of Königslutter next to Lothair and Richenza of Northeim. His son Henry the Lion was underage and was later given Saxony, while Henry II, Duke of Austria received Bavaria. Conrad the Priest probably wrote the Rolandslied, a German version of the Chanson de Roland, in Henry's service at the request of Queen Gertrude.
henry-v-holy-roman-emperor: Henry V was the fourth and last ruler of the Salian dynasty, the son of Emperor Henry IV and Bertha of Savoy. Only the date of his accolade at Easter 1101 can be confirmed. His father had long been in conflict with the pope, the bishops and the princes. Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV in 1077, and he was excommunicated again in 1080 and 1094. Henry V joined the opponents of his father and forced him to abdicate on 31 December 1105. Historians still debate why: one view stresses religious reform and the influence of young Bavarian counts, another the murder of Sieghard of Burghausen in 1104.

In spring 1106 Henry reflected that disregard for the princes had been the downfall of the empire. For some years he ruled with their advice and reinstated bishops banned by his father. His main concern was the Investiture Controversy. When negotiations failed he marched on Rome in 1110, and in 1111 he captured Pope Paschal II and forced him to crown him emperor. Afterwards he returned to autocratic rule and numerous clergy deserted him. He held Archbishop Adalbert of Mainz for over three years, and Adalbert became his great opponent.

In 1110 he was engaged to Matilda, the eight-year-old daughter of King Henry I of England; the wedding took place at Mainz on 7 January 1114. On 7 August 1111 he buried his father at Speyer Cathedral and granted Speyer's citizens privileges that gave them unprecedented civil liberties. After Matilda of Tuscany died in July 1115 he went to Italy to secure her estates. In 1122 he and Pope Callixtus II ended the Investiture Controversy in the Concordat of Worms.

Henry died of disease at Utrecht on 23 May 1125 and was buried at Speyer. With no legitimate children he left his possessions to his nephew Frederick II of Hohenstaufen, and the Salian line ended. At Mainz on 24 August 1125 the princes elected Lothair III instead, so that legitimacy came by election, not inheritance. Medieval judgements were harsh, especially in France, where the abbot Suger called him a troublemaker.
henry-vi-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was the second son of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and Beatrice I, Countess of Burgundy. His father had him elected King of the Romans at a diet in Bamberg at Pentecost 1169, when he was four. He was well educated in Latin and in Roman and canon law, and he was a patron of poets and a skilled poet himself; the Codex Manesse, a 14th-century songbook, portrays him first among its poets. In 1186 he married Constance of Sicily at Milan. When Barbarossa died on the Third Crusade in 1190, Henry became sovereign ruler of the Empire.

When William II of Sicily died in November 1189, the Sicilian nobility chose Count Tancred of Lecce as king, and Henry had to enforce his wife's claim. Pope Celestine III crowned Henry and Constance emperor and empress in Rome on 15 April 1191. His siege of Naples failed that summer after an epidemic hit his army, and Constance, left at Salerno, was handed over to Tancred. She was freed in June 1192.

In 1193 Duke Leopold V of Austria handed over Richard I of England, whom he had captured on his return from the crusade. Henry held him at Trifels Castle for a ransom of 150,000 silver marks, and Richard was released in 1194 after swearing allegiance to him. With that money Henry conquered Sicily. He entered Palermo on 20 November 1194 and was crowned king on 25 December; the next day Constance gave birth to their son, the future Frederick II. Henry crushed a plot at once, and in Sicily he had a name for ruthless treatment of opponents.

Henry also imposed suzerainty over King Aimery of Cyprus and King Leo I of Armenia and drew a ransom from the Byzantine emperor Alexios III Angelos. In 1195 and 1196 he proposed making the imperial crown hereditary, but the princes rejected the plan.

Henry vowed to go on crusade in 1195, and in 1197 a revolt in Sicily was put down harshly. While preparing the expedition at Messina he fell ill with chills after hunting and died on 28 September 1197, probably of malaria. He was buried at Messina and moved to Palermo Cathedral in 1198. His son Frederick was a child, and a quarrel over the German throne between Philip of Swabia and the Welf Otto of Brunswick lasted nearly twenty years, until Frederick was elected king again in 1212.

Historians generally judge Henry a talented ruler, and Koenigsberger calls him an immensely able politician. At his death he held the imperial crown and the kingdoms of Germany, Burgundy, Italy and Sicily. The empire, which depended on the ruler, did not hold together after him. Present-day research treats him as a capable man who overstretched the Hohenstaufen realm.
henry-vii-holy-roman-emperor: Henry was a son of Count Henry VI of Luxembourg and Béatrice of the House of Avesnes. He was raised at the French court and held comparatively small properties in a peripheral, mostly French-speaking part of the empire. As Count of Luxembourg he agreed to become a vassal of King Philip the Fair of France.

After the assassination of King Albert I on 1 May 1308, Philip spread French money among the German electors to win the crown for his brother, Charles of Valois. Many electors, and Pope Clement V, did not want French power to grow. Henry's brother Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, won over several electors, and Henry was elected with six votes at Frankfurt on 27 November 1308, then crowned at Aachen on 6 January 1309. Clement confirmed the election in July 1309 and agreed to crown him emperor in 1312.

Henry crossed the Alps in October 1310, and Guelph and Ghibelline nobles at first greeted him alike. He required Lombard cities to take back their exiles and the rulers to surrender their keys, and he was crowned King of Italy with the Iron Crown of Lombardy at Milan on 6 January 1311. He appointed Matteo I Visconti imperial vicar of Milan. A levy on the towns and his claims on communal rights turned the Guelph cities against him. Cremona fell to him on 26 April 1311 and he razed its walls, and a four-month siege of Brescia ended in September 1311.

Florence led a Guelph alliance with Lucca, Siena and Bologna, and King Robert of Naples opposed him. The Colonna family supported him in Rome, but Robert's troops held the Vatican quarter, so Henry was crowned emperor on 29 June 1312 at the Lateran by three Ghibelline cardinals. He later besieged Florence for six weeks without success, and in 1313 charged Robert with treason. He began a campaign against Naples on 8 August 1313, but fell ill with malaria while besieging Siena.

Henry died at Buonconvento on 24 August 1313, and the hope of effective imperial power in Italy died with him. His son John the Blind became King of Bohemia. Ludwig of Bavaria and Frederick of Habsburg then both claimed the crown, until Ludwig won the Battle of Mühldorf on 28 September 1322. Two of the vicars Henry appointed, Cangrande I della Scala of Verona and Matteo Visconti of Milan, had successful careers. Dante praised him as the savior who would restore imperial rule to Italy.
henry-vii-of-england: Henry was the only child of Lady Margaret Beaufort, then 13, and Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, who died three months before his birth. Margaret was a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt, so Henry's claim to the throne descended from Edward III through the Beaufort line. Edmund was the half-brother of the Lancastrian king Henry VI. Henry was raised by his uncle Jasper Tudor, a Lancastrian, and by William Herbert, a Yorkist supporter. After Edward IV retook the throne in 1471, Henry spent 14 years in exile in Brittany.

At Rennes Cathedral on Christmas Day 1483 Henry pledged to marry Elizabeth of York, eldest daughter of Edward IV. A first attempt to land in England failed. He then escaped to France, which supplied troops, and landed at Mill Bay near Dale in Pembrokeshire with a small French and Scottish force. Although outnumbered, he defeated Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485, after several of Richard's allies, among them the Earl of Northumberland and Lord Stanley, changed sides or left the field. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 30 October, married Elizabeth in 1486 and defended the crown at Stoke Field in 1487.

Henry came to the throne with no experience of financial administration, yet restored an effectively bankrupt exchequer. He kept the same advisers throughout and introduced efficient mechanisms of taxation, supported by his chancellor, Archbishop John Morton, whose argument, known as Morton's Fork, held that nobles who spent little must have savings and those who spent much could afford to pay. The Magnus Intercursus of 1496 restored trade with the Burgundian Netherlands after his embargo of 1494. To curb powerful nobles he passed laws against livery and maintenance and used the Court of Star Chamber.

In 1502 his heir Arthur, Prince of Wales, died at Ludlow Castle, very likely of the sweating sickness, and Elizabeth died the following year; the king, normally reserved, grieved intensely. Henry VII died on 21 April 1509, after nearly 24 years on the throne, and was peacefully succeeded by Henry VIII. Historians have compared him with Louis XI of France and Ferdinand II of Aragon, and Francis Bacon published a History of the Reign of King Henry VII in 1622.
henry-vii-of-germany: Henry was born in Sicily, the only son of King Frederick II and his first wife Constance of Aragon, and was the elder brother of Conrad IV. While Frederick sought election as German king against Otto IV, he had his infant son crowned King of Sicily in March 1212 by Pope Innocent III. After the pope's death in 1216 Frederick called Henry to Germany and entrusted him with the Duchy of Swabia. On 20 or 26 April 1220 the princes assembled at Frankfurt elected Henry King of the Romans, in return for Frederick's confirmation of privileges to the prince-bishops, but Pope Honorius III did not recognise the election.

After Frederick returned to Italy in 1220, Henry was placed under the tutelage of Archbishop Engelbert I of Cologne, who crowned him at Aachen on 8 May 1222. After Engelbert's death in 1225 Duke Louis I of Bavaria took over the guardianship. On 29 November 1225 Henry married Margaret of Babenberg, daughter of Duke Leopold VI of Austria, they had two sons, Henry and Frederick, who both died young. Around Christmas 1228, after a falling-out with Louis of Bavaria, Henry took over the rule for himself.

The German princes, angered by his city-friendly policies, forced Henry to issue the Statutum in favorem principum at Worms on 1 May 1231, and their complaints turned Frederick against him. In 1233 and 1234 Henry angered his father again by intervening against the Archbishop of Bremen's crusade against the peasants of Stedingen; Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him, and Frederick outlawed him on 5 July 1234. Henry revolted but was deserted by most of his followers and submitted to his father at Wimpfen on 2 July 1235. On 4 July 1235 Frederick and the princes tried Henry at Worms and dethroned him, and his brother Conrad was elected King of the Romans in his place.

Henry was kept prisoner in several places, among them Heidelberg, Apulia and Rocca San Felice in Campania. Analysis of his skeleton in 1998 and 1999 showed that he had suffered from advanced leprosy in his last years, perhaps the reason the emperor never forgave him. He died near Martirano in Calabria in February 1242 after a fall from his horse. He was buried with royal honours in the cathedral of Cosenza. He is numbered only in parentheses, as he did not hold sole kingship, and was long disparaged as Parentheses Henry, though several historians have recently taken a more positive view of his policies.
henry-viii-of-england: Henry was born on 28 June 1491 at the Palace of Placentia in Greenwich, the second son of King Henry VII and Elizabeth of York. As a small child he was given many offices, including Constable of Dover Castle and Duke of York, which allowed his father to keep lucrative positions in personal control. His elder brother Arthur, Prince of Wales, died in 1502, making Henry the heir. He succeeded at 17 in April 1509 and married his brother's widow, Catherine of Aragon, on 11 June 1509.

Henry joined the Holy League against France in 1511, and his invasion force of 1513 numbered some 30,000 men. In the later 1520s he grew impatient with Catherine's failure to produce a male heir and became enamoured of Anne Boleyn. Historians such as E. L. Woodward see the annulment as the occasion rather than the cause of the English Reformation. On 23 May 1533 Thomas Cranmer declared the marriage to Catherine void, and Anne was crowned on 1 June. Their daughter Elizabeth was born on 7 September 1533.

In 1536 Henry assented to the Laws in Wales Act, which united England and Wales. The day after Anne Boleyn's execution he became engaged to Jane Seymour; his minister Thomas Cromwell later arranged the marriage to Anne of Cleves, and Henry afterwards married Catherine Howard, who was beheaded, and Catherine Parr in July 1543. In 1538 the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury was dismantled, and in 1542 the remaining monasteries were dissolved and their property transferred to the Crown.

Henry's later years were marked by obesity and a leg wound that festered after a jousting accident on 24 January 1536. He died on 28 January 1547 and was succeeded by his only surviving son, Edward VI, aged nine. Henry's will named sixteen executors, and Edward Seymour became Lord Protector. It excluded the Stuart descendants of his sister Margaret, a provision that failed when James VI of Scotland became king of England in 1603. John D. Mackie judged that Henry carried England through a perilous time of change.
henry-wadsworth-longfellow: Longfellow was born on 27 February 1807 in Portland, then a town of the District of Maine in Massachusetts. His father, Stephen Longfellow, was a lawyer, and his maternal grandfather, Peleg Wadsworth, had been a general in the American Revolutionary War and a member of Congress. He was the second of eight children and descended from English colonists of New England, among them Mayflower Pilgrims. A studious child fluent in Latin, he published his first poem at the age of 13, a patriotic piece in the Portland Gazette on 17 November 1820.

After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he was offered a professorship of modern languages there. He toured Europe from May 1826 to August 1829, learned French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and German mostly without formal instruction, and met Washington Irving in Madrid, who encouraged him to write. At Bowdoin he translated textbooks, and his first published book, in 1833, was a translation of the poems of the medieval Spanish poet Jorge Manrique. He later taught at Harvard College. His collections Voices of the Night (1839) and Ballads and Other Poems (1841) made him instantly popular. He retired from teaching in 1854 to devote himself to writing.

His first wife, Mary Potter, died in 1835 after a miscarriage. In 1843 he married Frances Appleton, daughter of the Boston industrialist Nathan Appleton, after a long courtship. She died on 10 July 1861 after her dress caught fire, and Longfellow, burned while trying to save her, could not attend her funeral. He grew a beard from then on. He turned for a time to translation and, from 1864, met friends every Wednesday in the Dante Club to refine his version of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, published in three volumes in 1867. He was the first American to translate it completely.

Longfellow wrote lyric poems known for their musicality, many telling stories from mythology and legend, and he used many forms, including hexameter, blank verse, ballads and sonnets. His best-known works include Evangeline (1847), The Song of Hiawatha (1855) and Paul Revere's Ride. He supported abolitionism and, after the American Civil War, hoped for reconciliation between North and South. His poem Christmas Bells later became the basis of a carol. He died on 24 March 1882.

He was the most popular American poet of his day and had success overseas. His seventieth birthday in 1877 took on the air of a national holiday. Soon after his death his reputation declined, as academics turned to Walt Whitman, Robert Frost and others, and critics judged his verse sentimental and derivative of European models. In 2020 Nicholas A. Basbanes defended him as the victim of an orchestrated dismissal.
henryk-sienkiewicz: Henryk Sienkiewicz was born on 5 May 1846 at Wola Okrzejska in the Kingdom of Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. His family were impoverished Polish nobles, on his father's side descended from Lipka Tatars who had settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. He grew up on family estates and in Warsaw, where he studied at the Imperial University and moved from medicine and law to the Institute of Philology and History. He finished in 1871 without a diploma, having failed the examination in Ancient Greek, and lived in poverty as a part-time tutor.

He debuted as a journalist in 1869 and wrote under the pen name Litwos. In 1876 he went to the United States with the actress Helena Modrzejewska, and Gazeta Polska paid for his journey in exchange for travel essays, which won him a popular following. He stayed in California and returned to Poland in 1879. From 1883 he turned to historical novels. With Fire and Sword was serialised from 1883 to 1884, The Deluge from 1884 to 1886 and Sir Michael from 1887 to 1888. Together these make the Trilogy, which established him as the most popular contemporary Polish writer.

He wrote the first chapters of Quo Vadis in February 1895, and the novel was finished by March 1896 and soon gained international renown. He began serialising Krzyżacy, The Teutonic Knights, in 1897, and it was finished in 1900. In 1900 the Polish people gave him an estate at Oblęgorek near Kielce, where he later opened a school for children.

Poland remained partitioned between Russia, Austria and Prussia, later Germany, and Sienkiewicz used his fame to influence world opinion for the Polish cause. He criticised the policy of Germanization of the Polish minority in Germany, supported the Września schoolchildren in 1901, and in 1907 appealed to the intellectual community amid German attempts to expropriate Polish land. A moderate, he declined to stand for the Russian Duma and gave to struggling writers.

In 1905 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his merits as an epic writer. In his acceptance speech he said that Poland had been pronounced dead and that the prize was proof that she lived. He died on 15 November 1916.
hephthalites: The Hephthalites, sometimes called the White Huns, called themselves Ebodalo, a name they wrote in the Bactrian script on some of their coins. Sources for their history are sparse, there is no king-list, and historians disagree about how the group arose and what language it first spoke. The most prominent view at present is that they were of Turkic origin and later adopted Bactrian, an Eastern Iranian language written in the Greek alphabet, as their official language. Chinese chronicles derived them from the Gaoju or the Da Yuezhi. Scholars have reached no consensus on any link with the Huns of Eastern Europe.

The Hephthalites were at first vassals of the Rouran Khaganate and borrowed much of their political organisation from it, including the title khan. They split from their overlords in the early fifth century. Persian sources show them fighting Yazdegerd II from 442. In 458 a Hephthalite king named Akhshunwar helped Peroz I seize the Sasanian throne from his brother, and with Hephthalite aid Peroz reportedly ended Kidarite rule in Transoxiana by 467.

Their stronghold was Tokharistan, on the northern slopes of the Hindu Kush, and their capital was probably Kunduz. They may have conquered Sogdia as early as 479. In the late fifth century they crossed the Pamir Mountains and took the western Tarim Basin, including Kashgar and Khotan, from the weakening Rourans, and by the early sixth century they were sending embassies to the Northern Wei. They did not go beyond the Hindu Kush, which the Alchon Huns held, a people once thought to be part of the Hephthalites and now usually treated as separate.

Their power ended when the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanians under Khosrow I allied against them and defeated them after an eight-day battle near Qarshi, the Battle of Gol-Zarriun, perhaps in 557. Afterwards Hephthalite principalities remained in Tokharistan until the Tokhara Yabghus took over in 625.

The Hephthalites were a tribal confederation that included both nomadic and settled urban communities, and many of the people they ruled were probably Iranian speakers. Central control was weak, and local dynasties paid tribute. The Chinese considered them excellent archers, and they probably had a strong cavalry. Chinese sources report that brothers shared one wife, with the number of horns on a married woman's headdress matching the number of her husbands. Murals at Balalyk tepe and at the Buddhas of Bamiyan show figures with round beardless faces and cropped hair. The complex at Bamiyan was developed under Hephthalite rule.
hera: The name Hera is attested in Mycenaean Greek, written e-ra in Linear B on tablets from Pylos and Thebes, and it has no clear etymology. A Pylos tablet mentions offerings to Zeus-Hera-Drimios. Hera was the protecting goddess of Argos and may have Mycenaean origin. Homer's formula boōpis potnia Hērē, cow-eyed mistress Hera, probably relates her to a Mediterranean goddess of nature. Scholars have proposed Near Eastern and Indo-European origins, and some think that in certain cults she was an earth goddess. Others, following Johann Jakob Bachofen, have asked whether she was originally the goddess of a matriarchal people who lived in Greece before the Hellenes.

In historical times most Greeks recognised Hera as the consort of Zeus. She was the goddess of marriage, women and family and the protector of women in childbirth, and queen among the twelve Olympians. In myth she is the daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea. Her marriage with her brother Zeus is the main theme of most festivals held for her, in which young married women performed dances and rites. Her epithets include Gamēlios, presiding over marriage, and Anassa, queen.

Myths show her as jealous and vengeful towards Zeus's lovers and their children. She tricked Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his true form, which destroyed her. She delayed the birth of Heracles, whose name means glory of Hera, so that Eurystheus was born first. In art she is a dignified, matronly figure, upright or enthroned, crowned with a polos or diadem and sometimes veiled. Her sacred animals included the cow and the cuckoo, and in Hellenistic times the peacock.

The chief centre of her cult was the north-eastern Peloponnese, around Argos, Tiryns and Corinth. The oldest temple at Olympia belonged to her, and she was worshipped on Samos, Euboea, Rhodes and Crete. One of the earliest Greek temples was her temple of Hera Akraia at Perachora, built in the 9th century BCE. Her Roman counterpart is Juno, and Renaissance art joined Hera and Juno in one iconography.
heracleidae: The Heraclidae were the numerous descendants of Heracles, applied especially to those of Hyllus, the eldest of his four sons by Deianira. According to the tradition, Heracles had been meant by Zeus to rule Argos, Lacedaemon and Messenian Pylos, but Hera's cunning put those lands in the hands of Eurystheus, king of Mycenae. After Heracles died, his children found refuge at Athens, where Eurystheus attacked and was defeated and slain.
