Hyllus and his brothers then invaded the Peloponnese but were forced out by a pestilence and withdrew to Thessaly, where Aegimius, the mythical ancestor of the Dorians, adopted Hyllus and gave him a third of his territory.

Hyllus consulted the Delphic oracle, which told him to wait for the third fruit and to enter the Peloponnese by a narrow passage by sea. He was killed in single combat by Echemus, king of Tegea, and later attempts under Cleodaeus and Aristomachus also failed. Aristomachus's sons Temenus, Cresphontes and Aristodemus learned that the third fruit meant the third generation and the narrow passage the straits of Rhium. Guided by the one-eyed Oxylus of Aetolia, they crossed and defeated and killed Tisamenus, son of Orestes. Tradition dated this conquest eighty years after the Trojan War.

The Heraclidae divided the land by lot. Argos fell to Temenus, Lacedaemon to Procles and Eurysthenes, the twin sons of Aristodemus, and Messenia to Cresphontes, who by tradition cheated to obtain it. Elis was reserved for Oxylus. The Heraclidae ruled in Lacedaemon until 221 BCE but disappeared much earlier elsewhere. This conquest, commonly called the Dorian invasion or the Return of the Heraclidae, has been linked to a Dorian invasion since Karl Otfried Müller's Die Dorier of 1830. Neither Homer nor Hesiod mentions the Heraclidae or their return.

The theme asserted the primal legitimacy of a ruling clan that traced its origin to Heracles. In the historical period the Agiads and Eurypontids of Sparta claimed descent from him, as did the Argead dynasty of Macedonia, which traced its line to Temenus of Argos. Sources differ on which Temenid founded the Macedonian line: Herodotus and Thucydides name Perdiccas, later sources Caranus. A Heraclid family also ruled Lydia, ending when Gyges overthrew Candaules and founded the Mermnad dynasty. In the seventeenth century the Spanish king Philip IV, a descendant of both Burgundy and Castile, which claimed the same lineage, commissioned Francisco de Zurbarán to paint ten works depicting Hercules.
heracles: Heracles, whose name means glory of Hera, was born Alcaeus or Alcides. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene and the foster son of Amphitryon. Hera's hatred shaped his myths, since she plotted against Zeus's mortal children as revenge for his infidelities. Unlike other Greek heroes, no tomb was identified as his. At some festivals he received sacrifice first as a hero and then as a god upon an altar, so that he is the closest Greek approach to a demigod. His figure drew at first on Near Eastern motifs such as the lion fight.

In one tradition Hera drove Heracles mad and he killed his wife Megara and their children. The Oracle of Delphi told him to serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform ten tasks. Eurystheus added two more, which gave the twelve Labours. They included killing the Nemean lion and the Lernaean Hydra, stealing the golden apples of the Hesperides and capturing Cerberus. Other stories have him sailing with the Argonauts, killing the eagle that tormented Prometheus and sacking Troy before the Trojan War. After killing Iphitus in another fit of madness, he served a year as the slave of Omphale, queen of Lydia.

He married four times. His wife Deianira was deceived by the dying centaur Nessus into giving him a tunic smeared with poisoned blood. Unable to remove it, he burned himself on a pyre on Mount Oeta, and he ascended to Olympus as a god and married Hebe. His descendants are the Heracleidae. He is shown with a lion skin and a club, and was patron of young men and gymnasia.

The Greeks held the festival of the Heracleia, which commemorated his death, in late July or early August, and several ancient cities were named Heraclea for him. In the 5th century BCE he was increasingly given an ethical character, as in the parable of the Choice of Heracles, in which he chooses a severe but glorious life over an easy one. In Rome he was honoured as Hercules, and Roman emperors such as Commodus and Maximian identified themselves with him.

Herodotus connected him to the Egyptian god Shu and to the Phoenician god Melqart. Christian writers read the cult in a Euhemerist way, treating him as a historical king of Argos who was deified after death. Through Greco-Buddhist culture, Heraclean symbolism travelled to the Far East, and an example survives in the Nio guardian deities at Japanese Buddhist temples.
heraclitus: Little is known of the life of Heraclitus. He was the son of Blyson and came from the Ionian city of Ephesus, a port on the Cayster River on the western coast of Asia Minor, which was then part of the Persian Empire. Ephesus appears to have kept a close relationship with Persia; when Darius the Great suppressed the Ionian revolt in 494 BCE, Ephesus was spared, while Miletus, home of the earlier philosophers, was sacked.

The main source for his life is the doxographer Diogenes Laërtius, whose information is mostly unreliable. His story that Heraclitus gave up the hereditary title of king to his younger brother may at least suggest an aristocratic family. Heraclitus appears to have had little sympathy for democracy or the masses.

Heraclitus is said to have produced a single work on papyrus, which has not survived; more than 100 fragments are preserved in quotations by other authors. Its title is unknown, though later writers call it On Nature. According to Diogenes Laërtius he deposited it in the Artemision as a dedication. Its oracular, wordplay-filled style earned him the epithets the dark and the obscure, and the weeping philosopher, in contrast to the laughing Democritus.

The hallmarks of his thought are the unity of opposites and constant change. He is quoted as saying that everything flows and that no man steps in the same river twice. Among his sayings on opposites are 'The way up is the way down' and 'The straight and the crooked path of the fuller's comb is one and the same'. He saw harmony and justice in strife, and he stands opposed to Parmenides, who believed in a static being.

Like the Milesians before him, Heraclitus named a fundamental element, the arche: Thales had chosen water, Anaximander the apeiron and Anaximenes air, while Heraclitus chose fire. In one fragment he calls the world-order 'ever-living fire, kindling in measures and being quenched in measures'. He also spoke of the logos, a word meaning speech, discourse or reason, which seems to designate the rational structure of the world and a kind of divine law.

His writings influenced Plato, Aristotle and the Stoics, and later Hegel, Nietzsche and Heidegger. Plato presented Cratylus as a Heraclitean, and according to Aristotle Cratylus went further, saying that one cannot step into the same river even once. Two of his fragments occur in the Derveni papyrus, an Orphic poem. Whether he had students in his lifetime is unknown.
heraclius: Scholars debate the origin of Heraclius, chiefly because they debate that of his father, Heraclius the Elder, who is often considered of Armenian descent. Little is known of his life before he became emperor. In 608 the elder Heraclius, Exarch of Africa, renounced his loyalty to the unpopular emperor Phocas. His nephew Nicetas invaded Egypt, while the younger Heraclius sailed east with a second force. When he reached Constantinople the Excubitors deserted to him, and he entered the city without serious resistance. Phocas was executed, and Heraclius was crowned on 5 October 610.

The war with Sasanian Persia had begun in 602, when Khosrow II used the murder of the emperor Maurice as an occasion to attack. The Persians took Damascus in 613, Jerusalem in 614, where they captured the True Cross, and Egypt by 622. Heraclius himself was defeated near Antioch in 613. He raised money by borrowing Church treasure and cutting other spending, and left Constantinople on 4 April 622 to campaign in Armenia and the Caucasus. In 626 the Avars and Slavs, supported by a Persian army, besieged Constantinople, and the siege failed.

Late in 627 Heraclius launched a winter offensive into Mesopotamia and defeated the Persians at the Battle of Nineveh. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his son Kavad II, who sued for peace and agreed to withdraw from all occupied territory. In 629 Heraclius restored the True Cross to Jerusalem. The recovered lands were soon exposed to the Arabs: after the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 the Levant was lost within three years, and most of Egypt had fallen by 641. He also promoted Monothelitism in his Ecthesis, hoping to reconcile the Miaphysites, but the popes condemned it.

Heraclius died of an illness on 11 February 641, aged sixty-six, and was succeeded by his sons Heraclius Constantine and Heraclonas. Edward Gibbon judged his reign inconsistent, with a brilliant middle between idle first and last years. Warren Treadgold praises his success against the Persians and thinks his performance against the Arabs respectable, since he preserved the empire where the Persian king Yazdegerd III lost his. Greek became the official language of the state during his reign, and in 629 he began to use the title Basileus. Western medieval Christians remembered him as the first crusader, for the recovery of the True Cross.
heraion-of-samos: The Heraion lay 6 kilometres southwest of the ancient city of Samos, in the low, marshy basin of the Imbrasos river near where it enters the sea. Evidence of cult activity on the site goes back to about 1700 BCE, and the first temple of Hera was built in the eighth century BCE. According to local tradition the goddess was born under a lygos tree, the chaste-tree. At the annual festival called the Toneia, the binding, her cult image was bound with lygos branches and carried down to the sea to be washed.

The sanctuary was richest from the late seventh century BCE, when the Hekatompedos II temple, the south stoa, two colossal kouroi and the Sacred Way to the city were built. A second and greater phase of building in the second quarter of the sixth century added the monumental altar and the Rhoikos Temple, and a third phase began a still larger temple under the tyrant Polycrates.

Herodotus called its temple the largest of all those he knew and counted it with the Tunnel of Eupalinos and the harbour mole as the three great engineering feats of Samos. The Rhoikos temple, built by the architects Rhoikos and Theodoros between 600 and 570 BCE and finished around 560, was about 100 metres long and 50 wide, and was the first of the massive Ionian temples. It stood only about a decade before it was destroyed around 550 BCE, perhaps by an earthquake or because its marshy foundations were unstable.

The Great Temple, 108.6 metres long and 55.2 wide, replaced it about 40 metres to the west, and was never wholly finished. The altar, rebuilt seven times, reached about 35 metres by 16 and 20 metres high, with floral and animal reliefs. Aristocrats dedicated kouroi and korai, among them the Kouros of Samos of about 580 BCE, at about three times life size. Waterlogged soil preserved wooden votives, which are exceptional for Greece, and offerings came from Egypt, Syria and Babylonia.

Worship of Hera at the site ceased in 391 CE. In Byzantine times the Great Temple served as a quarry, and little but its foundations and one column survived. Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, the first Westerner to visit, published engravings of the ruins after his visit in 1704. Silt, reeds and a high water table protected the site until the first excavations of 1890–92 by Panagiotis Kavvadias and Themistoklis Sofoulis.

Theodor Wiegand's campaign of 1910–14 revealed the third temple's foundations, and German archaeologists began a sustained campaign in 1925, resumed in 1951 after the Second World War. The ruins and Pythagoreion were designated UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1992.
herakleopolis-magna: Herakleopolis Magna was the capital of Noret-Khent, the 20th nome of Upper Egypt. Its site lies about 15 kilometres west of the modern city of Beni Suef in the Beni Suef Governorate. In ancient Egypt it was called nn nswt, Child of the King. The Greek name meant City of Heracles, with Great added to distinguish it from other towns of the name; the Greek rulers of the Ptolemaic period associated the local god Haryshef with Heracles. Its modern names are Ihnasiyya Umm al-Kimam and Ihnasiyya al-Madina.

An entry on the Palermo Stone, reporting a visit by King Den to the sacred lake of Heryshef, suggests the city existed by the mid First Dynasty, about 2970 BCE. It rose to prominence in the First Intermediate Period, from 2181 to 2055 BCE, after the Old Kingdom collapsed. Egyptologists sometimes call the time of the 9th and 10th Dynasties, 2160 to 2025 BCE, the Herakleopolitan Period, and the city often fought Thebes. It became the cult centre of Heryshaf, and its temple was built around then. Mentuhotep II defeated the city and its dynasty, about 2055 to 2004 BCE, which began the Middle Kingdom.

Pharaoh Horemheb may have come from the city, since his coronation text credits Horus of Hnes with placing him on the throne. In the Third Intermediate Period it again became an important religious and political centre, with renovation of temples and funerary buildings, and it was still an important religious and cultural centre in the Ptolemaic Kingdom. People lived there into Roman times.

Edouard Naville excavated what he took to be the whole Temple of Heryshef, but Flinders Petrie found that much remained, completing the temple, identifying a second temple he attributed to the 19th Dynasty, and finding Roman houses and many objects of every period.

A Spanish team worked at the site in the 1980s and revealed a libation altar and a pair of decorated eyes from a Third Intermediate Period temple. In 2008 it found a tomb with several false doors from the First Intermediate Period, the funerary chapel of the official Neferjau and his wife Sat-Bahetep, and the tomb of Khety, an officer of the late 11th Dynasty.
heraklion: The name Herakleion comes from an ancient port, Heracleium, the harbour of Knossos, named for the hero Heracles. Knossos had a port on the site from the start of the Early Minoan period. After the fall of the Minoans the area developed little, and early in Byzantine times it abounded with pirates and bandits. The Arabic name of the city meant Castle of the Moat and became Chandax in Greek, which gave Candia. That name was used for the whole island as well as the city. After the Byzantine reconquest the city was locally known as Megalo Kastro, meaning Big Castle.

Moors expelled from Al-Andalus under Abu Hafs Umar took Crete from the Eastern Roman Empire and chose the site as capital in 824. They dug a moat round the city, and the Emirate of Crete lasted from about 827 to 961. When Nikephoros Phokas took the city in March 961 after a prolonged siege, the inhabitants were slaughtered and the city was looted and burned. It stayed Byzantine for 243 years. In 1204 the Republic of Venice bought it as part of a political deal arising from the Fourth Crusade. The Venetians built a wall in places up to 40 metres thick with seven bastions, and made Candia the capital of the Regno di Candia.

The meeting of Venetian and Cretan cultures led to the Cretan Renaissance in letters and the arts. In the Cretan War the Ottomans besieged the city for 21 years, from 1648 to 1669, and Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha took it in 1669. Under the Ottomans the harbour silted up and shipping moved to Chania, which became the capital of Crete in 1849. An earthquake on 12 October 1856 destroyed most of the city's over 3,600 homes. The city joined the Kingdom of Greece in 1913, was badly damaged in the German invasion of May 1941, and became capital of Crete again in 1971.

Heraklion is the fourth largest city in Greece, with a municipal population of 179,302 in 2021. Its Venetian walls, the Koules Fortress and the arsenal dominate the port area. The Heraklion Archaeological Museum and the University of Crete are among its institutions. The writer Nikos Kazantzakis and the painter El Greco were born there.
herat: Herat lies in western Afghanistan, south of the Paropamisus Mountains in the fertile valley of the Hari River. It stands on the Silk Road between West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and East Asia and was traditionally known for its wine. The city and its district take their ancient name from the river: under the Achaemenid Empire (550-330 BCE) the district was called Haraiva, and classical sources call the region Areia.

The date of Herat's foundation is unknown. At the time of the Arab invasion in the middle of the 7th century, Sasanian power in the province was largely nominal, and Hephthalite tribal lords had settled in the region. The Hephthalites and some Turks opposed the invaders at the battle of Qohestān in 651-52 but were defeated. In the Middle Ages Herat was one of the important cities of Khorasan, known as the Pearl of Khorasan. In 994 Alptegin and Mahmud of Ghazni defeated its rebellious governor Faik and annexed Herat, Nishapur and Tous.

After its conquest by Timur the city became an important centre of intellectual and artistic life in the Islamic world. Under Shah Rukh and Husayn Bayqara it was the focal point of the Timurid Renaissance, whose grandeur is thought to have matched that of Florence in the Italian Renaissance. It then remained part of Safavid Iran until the early 18th century. In 1716 the Abdali Afghans in the city revolted and set up the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat, and in 1732 it became part of Afsharid Iran. Ahmad Shah Durrani took it in 1747. In the first half of the 19th century it was an independent city-state and faced several invasions from Qajar Iran. It was incorporated into Afghanistan in 1863.

Herat is the capital of Herat Province and a major industrial and trading centre of Afghanistan. Most of its people speak Dari, a form of Persian, and Pashto is the second major language. Its historic sites include the Great Mosque of Herat, the Herat Citadel and the Musalla Complex.
herbert-kitchener: Horatio Herbert Kitchener was born on 24 June 1850 at Gunsborough Villa, north of Listowel in County Kerry, Ireland. His father was an army officer who had recently sold his commission and bought land in Ireland, and his mother, Frances Anne Chevallier, was of French Huguenot descent. In 1874, at 24 and an officer of the Royal Engineers, he joined Claude R. Conder on the Palestine Exploration Fund's survey of western Palestine. They worked there until 1877, with a brief return in 1875 after an attack at Safed. The survey was published in eight volumes, and Kitchener wrote part of the first three. He was fluent in Arabic.

In January 1883 Kitchener was sent to Egypt to take part in rebuilding the Egyptian Army, and in 1884 he took part in the failed Nile expedition to relieve Charles George Gordon in the Sudan. In 1896 Prime Minister Lord Salisbury, fearing the French expedition of Jean-Baptiste Marchand would take the Sudan, ordered him to invade northern Sudan. Kitchener was credited with winning the Battle of Omdurman in 1898 and securing control of the Sudan, and was made Baron Kitchener of Khartoum.

In the Second Boer War he arrived in South Africa in December 1899 as chief of staff to Lord Roberts and succeeded him as commander-in-chief when Boer forces had turned to guerrilla fighting. British forces then imprisoned Boer and African civilians in concentration camps. Kitchener also signed the death warrants of Harry Morant and Peter Handcock, executed on 27 February 1902 for killing prisoners. From 1902 to 1909 he was commander-in-chief of the Army in India, where he reorganised the army and quarrelled with the viceroy Lord Curzon, who eventually resigned. In 1911 he returned to Egypt as British agent and consul-general.

At the start of the First World War Prime Minister Asquith appointed Kitchener secretary of state for war. He foresaw a war of at least three years, organised the largest volunteer army Britain had seen and expanded the production of munitions. He was blamed for a shortage of shells in the spring of 1915 and was stripped of control over munitions and strategy. On 5 June 1916 he sailed on the armoured cruiser HMS Hampshire for talks in Russia with Emperor Nicholas II.

The ship struck a German mine west of Orkney in bad weather and sank, and he was among 737 who died. Since 1970 new records have led historians to rehabilitate his reputation to some extent, praising his groundwork for munitions production and the raising of the army.
herbert-samuel: Herbert Samuel was born in Toxteth, Liverpool, in 1870. His uncle Samuel Montagu founded the bank of that name. He was educated at University College School in Hampstead and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he renounced all religious belief in 1892, influenced by Charles Darwin. He nonetheless remained a member of the Jewish community to please his wife and kept the Sabbath and Jewish food laws at home for hygienic reasons.

After two unsuccessful general elections he was elected for the Liberals at the Cleveland by-election of November 1902. In 1909 Prime Minister H. H. Asquith brought him into the Cabinet, and he served as Postmaster General, President of the Local Government Board and Home Secretary. He resigned in December 1916 when Lloyd George replaced Asquith.

In January 1915 Samuel circulated to his Cabinet colleagues a memorandum, The Future of Palestine, proposing that Britain take Palestine to protect the Suez Canal and make it a home for the Jewish people. The final version of March 1915 ruled out an immediate Jewish state and insisted on equal treatment for non-Jews. His ideas influenced the Balfour Declaration. On 23 October 1918 he moved the motion that allowed women to stand for Parliament, which passed by 274 votes to 25.

Appointed High Commissioner for Palestine in 1920, before the League of Nations had approved the mandate, he served until 1925. Zionists welcomed the appointment, while the military government under Edmund Allenby and Louis Bols called it highly dangerous. Samuel tried to mediate, slowing Jewish immigration and seeking Arab participation, but refused the Arabs any power to stop immigration or land purchase. He recognised Hebrew as one of three official languages and chose Haj Amin al-Husseini as Grand Mufti of Jerusalem.

Samuel returned to the Commons in 1929 and led the Liberal Party from 1931 to 1935, serving as Home Secretary in the National Government from 1931 to 1932. The Liberal ministers resigned in October 1932 over tariffs, and in November 1933 he and most Liberal MPs crossed the floor to oppose the government. Seats fell from 59 to 21 under his leadership. He became Viscount Samuel in 1937 and led the Liberals in the House of Lords from 1944 to 1955. He died on 5 February 1963. Neither Zionist historians nor Arab nationalists remember his Palestine years kindly, a judgement the historian Wasserstein finds mistaken on both sides.
herbert-spencer: Spencer was born in Derby on 27 April 1820. His father, William George Spencer, a religious dissenter, ran a school based on the teaching methods of Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi and served as secretary of the Derby Philosophical Society, founded in 1783 by Erasmus Darwin. Through its members Spencer met pre-Darwinian ideas of biological evolution, particularly those of Erasmus Darwin and Jean-Baptiste Lamarck. His uncle, the Reverend Thomas Spencer, taught him some mathematics, physics and Latin, and passed on firm free-trade and anti-statist views. Otherwise Spencer was an autodidact.

He worked as a civil engineer during the railway boom of the late 1830s while writing for radical provincial journals. While sub-editor of The Economist from 1848 to 1853 he published Social Statics, in which he predicted that humanity would become adapted to life in society and that the state would wither away. Through the publisher John Chapman's salon he knew John Stuart Mill, Harriet Martineau, George Henry Lewes and Mary Ann Evans, and he introduced Thomas Henry Huxley, who became a lifelong friend. Lewes and Evans acquainted him with Auguste Comte's positivism, from which he strongly dissented.

Spencer set out his evolutionary view in the essay Progress: Its Law and Cause in 1857. He held that all structures in the universe develop from a simple, undifferentiated sameness to a complex, differentiated variety, a law he applied to stars, organisms, societies and the human mind. His agnosticism won him notoriety, though he said he wanted to reconcile science and religion.

In his last decades Spencer was lonely and disillusioned. He never married and after 1855 was a lifelong hypochondriac. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1902, which went to Theodor Mommsen, and he died on 8 December 1903 at the age of 83. By the 1870s and 1880s he may have been the only philosopher to sell over a million copies in his own lifetime, yet his influence declined sharply after 1900. His name is often linked with Social Darwinism, although such themes are absent from his sociological works, and libertarians have claimed him as a precursor.
herceg-novi: Herceg Novi lies at the western entrance to the Bay of Kotor in the Coastal region of Montenegro, at the foot of Mount Orjen. Its municipality stretches from Prevlaka to the Verige strait, with an almost unbroken string of towns along the coast. The climate is humid subtropical, with much more rain in winter than summer, and the town has about 200 sunny days a year. The name appears in several languages: Castelnuovo in Italian, Neókastron in Greek and Kala-i Novi in Ottoman Turkish, all meaning new castle.

Finds from the Luštica peninsula and the Vranjaj cavern show that the area was settled in the Neolithic and early Bronze Age. Rome ruled it from the 3rd century BCE, after its victory over the Illyrians, and the Eastern Roman Empire afterwards. Slavic tribes settled in the 7th century, and the district of Dračevica later passed through the Principality of Travunija, the Kingdom of Serbia and the Balšić family.

In 1382 King Tvrtko I of Bosnia built a fortress on the site of a small fishing village. Bosnia's coast from the Neretva to the Bay of Kotor lacked a significant port, and Tvrtko, pressed by the War of Chioggia and a Ragusan embargo, wanted a new salt-trading centre. The fortress was named for Saint Stephen, but it was soon known as Novi. It passed to Duke Sandalj Hranić of the Kosača family, and then to his nephew Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, who made it his winter seat; his title herceg gave the town its present name.

The Ottomans held the town until 1687, apart from 1538–1539, when the Spaniards held it before they were defeated in the Siege of Castelnuovo. The Ottomans built the Kanli Tower, and an earthquake devastated the town in 1608. In 1687 the Republic of Venice took it under Girolamo Corner and placed it in Albania Veneta. Habsburg Austria annexed it in 1798, Russia occupied it in 1806–1807, and France took over in 1807, joining it to the Illyrian Provinces in 1809. Austria held the Bay of Kotor until 1918.

The municipality had 30,864 residents at the 2011 census. The Old Town keeps the Forte Mare fortress and the Kanli Tower, a clock tower built by the Austrians in the 19th century, and several Serbian Orthodox churches and monasteries, among them the Savina Monastery. The town was once a Catholic bishopric and remains a titular see, Novi. It is known as a spa and holiday destination.
herculaneum: Dionysius of Halicarnassus states that the Greek hero Heracles founded the town, while Strabo says the Oscans founded the first settlement. The town sided with the Allies against Rome in the Social War of 91–88 BCE and was defeated by Titus Didius, a legate of Sulla, and in 89 BCE it became a Roman municipium.

Smaller than Pompeii, with about 5,000 people, Herculaneum was wealthier. It flourished as a seaside retreat for the Roman elite, with a dense cluster of luxurious houses. The Villa of the Papyri, built on four terraces on the shore, is thought to have belonged to the consul Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, Julius Caesar's father-in-law.

The course of the eruption is reconstructed from excavation and from two letters of Pliny the Younger to Tacitus. Vesuvius began to throw out material at about one in the afternoon of the first day. The winds blew towards the south-east, so Pompeii received most of the fall, while only a few centimetres of ash fell on Herculaneum, which lies west of the mountain. The ash led most inhabitants to flee. At one in the morning the eruptive column collapsed, and the first pyroclastic surge swept through the town at about 160 km/h.

Six flows and surges buried the town to about 20 metres. In some areas they left buildings and objects almost intact; elsewhere they knocked down walls. Intense heat, of at least 250 °C, rather than suffocation, is now thought to have killed people within ten kilometres.

According to the usual account the town was found by chance in 1709, when a well was being dug; the Prince d'Elbeuf tunnelled from its bottom and reached a theatre. Regular excavation began in 1738 under Charles III of Spain, and the publication of Le Antichità di Ercolano influenced early Neoclassicism. Work stopped in 1762 after Winckelmann criticised its treasure-hunting methods, and Pompeii, covered by only four metres of material against twenty, drew attention away.

Between 1752 and 1754 workmen recovered blackened papyrus scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri. In 1980–1981 hundreds of skeletons were found in the boat houses by the ancient shore, showing that many people had not escaped. More than three quarters of the town remains buried, and the modern towns of Ercolano and Portici lie above it.
herero-and-nama-genocide: The Bantu-speaking Herero reached present-day Namibia from the north as early as the 12th century and lived mainly as cattle pastoralists. In the 19th century they fought over grazing and water with neighbouring Khoikhoi groups, among them the Nama. In 1884 the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck claimed Namibia. Settlers arrived in numbers from the mid-1890s, and under the governor Theodor Leutwein the colonial administration used treaties and force to reduce the indigenous peoples to a servile labour reserve. A rinderpest epidemic killed most Herero cattle.

A central Herero grievance was a judicial system under which several Africans could be executed for the death of a white person, while settlers could kill Africans with near impunity. The Herero chief Samuel Maharero launched the uprising on 12 January 1904. Between 123 and as many as 160 Germans were killed, mostly farmers and traders, while women, children and missionaries were generally spared.

Lothar von Trotha arrived on 11 June 1904 with orders from Kaiser Wilhelm II to crush the rebellion by all means necessary, and replaced Leutwein as military commander. The Herero were surrounded and routed at the Battle of Waterberg in August. They fled into the Omaheke Desert, where a majority died of thirst, starvation or small-scale massacres; some water sources were guarded and others poisoned. Trotha ordered the execution of all Herero men, and in practice women and children were killed as well. About 40,000 Herero died in the desert.

Wilhelm II ordered the expulsion and extermination policy abolished, and surviving Herero were imprisoned in concentration camps, the main ones at Windhoek, Okahandja, Karibib, Swakopmund and Lüderitz. Around half of those captured died of disease, malnourishment and overwork, and three quarters of the prisoners were women and children. The Nama, who had at first fought alongside the Germans, revolted in September 1904 under Hendrik Witbooi. Trotha issued a second extermination order on 22 April 1905 but offered surrender to the Nama, and most of those who surrendered died in the camps. The fighting lasted until 1908.

Between 40,000 and 80,000 Herero, 80 per cent of their prewar population, and about 10,000 Nama, half of theirs, died. Around 1,000 Herero, Samuel Maharero among them, fled to Bechuanaland. Survivors were dispersed to farms and ranches to work for German farmers. Historians who follow scholarly norms do not dispute that a genocide took place, and Horst Drechsler was the first historian to argue it, in the 1960s. Germany acknowledged in 2015 that a genocide had been committed.
herero-people: The Herero, or Ovaherero, speak Otjiherero, a Bantu language of the Niger–Congo family. Unlike most Bantu, who are primarily subsistence farmers, they are traditionally pastoralists. In the 15th century the Herero migrated to what is now Namibia from the east and established themselves as herdsmen.

Early in the 19th century the Nama from South Africa, who already had some firearms, entered the land, followed by white merchants and German missionaries. The Nama at first displaced the Herero, and bitter warfare between the two groups lasted for much of the century, before a period of cultural exchange. The death of Tjamuaha in 1861 led to hostilities with the Nama and made unity necessary, and on 15 June 1863 at Otjizingue the clans elected Maharero commander-in-chief. He later became the first Paramount Chief.

In 1883 the merchant Franz Adolf Eduard Lüderitz made a contract with local elders that later became the basis of German colonial rule, and the territory became German South West Africa. Disputes over land and water arose, as did legal discrimination against the native population. Between 1893 and 1903 Herero and Nama land and cattle were progressively taken by settlers, and in 1903 the Herero learned that they were to be placed in reservations. Samuel Maharero, who had become Paramount Chief in 1892 with the aid of the German governor Theodor Leutwein, led a rising on 12 January 1904, which at first had success.

General Lothar von Trotha took command in May 1904. In August the Herero were surrounded, with one route of escape into the desert, and were prevented from reaching waterholes; starvation followed. Von Trotha called the conflict a race war and issued an order that every Herero within the German borders would be shot. Roughly 80,000 Herero lived in the colony at the start of German rule; after the revolt about 15,000 remained, and about 65,000 had been killed. Survivors were held in concentration camps until 1915, and Samuel Maharero fled to Bechuanaland.

Cattle are the mainstay of the Herero economy and a symbol of wealth. Men herd and trade cattle, while women milk them and prepare sour milk, called omaere. The Herero have a double descent system: a person traces heritage through the mother's lineage, the eanda, while clan leadership passes through the father's lineage, the oruzo. Most Herero today are Christians.

Women wear the long, voluminous dresses, called ohorokova, adopted from German missionaries in the late 19th century, with the horned headdress, the otjikaiva, which honours cattle. On ceremonial occasions men wear military-style dress, including peaked caps and epaulettes, to honour fallen ancestors.
herge: Georges Prosper Remi was born on 22 May 1907 in Etterbeek, a suburb of Brussels, to a lower-middle-class family: his father Alexis Remi was a Walloon who worked in a confectionery factory, and his mother Elisabeth Dufour was Flemish. His first language was French, but he also learned Dutch. His pen name, Hergé, is the French pronunciation of his reversed initials, RG. He began his career contributing illustrations to Scouting magazines, and in 1926 started his first comic series, The Adventures of Totor, for Le Boy-Scout Belge.

Working for the conservative Catholic newspaper Le Vingtième Siècle, Hergé created The Adventures of Tintin in 1929 on the advice of its editor, Norbert Wallez. The early albums, Tintin in the Land of the Soviets, Tintin in the Congo and Tintin in America, were designed as conservative propaganda for children. From 1934, influenced by his friend Zhang Chongren, he put far more emphasis on background research. Casterman began publishing the albums in book form from the volume of Cigars of the Pharaoh, and Hergé also produced Quick and Flupke and The Adventures of Jo, Zette and Jocko. All were drawn in his distinctive ligne claire style.

After the Allied liberation of Belgium in 1944, the newspaper Le Soir, in which Tintin had appeared during the German occupation, was shut down, and its staff, including Hergé, were accused of collaboration. He was arrested on 3 September 1944 and was arrested on three further occasions, spending one night in jail. No charges were brought, but he faced accusations of being a traitor and collaborator for years afterwards. In 1946 he founded Tintin magazine with Raymond Leblanc, and in 1950 he established Studios Hergé, whose staff included Bob de Moor and Jacques Martin.

Hergé died on 3 March 1983. His work has been widely praised for its clarity of draughtsmanship and its meticulously researched plots, and he remains a strong influence on comics, particularly in Europe. He has also faced repeated accusations of racism, notably over the portrayal of the Congolese in Tintin in the Congo, which was not seen as controversial when it appeared and came to be seen as racist in the later twentieth century. The Hergé Museum, in Louvain-la-Neuve, opened in 2009.
herisau: Herisau lies in the former District of Hinterland, at the crossing point of two major routes through the region, the road from St. Gallen to the Toggenburg and the road from Gossau to Appenzell. It consists of the village of Herisau and scattered hamlets, together with residential and industrial districts. About one third of the population of the whole half-canton lives there. Before 1648 the municipality controlled about twice as much land as it does now, since Schwellbrunn was then part of it.

Herisau was first mentioned in 837 as Herinisauva, and its church is mentioned in 907. The place suffered repeatedly in the struggles with the monastery of St. Gallen. It was destroyed in 1084 during battles around the monastery, and again in 1248 and 1249 when the monastery destroyed it to establish loyalty. In 1401 Herisau joined an alliance with other places in Appenzell during the Appenzell Wars, and between 1517 and 1518 it managed to buy itself free from the monastery.

Herisau was already an important centre of trade and commerce by 1537. Its town hall was built in 1601, and in 1606 the town was largely destroyed by fire. In 1648 Schwellbrunn separated and became an independent village. Between 1798 and 1803 Herisau was the capital of the canton of Säntis.

Herisau is the capital of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden and the seat of its government and parliament, while the judicial authorities are in Trogen. Several buildings are listed as heritage sites of national significance: the central hamlet and the houses around the central square, the Protestant church of 1580, the houses Wetter and zur Rose, both of 1737, the hamlet of Schwänberg, and the government building with the state archive.

The majority of residents speak German. In 2003 Herisau was named Alpine Town of the Year, and with other Alpine towns it takes part in the association of that name, which works to put the Alpine Convention into effect and to achieve sustainable development in the Alpine region.
herman-boerhaave: Herman Boerhaave was born on 31 December 1668 at Voorhout near Leiden, the son of a Protestant pastor. In his youth he studied for a divinity degree and wanted to be a preacher. After his father's death he was offered a scholarship and entered the University of Leiden, where he took his master's degree in philosophy in 1690 with a dissertation on the difference of the mind from the body, attacking the doctrines of Epicurus, Thomas Hobbes and Baruch Spinoza.
He then turned to medicine and earned his doctorate at the University of Harderwijk in 1693, with a dissertation on examining the excrement of the sick as a sign of disease.

In 1701 Boerhaave became lecturer on the institutes of medicine at Leiden, and in 1709 professor of botany and medicine; he improved and enlarged the botanic garden. In 1714, as rector of the university, he succeeded Govert Bidloo in the chair of practical medicine and introduced the modern system of clinical instruction, though a medical historian has said he was neither an innovator of the practice nor an especially energetic practitioner of it. Four years later he was appointed to the chair of chemistry as well. In 1728 he was elected to the French Academy of Sciences, and two years later to the Royal Society of London.

Students came from every part of Europe, and princes sent him pupils. Peter the Great took lessons from him in 1716, and Voltaire and Carl Linnaeus visited him; Linnaeus named the genus Boerhavia for him. In 1729 declining health made him resign the chairs of chemistry and botany.

Boerhaave was influenced by the mechanistic theories of René Descartes and Giovanni Borelli and proposed a hydraulic model of the body, with organs built from pipe-like structures and fluids that must move freely and in balance. He held that anatomy should rest on observation and experiment rather than on the teachings of Galen and Aristotle.

His Institutiones Medicae of 1708 was published in over five languages and went into about ten editions, and his Elementa chemiae of 1732 became a widely read chemistry textbook. A devout Christian, he admired Isaac Newton. He died at Leiden on 23 September 1738 after a lingering and painful illness. His operating theatre there is now at the centre of a museum named after him.
hermann-goring: Hermann Wilhelm Göring was born on 12 January 1893 in Rosenheim, Bavaria. His father, Heinrich Ernst Göring, had been the first governor-general of German South West Africa. His godfather, Hermann Epenstein, a wealthy Jewish physician and businessman, provided the family with a home in Berlin and then with a small castle. In the First World War Göring served in an infantry regiment, then transferred to the air service. He became a fighter pilot, received the Pour le Mérite and was the last commander of Jagdgeschwader 1, the wing once led by Manfred von Richthofen. After the war he worked as a pilot in Denmark and Sweden and married Carin von Kantzow on 3 February 1922.

Göring joined the Nazi Party in 1922 after hearing a speech by Adolf Hitler and took command of the Sturmabteilung in March 1923. He was wounded in the Beer Hall Putsch that year and became addicted to morphine. When Hitler became chancellor on 30 January 1933, Göring was made minister without portfolio and, on 11 April, Minister-President of Prussia and chief of the Prussian police. He oversaw the creation of the Gestapo, which he ceded to Heinrich Himmler in 1934. After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 he called for a crackdown on Communists, and some 4,000 party members were arrested. In 1936 he became Plenipotentiary of the Four Year Plan.

On 1 September 1939 Hitler designated him his successor. After the Fall of France in 1940 he received the specially created rank of Reichsmarschall. His standing declined as the Luftwaffe failed to stop Allied bombing and to supply the forces encircled at Stalingrad, and he devoted his attention to collecting property and art, much of it stolen from Jewish victims of the Holocaust. When he asked on 22 April 1945 to take over leadership of the Reich, Hitler regarded this as treason and ordered his arrest.

Göring supported the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and required the registration of all Jewish property. After Kristallnacht he proposed that Jews be fined one billion marks, and minutes read out at his trial showed his knowledge of and complicity in their persecution. He was convicted at the Nuremberg trials in 1946 of conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. His request to be shot was refused and he was sentenced to hang. On the night of 15 October 1946, before the execution, he died by suicide by taking cyanide.
hermann-hesse: Hermann Karl Hesse was born on 2 July 1877 in the Black Forest town of Calw, in Württemberg. His grandparents served at a Basel Mission in India, and his mother, Marie Gundert, was born at a mission in South India. The family lived in Basel from 1881 for six years before returning to Calw. In 1891 Hesse entered the Evangelical Theological Seminary at Maulbronn Abbey, where a serious personal crisis began. In March 1892 he fled the seminary and was found in a field a day later. After an attempt at suicide in May he spent time in institutions, and in 1893 he passed the examination that ended his schooling.

On 17 October 1895 Hesse began work in a bookshop in Tübingen, and after twelve-hour days he read theology, Goethe, Lessing and Schiller, and from 1895 Nietzsche. In 1904 he married Maria Bernoulli and settled in Gaienhofen on Lake Constance, where he wrote Beneath the Wheel, published in 1906.

When the First World War broke out in 1914 he registered as a volunteer and was assigned to the care of prisoners of war. On 3 November he published an essay, "O Friends, Not These Tones", urging intellectuals not to fall for nationalistic hatred. The German press attacked him, though Theodor Heuss and Romain Rolland supported him. By 1919 his marriage had fallen apart, and he resettled alone in Ticino, moving to Montagnola on 11 May. Siddhartha appeared in 1922. He married Ruth Wenger in 1924, divorced in 1927 and married Ninon in 1931.

Hesse's best-known novels are Demian, Steppenwolf, Siddhartha, Narcissus and Goldmund and The Glass Bead Game, each exploring an individual's search for authenticity, self-knowledge and spirituality. His interest in Eastern religious and philosophical traditions, and in Jungian analysis, shaped his work. He wrote that for different people there are different ways to God. He was widely read in the German-speaking world in his lifetime and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946. His works were little read in the United States when he died in 1962, but in the mid-1960s they became bestsellers there in paperback, a revival credited to their association with themes of the counterculture.
hermann-von-salza: Hermann von Salza was born about 1165 into a dynasty of ministeriales of the Thuringian landgraves, probably at Dryburg Castle in Langensalza. He may have taken part with Landgrave Louis III of Thuringia in the siege of Acre of 1189/91, where the Teutonic Order was founded, and possibly joined the Crusade of 1197 with Landgrave Hermann I.

That crusade was aborted on the death of Emperor Henry VI, after which the Teutonic Knights were re-established as a military order under Grand Master Heinrich Walpot von Bassenheim. The time of Hermann's entry into the Order is unknown. He first appears as Grand Master at the coronation of Count John of Brienne as King of Jerusalem in 1210.

Hermann was the fourth Grand Master of the Teutonic Knights, serving from 1210 to 1239. He was a friend and counsellor of the Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick II and from 1222 represented him as a mediator at the papal curia. Pope Honorius III recognised his capabilities and granted the Order equal status with the Knights Hospitaller and the Knights Templar.

At the request of King Andrew II of Hungary, Hermann placed Teutonic Knights in the Burzenland in Transylvania in 1211 to defend against the Cumans, but Hungarian nobles complained and the Order was forced to leave by 1225. He accompanied Frederick on the Fifth Crusade against Damietta in 1219, where John of Brienne decorated him for bravery, and later convinced Frederick to undertake the Sixth Crusade.

After returning to Europe he helped to end the War of the Keys and to lift Frederick's excommunication. Konrad I of Masovia then asked him to fight the pagan Old Prussians, and with the approval of Pope and Emperor the knights began their long campaign to Christianize Prussia in 1230. Visits to the Pope or the Emperor brought new privileges and donations, and in 1237 Hermann obtained the incorporation of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword into the Order.

The knights grew dissatisfied at the absence of their Grand Master and recalled him from political life, though he was less successful as a religious leader. He retired to Salerno in 1238 and died there on 20 March 1239. All communication between Frederick II and Pope Gregory IX broke off with his death, which shows how important his mediation had been. A marble bust of him stood in the Siegesallee in Berlin and has been in the Spandau Citadel since May 2009, and a memorial plaque for him is in the Walhalla memorial near Regensburg.
hermeric: Nothing is known for certain about Hermeric before 419, when the bishop Hydatius, who wrote his chronicle around 470, first mentions him as king of the Suebi at Braga, Bracara Augusta. Isidore of Seville, writing two centuries after the events, claims he was king from 406, but the authors on whom Isidore drew do not mention him earlier. Hermeric was a pagan and an enemy of the Roman Empire throughout his life.

Historians reconstruct the movements of the Suevi differently. Thompson reads Isidore as having the Suevi cross the Rhine with the Vandals and Alans in December 406 and settle in Hispania, while Kulikowski argued that they probably stayed in northern Gaul from 407 to 409 and moved to Galicia between 409 and 411. In 411 the barbarian peoples divided Iberia by lot: the west of the province of Gallaecia, with Braga, fell to the Suevi and the east to the populous Hasdingi. Between 416 and 418 the Visigoths under Wallia made war on Hermeric on behalf of Rome.

In 419, after a personal dispute between Hermeric and the Vandal king Gunderic, the Vandals attacked the Suevi and trapped Hermeric in the Narbasian Mountains until the Roman general Asterius intervened. Hermeric stayed peaceful until the Vandals left Iberia for Africa in 429, but in 430 he began to raid Gallaecia. In 431 a Gallaecian named Hydatius appealed to Flavius Aëtius for help, and the comes Censorius was sent in 432. According to Hydatius, the Gallaecian plebs in the better-fortified strongpoints defeated Hermeric's men, inflicting heavy casualties and forcing the release of captured families.

In 435, on episcopal intervention, possibly that of Hydatius, Hermeric made peace with the Gallaecians, and in the same year he negotiated with the western Roman emperor through the Catholic bishop Symphosius. Censorius made a second expedition in 437 with Fretimund. After seven years of illness Hermeric retired in 438 and passed the kingship to his son Rechila. Isidore's story that Hermeric afterwards sent Rechila against Andevotus in Baetica is false, since no contemporary evidence shows that he kept any authority. Hermeric died in 441, and his royal line lasted until 456.
hermes: The earliest written record of Hermes comes from Linear B tablets of the Mycenaean Bronze Age found at Pylos, Thebes and Knossos, where his name appears as e-ma-a, always beside those of goddesses. Later worship of Hermes also took place mostly within sanctuaries dedicated chiefly to goddesses such as Hera and Demeter. The name has long been derived from the Greek herma, a heap of stones, but this is disputed. Hermes began as a god with strong underworld associations, a psychopomp who led souls along the road between the upper and lower worlds. This role widened to roads in general and then to boundaries, travellers, sailors and commerce. He is described as the youngest Olympian and may have joined the Olympian pantheon late.

In myth Hermes is the herald and messenger of the gods, often presented as the son of Zeus and Maia. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the best-known account of him as a divine trickster. He killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus, which earned him the epithet Argeïphontes. He wore winged sandals, and in Roman art a winged cap, and carried the caduceus, a winged staff entwined with snakes. He was also the patron of flocks and shepherds.

His name was given to the herma, first a roadside pile of stones to which each traveller added one. In the 6th century BCE Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, replaced the cairns that marked the midway points between Athenian demes with pillars topped by a bust of Hermes. Such herms stood at crossroads and doorways, served as boundary and grave markers, and were thought to protect a household. Only three temples dedicated to him in Classical Greece are known, all in Arcadia, where Mount Cyllene was among the oldest places of his worship.

In Ptolemaic Egypt Greeks identified the god Thoth with Hermes, and their city Khemenu became Hermopolis. Hermes thereby gained the character of a god of learning and secret wisdom. The Romans adopted him as early as the 4th century BCE under the name Mercury, combining his attributes with those of the Etruscan Turms. After the Christian suppression of pagan worship in the 4th century CE, Christian scholars still treated Hermes Trismegistus as a mortal prophet who had foretold Christianity, and Renaissance philosophers used the Hermetic writings to support a belief in a single true theology shared by all religions.
hermopolis: Hermopolis, or Hermopolis Magna, was a major city of antiquity near the boundary between Lower and Upper Egypt, and its remains lie near the modern town of el-Ashmunein in Mallawi, Minya Governorate. Its Egyptian name Khemenu means Eight-Town, after the Ogdoad, a group of eight primordial deities said to reside there. The name survived in Coptic as Shmun, from which the Arabic al-Ashmunayn comes. The Greeks called it City of Hermes because they identified Hermes with Thoth, the god of magic, healing and wisdom and patron of scribes, whose main cult centre it was.

The city was the capital of the Hare nome, the fifteenth of Upper Egypt, from the Old Kingdom. As a border town it was a place of resort and wealth, ranking second only to Thebes. A castle just south of it collected tolls from river craft from the Thebaid. The dead were ferried across the Nile to the grottos of Beni Hasan. Thoth was represented by the ibis.

In Roman Egypt it became a significant city of the province of Thebais Prima, and a surviving Oxyrhynchus Papyrus of the 3rd century CE indicates that houses of seven storeys stood there. It was an early Christian centre from the 3rd century; the first bishop listed, Conon, dates from about 250, and a tradition holds that the Holy Family found refuge there. The city was abandoned after the Muslim conquest of Egypt, though Arabic papyri from the 8th to 11th centuries refer to it as Ushmun.

The temple of Thoth has left only a portico, a double row of six pillars with architraves of five stones, about 40 feet high with capitals, painted in alternating yellow, red and blue bands; the buildings raised there under the Ptolemies were on a great scale, in an essentially Egyptian style.

Outside the temple precinct stand the remains of a basilica of the 5th century, 55 metres long, with a colonnaded transept ending in exedras. It was found in 1942 by Moharam Kamal and documented from 1987 to 1990 by a Polish-Egyptian expedition. A small open-air museum holds two large statues of Thoth as a baboon worshipping the sun.
hernan-cortes: Hernán Cortés was born around 1485 in Medellín, in Extremadura, to Martín Cortés, an hidalgo of distinguished ancestry but slender means, and Catalina Pizarro; through his mother he was a distant relation of Francisco Pizarro. At fourteen he was sent to study Latin with an uncle in Salamanca. He sailed for Hispaniola in 1504, registered as a citizen of Santo Domingo, received an encomienda and became a notary at Azua de Compostela. In 1511 he accompanied Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in the conquest of Cuba, where he served as clerk to the treasurer and became a magistrate of the second Spanish town.

In 1518 Velázquez put Cortés in command of an expedition to the mainland, then revoked his charter at the last minute. Cortés ignored the order and sailed in February 1519 with about 11 ships, 500 men, 13 horses and a few cannon. On the Yucatán coast he found Geronimo de Aguilar, a Spanish priest who had learned Chontal Maya, and he also used Doña Marina as his interpreter. He allied with some native peoples against others. In mid-August 1519 he marched on Tenochtitlán with 600 soldiers, 15 horsemen, 15 cannons and hundreds of indigenous carriers and warriors, after Moctezuma II had repeatedly refused to meet him.

Cortés's force reached Tlaxcala after the battle of Otumba, having lost 870 men. With their allies and reinforcements from Cuba, they prevailed. Cortés cut off supplies, subdued the cities allied to the Aztecs and built brigantines on the lake. He destroyed the city block by block, and the siege ended in Spanish victory and the destruction of Tenochtitlán. He wrote to Charles V asking to be rewarded rather than punished for mutiny, and received the title of Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca, while the viceroyalty went to Antonio de Mendoza in 1535. From 1524 to 1526 he led an expedition to Honduras, during which Cuauhtémoc was executed.

Cortés returned to Spain in 1541, hoping to answer lawsuits brought by his opponents, and joined the emperor's expedition against Algiers, in which he nearly drowned in a storm. Heavily in debt after financing his own expeditions, he made a claim on the royal treasury in February 1544 and was ignored for three years. He set out for Mexico in 1547 but was taken ill at Seville and died at Castilleja de la Cuesta on 2 December 1547, aged 62. His letters to Charles V, the cartas de relación, are his only surviving writings. Mexico City was built on the ruins of Tenochtitlán, and the Paso de Cortés, the pass between the volcanoes Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl through which he led his soldiers, bears his name.
hernan-siles-zuazo: Hernán Siles Zuazo was the illegitimate son of Hernando Siles Reyes, the last president of the Republican Party, and Isabel Zuazo Cusicanqui, and was raised by his mother. He was wounded and decorated in the Chaco War of 1932 to 1935, then took a law degree at San Andrés University. Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1940, he founded the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR) in 1941 with Víctor Paz Estenssoro and others.

Exiled to Argentina after Gualberto Villarroel was overthrown in 1946, he returned in 1949, was jailed on an island in Lake Titicaca, escaped to Peru and slipped back into Bolivia to take his seat in congress and demand his back pay.

The army refused to recognise Paz Estenssoro's win in the 1951 election, and from 9 to 11 April 1952 the MNR led the Bolivian National Revolution. Siles played a major part while Paz was in exile, and he served as provisional president from 11 to 16 April 1952, then as vice-president. The government introduced universal suffrage, nationalised the largest mines and adopted an agrarian reform.

After his first term, Paz sent him as ambassador to Uruguay and then to Spain. He broke with Paz in 1964 and formed the MNRI in 1971. In 1978 he built the leftist alliance known as the UDP, which led the elections of 1978, 1979 and 1980; the coup of 17 July 1980 kept him from office and he went into exile in Peru.

As president from 6 August 1956 he faced collapsing production and rising inflation. He accepted the United States's Eder plan, cut spending and social programmes in return for aid, and disarmed the worker and miner militias.

Congress elected him again on 5 October 1982, and he took office on 10 October. He restored relations with Cuba in 1983 and extradited the Nazi war criminal Klaus Barbie to France that year. He was abducted for ten hours on 30 June 1984 during a failed military coup. Hyperinflation, strikes led by Juan Lechín and the desertion of his vice-president, Jaime Paz, weakened him, and Congress called early elections. Paz Estenssoro won in 1985. Siles died in Montevideo in August 1996.
hernando-de-soto: Hernando de Soto was born in Extremadura, in what is now the province of Badajoz, to parents who were both hidalgos, nobles of modest means. Badajoz, Barcarrota and Jerez de los Caballeros each claim to be his birthplace; Ursula Lamb considers Jerez most likely, and his will asked that his body be buried there. The region was poor, and young men sought fortune overseas. He sailed to the New World with Pedro Arias Dávila, the first governor of Panama, landing as a teenager in 1514.

De Soto took part in an expedition to Veragua in 1520 and in the conquest of Nicaragua from 1524, where he received an encomienda and an office in León. He became known as a horseman and tactician, and for extorting native villages by seizing their chiefs. He then joined Francisco Pizarro and became one of his captains. At Cajamarca he led one of three mounted groups in the attack on the Inca Atahualpa. During the king's captivity in 1533 he grew friendly with him and taught him chess. He returned to Spain in 1536 with plunder from Peru, entered the Order of Santiago and married Isabel de Bobadilla.

The crown granted him the governorship of Cuba and the right to conquer Florida. With about 620 Spanish and Portuguese men, among them Atlantic Creoles who were enslaved, and with horses and pigs, he landed on the Florida coast in May 1539. He found Juan Ortiz, a Spaniard living among the Mocoso, who served as interpreter in Timucuan-speaking areas. The expedition wintered at the Apalachee village of Anhaica, then went north-east through Georgia and was received by the female chief of Cofitachequi in South Carolina, where it found no gold.

The army crossed the Appalachian Mountains into eastern Tennessee, and reached the Mississippi on 8 May 1541, building flatboats and crossing at night. It then travelled west through Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas. De Soto died of a fever on 21 May 1542 in the native village of Guachoya. He had persuaded local people that he was an immortal Son of the Sun, so his men hid his death, and by one account sank his body in the Mississippi. Luis de Moscoso Alvarado took command, and the survivors built boats and descended the river. The expedition had lost nearly half its men and found neither treasure nor a site for a colony.

The Spanish counted it a failure. Its pigs escaped and became ancestors of feral razorbacks, and clashes it provoked set many peoples against Europeans. Whether it brought epidemics is disputed, since the first documented smallpox epidemic in the south-east dates from 1696. The route is debated beyond Mabila in Alabama, where John R. Swanton and Charles M. Hudson differ.
hero-and-leander: The myth is attested in Ovid's Heroides and in the epic poem of Musaeus, and Virgil's Georgics allude to it. Ovid is credited with the Double Heroides, which treats it in letters 18 and 19, an exchange between the lovers. In the first Leander has been unable to swim to Hero because of bad weather, and her summons to him to make the effort proves fatal to her lover.

Musaeus was a Byzantine poet of the 6th century. Aldus Manutius made his poem one of the first publications of his press at Venice, around 1493. Bernardo Tasso, Boscán and Clément Marot made early translations into Italian, Spanish and French. In the Renaissance the poem was widely believed to be older than Homer, and George Chapman wrote that the dead lovers were the first that ever poet sung.

Hero was a priestess of Aphrodite who lived in a tower at Sestos on the European side of the Hellespont. Leander came from Abydos on the opposite shore. In the usual telling he persuaded Hero with soft words and with the argument that Aphrodite, as goddess of love, would scorn the worship of a virgin. Their secret affair lasted through a warm summer, and as winter and rough weather approached they agreed to part and resume in the spring.

On a stormy winter night Leander saw the lamp on Hero's tower and set out to swim to her, but a strong wind blew out the light, he lost his way and he drowned. Hero threw herself from the tower when she saw his body. Their bodies washed up together on the shore and were buried in a lovers' tomb.

Christopher Marlowe began a long poem on the subject that ends after the two have become lovers, without the swim or the lamp. George Chapman completed it after Marlowe's death, and the result was often reprinted in the first half of the 17th century, in editions from 1598 to 1637. Walter Raleigh alluded to the story, and John Donne summed it up in a two-line epigram. Lord Byron swam the Hellespont in May 1810, inspired by the myth, and wrote of the feat.

Composers and painters returned to it. Peter Paul Rubens painted it in 1604, George Frideric Handel wrote the solo cantata Ero e Leandro in 1707, and William Etty showed Hero dying on Leander's body in 1829. Franz Grillparzer made it a tragedy in 1831, and Keats wrote a sonnet about an engraved gem of Leander in 1817. Lafcadio Hearn noted a Japanese tale of a girl who swims to her lover guided by a lantern, and observed that in the Far East it is Hero who does the swimming.
hero-of-alexandria: Almost nothing is known of the life of Hero of Alexandria, including his birthplace and background. The first surviving mention of him is in the Collection of Pappus in the 4th century, and scholarly estimates of his dates range widely. Alexandria had been founded by Alexander the Great and was by his time a cosmopolitan city of the Roman Empire, its intellectual life centred on the Mouseion, whose members spoke and wrote in Greek. Because some of his writings read like lecture notes or textbooks in mathematics, mechanics, physics and pneumatics, it has been inferred that he taught there.

Many devices are ascribed to Hero, some of them developed from the work of Ctesibius. The best known is the aeolipile, a steam-driven reaction engine; another engine used air heated in a closed chamber by an altar fire to push water from a sealed vessel, and the weight of the water collected pulled a rope that opened temple doors.

He described a coin-operated machine that released a fixed measure of water for ablutions, a force pump used in a fire engine, a fountain driven by its own water pressure, a self-filling wine bowl with a float valve and a wind-wheel that drove an organ. His mechanical theatre ran an entire play of almost ten minutes from ropes, knots and a rotating cogwheel.

In mathematics he wrote a commentary on Euclid's Elements and the Metrica, a work on applied geometry. The Metrica contains an iterative method for square roots, now called Heron's method, and the formula for the area of a triangle from the lengths of its sides, with which his name is chiefly linked.

He also treated a problem of the shortest path between two points by way of a line, from which he drew the principle that light travelling between two points in one medium takes the shortest path. In the Middle Ages Ibn al-Haytham extended the principle, and Pierre de Fermat stated it in a more general form in 1662.

Much of Hero's original writing has been lost. Some works survive in manuscripts from the Byzantine Empire and, to a lesser extent, in Latin or Arabic translations. Historians have sometimes run the aeolipile together with the temple-door engine and claimed that it did useful work, which the sources do not show.
herod-agrippa-i: Herod Agrippa was born around 11 BCE, the son of Aristobulus IV, a child of Herod the Great and Mariamne the Hasmonean. His mother Berenice was a daughter of Salome, sister of Herod the Great, so he descended from both the Hasmonean and Herodian dynasties. His parents named him after Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, a close collaborator of Emperor Augustus. He spent his childhood and youth at the imperial court in Rome, where he became a friend of the princes Claudius and Drusus.

After the death of Drusus he fell into disgrace and returned to Judaea, having squandered much of his fortune on the favour of the freedmen of Tiberius. Around 26 he married his cousin Cypros, and they lived modestly in a fortress at Malatha in Idumea. Their son became Herod Agrippa II. Pursued for debts, he left for Alexandria, borrowed money there, and sailed for Italy in the spring of 36.

In Rome Tiberius made him guardian of his grandson Tiberius Gemellus, but Agrippa courted the other designated heir, Caligula. When Caligula took the throne, Agrippa received the old tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias, with the title of king over Batanea, Trachonitis, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Paneas and Iturea. He travelled to his territories in the summer of 38, passing through Alexandria during a period of anti-Jewish feeling in which he was mocked in a street masquerade. In 40 he gained Galilee and Perea after the disgrace of his uncle Herod Antipas.

Caligula was assassinated on 24 January 41. Agrippa's support and manoeuvres seem to have been decisive in raising Claudius to power, and he was rewarded with Idumea, Judea and Samaria, so that he ruled a realm as large as that of Herod the Great. He interceded with Claudius for the Jews, and edicts confirmed the privileges of the Alexandrian Jews and extended them across the diaspora. His regional ambitions drew the opposition of Gaius Vibius Marsus, governor of Syria, who halted the fortification of Jerusalem on the emperor's orders.

Agrippa died unexpectedly in 44, after about three years as king of Judaea. The cause is unknown and rumours of poisoning circulated; some researchers think Romans worried by his ambitions may have been responsible. Acts of the Apostles tells that after a delegation from Tyre and Sidon called his answer the voice of a god, an angel struck him down and worms devoured him. Claudius did not give the kingdom to Agrippa II but made it a Roman province under the procurator Cuspius Fadus.

Josephus describes him as gentle and generous, and rabbinical sources present him as pious. The pagan inhabitants of Caesarea and Sebaste rejoiced at his death. For many Jews the end of his rule closed hopes of even a symbolic independence, and messianic, anti-Roman movements appeared afterwards.
herod-antipas: Antipas was a son of Herod the Great and Malthace, a woman from Samaria. His date of birth is unknown, but he, his full brother Archelaus and his half-brother Philip were educated in Rome. He was not Herod's first choice of heir. That place went to Aristobulus and Alexander, sons of the Hasmonean princess Mariamne, until they were executed, and to Antipater, who was convicted of trying to poison his father. In Herod's final will Archelaus was to be king, while Antipas would rule Galilee and Perea as tetrarch. The three heirs travelled to Rome, where Augustus largely confirmed the division of territory.

Galilee and Perea were separated by the Decapolis, and both were unsettled. While Antipas was in Rome, dissidents had attacked the palace of Sepphoris, and Quinctilius Varus, the Roman governor of Syria, burned the town and sold its inhabitants as slaves. Antipas rebuilt and fortified Sepphoris and added a wall to Betharamphtha in Perea, later called Livias and then Julias. His main construction was his capital Tiberias on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, named for the emperor Tiberius. Pious Jews at first refused to live there because it was built over a graveyard, so Antipas settled it with foreigners, forced migrants, poor people and freed slaves. His coins carried no images, out of respect for Jewish prescriptions against idolatry.

He divorced his first wife Phasa'el, daughter of King Aretas IV of Nabatea, in order to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother Herod II. According to the Gospels, John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and Antipas had him imprisoned at Machaerus and beheaded. Josephus says instead that John's influence made Antipas fear rebellion. In Luke's account Pilate, learning that Jesus was a Galilean, sent him to Antipas, who questioned and mocked him and sent him back. Some scholars doubt that this trial took place.

The divorce added to disputes with Aretas over the border, and in a war around 36 Antipas's army was defeated. Tiberius ordered a counter-offensive under Lucius Vitellius, but it was abandoned when Tiberius died in March 37.

Antipas's nephew Agrippa, brother of Herodias, became a friend of Caligula and received Philip's former tetrarchy with the title of king in 37. According to Josephus, Herodias urged Antipas to ask for the title of king too, but Agrippa accused him before Caligula of conspiring with Sejanus and with King Artabanus. In the summer of 39 Antipas was exiled and his territory passed to Agrippa. Josephus names Lugdunum in Gaul and, elsewhere, Hispania as the place. He died in exile at an unknown date.
herod-archelaus: Herod Archelaus was the son of Herod the Great and Malthace the Samaritan, brother of Herod Antipas and half-brother of Herod II. His name means leading the people. Shortly before his death, according to Josephus, Herod the Great had been involved in a religious crisis: he had placed a golden eagle over the Temple entrance, which was seen as blasphemous, and it was chopped down with axes. Two teachers and about 40 youths were arrested for the act and burned. Archelaus came to power at his father's death in 4 BCE, and ruled over one half of his father's territories.

Josephus describes Archelaus before the Passover of 4 BCE, dressed in white and seated on a golden throne. He appeared kind to the people of Jerusalem, who wanted lower taxes and an end to the imprisonment of Herod's enemies. The crowd then demanded punishment for those who had ordered the deaths of the two teachers and 40 youths, and the replacement of Herod's High Priest by one of greater piety and purity. Archelaus agreed to the latter and asked for moderation until Augustus confirmed him as king.

As the crowd in the Temple area grew threatening, he sent a general and a tribune to reason with them; they were stoned, and many were killed. After midnight Archelaus sent the whole army into the city, and Josephus records a death toll of 3000. Passover was cancelled. The army proclaimed him king, but he declined the title until Augustus had heard his claims, and he sailed to Rome. There his brother Antipas accused him over the uproar and disputed the succession, relying on an earlier will. Nicolaus of Damascus argued for Archelaus, and Augustus divided the kingdom, giving him Judea with the title of ethnarch.

Archelaus divorced his first wife, Mariamne, to marry Glaphyra, the widow of his brother Alexander. Her second husband, Juba, king of Mauretania, was still alive, and his subjects complained to Augustus that the marriage broke the Mosaic law. Archelaus fell into disrepute and was deposed in the tenth year of his rule and banished to Vienne in Gaul. His lands became the Roman province of Judaea.

Archelaus appears in the Gospel of Matthew, in which Joseph, returning from Egypt, hears that Archelaus rules Judaea and is afraid to go there, and turns aside to Galilee; this is Matthew's explanation of why Jesus grew up in Nazareth. Some interpreters think the opening of the parable of the minas in the Gospel of Luke refers to his journey to Rome, while others see a later adaptation in oral tradition.
herod-the-great: Herod was born in Idumea, south of Judea, the second son of Antipater the Idumaean, a high-ranking official under the ethnarch Hyrcanus II, and Cypros, a Nabatean princess from Petra. His father was by descent an Edomite, and his ancestors had been forcibly converted to Judaism. Herod was raised as a Jew. Historians dispute his ethnic background: Strabo held that the Idumaeans were of Nabataean origin, while others argue that the Edomites were not Arab. Josephus, whose works record many details of his life, made him a descendant of the Hasmoneans.

Judea had been ruled by Hasmonean kings from 140 until 63 BCE, when Pompey's conquest made them clients of Rome. Herod's war against the Hasmonean Antigonus began in 39 BCE, and after the conquest of Jerusalem Mark Antony executed Antigonus. Herod ruled under Roman overlordship until his death and established the Herodian dynasty. In 30 BCE Octavian confirmed him as King of Judea at Rhodes.

His most ambitious project was the expansion of the Second Temple in Jerusalem, begun in 20-19 BCE, for which he employed 1,000 priests as masons and carpenters to comply with religious law. It was destroyed in 70 CE, and only the retaining walls remain, including the Western Wall. He also built the fortresses of Masada and Herodium and founded Caesarea Maritima. Late in his reign he had his sons Alexander and Aristobulus tried before a Roman court at Beirut, and they were executed. The Gospel of Matthew describes him ordering the killing of all boys of two and under in Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents.

Herod died in Jericho after a painful illness. Josephus says the pain led him to attempt suicide by stabbing, and that his cousin stopped him. Most 20th-century scholarship followed Emil Schürer's chronology of 1896 in dating his death to 4 BCE. Josephus says he was buried at Herodium, and in 2007 a team led by Ehud Netzer announced the discovery of a tomb there, with a broken sarcophagus but no remains.

Augustus respected Herod's will and divided the kingdom among three sons. Herod Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea, Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea, and Philip tetrarch of the lands north and east of the Jordan.
herodias: Herodias was the daughter of Aristobulus IV and his wife Berenice, and a full sister of Herod V, king of Chalkis, and of Herod Agrippa, king of Judea. Herod the Great executed her father and his brother Alexander in 7 BCE and engaged her to Herod II, her half-uncle. Antipater II, Herod the Great's eldest son, opposed the marriage, but he was executed in 4 BCE for plotting to poison his father. Days before he died, Herod the Great divorced Herod II's mother Mariamne and dropped her son from the line of succession.

Herodias and Herod II had a daughter, Salome. The Gospels of Matthew and Mark name her husband Philip, but many scholars regard this as an error, since Josephus names him Herod and the Gospel of Luke drops the name Philip. Herodias later divorced him while he was alive, which Josephus says confounded the laws of the country, and she married his half-brother Herod Antipas.

Antipas divorced his first wife Phasaelis, daughter of King Aretas IV of Nabatea, in order to marry her. According to Matthew and Luke it was this proposed marriage that John the Baptist publicly criticised. The divorce also added a personal grievance to earlier disputes between Antipas and Aretas over territory on the border of Perea and Nabatea. Aretas sent an army against him with a disastrous result for Antipas, and a Roman counter-offensive ordered by Tiberius was abandoned on the emperor's death in 37 CE. In 39 CE his nephew Agrippa I accused Antipas of conspiracy against the emperor Caligula, who exiled him to Gaul. Herodias accompanied him there.

In Matthew and Mark, Herodias plays a major part in the execution of John the Baptist: her daughter's dance before Antipas and his guests leads to her request for the Baptist's head. In Mark, Antipas does not wish to kill John, whom he liked to hear preach. Some biblical scholars question whether the Gospels give an accurate account, and some see in the struggle a recollection of the conflict between Ahab and Jezebel and the prophet Elijah.

In medieval Europe her name became associated with beliefs about witches and the supernatural leader they joined at night.
