De trinitate, in twelve books, composed in 359 and 360, was the first successful expression in Latin of the theology worked out in Greek. Some regard him as the first Latin Christian hymn writer. Pope Pius IX recognised him as a Doctor of the Church in 1851, and his feast day is 13 January.
hildburghausen: Hildburghausen lies in the Franconian part of Thuringia, south of the Thuringian Forest, in the valley of the Werra River. The town centre is about 20 kilometres south of Suhl and 20 kilometres north-west of Coburg. It is the capital of the Hildburghausen district.

The settlement of Hilteburgehusin is first mentioned in a deed of 1234, when the Counts of Henneberg sold it to the Prince-Bishops of Würzburg. The Henneberg lords repurchased it in 1316, gave the citizens town privileges in 1324 and had city walls built. In 1353 the estates of Hildburghausen were inherited by the Wettin landgrave Frederick III of Thuringia, and under the Treaty of Leipzig of 1485 they became part of the Ernestine duchies.

The citizens turned Protestant in 1528. The town fell to the newly established Duchy of Saxe-Coburg in 1572 and, when that line became extinct in 1638, passed to the Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg. In 1680 it became the residence of the Ernestine dukes of Saxe-Hildburghausen, which lasted until the duchy was dissolved in 1826, after which the town passed to the Duchy of Saxe-Meiningen. It became part of the new state of Thuringia in 1920.

Among the sights of the town are the ducal palace, built between 1685 and 1695, with a park containing a monument to Queen Louise of Prussia, the old town hall, and a monument to the citizens who died in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71. People born in Hildburghausen include Karoline von Feuchtersleben, who was born in 1774, and the cellist and composer Friedrich Dotzauer, who lived from 1783 to 1860. Others connected with it are Princess Charlotte and Princess Louise of Saxe-Hildburghausen, the publisher Joseph Meyer, who lived from 1796 to 1856, and the geologist Hans Meyer, who lived from 1858 to 1929.
hildegard-of-bingen: Hildegard was born around 1098 to Mechtild of Merxheim-Nahet and Hildebert of Bermersheim, a family of the free lower nobility in the service of Count Meginhard of Sponheim. Sickly from birth, she is traditionally considered their youngest and tenth child, although there are records of only seven older siblings. She said that she first saw what she called the Shade of the Living Light at the age of three, and understood by five that she was having visions.

Her parents offered her as an oblate to the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg. The date of her enclosure is debated: her Vita says she was eight when she was professed with Jutta, daughter of Count Stephan II of Sponheim, but Jutta's enclosure is known to have been in 1112, when Hildegard would have been 14, and some scholars think the two were enclosed together then.

Her three volumes of visionary theology are Scivias, composed 1142 to 1151, the Liber Vitae Meritorum, composed 1158 to 1163, and the Liber Divinorum Operum, begun around 1163 or 1164. In each she first describes a vision and then interprets it in the words of the voice of the Living Light. For Scivias, a contraction of Sci vias Domini, she perceived a command to write what she saw and heard, and the work records 26 visions. She also wrote two volumes on natural medicine, which spring from her work in the monastery's herbal garden and infirmary and from her reading in its library.

Sixty-nine musical compositions, each with its own poem, survive, among the largest repertoires of any medieval composer, together with the Ordo Virtutum, a Latin morality play with 82 songs, which is thought to date as early as 1151 and is not attached to any liturgy. She also invented the Lingua ignota, about 1,000 invented nouns with German and Latin glosses, and an alphabet, the Litterae ignotae; scholars differ on whether the language was meant to bind her nuns together or to serve the abbey more widely.

Hildegard died on 17 September 1179. Her hagiography, the Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, was compiled after her death by the monk Theoderic of Echternach from the Libellus begun by Godfrey of Disibodenberg and the sources Guibert of Gembloux left. Her name appears in the Roman Martyrology from the end of the 16th century, with her feast on 17 September. On 10 May 2012 Pope Benedict XVI extended her veneration to the whole Catholic Church by equivalent canonization, and on 7 October 2012 he named her a Doctor of the Church. Her relics are in the pilgrimage church at Eibingen.
hilderic: Hilderic, born about 460, was the grandson of Gaiseric, founder of the Vandal kingdom in Africa. His father was Gaiseric's son Huneric and his mother was Eudocia, daughter of the Roman emperor Valentinian III and Licinia Eudoxia. Most Vandals were Arians who had persecuted Chalcedonians, but Hilderic favoured Chalcedonianism as the religion of his mother, which made his accession in 523 controversial.

Soon after becoming king, Hilderic had his predecessor's widow, Amalafrida, imprisoned. He avoided war with her brother, the Gothic king Theoderic the Great, only because Theoderic died in 526. His reign was marked by excellent relations with the Eastern Roman Empire; Procopius writes that he was a very particular friend and guest-friend of Justinian, who had not yet come to the throne, and that they exchanged large gifts of money. Hilderic allowed a new Chalcedonian bishop to take office in Carthage, and many Vandals began to convert, to the alarm of the Vandal nobility.

He was at least in his fifties, and perhaps over sixty, when he took the crown. According to Procopius, for that reason he took no interest in Vandal military operations and left them to other family members, of whom Procopius singles out his nephew Hoamer.

On 15 June 530 Hilderic fell victim to a revolt led by his cousin Gelimer, who restored Arianism as the official religion. Gelimer imprisoned Hilderic, Hoamer and Hoamer's brother Euagees but did not at first kill them. Justinian demanded that Gelimer return the kingdom to Hilderic; Gelimer sent the envoys away, blinded Hoamer and confined Hilderic and Euagees more closely, claiming that they had planned a coup against him.

Gelimer answered a second embassy in effect that Justinian had no authority to make such demands. Justinian then ended his war with the Sassanian Empire and prepared an expedition against the Vandals in 533. When Gelimer learned that the Roman army had arrived, he had Hilderic murdered, together with Euagees and other supporters he had imprisoned. A later legend gave Hilderic a daughter, Hildis, who, with her son Halfdan the Old in the same legend, was an ancestor of Ragnar Lodbrok.
hildesheim: Hildesheim lies on the Innerste river, a tributary of the Leine. According to tradition the city was named after its founder Hildwin. It may have been founded when the bishop moved from Elze to the ford across the Innerste, an important market on the Hellweg trade route. The settlement around the cathedral grew quickly into a town, and King Otto III granted it market rights in 983. The present market place was laid out at the beginning of the 13th century, when the city had about 5,000 inhabitants.

Hildesheim obtained city status in 1249 and was then one of the biggest cities in northern Germany. The clergy ruled it for four centuries, until a town hall was built, work on the present one beginning in 1268. It joined the Hanseatic League in 1367. Most of its inhabitants became Lutherans in 1542, and during the Thirty Years' War it was besieged and occupied several times. The Kingdom of Hanover, to which it belonged, was annexed by Prussia after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866.

On 22 March 1945 British air raids bombed the historic centre, which had kept its medieval character, and almost levelled it. Some 29 per cent of the houses were destroyed and 45 per cent damaged, and around 200 of 800 half-timbered houses survived. Most of the major churches were soon rebuilt in their original style, and reconstruction of the historic centre began in the 1980s.

The Romanesque cathedral, with its ancient bronze doors made around 1015, and St. Michael's Church, an early Romanesque church of Ottonian architecture built from 1010 to 1022, are both on the UNESCO World Heritage list. A rose bush on the wall of the cathedral apse, reputed to be 1,000 years old, still flowers. The market place was reconstructed in 1984–90, and the University of Hildesheim was founded in 1978.
hill-forts-of-rajasthan: Rajasthan has over one hundred fortifications on hills and mountainous terrain. The Hill Forts of Rajasthan were first submitted to UNESCO as a serial property of five Rajput forts in the Aravalli Range; Jaisalmer was added later. Rajput builders followed architectural texts that sorted forts by geography, and the earliest literary references distinguish hilltop, water, forest and desert forts. The series was made solely of hilltop forts.

The selection followed four criteria: the fort was adapted to the geography of its hilltop, it was a centre of power, it included sacred ground, and it was designed with an urban settlement. The Archaeological Survey of India's records gave an initial list, of which 54 forts were examined, then 24, then 13. Junagarh Fort, a ground fort, was left out, as was Mehrangarh at Jodhpur: a hill fort, but a citadel for the court with no settlement for civilians.

Chittor Fort, the capital of Mewar, covers a hill 180 metres high and 280 hectares above the Berach River valley. Legend credits it to a local Mori ruler, Chitrangada Mori, or to the hero Bhima, and Buddhist stupas of the ninth century have been found beside the Jaimal Patta lake. Kumbhalgarh, also called the Great Wall of India, was built by Rana Kumbha of the Sisodia clan with the architect Mandan, on the site of an older fort; it holds over 70 Jain and Hindu temples. Amber Fort was begun by Raja Man Singh and expanded by Jai Singh I, until the Kachwahas moved their capital to Jaipur in 1727.

Ranthambore Fort lies in Ranthambore National Park. Its origin is disputed, though a settlement stood there as early as the eighth century and building probably began in the mid-tenth, under the Chahamanas; the Delhi Sultanate briefly captured it in the thirteenth century. Gagron Fort was built in the twelfth century by Bijaldev Singh Dod at the meeting of the Ahu and Kali Sindh rivers, surrounded by water on three sides and a moat on the fourth, and reportedly saw 14 battles and two jauhars of queens. Jaisalmer Fort was built by Rawal Jaisal, a Bhati Rajput, according to legend in 1156, and nearly a quarter of the old city's people still live inside it.
hill-of-tara: The name Tara is an anglicisation of the Irish Teamhair, also called Teamhair na Rí, Tara of the kings. It is believed to come from a Proto-Celtic word for a sanctuary or sacred space cut off for ceremony. The remains of twenty ancient monuments are visible, and surveys have found at least three times as many. The oldest is the Mound of the Hostages, a Neolithic passage tomb built around 3,200 BCE, which held almost 300 burials in about a century and 33 more a millennium later. In the Iron Age large round enclosures were built; the biggest, Ráth na Ríogh, contains the Forradh, with a standing stone believed to be the Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny.

According to legend the Lia Fáil cried out when the rightful king touched it. By the start of Ireland's historical period Tara was the seat of a sacral kingship, but John T. Koch explains that no king was likely to have had enough authority to dominate the whole island before the 9th century. Tara was probably controlled by the Érainn before the Laigin seized it in the third century. Niall of the Nine Hostages displaced the Laigin in the fifth century, and it became the ceremonial seat of the Uí Néill. The kingship alternated between Southern and Northern Uí Néill until the eleventh century, and the annals record a Battle of Tara in 980 between Máel Sechnaill mac Domnaill and Amlaíb Cuarán of Dublin.

United Irishmen camped on the hill during the rebellion of 1798, and British troops defeated them on 26 May. In 1843 Daniel O'Connell held a demonstration there for Irish self-governance that drew over 750,000 people. At the turn of the 20th century British Israelites, who believed the hill held the Ark of the Covenant, dug at the Rath of the Synods, and nationalists including Douglas Hyde, Maud Gonne and W. B. Yeats protested. The Irish government bought the southern part of the hill in 1952 and the northern part in 1972. Tara is a protected national monument in the care of the Office of Public Works, which runs a visitor centre in Saint Patrick's church.
hilla: Hilla lies on the Hilla branch of the Euphrates, about 100 km south of Baghdad. The river runs through the middle of the town, which is surrounded by date palms. It stands in a mainly agricultural region irrigated by the Hilla canal, which supplies crops, fruit and textiles. Babylon lies 5 km to the north, and the ancient cities of Kish and Borsippa are also close. The Arabic name may come from a word for beauty.

A town called Al-Jamain already stood on the site in the 10th century, and the Banu Mazid had settled at nearby Nile in 1014. Sadqa ibn Mansur founded Hilla in 1101 on the west bank of the river, moving from Nile. Bricks taken from Babylon were used for its houses. After the Mongols took Baghdad, a group of the city's scholars, among them Sayyid Majd al-Din ibn Tawus, wrote to Hulagu Khan offering submission. According to the account, Hulagu left local government in the Euphrates region to Ibn Tawus and spared Hilla and the two shrines, so the city kept its centre of learning. The Jalairid state made it a capital around 1410.

Under the Ottomans Hilla became an administrative centre, first a district and later a mutasarrifate, and the Great Hillah Mosque was built in 1713. In 1916 the commander Akif Bey bombarded the city after a revolt, destroying three neighbourhoods; 126 men were executed and many women were taken to Anatolia. British forces occupied Hilla on 9 March 1917. During the uprising of 1920 it became the last British stronghold in the central Euphrates by August, and an assault on it at the end of July failed.

In the 19th century the Hilla branch silted up and much farmland was lost. The Hindiya Barrage, built in 1911 to 1913, diverted water from the Hindiya branch into the Hilla canal and reversed the decline.

Hilla is the capital of Babylon Province, with a population estimated at about 455,700 in 2018. The University of Babylon, founded in 1991, is among the province's five universities. The city was chosen cultural capital of Iraq in 2008. The scholar al-Allama al-Hilli was born there, as were Muhaqqiq al-Hilli and Ibn Tawus. The tomb of the prophet Ezekiel is reputed to lie in the nearby village of Al Kifl.
himachal-pradesh: Himachal Pradesh lies in the western Himalayas and is India's northernmost state. It borders Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to the north, Punjab to the west, Haryana to the south-west and Uttarakhand to the south-east, and it shares an international border with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China to the east. It covers 55,673 square kilometres. The Zanskar range runs in the north-east, the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal ranges form much of the core, and the Shiwalik range forms the south and west. Reo Purgyil, at 6,816 metres, is the highest peak. The name means snowy slopes, from the Sanskrit hima, snow, and acala, slopes or abode.

Tribes such as the Koli, Hali, Dagi, Dhaugri, Dasa, Khasa, Kanaura and Kirata inhabited the region from prehistoric times, and the foothills were inhabited by people of the Indus Valley Civilisation. For most of its history the region was ruled by local kingdoms, some of which accepted the suzerainty of larger empires. Before independence it comprised the hilly regions of the Punjab Province of British India.

After independence the Chief Commissioner's Province of Himachal Pradesh was organised on 15 April 1948 by the integration of 30 small princely states of the western Himalayas with four southern hill states of the Punjab. The State of Bilaspur was merged into it on 1 July 1954. It later became a union territory, hilly areas of neighbouring Punjab were merged into it in 1966, and it was granted full statehood in 1971.

Shimla is the summer capital and Dharamshala the winter capital. The state is divided into 12 districts. Agriculture, horticulture, hydropower and tourism are the main parts of its economy, and its perennial rivers supply hydroelectric plants. Hill stations such as Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala and Dalhousie attract visitors.
himalayas: The Himalayas run west-northwest to east-southeast in an arc 2,400 km long, between the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the south and the Tibetan Plateau in the north. Nanga Parbat anchors the western end, near the northernmost bend of the Indus, and Namcha Barwa the eastern end, near the great bend of the Yarlung Tsangpo. The range is 350 km wide in the west and 151 km in the east. It consists of four parallel ranges from south to north: the Sivalik Hills, the Lower Himalayan Range, the Great Himalayas, which is the highest and central range, and the Tibetan Himalayas. More than 100 peaks exceed 7,200 metres, and the Mahalangur Himal holds four of the world's six highest mountains, including Everest.

The mountains were uplifted after the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. India had begun to split away from Gondwana about 70 million years ago and moved north. Its thick, buoyant continental plate could not subduct, and the upper crust piled up in sheets called nappes. The geophysicist Peter Molnar noted that most of the Himalayas are slices of rock that once were the top part of India's crust.

The Himalayas span Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan, and the sovereignty of the range in Kashmir is disputed. The Indus, the Ganges and the Tsangpo–Brahmaputra rise in the range, and their drainage basin is home to some 600 million people, while 53 million live in the Himalayas themselves. The range holds about 15,000 glaciers and is sometimes called the Third Pole. Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal, is the largest city in the Himalayas. The snow leopard is the main predator at high altitudes, and the red panda lives in the bamboo forests of the eastern Himalayas.

The name comes from the Sanskrit Himālaya, abode of snow. The range has profoundly shaped the cultures of South Asia and Tibet. For Hindus the Himalayas are personified as Himavat, king of the mountains and father of the goddess Parvati, and the temples at Pashupatinath and Muktinath are major pilgrimage places. Muktinath is also a pilgrimage place for Tibetan Buddhists, and Paro Taktsang is where Padmasambhava is said to have founded Buddhism in Bhutan. In Jainism, Mount Ashtapada is where the first tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, attained moksha. The summits of several peaks, including Nanda Devi and Gangkhar Puensum, are off limits to climbers.
himiko: Himiko, also called Pimiko, was a shaman queen of Yamatai-koku in Wakoku, the land of the Wa. Her earliest account is in the Book of Wei of the Records of the Three Kingdoms, a Chinese text compiled about 297, which gives neither her birth date nor her birthplace.

It says the country once had a male ruler, followed by some seventy or eighty years of disturbances and warfare, until the people agreed upon a woman as ruler. Christopher Harding estimates that she came to power about 190 at about twenty years old. The Book of Wei says she was occupied with magic and sorcery and remained unmarried, and that her younger brother assisted her in governing.

After she became queen few people saw her. She lived in a palace surrounded by towers and stockades with armed guards, and one man served her food and drink and carried messages. The historian Akiko Yoshie argues against treating her as a mere religious figurehead, noting her active diplomacy with Wei. Her first recorded embassy went to Daifang Commandery on the Korean Peninsula, which arranged an escort to the Cao Wei court.

The Wei emperor gave her the title Queen of Wa Friendly to Wei and a gold seal with a purple ribbon, with gifts that included one hundred bronze mirrors. Envoys from Daifang brought the decree to Wa in 240, and she sent another embassy in 243. In 247 she reported fighting with the ruler of Kuna, and Wei sent an official, Zhang Zheng, with a decree and a yellow banner.

Her death is generally dated to 247 or 248. The Book of Wei describes a great mound, more than a hundred paces across, raised for her burial. A male ruler placed on the throne was not accepted and fighting resumed until order was restored by installing her thirteen-year-old relative Iyo as queen.

Neither the Kojiki nor the Nihon Shoki names Himiko, though the Nihon Shoki quotes the Book of Wei, and later scholars have compared her with figures of early tradition such as Empress Jingū. Debate over whether Yamatai lay in northern Kyūshū or in the Yamato region began in the Edo period. Many scholars have proposed Hashihaka Kofun in Nara Prefecture as her burial site.
himilco: Himilco, a Carthaginian navigator and explorer, flourished in the early 5th century BCE. Little or nothing is known of his life. He was a contemporary of the Carthaginian explorer Hanno, who travelled south along the coast of West Africa. According to Duane W. Roller they probably belonged to the Magonid family and were perhaps brothers, and Stéphane Gsell, followed by B. H.

Warmington, suggested they were sons of Hamilcar I, who died at the battle of Himera in 480 BCE. The date of Himilco's voyage depends on that of Hanno's, which is itself uncertain but perhaps fell shortly after 500 BCE. His own account, sometimes called the Periplus of the Northern Sea, is lost and survives only in brief notices preserved by Pliny the Elder and Avienus.

Himilco sailed beyond the Pillars of Heracles, today the Strait of Gibraltar, along the Atlantic seaboard, probably reaching Brittany and possibly the British Isles. Scholars debate whether the voyage served Carthaginian trade interests, perhaps a monopoly of the tin and lead trade, or was undertaken independently. Roller suggests he was sent to explore north-western Europe after reports from Tartessos, and perhaps from Greek traders, of wealthy lands beyond the continent that may have included sources of tin. Greek sailors such as the Phocaeans and Massalians had already reached at least Ophiussa, modern Portugal. Whether Himilco knew of those voyages is uncertain, because the Greek sailors kept them secret.

According to Avienus, Himilco reached a coastal zone four days beyond the Pillars of Heracles, used by the fishermen of Gades. The Ora maritima mentions the Oestrymnides, islands rich in tin and lead, and a Sacred Island two days from them, inhabited by the Hierni, with a nearby island of the Albiones. Himilco reported that the sea there could scarcely be crossed in four months, with no breeze, floating seaweed, shallow water and monsters of the deep. Historians think he may have exaggerated the danger to glorify his achievement and perhaps to deter Greek competition.

The Sacred Island may correspond to the ancient Greek name for Ireland, Iérnē, though this remains speculative. Some scholars therefore suggest that Himilco was the first Mediterranean sailor to reach and record Ireland's name, which otherwise does not reappear in surviving literature until the 1st century BCE. Avienus may also have taken the name Albiones from Himilco's report; it is related to Albion, the ancient name for Britain.
himmatnagar: The town was founded by Ahmad Shah of the Gujarat Sultanate, who named it Ahmednagar after himself and established it to keep the Raos of Idar State in check. In 1665 the emperor Aurangzeb, who had reintroduced the jizya in 1658, issued a ferman that forbade Jains and Hindus to close their shops on the festival of Paryushan and ordered that the Kolis of Himmatnagar should not disturb Muslims during their Friday prayers.

When the Marwar dynasty took Idar in 1728, Ahmednagar soon passed into its hands. After Maharaja Shivsing died in 1792, his brother Sangramsing took the town and its surrounding country and, despite the efforts of his nephew Gambhirsing, became an independent chief.

Sangramsing's son Karansing died in 1835, and the British Agent Erskine moved to Ahmednagar to prevent his queens from becoming satis. According to the account given, the dead ruler's sons pretended to negotiate while secretly summoning Bhils and other tribes, and during the night opened a way through the fort wall, so that the queens burned themselves with the body.

The sons fled, later surrendered and agreed terms with the British, and Takhtsing succeeded as Maharaja of Ahmednagar. He was later chosen for the vacant throne of Jodhpur. After a long discussion it was ruled in 1848 that Ahmednagar should revert to Idar State.

In 1912 Sir Pratap Singh, the Maharaja of Idar, renamed the town Himatnagar after Prince Himmat Singh. Under British rule the state belonged to the Mahi Kantha Agency, which later became part of the Western India States Agency. After 1947 Idar State merged with the Union of India. From 1947 to 1956 the area was Idar district of Bombay State, and from 1956 to 1960 Himatnagar was the largest city and administrative headquarters of the Dungarpur district of Rajasthan. Since 1961 it has been the headquarters of Sabarkantha district in Gujarat.

Himatnagar stands on the bank of the Hathmati river. The white sandstone and cement walls of the original fort still surround the heart of the town, though ruined in parts, and gateways such as the Prantij or Ahmedabad gate are examples of Muslim architecture. Other monuments include the Kazi ni Vavdi, a well with inscriptions in Arabic and Devnagri dated to 1417 and 1522, and the Navlakha Kund, a stepped pit with a spring-fed basin that tradition ascribes to a son of Sultan Ahmed. The Maharaja Himmat Singh Fort and the Daulat Vilas Palace survive as palaces.
The 2011 census recorded a population of 81,137. The town is a centre of the ceramics industry of Gujarat and has a railway station and a connection to National Highway 8.
himnusz: The title in Kölcsey's manuscript, Hymnus, is the Latin word for a hymn, which came into Latin from the Ancient Greek hýmnos, meaning song, hymn or ode. As the poem gained acceptance as the de facto national anthem of Hungary, the Hungarian form himnusz took on the meaning of a national anthem. The lyrics are a prayer that begins with the words "God bless the Hungarians" (Isten, áldd meg a magyart). Its full meaning is evident only to those well acquainted with Hungarian history.

Although Kölcsey finished the poem in 1823, it was first published only in 1829, in Károly Kisfaludy's Aurora, without the subtitle that had been part of the manuscript. It appeared in a collection of his works in 1832 with the subtitle restored. A competition for composers to make the poem suitable for singing by the public was held in 1844 and won by Ferenc Erkel, who conducted at the National Theatre. His setting was first performed there in July 1844, then before a larger audience on 10 August 1844. By the end of the 1850s it was customary to sing it on special occasions. The first stanza is sung at official ceremonies.

In the early 1900s members of the Hungarian parliament proposed making it the official anthem within Austria-Hungary, but the proposals never gained enough support. In the 1950s the communist leader Mátyás Rákosi planned to replace it, but the poet Gyula Illyés and the composer Zoltán Kodály, whom he had in mind for the task, both refused. Erkel's setting was officially recognised as the national anthem only in 1989, when the Constitution of Hungary named it. Vörösmarty's Szózat enjoys a nearly equal standing as a de facto second anthem; tradition has Himnusz sung at the beginning of ceremonies and Szózat at the end.
himyarite-kingdom: Himyar's original heartland lay in the southern highlands of present-day Yemen. Until around 110 BCE it formed part of the Qatabanian kingdom, after which it emerged as an independent state with its capital at Ẓafār. Its rulers were associated with dhū-Raydān, and they were first styled kings of Sabaʾ and dhū-Raydān. Himyar conquered Sabaʾ for the first time in about 25 BCE, Qataban in about 200 CE and Ḥaḍramawt around 300 CE. By the late third century it controlled the Sabaean kingdom for good and ruled most of South Arabia, uniting the region for the first time.

The kingdom was a confederation of tribes and a hub of trade linking the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India. Yemen supplied the Roman Empire with frankincense and myrrh, and Pliny the Elder called it one of the richest nations in the world. Himyarite ships regularly travelled along the East African coast. From the mid-fourth century inscriptions record expeditions into central Arabia, and by about 440 Himyar had annexed Maʿadd and placed garrisons there. It kept extensive control of the interior for nearly two centuries.

From the mid- to late fourth century the ruling class adopted Judaism or a Jewish-inflected monotheism. Inscriptions stopped naming polytheistic gods and instead invoked Rahmanan, the Lord of Heaven and Earth, and sometimes the God of Israel. Sources credit the change to Malkīkarib Yuha'min, who reigned about 375–400, while traditional Islamic sources place it under his son Abu Karib. Native Christian kings ruled from 500 to 521–522, and an Aksumite invasion brought Christian rule in the sixth century. Himyar then had an Aksumite-backed regime, and Abraha later sponsored churches and a restored Marib Dam, as an inscription of 548 records. Sasanian intervention brought Yemen under Sasanian influence in 575 or 578.

Himyarite families outlived the kingdom. The aristocratic Dhu'l-Kala and Dhu Asbah led South Arabian contingents in the Muslim conquest of Homs in 638 and made it a centre of South Arabian settlement and political power. Their chiefs supported Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan against Caliph Ali, and their influence waned after the Battle of Marj Rahit in 684 and the death of their leader at the Battle of Khazir in 686. Medieval Muslim genealogists placed Himyar among the southern Arabs descended from Qahtan, and after the spread of Islam in Yemen, Himyarite noble families re-established control over parts of the country.
hindko: The name Hindko means the Indian language, or language of Hind. It refers to the Indo-Aryan speech forms of the northern Indian subcontinent, in contrast to Pashto, the Iranic language of the neighbouring Pashtun people. Another local name is Hindki, and a speaker may be called Hindki, Hindkun or Hindkowan. Like other Lahnda varieties, Hindko derives from Shauraseni Prakrit. It is to some extent mutually intelligible with Standard Punjabi and Saraiki, with more affinities to the latter. It is a polyphyletic label for a diverse group of Lahnda dialects, and in recent decades Hindko-speaking intellectuals have begun to promote it as a separate language.

Varieties of Hindko are spoken in a core area in the district of Attock in the north-western corner of Punjab, and in two neighbouring regions: Peshawar to the north-west and Hazara to the north-east, both in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Hindko of Hazara extends into Azad Kashmir, where it predominates in the Neelum Valley and is locally called Parmi.

The central group includes Kohati, spoken in Kohat, and the closely related Chacchi, Ghebi and Awankari dialects of Attock District. Peshawari, the prestigious urban variety of Peshawar, forms a group of its own, has been influenced by Urdu and Standard Punjabi, and is promoted as a standardised literary language. The dialects of Hazara, called Hazara or Northern Hindko, include Kaghani and Tanoli. Ethnologue divides the continuum into Northern and Southern Hindko. Like other Punjabi varieties, Hindko has a system of pitch accent, commonly called tone, which in Punjabi arose from the loss of voiced aspirates.

Speakers belong to diverse ethnic groups and usually identify by larger families or castes. In Hazara they include Swatis, Yusufzais, Jadoons, Tareens, Sayyids, Awans, Mughals, Tanolis, Turks, Qureshis and Gujars, and many of them are Pashtuns. The most common second language of speakers in Pakistan is Urdu, and the next is Pashto.

Before the partition of British India in 1947 a substantial share of Hindkowans were Hindus and Sikhs, who migrated to India. After their exodus and the influx of Pashtuns into the urban economy of Peshawar and Kohat, there were signs of a shift towards Pashto in those cities. In Hazara, by contrast, Hindko was displacing Pashto among the Swati Pathans. There is a literary tradition based on Peshawari and another based on the language of Abbottabad. In the 2023 census of Pakistan, 5.6 million people declared their language to be Hindko.
hindu-arabic-numeral-system: The system is a base ten positional numeral system built on ten glyphs for the numbers from zero to nine, which allow any natural number to be written as a unique sequence of them. In a more developed form, with a decimal marker, a symbol for recurring digits and a minus sign, thirteen symbols can express any rational number. The glyphs are in principle independent of the system itself.

The glyphs in use descend from the Brahmi numerals and have split into three main families since the Middle Ages: the Eastern Arabic numerals used with the Arabic script, developed mainly in what is now Iraq; the Indian numerals of the Brahmic scripts; and the Western Arabic numerals, developed in al-Andalus and the Maghreb and used everywhere else.

The Brahmi numerals predate the Common Era and replaced the earlier Kharosthi numerals; both appear on the edicts of Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. They were not a positional system with a zero, and had separate numerals for each of the tens. Around 500 the astronomer Aryabhata used the word kha, meaning emptiness, to mark zero in tables, and the 7th century Brahmasphuta Siddhanta shows an advanced understanding of the role of zero. The first dated and undisputed inscription with a symbol for zero is at the Chaturbhuja Temple at Gwalior, dated 876 CE.

The Indian system was taken up in Islamic mathematics in the 8th century. Al-Khwarizmi wrote On the Calculation with Hindu Numerals in about 825 and al-Kindi On the Use of the Hindu Numerals around 830, books principally responsible for its spread through the Islamic world and ultimately to Europe. In the 10th century Abu'l-Hasan al-Uqlidisi was the first to describe positional decimal fractions.

The first mention of the numerals in Christian Europe, from one to nine without zero, is in the Codex Vigilanus, written in 976 by three monks of the monastery of San Martín de Albelda in Spain. Gerbert of Aurillac studied Arab science in the Catalan abbeys between 967 and 969 and, as Pope Sylvester II, introduced an abacus with tokens bearing the numerals. Fibonacci's Liber Abaci brought the method of the Indians, with zero and decimal place value, to the Latin world. European mathematics used the system from the 12th century, and it replaced Roman numerals in common use from the 15th. Adam Ries's book of 1522 did most to teach it to craftsmen's apprentices. China and Japan adopted it only in the 19th century.
hindu-kush: The range is about 800 kilometres long and lies west of the Himalayas, running from central and eastern Afghanistan into north-western Pakistan and far south-eastern Tajikistan. It divides the valley of the Amu Darya, the ancient Oxus, in the north from the Indus valley in the south. Its highest point is Tirich Mir, at 7,708 metres in Pakistan. Numerous high passes, known as kotal, make a network for caravans, and the Salang Pass north of Kabul is the most important in Afghanistan.

The name Hindu Kush is first mentioned by Ibn Battuta in the 14th century, who explained it as Hindu-slayer, because slaves taken from India to Turkestan died in the harsh climate. Other scholars take it as a corruption of Hindu Koh, mountains of India. In the time of Alexander the Great it was the Caucasus Indicus. Its significance was recorded from the time of Darius I of the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander's army crossed it in the spring of 329 BCE.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the region passed to the Seleucid Empire, then around 305 BCE to the Maurya Empire, and around the start of the common era to the Kushan Empire. Buddhism flourished there, with monasteries, trade networks and the rock-carved Bamiyan Buddhas. Kabul fell to the army of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun in 808. The Hindu Shahi dynasty of Kabul later held the range until Sabuktigin conquered its lands west of Peshawar. The people of Kafiristan kept polytheistic traditions until 1896, when Afghans under Amir Abdur Rahman Khan converted them, and the region was renamed Nuristan.

The mountains have long supplied lapis lazuli, mined in the Kowkcheh Valley, and emeralds from the Panjsher valley. Mountain areas are mostly barren or sparsely wooded, with coniferous forests at higher levels. Meltwater from the range feeds the Amu Darya, the Helmand River and the Kabul River, a major tributary of the Indus.
hindustan: Hindustan is the Persian name for India, used at different times for the northern part of the Indian subcontinent and for the whole of it. It comes from the Persian word Hindū, related to the Sanskrit Sindhu, meaning the Indus River. According to Asko Parpola, the Proto-Iranian change of s to h took place between 850 and 600 BCE, so that the Rigvedic sapta sindhava, the land of seven rivers, became hapta hindu in the Avesta. In 515 BCE Darius I annexed the Indus Valley, including Sindh, which Persian called Hindu.

The suffix -stān, meaning a country or region, was added in Middle Persian, probably from the first century CE. The inscription of Shapur I at Naqsh-e-Rustam, from about 262 CE, refers to Sindh as Hindūstān. The Arabic equivalent is al-Hind, which Arab traders used for a much wider region, from the Makran coast to the Indonesian archipelago.

The tenth-century Hudud al-Alam defined Hindustan as roughly the subcontinent, with the Indus as its western limit and Kamarupa, present-day Assam, as its eastern. With the Turko-Persian conquests from the eleventh century the name took a narrower sense. In the early eleventh century a satellite state of the Ghaznavids in the Punjab, with its capital at Lahore, was called Hindustan. Once the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was established, north India, especially the Gangetic plains and the Punjab, came to be called Hindustan, while the wider meaning continued beside it.

The Mughals (1526-1857) called their lands Hindustan, and the word grew as the empire expanded. Their sources also used it for the whole subcontinent, as the Baburnama and the Ain-i-Akbari do. In Mughal sources Hindustani commonly meant the Muslims of Hindustan, and non-Muslim Indians were called Hindus. Prithvi Narayan Shah, who unified Nepal, called his kingdom Asal Hindustan, the real Hindustan, because north India was ruled by the Mughals.

Europeans carried over the double meaning. James Rennel's atlas of 1792, Memoir of a Map of Hindoostan or the Mogul Empire, in fact showed the whole subcontinent. An Anglo-Indian dictionary of 1886 states that in native usage the word had come to mean the region north of the Narmada River, excluding Bihar and Bengal. In the independence movement Indians called their land India, Hindustan and Bharat, and Muhammad Iqbal's song Tarānah-e-Hindī was a popular patriotic anthem. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 the Dominion of India came to be called Hindustan in popular speech.
hipolito-yrigoyen: Juan Hipólito del Sagrado Corazón de Jesús Yrigoyen was born on 12 July 1852, a few months after the Battle of Caseros. His father, Martín Yrigoyen Dodagaray, was a Basque-French immigrant, and his mother, Marcelina Alén Ponce, was a half-sister of Leandro N. Alem. After finishing secondary school in 1869 he entered politics with his uncle Alem in the Autonomist Party of Adolfo Alsina, demanding free suffrage and judicial reform, and he later became a police commissioner in Buenos Aires.

In 1892 Alem and Yrigoyen issued a declaration calling for an armed uprising against the regime, and the Civic Radical Union's convention approved a manifesto describing the government's power as based on fraud and violence. Yrigoyen took part in the radical revolution of 1905, which failed when the revolutionaries could not seize the arsenal.

The Sáenz Peña Law of 10 February 1912 guaranteed secret and mandatory voting for men, and Yrigoyen's activism was the main impetus behind it. He won the first election held under it, on 2 April 1916. As president he held that Argentina should manage its own currency and credit and control its transport, energy and oil. He founded the state energy company YPF, drew up plans for a central bank, placed controls on the railways in British hands and defended non-intervention against the United States in Latin America.

His first term also saw laws on homework and minimum wages in 1918, workers' housing in 1919, rent increases in 1921, and pensions for railway workers. Workers' strikes were violently suppressed in the La Forestal massacre, the Tragic Week and the Patagonia Rebelde, often with the help of the paramilitary Argentine Patriotic League.

Elected again in 1928 after the end of Marcelo Torcuato de Alvear's term, he authorised funds for primary schools and in 1929 an eight-hour working day and forty-eight-hour week. The Great Depression, conservative army officers, and American oil companies that opposed YPF all worked against him, and he survived an assassination attempt on 24 December 1929.

On 6 September 1930 General José Félix Uriburu deposed him in a military coup. Yrigoyen was held under house arrest and confined several times on Martín García Island. He died in Buenos Aires on 3 July 1933 and was buried in La Recoleta Cemetery. He is known as the father of the poor, and supporters saw radicalism as the authentic expression of the nation against an oligarchic regime, while opponents accused him of arrogance toward Congress.
hippias-of-elis: Hippias was born at Elis around 460 BCE and was thus a younger contemporary of Protagoras and Socrates. He lived at least as late as Socrates's death in 399 BCE. He is said to have been a disciple of Hegesidamus. His fellow citizens used his services in political matters, including a diplomatic mission to Sparta.

Like other sophists of his time, Hippias travelled through the towns of Greece to teach and speak in public. He claimed to be an authority on every subject and lectured on poetry, grammar, history, politics and mathematics. His great skill seems to have lain in grand show speeches. Plato has him declaring that he would go to Olympia and give the assembled Greeks an oration on any subject proposed, and Philostratus speaks of several such orations there. No specimen has survived, apart from an epigram preserved by Pausanias.

Most of what is known of him comes from Plato, who portrays him as vain and arrogant. The Hippias Minor shows him as ridiculously vain, and the Hippias Major, whose authorship by Plato is sometimes doubted, puts his presumption in a ludicrous light.

Hippias was learned in rhetoric, philosophy and politics and also in poetry, music, mathematics, painting and sculpture. He boasted of wearing nothing he had not made himself, including his seal-ring, cloak and shoes. A lost work on the victors of the Olympiads placed the victory of Coroebus in 776 BCE and became the basis of all later lists. Plutarch criticised it, saying that Hippias had no authoritative basis for his chronology. A mathematical discovery ascribed to him is sometimes called the quadratrix of Hippias.

Hippias is credited with originating the idea of natural law, which he held to be universal. He also wrote about self-sufficiency as a binding principle. His ideas passed on through Cynicism and Stoicism.
hippias-tyrant: Hippias was born around 570 BCE as the eldest son of Pisistratus, the first tyrant of Athens. When his father was forced to flee to Eretria after offending Megakles, Pisistratus took counsel with his sons, and Hippias proposed that they retake the tyranny. Athens fell to Pisistratus for the third time in 546 BCE. Hippias was supported in the restoration by the family of the polemarch Charmus, an old ally of his father, and Pisistratus gave him Charmus's daughter in marriage.

Hippias succeeded his father as tyrant of Athens in 528 or 527 BCE, when Pisistratus died of old age. He was a patron of poets and craftsmen, and Athens enjoyed prosperity under his rule. His brother Hipparchus, who may have ruled jointly with him, was murdered at the Panathenaic festival in 514 BCE by Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Aristogeiton resented Hipparchus's advances toward Harmodius, and the plotters meant to kill both brothers.

Only Hipparchus died. Hippias's soldiers captured the group, and Aristogeiton was executed after torture while Harmodius was killed on the spot. It was said that Hippias afterwards became bitter and cruel over four years, unlike his moderate father. He executed many citizens, exiled others and imposed harsh taxes.

The Alcmaeonidae, whom Pisistratus had exiled in 546 BCE, were concerned about his alliances with the Persian ruling class and planned an invasion. Cleisthenes, who had been archon in 525/4 BCE, is said to have bribed the Pythian priestess of Delphi to tell the Spartans to liberate the Athenians. After a failed expedition, Cleomenes I of Sparta invaded in 510 BCE and trapped Hippias on the Acropolis, took the children of the Peisistratids hostage and made him leave to have them returned. Power passed to the Athenian magistrates, which began Athenian democracy.

Hippias went to Sigeion, then to Lampsakos and to King Darius in Persia. The Spartans later tried to restore him, but the Corinthians and other allies refused to see a tyranny imposed on a Greek city. He made his illegitimate son Hegesistratus tyrant of Sigeion and railed against the Athenians to Artaphrenes, the governor of Sardis. In 490 BCE he urged Darius I to attack Athens, accompanied the Persian fleet and proposed Marathon as suited to their cavalry. According to Herodotus he dreamt the night before that he lay with his mother, which he took as an omen of a return, but a loose tooth fell out on the beach.

He is said to have died at Lemnos on the way back from Marathon. His five sons joined Xerxes's army in 480 BCE, and the Peisistratids never again had influence in Athens. Building continued under his rule on the temple of Olympian Zeus, which was not finished until Hadrian's time.
hippo-regius: Hippo takes its name from a Phoenician word, probably related to the word for harbour, and Phoenicians from Tyre first settled the town around the 12th century BCE. The Romans called it Hippo Regius, the Royal Hippo, because it was one of the residences of the Numidian kings, and to tell it from Hippo Diarrhytus, modern Bizerte. It lay near the mouth of the river Ubus, now the Seybouse, on the bay that was known as Hippo Bay.

Hippo became a Roman colony that prospered into a major city of Africa Province, and was later included in the Diocese of Africa under Diocletian's reforms. The diocese was established around 250. Councils met there in 393, 394 and 426, and the synod of 393 and the Synod of Carthage in 397 drew up a list of the books of scripture still regarded as the Catholic canon. Augustine of Hippo, a Church Father, served as bishop in his later years.

In 430 the Vandals advanced along the coast and besieged the walled city. Augustine died on 28 August 430, three months into the siege, perhaps from starvation or stress. The Vandals lifted the siege after 14 months, and the peace treaty of 435 acknowledged their possession of the city. King Geiseric made it the capital of the Vandal Kingdom until the capture of Carthage in 439. The Eastern Roman Empire conquered Hippo in 534 and held it until the Muslim conquest in 698.

The Caliphate rebuilt the town in the eighth century, and in the eleventh the Berber Zirids founded the town of Beled el-Anab about three kilometres away. France took it in 1832 and renamed it Bône. Hippo Regius is the ancient name of the modern city of Annaba, Algeria. Some ancient ruins remain, together with a basilica dedicated to St Augustine.
hippocrates: Historians agree that Hippocrates was born around 460 BCE on the island of Kos; other biographical information is likely to be untrue. Soranus of Ephesus, a 2nd-century Greek physician, was his first biographer and is the source of most personal information. Hippocrates is mentioned in passing by two contemporaries, in Plato's dialogues Protagoras and Phaedrus and in Aristotle's Politics.

According to Soranus his father Heraclides was a physician and his mother was Praxitela. He learned medicine from his father and grandfather, and studied other subjects with Democritus and Gorgias. He was probably trained at the asklepieion of Kos, and took lessons from the Thracian physician Herodicus of Selymbria. He taught and practised medicine throughout his life, travelling at least as far as Thessaly, Thrace and the Sea of Marmara.

Hippocrates is credited as the first person to hold that diseases had natural causes rather than being sent by gods. In On the Sacred Disease, on epilepsy, the writer argues that the disease is no more divine than others and that people regard it as divine from ignorance and wonder. Hippocratic medicine held that disease came from environmental factors, diet and living habits, though it also held convictions based on incorrect anatomy and physiology, such as humorism. Its therapy was gentle and passive, resting on the healing power of nature, and it gave weight to prognosis and to careful case histories.

The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around seventy early medical works, written in Ionic Greek and gathered in Alexandrian Greece. Whether Hippocrates himself wrote any of them has not been conclusively answered, and given the variety of subjects and styles the corpus could not have been written by one person. It includes the Hippocratic Oath, Aphorisms and On Airs, Waters and Places, and its works sometimes contradict one another. Very little is known concretely about what Hippocrates himself thought, wrote and did.

Several accounts of his death exist. He died probably in Larissa, at the age of 83, 85 or 90, though some say he lived well over 100. Although he neither founded the school of medicine named after him nor wrote most of the treatises attributed to him, he is traditionally regarded as the Father of Medicine. His teachings were so revered that for a long time they were taken as too great to be improved upon. The Islamic world adopted its methods in the Middle Ages, and after the Renaissance they were revived in western Europe. Clubbing of the fingers is still called Hippocratic fingers, and the Hippocratic Oath is the foundation of later oaths taken by medical graduates.
hippocrates-of-chios: Hippocrates of Chios was born on the island of Chios, where he was originally a merchant. After misadventures, in which he was robbed by either pirates or fraudulent customs officials, he went to Athens, possibly for litigation, and there became a leading mathematician. On Chios he may have been a pupil of the mathematician and astronomer Oenopides of Chios. His mathematics probably shows some Pythagorean influence too, perhaps through contacts between Chios and the neighbouring island of Samos, a centre of Pythagorean thinking, and he has been described as a para-Pythagorean, a philosophical fellow traveller.

His major accomplishment was to write the first systematically organised geometry textbook, the Elements (Stoicheia), setting out basic theorems as building blocks of mathematical theory. It gave mathematicians a common framework to build on. Only one fragment survives, embedded in the work of Simplicius, in which the areas of some lunes, now called Hippocratic lunes, are calculated. This belonged to a programme to square the circle. Hippocrates failed in that, but he was the first to prove an equality of area between a curved shape and a polygonal one. Ferdinand von Lindemann showed in 1882 that the approach could not succeed.

In the century after him at least four other mathematicians wrote their own Elements, improving terminology and logical structure, and his work laid the foundation for Euclid's Elements of about 325 BCE. He is believed to have originated the use of letters for the points and figures of a proposition, as in triangle ABC, and the use of power for the square of a line. He found a way to approach the duplication of the cube, the problem of constructing a cube root, and invented the technique of reduction, which turns a specific problem into a more general one that is easier to solve.

In astronomy he tried to explain comets and the Milky Way. His ideas are not clearly handed down, but he probably thought both were optical illusions, caused by the refraction of sunlight by moisture exhaled by a putative planet near the Sun and by the stars. He also held that light rays originate in the eye rather than in the object seen.
hippodamus-of-miletus: Hippodamus was born in Miletus and lived during the 5th century BCE; his father was Euryphon. Ancient and later writers describe him as an architect, urban planner, physician, mathematician, meteorologist and philosopher. He is referred to in the works of Aristotle, Stobaeus, Strabo, Hesychius, Photius and Theano. Aristotle, in his Politics, records that he had a reputation as a lover of attention: some people thought he carried things too far, with his long hair, expensive ornaments and the same cheap warm clothing worn in winter and summer.

According to Aristotle, Hippodamus was the first urban planner to give attention to the proper arrangement of cities. He laid out the Piraeus, the port of Athens, for Pericles, with wide streets radiating from the central agora, which was generally called the Hippodameia in his honour. He is also said to have built the refounded city of Rhodes in the form of a theatre. In 440 BCE he went out among the Athenian colonists and planned the new city of Thurium, later Thurii, in Magna Graecia, with streets crossing at right angles; for this he is sometimes called Hippodamus of Thurium.

His plans were characterised by order and regularity, in contrast to the intricacy and confusion common to cities of that period, even Athens. The grid plans attributed to him consisted of broad, straight streets cutting one another at right angles, and Miletus offers the prototype, with a wide central area kept unsettled that in time evolved into the agora. His principles were later adopted in Halicarnassus, Alexandria and Antioch. Because rectangular plans were in use among the Greeks as early as the 8th century BCE, he cannot be considered the originator of the concept.

Aristotle treats Hippodamus as the first author to write on the theory of government without any experience of practical affairs. His ideal city was to be inhabited by 10,000 free male citizens, within a total population of 50,000 including women, children and slaves. He divided the citizens into three classes, soldiers, artisans and husbandmen, and the land into sacred, public and private. Aristotle objected that confining arms to one class would lead to the oppression of the others. He also criticised the proposal to reward those who discover something useful to the city, arguing that easy change weakens the force of law. Writings attributed to him include On the State and On Happiness.
hippodrome-of-constantinople: The first Hippodrome was built when the city was still called Byzantium, a provincial town of moderate importance. In 203 CE the Emperor Septimius Severus rebuilt the city and gave it a hippodrome. After his victory at the Battle of Chrysopolis, Constantine the Great refounded Byzantium in 324 as Nova Roma, a name that soon gave way to Constantinople, and he renovated the Hippodrome.

It is estimated to have been about 450 m long and 130 m wide, with starting gates, the carceres, at the northern end and the curved tribune, the sphendone, at the southern end of the U-shaped track. The stands held around 100,000 spectators. The emperor's lodge, the Kathisma, could be entered directly from the Great Palace by a passage reserved for the imperial family.

Through the Byzantine period the Hippodrome was the centre of the city's social life, and large sums were wagered on the races. Four teams took part at first, each backed by a political party: the Blues, the Greens, the Reds and the Whites. The Reds and Whites weakened and were absorbed by the other two. The meetings were among the few occasions on which the emperor and ordinary citizens shared one place, and political matters were often discussed there.

The rivalry of the Blues and Greens often merged with political or religious disputes and sometimes produced riots amounting to civil war. The worst were the Nika riots of 532, in which an estimated 30,000 people were killed and many buildings, including the second Hagia Sophia, destroyed. The last recorded race took place in 1200, and the sack of the city in the Fourth Crusade of 1204 ruined the Hippodrome. The Ottomans, who took the city in 1453, had no interest in chariot racing, and the site served as a source of building stone.

The site is now Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul. The original track lies some 2 m below the present surface. Three monuments of the central barrier survive in excavated pits. The Serpent Column is the base of a tripod cast to celebrate the Greek victory over the Persians in the 5th century BCE, which Constantine ordered moved from Delphi; its heads and top third were destroyed in 1700. The Obelisk of Thutmose III, first raised at Karnak about 1490 BCE, was brought by Theodosius the Great in 390, and its top section stands on a marble pedestal. The Walled Obelisk was built in the 10th century.
hippolytus-son-of-theseus: Hippolytus, in Ancient Greek Hippolutos, was in Greek mythology the son of Theseus and an Amazon, either Hippolyta or Antiope. His name means unleasher of horses, and it may be understood ironically, since the element -lytos suggests something that may be undone or destroyed, giving the sense destroyed by horses. He is a hunter and sportsman, more inclined to hunting than to marriage and love. He worships Artemis, the virgin huntress, scrupulously and refuses to honour Aphrodite. Offended, Aphrodite causes his stepmother Phaedra to fall in love with him. When he rejects her advances, events begin that lead to his death in a fall from his chariot.

In the tragedy of Euripides, Phaedra, the second wife of Theseus, is cursed by Aphrodite and falls so ardently in love that she becomes physically ill and decides to end her life. Her nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus and urges him to return her love, but he responds only with horror and disgust. In despair Phaedra hangs herself and leaves a note accusing him of raping her. Theseus, furious, uses one of three wishes given him by his father Poseidon to call for his son's death. Hippolytus has gone hunting, and Poseidon sends a sea-monster that terrifies his chariot horses. They become uncontrollable and hurl him out, and he is dragged, entangled in the reins, and fatally wounded.

Artemis then reconciles father and son by telling Theseus that Phaedra's accusation was false. She comforts the dying Hippolytus with a promise that he will be the subject of religious practice, so that his memory will live for ever, and she assigns a band of Trozenian maidens to preserve the story of Phaedra and Hippolytus in a ritual song.
Other writers told versions of the story, among them Seneca the Younger in Phaedra, Ovid in the Metamorphoses and Heroides, Jean Racine in Phèdre and Thomas Sturge Moore in Aphrodite against Artemis.

In Italy, in a later phase of Hellenization, Virbius, one of two figures tied to the ancient cult of Diana Nemorensis, was assimilated to Hippolytus. The version told by Ovid and Pausanias differs from that of Euripides: Asclepius brought Hippolytus back from the dead, but he refused to forgive Theseus, went to Italy, became king of the Aricians and named a city after Artemis. He ruled as Virbius from inside the shrine of Diana, which forbade horses to enter. His cult held that Artemis asked Asclepius to resurrect him because he had vowed chastity to her, and his followers cut off a piece of their hair to dedicate their chastity to him before marriage.
hipponax: Ancient authorities record only the barest details of the life of Hipponax, sometimes contradicting each other. He is dated to 541 or 540 BCE, a date supported by Pliny the Elder, who places the sculptors Bupalus and Athenis, his targets, in his lifetime. The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda records that he was expelled from Ephesus by the tyrants Athenagoras and Comas and settled in Clazomenae. According to Athenaeus he was small, thin and surprisingly strong, and tradition made him ugly. One scholiast reports that he sought to marry the daughter of Bupalus and was rejected, and that when Bupalus portrayed him as ugly Hipponax retaliated in verse so savage that Bupalus hanged himself. The story resembles that of Archilochus, which invites scepticism.

Hipponax composed within the iambic tradition, which in the work of Archilochus a century earlier seems to have been ritualised abuse tied to the cults of Demeter and Dionysus, and in his day served for entertainment. Unlike Archilochus he often names himself, and his world is sordid and unheroic. He was regarded as the inventor of the scazon, or choliamb, the halting iambic, which replaces the last iambus of the senarius with a spondee or trochee. Ancient scholars credited him with inventing parody. Except in parody he wrote as if Homer had never existed, and his Ionic Greek contains an unusually high proportion of Anatolian, particularly Lydian, loanwords.

Alexandrian scholars collected his poems in two or three books, and they influenced poets such as Callimachus and Herodas. Aristophanes borrowed from him, and in Frogs Dionysus exclaims, Wonderful poet, Hipponax! Few fragments survived the Byzantine period: the Christian fathers disapproved of his abusive verse, and the emperor Julian forbade initiates to read Archilochus or Hipponax. His Ionic dialect and foreign words also made him unsuited to an education built on Attic. The longest surviving run of consecutive verses is only six lines, and a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus published in 1941 has parts of over fifty choliambics.
hiraizumi: Hiraizumi lies in Nishiiwai District, Iwate Prefecture, in the Tōhoku region of northern Honshu. It is the smallest municipality in the prefecture by area, about 63 square kilometres, and sits in a basin surrounded by the Kitakami Mountains. Its neighbours are Ichinoseki and Ōshū, and it has a humid climate with mild summers and cold winters. Its population peaked around 1950 and has declined since. The modern village was created on 1 April 1889 and raised to town status on 1 October 1953. The local economy rests on agriculture and tourism.

The area was part of ancient Mutsu Province. It was the home of the Northern Fujiwara clan for about 100 years in the late Heian era and served as the de facto capital of Ōshū, an area covering nearly a third of Japan. At its height Hiraizumi had a population of 50,000 or more than 100,000, rivalling Kyoto in size and splendour. The first structure may have been Hakusan Shrine on Mount Kanzan, which a writer in 1334 recorded as already 700 years old.

About 1100 Fujiwara no Kiyohira moved his home from Fort Toyoda to Mount Kanzan. The site lay at the junction of the Kitakami and Koromo rivers, directly on the Ōshū Kaidō, the main road from Kyoto to the north, and was seen as the exact centre of Ōshū. The Koromo River traditionally marked the boundary between Japan to the south and the Emishi peoples to the north; by building south of it, Kiyohira, himself half Emishi, signalled his intention to rule Ōshū without the court's sanction.

He built the temple complex Chūson-ji, beginning with a large pagoda, and set small reliquaries every hundred metres along the road. The Konjiki-dō was built to represent the Buddhist Pure Land and to be the final resting place of the Fujiwara lords. The golden age lasted nearly a century and ended in 1189, when the town was destroyed. Most of its buildings were lost. In 1689 the poet Matsuo Bashō saw its state and wrote a haiku on the impermanence of glory: 'Ah, summer grasses! All that remains of the warriors' dreams. '

The Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011. Chūson-ji with the Konjikidō Golden Hall, Mōtsū-ji with its Pure Land garden, the ruins of Kanjizaiō-in and Muryōkō-in, the Takkoku-no-Iwaya Bishamon chapel, the Takadachi Gikeidō and the Yanagi-no-Gosho palace site are among its listed sites.
hiram-bingham-iii: Hiram Bingham III was born in Honolulu on 19 November 1875, the son of Hiram Bingham II, an early Protestant missionary to the Kingdom of Hawaii, and grandson of the missionary Hiram Bingham I. He attended Oʻahu College, now Punahou School, then Phillips Academy in Andover, and took a B.A. at Yale in 1898, a degree at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1900 and a Ph.D. at Harvard in 1905. He taught at Harvard and Princeton, and in 1907 became a lecturer in South American history at Yale, a pioneer of the subject in the United States.

Bingham was not a trained archaeologist. In 1908, returning from a scientific congress in Santiago, he visited the pre-Columbian city of Choquequirao in Peru. He then organised the 1911 Yale Peruvian Expedition, one aim of which was to find the last capital of the Incas. Guided by locals, he identified Vitcos and Vilcabamba, then called Rosaspata and Espíritu Pampa, but did not recognise Vilcabamba as the last capital. On 24 July 1911 Melchor Arteaga led him to Machu Picchu, which he took for the lost city of the Incas. The site was known to people in the neighbouring valley, and Agustín Lizárraga had left his name on a wall of the Temple of the Three Windows in 1902; Bingham noted this in his journal.

In 1916 he became a captain in the Connecticut National Guard, and in 1917 he became an aviator and organised schools of military aeronautics at eight universities and rose to lieutenant colonel. He was lieutenant governor of Connecticut from 1922 to 1924 and was elected governor in 1924, but on 16 December 1924 was also elected to the United States Senate. He served as governor for one day, 7 to 8 January 1925, before taking his Senate seat. He lost his seat in 1932, and the Senate censured him on 4 November 1929 over a lobbyist's arrangement.

Bingham died at his Washington home on 6 June 1956 and is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. His book Lost City of the Incas became a bestseller in 1948, and a road to the site is named for him. Modern research has found Machu Picchu to be a royal estate, not the religious centre he proposed, and Vilcabamba was later shown to have been the last capital. The roughly 40,000 objects he took to Yale were the subject of an agreement of 2007 for their return to Peru, which began in 2012.
hiram-i: Hiram I was a Phoenician king of Tyre, the son of Abibaal, and was succeeded by his son Baal-Eser I. His regnal years have been calculated by some as 980 to 947 BCE, though the dates are debated. The calculation rests on the Tyrian records and the writings of Menander of Ephesus, preserved in Josephus's Against Apion, which say that Solomon's Temple was begun in the twelfth year of Hiram's reign and that 143 years passed from that start to the founding of Carthage. Josephus adds that Hiram lived 53 years and reigned 34.

During Hiram's reign Tyre grew from a satellite of Sidon into the most important Phoenician city and the centre of a large trading empire. He suppressed the rebellion of Utica, the first Tyrian colony. Josephus says that he extended the harbour, enlarged the city by joining the two islands on which it was built, and constructed a royal palace and a temple for Melqart. The "Tomb of Hiram" near Tyre, a colossal limestone sarcophagus on a pedestal, dates from the Persian period, four to six centuries after the presumed time of Hiram.

The Hebrew Bible says that he allied himself with David, king of Judah, and that his artisans built David's palace in Jerusalem of Lebanon cedar. He kept the alliance with David's son Solomon, addressing him as an equal, "my brother". For the Temple and the royal palace he sent architects, workmen, cedar and cypress wood and gold, and Solomon gave wheat, barley, olive oil and wine in return. The two kings also opened a trade route over the Red Sea from the harbour of Ezion-Geber to a land called Ophir. Beyond the Bible and Josephus the evidence is limited, and the biblical account may be embellished.
hiri-motu: Hiri Motu is also called Police Motu, Pidgin Motu or simply Hiri. It is a simplified version of Motu, a language of the Austronesian family, and is spoken around Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea. It is strictly neither a pidgin nor a creole, though it has features of both. Differences in sound and grammar make it not mutually intelligible with Motu, although the two languages are very similar in vocabulary and share a simplified Austronesian structure.

The word hiri names the traditional trade voyages that shaped the way of life of the Motu people, who live along the southern coast of their country. The voyages carried prized goods to the peoples of the Gulf of Papua. The language developed among those taking part in the hiri trade, chiefly in sago and clay pots, between the Motu and their neighbours on the south-east coast of New Guinea, and it is older than European contact.

In early colonial times the use of Hiri Motu spread because the Royal Papuan Constabulary adopted it, which is why it was called Police Motu. By the early 1960s it was the lingua franca of a large part of the country, and it was the first language of many children of policemen and other public servants whose parents came from different language groups.

The name Hiri Motu was proposed in the early 1970s at a conference held by the Department of Information and Extension Services. The committee argued that the New Guinea Police Force had taken up Pidgin when the forces were united in 1946, and that the name should reflect the language's legacy and everyday use rather than the police. Since the early 1970s or earlier its use has declined in favour of English and Tok Pisin. Today its speakers tend to be elderly and concentrated in Central and Gulf provinces, and younger speakers of Motu proper often understand it poorly. It has some statutory recognition.

Hiri Motu has two dialects, called Austronesian (or central) and Papuan (non-central), named for the first languages of the people who used it as a lingua franca. The Papuan dialect was more widely spoken and has been the standard of official publications since about 1964, while the Austronesian dialect, closer to Motu in grammar and sound, was the prestige form. It uses postpositions, such as ai for in, on or at. Sentences end with a verb, and either subject–object–verb or object–subject–verb order is used; a subject marker, ese, is used when meaning would otherwise be unclear. Its pronouns distinguish an inclusive we from an exclusive we.
hirohito: Hirohito was born on 29 April 1901 at Tōgū Palace in Aoyama, Tokyo, the first son of Crown Prince Yoshihito, the future Emperor Taishō, during the reign of his grandfather Emperor Meiji. Ten weeks after his birth he was placed in the care of Count Kawamura Sumiyoshi, and he returned to court at the age of three when Kawamura died. He was proclaimed crown prince on 2 November 1916.

From March to September 1921 he visited the United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Vatican City and Malta, the first European visit by a Japanese crown prince, achieved despite strong opposition in Japan. On his return he became regent on 25 November 1921 in place of his ailing father. He married Princess Nagako Kuni on 26 January 1924.

Hirohito became emperor on 25 December 1926, and the Shōwa era began. The early reign unfolded against financial crisis and growing military power in government. The killing of Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi in 1932 marked the end of civilian control of the military. In 1931 Japan staged the Mukden incident as a pretext to invade Manchuria, and Hirohito did not voice objection. On 27 September 1940 Japan joined Germany and Italy in the Tripartite Pact.

Hirohito formally sanctioned the decision to go to war against the United States and its allies on 1 December 1941. After the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Korea, he called on the armed forces to surrender in a radio broadcast on 15 August 1945. Historians agree that he was involved to some extent in strategy and war crimes, but the degree remains disputed.

He was not tried by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East. General Douglas MacArthur believed a cooperative emperor would help a peaceful occupation, and evidence that could have incriminated him was excluded. In 1946 he renounced his divinity, and the constitution of 1947 defined him as the symbol of the State and of the unity of the People.

Hirohito died on 7 January 1989 at the age of 87 and was succeeded by his son Akihito, beginning the Heisei era. His reign of more than sixty years was the longest of any historically attested emperor of Japan.
hiroshima: The site was originally a small fishing village on the shores of Hiroshima Bay, which from the 12th century prospered through its ties to a Zen Buddhist temple, Mitaki-dera, and through growing trade with the rest of Japan under the Taira clan. The warlord Mōri Terumoto founded Hiroshima in 1589 on the delta coast of the Seto Inland Sea, and the name means wide island. His castle was quickly built, and he moved in in 1593. After Terumoto sided with the losers at the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu took most of his fiefs, including Hiroshima, and gave Aki Province to the daimyō Masanori Fukushima. From 1619 until 1871 the Asano clan ruled the city.

After the han was abolished in 1871 the city became the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and, with the building of Ujina Harbor in the 1880s, an important port. The San'yō Railway reached it in 1894. During the First Sino-Japanese War the government moved there temporarily, and Emperor Meiji kept his headquarters at Hiroshima Castle from 15 September 1894 to 27 April 1895. In the Second World War the Second General Army and the Chūgoku Regional Army were headquartered there, and the port was a key centre for shipping and supply depots.

At 8:15 a.m. on Monday, 6 August 1945, the American B-29 Enola Gay, flown by Paul Tibbets, dropped the bomb Little Boy on the city. It directly killed at least 70,000 people, among them thousands of Korean forced labourers, and fewer than 10 per cent of the casualties were military. The population before the bombing was about 345,000. About 70 per cent of the buildings were destroyed and another 7 per cent badly damaged.

Hiroshima is the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture and the largest city of the Chūgoku region of western Honshu. In 1949 the national parliament proclaimed it a City of Peace and passed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law to help rebuild it. The Peace Memorial Park was designed that year, and the Peace Memorial Museum opened in 1955. The Genbaku Dome, formerly the Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall and the building closest to the explosion that survived, is part of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, a World Heritage Site since 1996. The castle was rebuilt in 1958. The population, which had dropped to 137,197 after the bombing, had returned to its prewar level by 1955.
hiroshima-prefecture: The prefecture covers 8,479 square kilometres and borders Okayama Prefecture to the east, Tottori to the north-east, Shimane to the north and Yamaguchi to the south-west. It also touches Ehime Prefecture for 74 metres on the island of Hyōtanjima. Most of it is mountainous, with the Chūgoku Mountains in the north leading towards Shimane, and rivers have made rich plains near the coast. It faces Shikoku across the Seto Inland Sea, where Hiroshima Bay opens, and it includes many small islands. The sheltered Inland Sea makes the climate very mild.

The area was formerly divided into Bingo Province and Aki Province. It has been a centre of trade and culture since the beginning of Japan's recorded history. Hiroshima is a traditional centre of the Chūgoku region and was the seat of the Mōri clan until the Battle of Sekigahara. The prefecture is known worldwide for the atomic bombing of 1945, after which the city was rebuilt as a major regional centre of industry, education and culture. The Atomic Dome, one of the few remnants of prewar Hiroshima, stands as a reminder of that event.

Hiroshima is the capital and the largest city of the Chūgoku region, and other major cities are Fukuyama, Kure and Higashihiroshima. The population is 2,811,410 in 2019. With Nara and Tokyo it is one of three prefectures with more than one UNESCO World Heritage Site: the Atomic Dome and the Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima, famed for appearing to float when the tide fills round it. Mazda has its headquarters in the prefecture, and automobile manufacturing and tourism are among its main industries. Fukuyama and Hiroshima are international container ports, and ferries link Hiroshima Port with Miyajima, Matsuyama and Beppu.
hisham-i-of-cordoba: Hisham was born in Córdoba on 26 April 757, the son of Abd al-Rahman I and his wife Halul and the younger half-brother of Suleiman. By reputation he was pious, sober and capable, and Abd al-Rahman favoured him. He came to the throne in 788 with considerable experience and the support of the religious elite.

He was at once opposed by his elder brother Sulayman, who ruled in Toledo, was a seasoned fighter and enjoyed the loyalty of the Syrian troops. Sulayman recruited another brother, Abd Allah. After losing Toledo to Hisham and failing to regain the initiative, the two agreed to accept permanent exile in the Maghrib together with a large cash settlement.

His reign was comparatively stable. At home Hisham continued his father's work, completing the mosque of Córdoba and improving the city, including repairs to the great Roman bridge. He relied heavily on Umayyad family clients and entrenched the emerging Maliki school of scholars in the emirate's power structure; Malik ibn Anas himself was said to have praised him as an example of piety and justice.

In 793, facing Carolingian pressure across the Pyrenees, he called a jihad against the Franks and sent troops to Girona and Narbonne, which held out. His general Abd al-Malik ibn Abd al-Wahid ibn Mughith was more fortunate near Carcassonne, where he defeated William of Orange. The expedition brought loot and many slaves, which paid for the expansion of the Great Mosque of Córdoba and for new mosques.
