hudsons-bay-company: For much of the 17th century the French colonists of New France held a de facto monopoly of the North American fur trade. Two French traders, Pierre-Esprit Radisson and his brother-in-law Médard des Groseilliers, learned from the Cree that the best fur country lay north and west of Lake Superior, with a frozen sea still further north. They sought French backing for a post on what they took to be Hudson Bay, but the French governor refused permission. They went to the upper Great Lakes in 1659 anyway and returned to Montreal with valuable furs, but French authorities arrested them for trading without a licence and confiscated the furs.

The royal charter of 2 May 1670, issued by Charles II, gave the company the right of sole trade and commerce over Rupert's Land, a territory based on the Hudson Bay drainage basin. Prince Rupert of the Rhine was its first governor.

The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 required France to give up all claims to Hudson Bay. The main rival in the fur trade was the North West Company, and the competition led to the Pemmican War and the Battle of Seven Oaks on 19 June 1816. In 1821 the British government forced the two companies to merge. Of 175 posts, 52 were kept, and the territory reached the Arctic Ocean and, through the Columbia Department, the Pacific.

In 1849 Guillaume Sayer, a Métis trader, was tried for illegal trading before a jury of company officials and supporters while an armed crowd led by Louis Riel Sr. gathered outside. Sayer was found guilty but not punished, and the Métis cry of "Le commerce est libre!" marked the loosening of the company's control of the courts.

The company later turned to retail. Its first department store opened in Winnipeg in 1881, and the first of its grand original six was built in Calgary in 1913. In 1970 it moved its head office from London to Canada and was rechartered under Canadian law. It was the oldest commercial corporation in North America. Its stores closed in 2025 and the company was liquidated, and its royal charter and art collection were auctioned. Its archives were donated to the Archives of Manitoba in 1994.
hue: The Perfume River passes through the centre of Huế, which lies roughly in the middle of Vietnam on the transition between the north central and south central regions. The area includes the Tam Giang–Cau Hai lagoon, 68 km long, and has about 128 km of coastline. Mountains line its western and south-western borders, and the climate is tropical monsoon, with most rain falling from September to December.

The oldest ruins in the area belong to the kingdom of Lâm Ấp and date to the 4th century CE. The region, called Thuận Hóa, was ceded by Champa to Đại Việt in 1306: the Cham king Chế Mân gave two prefectures in exchange for marriage with a Vietnamese princess, Huyền Trân.

In the 16th century Nguyễn Hoàng asked to govern Thuận Hóa, then the southernmost region of Vietnam. After he pacified it, he and his heir Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên made it loyal to the Nguyễn family and rose against the Trịnh lords, and Vietnam divided between two ruling clans. The Nguyễn lords moved their palace to Kim Long in 1636 and based themselves at Phú Xuân, the future Huế, in 1687. The Trịnh captured it in 1775, and the Tây Sơn, whose rebellion had broken out in 1771, defeated the Trịnh garrison in 1786 and took Phú Xuân.

Nguyễn Ánh, a successor of the Nguyễn lords, recaptured Phú Xuân and unified the country. He rebuilt the citadel entirely and, as Emperor Gia Long, made Huế the national capital. After the French conquest Phú Xuân was officially renamed Huế in 1899, and the city remained capital of Annam within French Indochina. The imperial court stayed there until Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated in 1945.

Huế became a centrally governed city of Vietnam in 2025, when it was merged with the rest of Thừa Thiên Huế province. Its complex of imperial palaces, tombs and temples is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, including the Imperial City and the Forbidden Purple City, once the emperor's home. The tombs of emperors such as Minh Mạng, Khải Định and Tự Đức lie along the Perfume River, and the Thiên Mụ Temple, the largest pagoda in the city, is its official symbol.
huelva: Huelva lies in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula on the Gulf of Cádiz, facing the Atlantic. It stands on the estuary formed where the Odiel and Tinto rivers meet, between the two rivers. In ancient times the estuary was rather wide, and it has progressively silted up.

Historians long held that Huelva began as a native Tartessian settlement. Finds of Phoenician material at the Méndez Núñez-Las Monjas site led to the Phoenician chronology being reassessed, and the evidence now favours seeing Huelva as a very early Phoenician colony, founded roughly in the 9th century BCE, though a 10th-century date has also been argued. The Phoenicians called it ʿunʿu baʿl, 'Baal's fort', which Greek texts corrupted to Onoba. The outpost exported silver, copper, purple dye and salted fish and was a node on routes linking the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The Tartessian world entered a crisis in the 6th century BCE, and the town passed slowly to the Turdetani.

Under Rome it was Onoba or Onuba and had a mint. Musa ibn Nusayr's troops seized it by April 712, and its name became Walba. It was a short-lived independent taifa from 1012 to 1051, was then annexed by Seville and was occupied by the Almoravids in 1091. Alfonso X of Castile took it in 1262.

Huelva was a leading fishing town of Andalusia in the 16th century, became a provincial capital in 1833 and a city by royal decree on 17 September 1876. Mining by Rio Tinto, the main company from about 1873, sent copper and pyrite to its port. On 4 February 1888 soldiers fired on demonstrators against ore-smelting pollution at Rio Tinto, and historians estimate 100 to 200 deaths.

Huelva is the capital of its province in Andalusia, with a population of 149,410 at the 2010 census. Its port still handles copper and pyrite from mines inland. Recreativo de Huelva, founded in 1889 by workers of Rio Tinto, is the oldest football club in Spain, and the Fiestas Colombinas honour Christopher Columbus's departure from the port on 3 August 1492.
huesca: Huesca lies on a plateau in northern Aragon at an elevation of 488 metres, close to the Sierra de Guara, which reaches 2,077 metres. It is the capital of the Spanish province of the same name and one of the smallest provincial capitals in Spain, 71 kilometres from Zaragoza. Its coat of arms carries a block with a V-shaped notch, commonly said to represent the Salto de Roldán, or Roland's Leap, a rock formation about 25 kilometres to the north.

The city dates from before the Roman period, when it was called Bolskan in the Iberian language. As Osca it became a Roman colony under Quintus Sertorius, who made it his base. It minted its own coinage and had a school, founded by Sertorius, where young Iberians were taught Latin and Roman customs. Augustus made it a municipium in 30 BCE. The Arabs conquered the city in the late 8th century and called it Washqah. Part of the Upper March of the Emirate of Córdoba, it was repeatedly troubled by rebellion as the Banu Qasi, Banu Amrus and Banu al-Tawil clans and the Arista dynasty of Pamplona struggled for control. In 1018 it became part of the Taifa of Zaragoza.

In 1094 Sancho Ramírez built the Castle of Montearagón nearby in order to besiege the city, but was killed by a stray arrow as he reached its walls. Peter I of Aragon conquered it in 1096 and moved the royal capital there from Jaca. Peter IV of Aragon founded the University of Huesca in 1354; it was abolished in 1845. Huesca had one of the most important Jewish communities in Aragon, which flourished until the expulsion of 1492. During the Spanish Civil War the city was held by the Nationalists and besieged by the Republicans, among them George Orwell, but did not fall.

Huesca had 52,059 inhabitants in 2009, almost a quarter of the province's population. Its Gothic cathedral was begun by James I of Aragon around 1273, on the foundations of a mosque. The Abbey of San Pedro el Viejo, built between 1100 and 1241, is one of the oldest Romanesque structures in the Iberian Peninsula. The city celebrates the Fiestas de San Lorenzo from 9 to 15 August, in honour of Saint Lawrence, a native of Huesca martyred in 268 CE.
huey-tlatoani: Tlahtoāni is a historical title used by the dynastic rulers of the āltepēmeh, the autonomous city-states that many pre-Columbian Nahuatl-speaking peoples formed in the Valley of Mexico during the Postclassic Period. The word is an agent noun from the verb tlahtoa, meaning to speak, so that it literally means one who speaks. English renders it as king, sovereign, ruler or speaker. The title huēyi tlahtoāni, great ruler or emperor, was used by the rulers of the Aztec Empire, the alliance of Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan. Related titles include tlahtohcāpilli, for princes and prominent noblemen, and cihuātlahtoāni, for noblewomen such as consorts or princesses.

Each āltepētl had its own tlahtoāni, who was at once its ruler, high priest and commander-in-chief. He held ultimate authority over all land in the city-state and oversaw tribute collection, market activities, temple affairs and the settling of judicial disputes. He was typically a ruler from the royal lineage and served for life, although in some cases a council of nobles, elders and priests could elect one from a pool of four candidates. The cihuācōātl, a noble who served as supreme judge, appointed the lower court judges and handled financial affairs, was second in command.

In war the tlahtoāni drew up battle plans from the reports of scouts, messengers and spies sent to an enemy city, and was the main decision-maker. He sought the support of allied rulers by sending gifts and emissaries, was told at once of warriors killed or captured, informed the citizens, and presented gifts to the successful.

There were eleven tlahtohqueh of Tenochtitlan: Acamapichtli (1376 to 1395), Huitzilihuitl (1395 to 1417), Chimalpopoca (1417 to 1427), Itzcoatl (1427 to 1440), Moctezuma I (1440 to 1469), Axayacatl (1469 to 1481), Tizoc (1481 to 1486), Ahuitzotl (1486 to 1502), Moctezuma II (1502 to 1520), Cuitláhuac (1520) and Cuauhtémoc (1520 to 1521). From Itzcoatl onward, the tlahtoāni of Tenochtitlan was also the huēyi tlahtoāni of the Aztec Empire.
hugh-capet: Hugh was the son of Hugh the Great, Duke of the Franks, and Hedwige of Saxony, daughter of the German king Henry the Fowler. Through his mother he was a nephew of Otto I, and through his paternal grandmother he descended from Charlemagne. His family, the Robertians, were powerful landowners in the Île-de-France, and two of them, Odo I and Robert I, had been chosen as kings in place of Carolingians. When his father died in 956 Hugh, the eldest son, was about fifteen, and his neighbours took advantage: Theobald I of Blois took Chartres and Châteaudun.

In 960 King Lothair agreed that Hugh should have his father's margraviate of Neustria and the title Duke of the Franks. In 978, when Otto II invaded France and besieged Lothair in Paris, a relief army under Hugh helped force him to lift the siege on 30 November, and Otto's rearguard was destroyed crossing the flooded Aisne. The victory restored Hugh's position as the first noble of the kingdom.

Lothair's son Louis V died in a riding accident while hunting in the forest of Senlis on 22 May 987, leaving no children. Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, a Carolingian claimant, was accused of having made himself a vassal of the emperor. Adalberon, Archbishop of Reims, argued that the throne was not acquired by hereditary right. Hugh was crowned rex Francorum at Noyon on 1 June and again in Paris on 3 July 987, and he had his son Robert crowned on 25 December that year.

Charles of Lorraine took Laon, and Hugh and Robert twice besieged it without success. Adalberon, Bishop of Laon, then seized Charles in his sleep and delivered him to Hugh, who imprisoned him at Orléans until his death. Hugh's power was narrow. He held towns and estates between Paris and Orléans of about 400 square miles, and a plot of 993 to hand him to Otto III went unpunished, which shows how tenuous his hold was. He had to seek military aid from Richard I of Normandy, though his unanimous election gave him moral authority.

Hugh died on 24 October 996 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. His son Robert continued to reign, and the direct Capetians ruled France from 987 to 1328, with cadet branches after that until 1848.
hugh-the-great: Hugh the Great was the son of King Robert I of France and Béatrice of Vermandois, a descendant of Charlemagne, and was born in Paris. His family is known as the Robertians. In 922 the barons of Western Francia revolted against the Carolingian King Charles the Simple, who fled, and elected Robert as king. When Robert died in battle at Soissons in 923, Hugh refused the crown, and it went to his brother-in-law Rudolph. Charles the Simple had sought help from Hugh's cousin Count Herbert II of Vermandois, who instead imprisoned him and used the threat of releasing him to press his own ambitions until Charles died in 929.

At Rudolph's death in 936 Hugh held nearly all the land between the Loire and the Seine, the ancient Neustria, except Anjou and the territory ceded to the Normans in 911. He took an active part in bringing King Louis IV back from England that year. Historians have wondered why he called the young Louis to the throne instead of taking it himself. He had rivals, especially Hugh, Duke of Burgundy, and Herbert II, who would probably have challenged his election, and Richer explains that he remembered his father, who had died for his pretensions.

Hugh married three times: Judith of Maine in 922, Eadhild, a daughter of Edward the Elder, in 926, and in 937 Hedwig of Saxony, sister of Otto the Great and of Gerberga, Louis's wife. Soon afterwards he was drawn into a long quarrel with Louis. In 939 he, Herbert, Count Arnulf I of Flanders and Duke William Longsword of Normandy paid homage to Otto against Louis. When the Normans handed Louis over to him in 945, Hugh released him in 946 on condition that he surrender the fortress of Laon. In 948 a church council at Ingelheim excommunicated Hugh in absentia, and he responded by attacking Soissons and Reims. In 953 he made peace with Louis, the church and Otto.

When Louis died, Hugh was among the first to recognise his son Lothair as king and, at the request of Lothair's mother Gerberga, helped to have him crowned. In return Lothair invested Hugh with the duchies of Burgundy and Aquitaine. Duke Gilbert of Burgundy had acknowledged himself Hugh's vassal and betrothed his daughter to Hugh's son Otto-Henry, and when Gilbert died on 8 April 956 Hugh became effective master of the duchy. He died at Dourdan on 16 June 956. His son Hugh Capet became King of France in 987.
hugo-banzer: Hugo Banzer Suárez was born on 10 May 1926 at the hacienda Concepción in Santa Cruz. His grandfather Georg Banzer was a German immigrant from Osnabrück. He entered the Army Military College at fourteen in 1941 and graduated as a second lieutenant in 1947. He trained in Argentina, at Fort Hood in the United States and at the School of the Americas in Panama. Promoted colonel in 1961, he headed the Ministry of Education and Culture from 1964 to 1966 under General René Barrientos, a personal friend, was military attaché in Argentina, and from 1969 to 1971 directed the Military Academy. He sided with the right wing of the army.

In 1970 President Juan José Torres was leading Bolivia in a leftist direction, with a People's Assembly of miners, teachers, students and peasants, which angered conservative circles and the Nixon administration. An attempt to unseat him in early 1971 failed and Banzer fled to Argentina. On 17 August 1971 he led a successful uprising from Santa Cruz de la Sierra and on 22 August was given full power. According to Stephen Zunes, the coup had significant clandestine financial and advisory support within the Nixon administration. Torres was killed in exile in Buenos Aires in 1976.

Banzer banned left-leaning parties, suspended the Central Obrera Boliviana and closed the universities. From 1974, when it was clear he would hold no elections, he banned all political activity. Human rights groups claim that several thousand Bolivians sought asylum abroad, 3,000 were arrested, 200 were killed and many were tortured. Foreign credit sustained the regime, and external debt rose to record levels. In 1978, under pressure from the Carter administration, he opened a regulated move to elections. After the vote of 9 July was found to be rigged, Banzer had it annulled, and Juan Pereda overthrew him on 21 July.

He then founded the party Acción Democrática Nacionalista and ran for president in 1979 and 1980, finishing third both times. In 1997 he won by a small plurality, at 71, and returned as president with a grand coalition. In 2000, during the Cochabamba Water War, protests over the privatization of the city's water works led to clashes, and he declared a state of siege. The government declared the contract void in April 2000.

Diagnosed with lung cancer in June 2001, Banzer resigned on 7 August and was succeeded by his vice president, Jorge Quiroga. He died of heart failure at Santa Cruz de la Sierra on 5 May 2002, aged 75. He was the first former dictator in recent Latin American history to return to power by election.
hugo-chavez: Hugo Rafael Chávez Frías was born on 28 July 1954 in the rural village of Sabaneta, in Barinas State, in his paternal grandmother's three-room house. His family was of Amerindian, Afro-Venezuelan, Spanish and Italian descent, and his parents were schoolteachers. At 17 he entered the Venezuelan Academy of Military Sciences in Caracas, where a curriculum known as the Andrés Bello Plan brought in civilian professors to teach the cadets. He served as a communications officer in a counterinsurgency unit and, after fighting a Marxist–Hoxhaist insurgency in Anzoátegui in 1977, began to doubt the army.

Chávez formed a secret cell within the military, later the Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200 (MBR-200), inspired by Simón Bolívar, Simón Rodríguez and Ezequiel Zamora. Dissatisfied with a political system based on the Puntofijo Pact, he led it in an unsuccessful coup against President Carlos Andrés Pérez in 1992 and was imprisoned. President Rafael Caldera freed him in 1994. He then founded the Fifth Republic Movement and won the 1998 presidential election with 56.2 per cent of the vote. He took office on 2 February 1999 and was re-elected in 2000, 2006 and 2012.

With the high oil revenues of the 2000s his government nationalised key industries, created Communal Councils and ran the Bolivarian missions to widen access to food, housing, healthcare and education. Poverty and inequality fell between about 2003 and 2007, though structural inequalities remained. Critics point to his packing of the Supreme Court, pressure on the media and rising murder and kidnapping rates. Deficit spending and price controls later proved unsustainable, and shortages and inflation grew.

In June 2011 Chávez announced from Havana that he had had operations, including the removal of a tumour with cancerous cells. He won a fourth election on 7 October 2012, but his inauguration was cancelled because of his treatment, and he died in Caracas on 5 March 2013, aged 58. His ideas form the basis of Chavismo, close to Bolivarianism. He supported regional bodies such as the Union of South American Nations and the television network TeleSUR, and he is regarded across the political spectrum as one of the most influential and controversial figures in the modern history of Venezuela and Latin America.
hugo-grotius: Hugo Grotius, also called Hugo de Groot, was born in Delft on 10 April 1583, during the Dutch Revolt, into a patrician family. His father, who had studied with Justus Lipsius, translated Archimedes and gave his son a humanist education. Grotius entered Leiden University at eleven, and at sixteen published an edition of Martianus Capella's work on the seven liberal arts, which remained a reference for centuries. In 1603 his cousin Captain Jacob van Heemskerk captured the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina off present-day Singapore, and the Company he served asked Grotius to defend the seizure. His treatise of 1604 to 1605, later called De Jure Praedae, grounded it in natural justice and was not published in full in his lifetime.

Grotius advanced as an associate of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, becoming Pensionary of Rotterdam in 1613. A theological dispute between the followers of Jacobus Arminius, the Remonstrants, and the strongly Calvinist followers of Franciscus Gomarus divided the Republic. Grotius drafted for the States of Holland an edict of toleration, which held that only the tenets needed for civil order should be enforced. When Maurice of Nassau moved against Oldenbarnevelt, Grotius was imprisoned at Loevestein Castle. He escaped hidden in a chest of books and fled to Paris.

In France, where he lived almost continuously from 1621 to 1644, he published in 1625 De jure belli ac pacis, On the Law of War and Peace, dedicated to Louis XIII. Begun in prison, it was an effort to restrain conflict on the basis of a broad moral consensus. In 1634 Sweden named him ambassador to France, a post he kept for ten years.

In the summer of 1645 he left Sweden, was shipwrecked and washed up near Rostock ill, and died there on 28 August 1645. His body was laid in the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft. His thought on natural law influenced Samuel Pufendorf and John Locke, and along with the earlier works of Francisco de Vitoria and Alberico Gentili his writings laid foundations for international law. His influence declined with the rise of positivism, but revived after the First World War.
hugo-junkers: Hugo Junkers was born in Rheydt in the Prussian Rhine Province, the son of a wealthy industrialist. After his Abitur in 1878 he studied at the Technische Hochschulen in Charlottenburg and Aachen and completed his engineering studies in 1883. He first worked in his father's company, then attended lectures by Adolf Slaby, who placed him with the Continental-Gasgesellschaft in Dessau, where he worked on the first opposed-piston engine.

Junkers patented a calorimeter and founded a manufacturing company in 1892; the calorimeter won a gold medal at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. He patented a gas-fired bath boiler the next year and founded Junkers & Co. in 1895. From 1897 to 1912 he was a professor of mechanical engineering at Aachen, while his firm produced calorimeters, gas stoves, pressure regulators and fan heaters.

His aeronautical work began in earnest at the age of 50, with the engineer Hans Reissner. Junkers had a wind tunnel built and invented a hydraulic brake. During the First World War the government forced him to concentrate on military aircraft. In 1915 he developed the Junkers J 1, the first practical all-metal aircraft, with a cantilever wing with almost no external bracing. In 1917 the military inspectorate compelled him to merge his firm with Anthony Fokker's.

The F 13 of 1919 was the first of several civil designs, followed by the Ju 52/3m of 1932, and Junkers helped found airlines including Deutsche Luft Hansa. A Junkers W 33 made the first heavier-than-air crossing of the Atlantic from east to west. He also supported the Bauhaus and helped it move from Weimar to Dessau in 1925.

When the Nazis came to power in 1933 Junkers opposed their rearmament plans. They demanded ownership of all patents and market shares of his remaining companies, under threat of imprisonment for high treason. He was placed under house arrest in 1934 and died on 3 February 1935, his 76th birthday, after a visit from Nazi officials. The designers Andrei Tupolev and William Bushnell Stout drew on his corrugated, light-metal construction.
huguenots: The term Huguenot was in common use by around 1550 and was originally a term of derision whose source is unclear. One hypothesis links it to Besançon Hugues, a burgomaster who defended Geneva against Catholic Savoy. The Huguenots called themselves reformés. Their numbers grew rapidly between 1555 and 1561, chiefly among nobles and city dwellers, and they held their first national synod in Paris in 1558. They were concentrated in the south and west of France, whereas the Protestants of Alsace, Moselle and Montbéliard were mainly Lutherans.

Eight civil wars between 1562 and 1598 took on a dynastic character, as a feud between the Houses of Bourbon and Guise. The Huguenots were led by Jeanne d'Albret, her son, the future Henry IV, and the princes of Condé. On the eve of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572 the community made up as much as 10 per cent of the French population. Catholics killed thousands of Huguenots in Paris between 24 August and 3 October 1572, and similar massacres followed in Aix, Bordeaux, Lyon, Rouen, Toulouse and other towns. Henry IV, who had converted to Catholicism to gain the crown, issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Protestants equality under the crown and a degree of religious and political freedom.

Rebellions in the 1620s cost the Huguenots their political and military privileges. Louis XIV first sent missionaries, then closed Huguenot schools, excluded them from favoured professions and billeted troops in their homes in the dragonnades. In 1685 the Edict of Fontainebleau revoked the Edict of Nantes and made Protestantism illegal. Some converted, others emigrated, chiefly to the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg-Prussia and Switzerland. Persecution ended officially with the Edict of Versailles in 1787, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 gave Protestants equal rights.

The exodus drained France of people who had held important places in society, and the kingdom did not fully recover for years. In England some 40,000 to 50,000 settled, and they founded the silk industry there. In Brandenburg-Prussia, Frederick William granted them privileges by the Edict of Potsdam of 1685. In South Africa many Afrikaners bear French surnames. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France merged with the Evangelical Lutheran Church to form the United Protestant Church of France. In 1985 President François Mitterrand announced a formal apology to the descendants of the Huguenots.
huitzilopochtli: The name combines huitzilin, hummingbird, and opochtli, left-hand side, and is often translated Left-Handed Hummingbird or Hummingbird of the South. Scholars disagree about its full significance. In one account he was the smallest of four sons of the creator couple, with Quetzalcoatl, Xipe Totec and Tezcatlipoca as brothers. In another, the goddess Coatlicue was made pregnant by a ball of feathers on Mount Coatepec. Her other children conspired to kill her, and Huitzilopochtli burst from her womb in armour, beheaded his sister Coyolxauhqui and scattered his brothers across the sky.

In the legend of the Aubin Codex, Huitzilopochtli told the Aztecs to leave Aztlan and to call themselves Mexica, and guided them on their journey. He told them to build their city where an eagle perched on a cactus, eating a serpent. They settled on an island in Lake Texcoco, the site of Tenochtitlan.

Huitzilopochtli was the solar and war deity of the Mexica and patron god of Tenochtitlan. In myth he is the sun, his siblings the stars and the moon, and the daily sunrise was read as his battle with them. Originally of little importance to the Nahuas, he was raised by Tlacaelel's reform of religion to the level of Quetzalcoatl, Tlaloc and Tezcatlipoca. He was shown as a hummingbird or as a figure with a hummingbird helmet and a blue-painted body. Warriors who died in battle or as sacrifices were thought to join him as hummingbirds.

The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan was dedicated to him and to the rain god Tlaloc, his shrine red and on the south side, Tlaloc's blue and on the north. At the base of the stairway lay the Coyolxauhqui stone, showing the dismembered goddess, so that the temple recalled the mountain of Coatepec.

Aztec worship held that the sun needed nourishment in human blood and hearts, and that the Mexica as people of the sun had to provide it. Captives were sacrificed on a stone, their hearts cut out and their bodies sent down the pyramid, and a warrior who took a victim rose in the social hierarchy. The month of Panquetzaliztli was his festival, with processions, dances and sacrifices of victims dressed in his costume, and a statue of amaranth seeds and honey was eaten in pieces. The Aztecs reported that about 20,400 prisoners were sacrificed at the reconsecration of the Great Pyramid in 1487, a figure some scholars accept and others consider Aztec propaganda.
hulagu-khan: Hulagu, also written Hulegu or Hülegü, was born around 1217 to Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan, and Sorghaghtani Beki, an influential Keraite princess. He was a brother of Möngke Khan, Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke. Little is known of his childhood. His mother, a Christian of the Church of the East, arranged for all her sons to become Mongol leaders, and Hulagu was friendly to Christianity; his favourite wife, Doquz Khatun, and his closest friend and general, Kitbuqa, were also Christians.

Möngke, installed as Great Khan in 1251, charged Hulagu with conquering or destroying the remaining Muslim states of south-western Asia, including the Abbasid Caliphate. Two-tenths of the empire's fighting men were gathered for his army in 1253. The Lurs were destroyed and the Assassins surrendered their fortress of Alamut in early 1256. He chose Azerbaijan as his base.

The army set out for Baghdad in November 1257, and the Mongols laid siege on 29 January 1258. The city surrendered on 10 February, and the Mongols entered on 13 February and began a week of destruction, including that of the Grand Library. Death counts vary widely, from a low estimate of about 90,000 to a million. In 1260 the Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus, but Hulagu then withdrew most of his force and left for Mongolia over the succession after Möngke's death. At the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260 the Mamluks of Qutuz and Baybars destroyed the Mongol force left behind.

After Kublai became Great Khan, Hulagu returned to his lands by 1262. He was drawn into war with Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, a Muslim convert who had allied with the Mamluks, and suffered a severe defeat north of the Caucasus in 1263. He sent letters to Europe seeking an alliance, among them one of 10 April 1262 to Louis IX of France, but never gained one. He fell ill in January 1265 and died on 8 February 1265; he was buried on Shahi Island in Lake Urmia, and his tomb has never been found.

He founded the Ilkhanate. He employed Shams al-Din Juvayni as sahib-divan, while Ata-Malik Juvayni governed Baghdad and helped repair it, and he patronised Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, for whom the Maragheh observatory was built.
huldrych-zwingli: Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 at Wildhaus in the Toggenburg valley, the third of eleven children in a farming family. His father Ulrich was the chief local magistrate. At ten he was sent to Basel for secondary schooling. He studied at the University of Vienna and then at Basel, where he received his Master of Arts in 1506. He served as a pastor in Glarus and later in Einsiedeln, and the writings of Erasmus influenced him.

On 1 January 1519 Zwingli gave his first sermon as people's priest of the Grossmünster in Zurich. Instead of preaching on the Sunday's set Gospel, he read through Matthew verse by verse, and went on through the rest of the New Testament and the Old. In Lent 1522 he and about a dozen others ate sausages in breach of the fast, and the Affair of the Sausages is considered the start of the Reformation in Switzerland. After the first Zurich disputation, on 29 January 1523, the city council allowed him to go on preaching. Zurich severed its ties with the bishop of Constance in 1524 and replaced the Mass with a new communion liturgy in 1525.

Zwingli clashed with the Anabaptists, and after a public debate on 17 January 1525 the council ordered those who refused to have their children baptised to leave Zurich. A Christian Civic Union of Reformed cities was formed in 1528. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529 he and Martin Luther agreed on many points but not on the Real Presence in the Eucharist, which Zwingli took to be symbolic.

In 1531 the Reformed alliance's food blockade of the Catholic cantons failed. The cantons attacked when Zurich was ill-prepared, and Zwingli died on the battlefield on 11 October 1531. The Zurich council chose Heinrich Bullinger as his successor, who defended him as a prophet and martyr and consolidated his reforms. Zwingli's legacy lives on in the confessions, liturgy and church orders of the Reformed churches.
huliaipole: Huliaipole, whose Ukrainian name means walk-about field, lies in the valley of the Haichul river in Polohy Raion of Zaporizhzhia Oblast. The name of the river is derived from Turkic words meaning free and steppe. The town is 98 kilometres from the regional centre of Zaporizhzhia and 8 kilometres from the railway station of the same name. It is a small city; in January 2022 its estimated population was 12,786.

Before the Russian Empire annexed the Crimean Khanate, the area was settled mostly by Zaporozhian Cossacks and the nomadic Lesser Nogai Horde. The settlement arose in the 1770s after the Dnieper defensive line was built on former lands of the Zaporozhian Sich. When Catherine the Great dissolved the Sich, local Cossacks fled or were brought into serfdom under the Shabelskiys. In 1785 the Yekaterinoslav Governorate ordered a state military settlement founded here for protection from the Crimean Khanate. Its name reflected the fairs that had long been held on the spot.

From the middle of the nineteenth century the village became a commercial and industrial town. The first trades fair took place in 1859, with more than fifty trading companies and a turnover of 1 million rubles. Factories making agricultural machinery opened from 1882, and the Chaplyne–Berdyansk railway was laid nearby in 1898. Between 1917 and 1921, in the turbulence of the Russian Civil War and the Ukrainian War of Independence, the town changed hands no fewer than sixteen times, among Austro-Hungarian forces, the Red Army, the Ukrainian People's Republic, the Hetmanate, Anton Denikin's White Army and Nestor Makhno's Insurgent Army. It became widely known as the headquarters of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine and the capital of the Makhnovshchina.

Huliaipole gained city status in 1938 during rapid industrial development in the 1930s; at least 108 of its residents died in the Holodomor of 1932–1933. German forces occupied it on 5 October 1941, and Soviet troops retook it on 16 September 1943.

Notable natives include Makhno himself, born in 1888, and the anarchists Semen Karetnyk, Oleksiy Marchenko and Voldemar Antoni, who founded the Union of Poor Peasants. After Ukrainian independence the town's economy rested on an agricultural machinery plant, a paint plant, a shoe factory and food enterprises. In 2020 the city became part of Polohy Raion.
human-sacrifice: Human sacrifice is the killing of one or more people as part of a ritual. It is typically meant to please or appease gods, a human ruler, a priestly figure or the spirits of dead ancestors. Its forms include retainer sacrifice, in which a monarch's servants are killed so that they may go on serving him in the next life. The reasons given are those that motivate religious sacrifice in general: to bring good fortune, to pacify the gods when a temple or bridge is dedicated, to win favour in war, or to promote fertility, as in sacrifices to the Aztec god of agriculture Xipe Totec. Closely related practices in some tribal societies are cannibalism and headhunting.

The practice is found in many societies from prehistoric times. At Herxheim in southwestern Germany a Linear Pottery enclosure of the fifth millennium BCE held the fragmented remains of more than 1,000 individuals, and whether they were war captives, sacrificial victims or victims of other ritual violence is debated. At Abydos in early dynastic Egypt there may be evidence of servants buried with a king, but any such evidence disappears at about 2800 BCE. In China the Shang practised sacrifice on a large scale: at least 14,197 victims are mentioned in inscriptions. Slaves were buried alive with their owners under the Shang and Zhou, and Ximen Bao of Wei outlawed the drowning of victims to the river god Hebo.

In the Americas it continued, to varying degrees, until European colonisation. For the re-consecration of the Great Pyramid of Tenochtitlan in 1487 the Aztecs reported that they killed about 80,400 prisoners over four days, while Ross Hassig puts the number between 10,000 and 80,400. In Tahiti, during James Cook's visit in 1777, the chief Tina offered a servant to the war god ʻOro before a campaign. In West Africa the Annual Customs of Dahomey were the most notorious example, and sacrifices followed the deaths of kings and queens, with recorded cases of hundreds or thousands of slaves killed; Rudolph Rummel reports as many as 4,000 in 1727.

By the Iron Age, with the religious developments of the Axial Age, the practice was becoming less common across Africa, Europe and Asia, and in classical antiquity it came to be looked down on as barbaric. Greek myth may preserve a memory of its abandonment: Iphigenia, whom her father Agamemnon was to sacrifice to Artemis, is saved by the goddess, who substitutes a deer. In India human and animal sacrifice became less common after the Vedic period as ahimsa, non-violence, entered mainstream religious thought. Judaism explicitly forbids human sacrifice as murder, and Jews see the Akedah as central to its abolition. Modern secular laws treat it as murder.
humayun: Humayun was born Nasir al-Din Muhammad on 6 March 1508, the son of Babur and his favourite wife Māham Begum. On 26 December 1530 he succeeded his father at 22, an inexperienced ruler. His half-brother Kamran Mirza inherited Kabul and Kandahar, and the two became bitter rivals. Babur had divided his lands between sons, a Central Asian practice since Genghis Khan, and not all nobles saw Humayun as the rightful successor.

Humayun's first campaign was against Sher Shah Suri in Bihar, but he broke it off to annex Gujarat, Malwa and the fort of Mandu. While he was there, Sher Shah invaded Bengal and besieged its capital Gaur, and its wealth gave him a war chest. At the battle of Kannauj on 17 May 1540 Humayun was soundly defeated and retreated to Lahore. Kamran offered to join Sher Shah against him, but Humayun refused to kill his brother, citing Babur's last words: do nothing against your brothers, even though they may deserve it.

He withdrew across the Thar Desert, where his wife Hamida Bano, eight months pregnant, was left without a horse; he later called it the lowest point of his life. He crossed the Indus on 11 July 1543 and fled with a small party to the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, who received him as a royal guest at Herat. With 14,000 Persian soldiers he besieged Kandahar from 21 March 1545 and entered Kabul on 18 November 1545. At the Battle of Sirhind on 22 June 1555 his general Bairam Khan decisively defeated Sikandar Shah Suri, and the Mughal Empire was re-established.

On 24 January 1556 Humayun was descending the staircase of his library, Sher Mandal, with his arms full of books when the muezzin called the prayer. Trying to kneel, he caught his foot in his robe, fell several steps and struck his temple on a stone edge. He died three days later.

He was buried at last in Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, commissioned by his chief wife Bega Begum, the first very grand garden tomb of Mughal architecture, which set the precedent for the Taj Mahal. His return from Persia brought Persian noblemen to the Mughal court and changed its culture, and he left a substantial legacy to his son Akbar.
humayuns-tomb: Humayun died on 27 January 1556. His body was first buried in his palace in the Purana Quila at Delhi, then taken to Sirhind in Punjab by Khanjar Beg. His widow and chief consort, Bega Begum, devoted herself to building a memorial that would be the grandest mausoleum in the Mughal empire. According to the Ain-i-Akbari she supervised the work after returning from the Hajj. Construction began in 1565 and ended in 1572, and the whole cost of 1.5 million rupees was paid by her. The emperor Akbar visited the tomb in 1571, when it was nearly complete.

The site beside the Yamuna was chosen for its nearness to the Nizamuddin Dargah, the shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, whom the rulers of Delhi revered. Abd al-Qadir Bada'uni, one of the few contemporary historians to mention the building, says the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, whom the empress chose and brought from Herat, designed it. His son Sayyid Muhammad completed it.

The tomb is built of rubble masonry and red sandstone, clad in white marble, which is also used for the floors, lattice screens, door frames, eaves and the main dome. It stands on a vaulted terrace eight metres high and is essentially square, with chamfered corners that make it look octagonal. A high rubble wall encloses the complex, entered through two double-storeyed gateways 16 metres high. The terrace holds fifty-six cells with over 100 graves.

It stands at the centre of a 30-acre charbagh, a Persian-style garden divided into four squares by paved walkways and two crossing water channels that recall the four rivers of paradise. Each square is divided again into smaller gardens, 32 in all. It was the first such garden on this scale in South Asia, and the first structure to use red sandstone on such a scale. The tomb was modelled on Gur-e Amir, the tomb of Timur at Samarkand.

The tomb marked a leap in Mughal architecture and set a precedent for later royal mausolea, which reached their height in the Taj Mahal at Agra. Beside Humayun it holds the graves of Bega Begum, Dara Shikoh and several later Mughals, among them Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar and Alamgir II. When William Finch visited in 1611 he described the central chamber richly furnished with carpets.

The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, took refuge here with three princes during the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and was captured by Captain Hodson and exiled to Rangoon. The tomb became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture and the Archaeological Survey of India restored the gardens and water channels between about 1999 and 2003.
humber: The Humber is formed at Trent Falls by the meeting of the tidal rivers Ouse and Trent. From there to the North Sea it forms part of the boundary between the East Riding of Yorkshire on the north bank and North Lincolnshire on the south bank, and it is tidal throughout. The River Hull joins it at Kingston upon Hull, and it reaches the sea between Cleethorpes and the headland of Spurn Head. During the Ice Age the Humber had a much longer freshwater course across Doggerland, now submerged beneath the North Sea. Ptolemy recorded it in the 2nd century as Ábou (Latin Abus), a name from an early Celtic word meaning "moving water".

The Humber appears regularly in medieval British literature. In the Welsh Triads it is one of the three principal rivers of Britain with the Thames and the Severn, and in Geoffrey of Monmouth's chronicle it is named for Humber the Hun, an invader who drowned there in battle. It remained an important boundary in the Anglo-Saxon period, separating Northumbria from the southern kingdoms; the name Northumbria means the people north of the Humber. Ptolemy gives the Coritani as the Iron Age tribe south of the Humber and the Parisi as the tribe to the north.

A ferry route from Hessle to Barton-upon-Humber is noted in the Domesday Book and in a charter of 1281. Steam ferries from Hull to New Holland began in 1841 and ran until the Humber Bridge opened in 1981. Until 1974 the Humber formed part of the boundary between Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, and from 1974 to 1996 the counties on both banks together formed Humberside. The Humber Forts at the mouth of the estuary were planned in 1914, begun in 1915 and completed in 1919, and abandoned for military use in 1956. On 23 August 1921 the airship R38 crashed into the estuary near Hull, killing 44 of the 49 crew.

The ports on the Humber include Hull, Grimsby and Immingham, and the estuary is navigable for the largest deep-sea vessels. It is used by wintering birds and forms part of the Severn-Trent flyway, a route for migratory birds crossing Great Britain. Salmon, sole, cod, eel and flounder are among the fish caught in it.
humbert-i-count-of-savoy: Humbert was the son of Amadeus, who may or may not have preceded him as count of Maurienne. His brother was Bishop Otto of Belley. The origins of the family are unknown: his ancestors are variously said to have come from Saxony, Burgundy or Provence. Because Humbert had close connections with Rudolf III of Burgundy, it is likely that his family was Burgundian, descended either from the dukes of Vienne or from an aristocratic family such as the Guigonids, ancestors of the counts of Albon. He was probably also related to Ermengarde of Burgundy, the second wife of Rudolf III. He first held lands around Belley and in the county of Sermorens, before gaining lands in Aosta and Valais.

His service to the Holy Roman Emperors Henry II and Conrad II was rewarded with the counties of Maurienne and Aosta and lands in Valais, all at the expense of local bishops and archbishops. After Rudolf III died in 1032, Humbert swore fealty to Conrad II. He supported the emperor in his campaigns against Odo II, Count of Blois, and Aribert, Archbishop of Milan. In return Conrad appointed him count of Savoy and granted him Maurienne, Chablais and perhaps Tarentaise. These grants to a loyal supporter secured key passes through the Alps, which controlled trade between Italy and Western Europe, and they formed the core of Savoy power for centuries.

Humbert married a woman named Ancelie, also written Auxilia or Ancilia. She may have been the daughter of Anselme of Aoste, or of the master of ceremonies of Burgundy, or a member of a northern Italian dynasty known as the Anselmids. They had at least four sons. Amadeus I and Otto both became counts of Savoy in succession, Aymon was Bishop of Sion and Burchard was Archbishop of Lyon. Humbert is often said to have died at Hermillon, in the Maurienne region of present-day Savoie, France. His descendants, the House of Savoy, held the county and expanded from it.
humberto-castelo-branco: Humberto de Alencar Castelo Branco was born on 20 September 1897 into a wealthy family of north-eastern Brazil with roots in Portugal. His father, Cândido Borges Castelo Branco, was a general, and his mother, Antonieta de Alencar, belonged to the family of the writer José de Alencar. He joined the army at the Rio Pardo Military School, entered the Military School of Realengo in 1918 and was commissioned a second lieutenant in 1921. He took part in the Revolution of 1930 and later studied at the French War College.

In the Second World War he headed the operations section of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force in Italy, where he planned manoeuvres at the Battle of Monte Castello and gained great prestige, according to Marshal Cordeiro de Farias. As a general he commanded the Command and General Staff College from 1954 to 1956, and he was chief of staff of the army from 13 September 1963 until April 1964.

Castelo Branco was one of the leaders of the 1964 coup that overthrew Goulart. Congress chose him on 11 April to complete Goulart's term, and he took the oath on 15 April 1964. The First Institutional Act gave him emergency powers, including the power to cancel the political rights of subversive elements for ten years, and he intended to hand power to a civilian in 1966, but hard-line officers backed by War Minister Artur da Costa e Silva wished to stay in power. When opposition candidates won the governorships of Minas Gerais and Guanabara in October 1965, he refused to annul the results, and Costa e Silva persuaded the hard-liners to accept them in return for a promise of a tougher policy.

On 27 October 1965 he issued the Second Institutional Act, which abolished all existing political parties, restored his emergency powers and extended his term to 1967. Two parties replaced them: the pro-government National Renewal Alliance, ARENA, and the opposition Brazilian Democratic Movement, MDB. In 1967 a commission of jurists drafted a new constitution, and a press law, which remained valid until 2009, was issued near the end of his term. His government relied on loans from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund and on American investment. He was succeeded by Costa e Silva at midnight on 15 March 1967.

Four months after leaving office Castelo Branco died on 18 July 1967 in a mid-air collision of two Piper aircraft near Fortaleza. He belonged to a more liberal legalist faction within the regime, as opposed to his more authoritarian successors, and he was the first leader of the military regime that lasted after the coup of 1964.
humboldt-university-of-berlin: The university arose during the Prussian Reform Movement on the initiative of the philosopher and linguist Wilhelm von Humboldt, with Johann Gottlieb Fichte and Friedrich Schleiermacher, under King Frederick William III. It was housed in the palace built for Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of Frederick the Great, on Unter den Linden. Humboldt met great resistance and submitted his resignation to the King in April 1810, so he was absent when it opened.

The first students were admitted on 6 October 1810 and the first semester began on 10 October, with 256 students and 52 lecturers in faculties of law, medicine, theology and philosophy. The university keeps 15 October 1810 as its opening date. It set up the world's first academic chair in history. From 1828 to 1945 it was named the Royal Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin.

In the 19th century the university grew to take in many new disciplines, and modern research facilities aided the natural sciences. Researchers such as the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz and the physicians Rudolf Virchow and Robert Koch built its fame. It absorbed other Berlin colleges, among them the Charité, which became its medical campus by 1829. Its principle of uniting teaching and research served as a model elsewhere, for institutions such as Johns Hopkins University.

After 1933 the Nazi regime affected the university like all German universities. Under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service, 250 Jewish professors and employees were dismissed in 1933-1934, and nearly a third of the staff was fired in all. On 10 May 1933 some 20,000 books were taken from libraries to be burned in the Opernplatz, now Bebelplatz.

After the Second World War the university lay in East Berlin and reopened in 1946 under the Soviet Military Administration, which required lectures to be approved by Socialist Unity Party officials. The Free University of Berlin was founded in West Berlin in 1948. Because the old name had monarchic origins, the university was renamed in 1949 after the brothers Alexander and Wilhelm von Humboldt.

After German reunification it was restructured by commissions led by West German professors. Alumni and faculty include Hegel, Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, Otto von Bismarck, W. E. B. Du Bois, Albert Einstein, Max Planck and the Brothers Grimm.
humphrey-gilbert: Humphrey Gilbert was the fifth son of Otho Gilbert of Compton, Greenway and Galmpton in Devon and of Catherine Champernowne. He was a maternal half-brother of Sir Walter Raleigh. Gilbert was educated at Eton College and the University of Oxford, where he learned French and Spanish and studied war and navigation, and his mentor was Sir Henry Sidney. He was wounded at the siege of Newhaven, in Le Havre, in June 1563.

From 1566 Gilbert served in Ireland under Sidney against Shane O'Neill, and after O'Neill's assassination in 1567 he became governor of Ulster. In 1569 he took part in the fighting that followed the first Desmond Rebellion, capturing thirty to forty castles in Kerry and Connello. Thomas Churchyard recorded that he had the heads of the dead laid along the path to his tent to terrify the people. Sidney knighted him in 1570, and he sat in the English Parliament for Plymouth in 1571.

In 1566 he argued before Queen Elizabeth for a Northwest Passage to Cathay, and Martin Frobisher's voyage of 1576 grew from the support he won. In 1573 he proposed an academy in London, which Sir Thomas Gresham eventually realised as Gresham College. After letters patent of 11 June 1578 he sailed with seven vessels that November, but storms scattered the fleet and forced it back some six months later. Failed expeditions exhausted his family fortune.

In June 1583 Gilbert sailed for North America with five vessels. On 5 August 1583 he took possession of Newfoundland for the English Crown at St. John's, by cutting turf in the manner of English common law. He claimed authority over the fish stations and taxed the fishermen. The ship Delight then ran aground on Sable Island after he ordered a controversial change of course, and only sixteen of its crew survived. He decided on 31 August to turn back.

On 9 September his small ship, the Squirrel, was nearly overwhelmed by heavy seas near the Azores. Gilbert refused to move to the larger Golden Hind and was seen reading in the stern. At midnight the Squirrel's lights went out, and the ship was lost with all hands. A. L. Rowse described him as passionate, impulsive and liable to violence and cruelty, but also visionary and original. His claim was realised in 1610, and the royal charter granted to Raleigh in 1584 drew in part on his patent.
hunan: Hunan lies on the south bank of the Yangtze River, about halfway along its length, and its name means south of the lake, the lake being Dongting. Mountains and hills cover more than 80 per cent of the province. The Wuling, Xuefeng, Nanling and Luoxiao ranges enclose it on the west, south and east, and the Xiang, Zi, Yuan and Li rivers converge on Lake Dongting in the north. The lake and the Xiaoxiang area figure prominently in Chinese poetry and painting, particularly in the Song dynasty, when they were associated with officials who had been unjustly dismissed. The area was under Chinese rule as far back as 350 BCE.

The forests were first occupied by the ancestors of the Miao, Tujia, Dong and Yao peoples. After Qin conquered Chu in 278 BCE the region came under Qin, and under the Han it formed the Changsha Kingdom. For hundreds of years Han Chinese settlers came from the north, displacing and assimilating the original inhabitants, clearing forests and farming rice in the valleys and plains. Migration was especially heavy when the north was ruled by non-Han groups and in disorder. In the Tang dynasty Changsha was a ceramics district, mass-producing tea bowls and ewers for export; the Belitung Shipwreck, an Arab dhow dated to the 830s, carried more than 60,000 pieces of such wares.

During the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period Hunan had its own independent regime, Ma Chu. Under the Yuan it was joined with Hubei in the province of Huguang, and the Red Turban Rebellions first rose up in Hunan in the 14th century. Hunan province was created in 1664 from Huguang and renamed in 1723. The Yuelu Academy at Changsha made it a centre of Confucian learning, and its grain surpluses fed many parts of China. By the 19th century it was overcrowded and prone to uprisings, among them the Miao Rebellion of 1795 to 1806. A Hunanese army under Zeng Guofan marched into Nanjing to put down the Taiping Rebellion in 1864.

A famine in 1920 killed an estimated 2 million people and led to the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 1927, led by the Hunan native Mao Zedong. Communists held a guerrilla army along the Hunan and Jiangxi border until 1934, when the Long March began. Changsha fell to the Japanese in 1944.

Hunan has a population of just over 66 million at the 2020 census, and Changsha is its capital and largest city. Han Chinese are the majority, with Tujia and Miao among the minorities. Wulingyuan, noted for its quartzite sandstone pillars, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Mount Heng at Hengyang is one of the Five Great Mountains of China.
hunayn-ibn-ishaq: The Ibad were an Arab community of different tribes that had converted to the Church of the East and lived in al-Hira, once the capital of the Lakhmid kingdom. They were known for their literacy and multilingualism, in Syriac and Arabic. Hunayn's father was a pharmacist, and although al-Hira was known for commerce and banking, Hunayn went to Baghdad to study medicine under the physician Yuhanna ibn Masawayh. His endless questions irritated his teacher, who scolded him and forced him to leave. Hunayn promised himself to return as a physician and went abroad to master Greek.

On his return he displayed his new skill by reciting the works of Homer and Galen, and ibn Masawayh, in awe, was reconciled with him; the two began to work together. The caliph al-Mamun noticed his talent and, placed him in charge of the House of Wisdom, though at least one scholar argues there is no evidence of this. He also gave Hunayn the chance to travel to Byzantium in search of manuscripts.

Hunayn worked with his son Ishaq ibn Hunayn and his nephew Hubaysh. He would translate Greek into Syriac, his nephew would then render the Syriac into Arabic, and Hunayn would correct any mistakes. Unlike many translators of the Abbasid period he largely did not follow the exact wording of a text, but summarised its subject and paraphrased it, and he edited technical works by comparing the available manuscripts. He wrote that he first translated Galen from a faulty Greek manuscript and later, at forty, collated several manuscripts into one correct copy.

His translations included Plato's Timaeus and Republic, Aristotle's Categories, Physics, Metaphysics and Magna Moralia, and the Old Testament, which he rendered from the Septuagint, though that version did not survive. He translated 129 works of Galen, and travelled to Damascus to find half of one of them. Some of Galen's works, lost in Greek, survive in his Arabic. When al-Mutawakkil named him his personal physician, the caliph ended the exclusive use of physicians of the Bukhtishu family.

Hunayn wrote 36 books of his own, 21 of them on medicine, as well as works on philosophy, religion and Arabic grammar. His Book of the Ten Treatises of the Eye, the first known systematic treatment of ophthalmology, describes the anatomy of the eye, its diseases, their symptoms and treatments, including surgery for corneal ulcers and cataracts. He insisted that the crystalline lens lies at the centre of the eye, an idea that was widely held from his lifetime until the late 1500s.
hundred-days-reform: The Hundred Days' Reform, also called the Wuxu Reform, ran from 11 June to 21 September 1898. It followed the defeat of Qing China by Japan in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894 and 1895, after which the Treaty of Shimonoseki forced China to recognise Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula and pay a large indemnity. Elites saw the defeat as proof that the Self-Strengthening Movement, which concentrated on weapons and arsenals, had failed, and that institutional change was needed.

Thinkers including Tan Sitong, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, influenced by the Meiji reforms in Japan, argued that China needed more than technical improvements. Parts of the Qing government were alarmed enough to let Kang and Liang put their proposals to the Guangxu Emperor, who agreed to an ambitious programme.

Over about a hundred days the emperor issued a rapid series of edicts on education, administration, the economy and the military. They called for a modern school system teaching mathematics and science, gradual replacement of the traditional civil service examinations, a bureau for railways and mines, a modern army and naval academy, and a move towards constitutional monarchy on the Meiji model. The Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University, was established.

Conservative opposition was intense among senior Manchu princes, Grand Councilors and provincial governors, who saw the changes to the examinations and the abolition of sinecures as threats to the social and political order. Empress Dowager Cixi supported the principles but feared that sudden change would be disruptive and that Japan and other powers would exploit any weakness. Later accounts say that Tan Sitong asked Yuan Shikai to kill Ronglu and march on Beijing to arrest Cixi, but Yuan told Ronglu instead.

With the support of conservatives and the forces of Yuan and Ronglu, Cixi staged a coup in September 1898 and took over the government. Guangxu was put under house arrest until his death in 1908. The reforms were reversed, and six leading reformers, the Six Gentlemen of Wuxu, including Tan Sitong, were ordered executed. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao fled to Japan, where they founded the Baohuang Hui and worked unsuccessfully for a constitutional monarchy.

Historians differ. The mainstream view sees heroic but disorganised reformers blocked by Cixi's conservative faction, while some late 20th-century historians hold that Kang and his allies were dreamers unaware of political realities. The failure of the later reforms helped revolutionary forces, and the Xinhai Revolution succeeded in 1911.
hundred-years-war: The tension between the two crowns went back to the Norman Conquest of 1066, which put the Duke of Normandy, a vassal of the king of France, on the English throne. English kings thereafter held lands in France, and the status of those fiefs was a lasting source of conflict.

The immediate cause was dynastic. After Louis X died in 1316, the French crown passed through his brothers, and when Charles IV died, Edward III claimed the succession through his mother Isabella, Charles's sister. In May 1337 Philip VI took Aquitaine back into his hands, since Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. Edward answered by challenging Philip's right to the throne, and in 1340 he formally took the title of king of France.

Historians usually divide the war into three phases, separated by truces. In the Edwardian phase, to 1360, Edward III and his son Edward the Black Prince won at Crécy in 1346 and at Poitiers in 1356, where King John II of France was taken prisoner. The Black Death, which spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351, killed 6 to 12 million people in France, over a third of the population, and 2 to 3 million in England.

In the Caroline phase, under Charles V and the commander Bertrand du Guesclin, the French reconquered most of the lands ceded to Edward at the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360; Charles created a professional standing army, the first in post-Roman western Europe. After the Truce of Leulinghem of 1389, Henry V of England used the madness of Charles VI and the civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians to renew the war. He won at Agincourt in 1415, where about 40 per cent of the French nobility was killed, and at Verneuil in 1424. In April 1429 Joan of Arc entered the besieged city of Orléans, and the English lifted the siege.

When the war ended, England had lost its continental possessions apart from Calais, which it held until 1558. The French and English monarchies stayed separate, although English sovereigns styled themselves kings of France until 1802. Historians point to the war's lasting effects on European warfare: professional armies replaced feudal levies, artillery became important, and stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms.
huneric: Huneric was the oldest son of Gaiseric and was sent to Italy as a hostage in 435, when his father made a treaty with the Western emperor Valentinian III. He married Eudocia, daughter of Valentinian III and Licinia Eudoxia, in 455 or 456, after she was taken following the Sack of Rome; their one child was the future king Hilderic. Huneric had earlier been married to a daughter of the Visigothic king Theodoric I. He divorced her on the claim that she had tried to poison someone, and she returned to the Visigothic Kingdom after her nose and ears were cut off, which soured relations between the Vandals and the Visigoths.

Huneric became king on his father's death on 25 January 477 and was the first Vandal king to use the title King of the Vandals and Alans. He abandoned his father's imperial politics and concentrated on internal affairs, and he lacked the prestige Gaiseric had enjoyed with other states. In 479 he conducted a purge, exiling his older brother Theoderic with his daughters and younger son. Theoderic's wife and eldest son were executed, as were the official Heldica and his family, and Jucundus, the Arian patriarch of Carthage, was publicly burned to death.

A fervent Arian, Huneric opened his reign with overtures to the Roman population. After an Eastern Roman mission led by Alexander, he restored properties his father had seized from the merchants of Carthage, and he allowed the Nicene Christians to hold a synod, which elected Eugenius as bishop of Carthage. He then reversed himself. On 24 February 484, three weeks after a meeting of Nicene and Arian bishops, he removed the Nicene bishops from office and banished some to Corsica. A few were executed, among them the former proconsul Victorian and Frumentius, killed at Hadrumetum after refusing to become Arians.

Yves Modéran estimated that around 20% of the bishops in Africa converted to Arianism in response. Huneric also murdered many members of the Hasdingi dynasty and persecuted Manichaeans, and near the end of his reign the Moors of the Aurès Mountains successfully rebelled against Vandal rule. He renamed Hadrumetum Hunericopolis. He died on 23 December 484 and was succeeded by his nephew Gunthamund, who allowed the exiles to return; among them was Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus, who published a treatise against Arianism. Only three pieces of Vandal legislation survive, all from Huneric's reign.
hungarian-revolution-of-1848: Unlike other Habsburg lands, the Kingdom of Hungary had an old constitution that limited the Crown, going back to the Golden Bull of 1222, and a separate parliament, the Diet. Under Metternich's policy of stability the Diet was not summoned after 1811, but writers such as Mihály Vörösmarty and Ferenc Kölcsey kept alive the ideal of political liberty. The crisis came from abroad: on 3 March 1848, after news of the revolution in Paris, Lajos Kossuth demanded parliamentary government for Hungary, and his speech was read aloud in Vienna before Metternich was overthrown on 13 March.

On 17 March 1848 the emperor assented, and Lajos Batthyány formed the first Hungarian responsible government. The Twelve Points, called the March Laws, received royal assent on 10 April. The April laws created a democratic political system: Act V of 1848 turned the feudal Diet into an elected parliament with the widest right to vote in Europe at the time and erased the privileges of the nobility. The government also demanded that taxes raised in Hungary be spent there and that parliament control the Hungarian regiments.

Conflict followed. Serbs and Romanians, whom the Austrian court manipulated with conflicting promises, took up arms against the Hungarian government, and brutal incidents occurred. When Batthyány resigned, Kossuth became President of the Committee of National Defence at the end of September. In December Austrian forces under Field Marshal Windisch-Grätz entered Hungary, and the government left Pest for Debrecen. Hungarian armies led by Artúr Görgei won victories in the spring of 1849, and General Bem drove the Austrian and Russian troops out of Transylvania.

Austria then sought help from Russia. Franz Joseph I kissed the hand of Nicholas I in Warsaw on 21 May 1849, and Nicholas sent about 200,000 men under Field Marshal Ivan Paskevich, while Julius Jacob von Haynau commanded the Austrian army. The Hungarian army of about 160,000 faced some 380,000 troops, and it was defeated.

Haynau was made plenipotentiary and ordered the execution of the 13 Martyrs of Arad, and Batthyány was executed on the same day in Pest. Hungary was placed under martial law, followed by passive resistance and, from 1851, the regency of Archduke Albrecht, who pursued a policy of Germanisation. Many Hungarians later served in the Union Army in the American Civil War. The revolution is a cornerstone of modern Hungarian national identity, and 15 March, the anniversary of its outbreak, is a national holiday.
hungary: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe that spans much of the Carpathian Basin. It is bordered by Slovakia to the north, Ukraine to the northeast, Romania to the east and southeast, Serbia to the south, Croatia and Slovenia to the southwest, and Austria to the west. The whole country lies within the drainage basin of the Danube, which flows north to south through its centre. Its traditional divisions are Transdanubia, the land between the Danube and the Tisza, and the land beyond the Tisza.

Transdanubia is mostly hilly, with the eastern edge of the Alps in the west and Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe. The Great Hungarian Plain covers most of the east and southeast. Kékes, at 1,014 metres, is the tallest mountain, in the foothills of the Carpathians near the Slovak border.

The Roman Empire took the land west of the Danube in 16 to 15 BCE, and Pannonia was recognised as Roman in 14 BCE. The province of Dacia, which included the east of present-day Hungary, was formed in 106 CE and remained under Roman rule until 271. Later arrivals included the Hunnic Empire (c. 370 to 469), the Gepids, and the Avars, who founded the Avar Khaganate in the 560s. The Franks under Charlemagne defeated the Avars in a series of campaigns during the 790s.

Statehood began in the late ninth century with the Principality of Hungary, which became a Christian kingdom under King Stephen I in 1000. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was divided into three regions for over 150 years, until it was reunited under Habsburg rule before the turn of the 18th century. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 set Hungary's modern borders and cost it 71% of its historical territory; a third of ethnic Hungarians were left outside the new borders.

The Hungarian People's Republic was established in 1949 as a satellite state inside the Warsaw Pact. The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was unsuccessful, and during the Revolutions of 1989 the country moved peacefully to a democratic parliamentary republic. Parliament has 199 members.

The population was 9,689,000 in 2021, down from a peak of 10.8 million in 1980, and around 70% of the population lives in cities and towns, and a quarter of Hungarians live in the Budapest metropolitan area. About 5 million Hungarians live outside the country.
hunminjeongeum: Before Hangul, Korea had used Hanja, Chinese characters, since antiquity. The difficulty of the script limited its use largely to the upper classes, and commoners were mostly illiterate. Hanja also suits Korean poorly, since the two languages belong to different families and differ in structure: Classical Chinese puts the verb before its object, Middle Korean after it.

Because of a lack of records it is unknown when work on Hangul began or how it proceeded. King Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, was responsible for it and deeply involved. Hangul was introduced to his court, probably in a mostly complete form, in the twelfth month of 1443 by the Korean calendar, between about 30 December 1443 and 28 January 1444. Work then began on applying the script and preparing official documentation. The base text claims publication in the ninth month of 1446. The postface of the commentary is dated to the first ten days of that month, which on the tenth day is 9 October, the date observed as Hangul Day in South Korea.

The base text, written by Sejong in Classical Chinese, has two parts: a short preface and a description of the alphabet, occupying four leaves in the Haerye edition. The preface says that the sounds of the country's language differ from those of the Middle Kingdom, so that ignorant people with something to say were often unable to express it. Sejong writes that he has newly designed twenty-eight letters for everyone to practise at their ease and use daily.

It then introduces the 17 consonants and 11 vowels, each with its shape and a Hanja character showing its sound, and sets out orthographic rules. Initial consonants can serve as final ones, consonants and vowels combine into syllables, and tone is marked by dots at the left of a character: none for the level tone, one for the departing tone and two for the rising tone.

The Hunminjeongeum Haerye, a commentary written separately by a group of scholars led by Chŏng Inji, is believed to be closest to the text as published in 1446. It was lost and forgotten, possibly by the early 16th century, and was rediscovered in 1940 in what is called the Kansong copy. That copy became a National Treasure of South Korea on 20 December 1962 and entered UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997. A second, Sangju copy was discovered in 2008.
Other versions include the text in the Veritable Records of Sejong, and Eonhae editions translated into Korean mixed script, the oldest known variant of which appears in the Wŏrin sŏkpo of 1459.
huns: The Huns left no sources of their own, and their origins and links to other steppe peoples remain uncertain. They probably came from Central Asia. Roman writers equated them with earlier steppe peoples, calling them Massagetae, Scythians or Cimmerians. In the 18th century Joseph de Guignes proposed that they were descended from the Xiongnu. Scholars still dispute the connection, though recent archaeogenetic studies show some Hun-era individuals with DNA similar to ancient Mongolian populations.

The Romans became aware of the Huns in 376, when their invasion of the Pontic steppes drove thousands of Goths to seek refuge on the Lower Danube. In 395 they began their first large-scale attack on the Eastern Roman Empire, striking Thrace, Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria. From 434 the brothers Attila and Bleda ruled together, and in 435 they forced the Eastern Roman Empire to sign the Treaty of Margus, which gave the Huns trade rights and annual tribute. Theodosius II gave in to their demands in the Peace of Anatolius in 443. Bleda died in 445 and Attila ruled alone.

In 451 the Huns invaded Gaul and fought a combined army of Romans and Visigoths at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields, and in 452 they invaded Italy. After Attila's death in 453 his empire faced a struggle between its Germanic vassals and the Hunnic rulers. At the Battle of Nedao, around 454, the Gepid king Ardaric led a Germanic coalition against Attila's son Ellak, and the Huns lost many of their vassals.

The Huns practised pastoral nomadism, and their main method of warfare was mounted archery. Under Attila their economy depended heavily on plunder and tribute from the Roman provinces. Their government is debated: Peter Heather sees a loose confederation, and Hyun Jin Kim argues for a far more centralised system. They ruled many peoples, among them Gepids, Sarmatians, Heruli, Rugii, Suebi and Sciri, whose own kings often remained in place.

Very few archaeological remains are firmly Hunnic. Large copper cauldrons are attributed to them, and between 50 and 80 per cent of burials in the Carpathian basin in the Hun period show artificial cranial deformation. Almost nothing is known of their religion, though divination is attested. Medieval Hungarian chronicles claimed descent from them, a claim mainstream scholarship has dismissed.
hunsruck: The Hunsrück is a long, triangular upland in Rhineland-Palatinate, bounded by the valleys of the Moselle and Saar, the Nahe and the Rhine, and a school rhyme teaches children its limits: Moselle, Nahe, Saar and Rhine enclose our Hunsrück. It continues as the Taunus beyond the Rhine and as the Eifel beyond the Moselle, and Koblenz lies at its north-eastern corner. The range is around 100 km long and 25 to 30 km wide. Its interior is rarely higher than 450 metres, and its highest peak is the Erbeskopf, at 816 metres. The Idar Forest, the Soonwald and the Bingen Forest form an almost unbroken belt of forest, and the climate brings frequent morning mists and more rain than the German average.

Stone axes show that the Hunsrück has been settled since the New Stone Age, and Gravettian sites mark the first settlements in the area. In the La Tène period the Hunsrück-Eifel culture, linked with the Celts, left the Waldalgesheim prince's grave, the circular rampart of Otzenhausen and the Pfalzfeld obelisk. The region was then the tribal area of the Treveri. Between about 50 BCE and 400 CE the Romans opened it up with a dense network of roads, the best known being the Via Ausonia, which linked Trier with Bingen.

The name Hundesrucha is first mentioned in a deed of 1074 from Ravengiersburg Abbey. In the Middle Ages the land was fragmented among the counts Palatine of the Rhine, the archbishops of Trier, the counts of Sponheim and the successors of the Emichones, the Wildgraves, the Raugraves and the counts of Veldenz. Many castles and customs stations were built between the 11th and mid 14th century. The Principality of Simmern emerged in 1410 under a side line of the counts Palatine. In 1689 French troops set fire to Kirchberg, Kastellaun, Simmern and Stromberg in the Nine Years' War.

After the French period, the Congress of Vienna gave most of the Hunsrück to Prussia's Rhine Province in 1815. Poor harvests and the famine of 1817 followed, and in 1823 the agent Georg Anton Schäffer, sent by Emperor Dom Pedro I of Brazil, recruited many emigrants there. The first settled near São Leopoldo in Rio Grande do Sul in 1824, and further waves left in the 1840s and 1861, for Brazil and North America.

The notable towns are Simmern, Kirchberg, Idar-Oberstein, Kastellaun and Morbach, and Frankfurt-Hahn Airport lies at the centre of the upland. Slate is still mined there. The region is best known culturally for the Hunsrückisch dialect and for its depiction in the Heimat film series.
hurrem-sultan: No document records Hürrem's life before she entered the harem, and her birth name is unknown. Legends of her origins arose in literature, and she has been claimed as Ukrainian, Russian or Polish. Many sources place her in Ruthenia, then part of the Polish Crown. The ambassador Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, in his Turkish Letters, published in 1581, called her Roxelana after Roxolania, the name often given to that territory. According to accounts, Crimean Tatars kidnapped her in a slave raid between 1512 and 1520, and she may have been taken first to Kaffa, a major centre of the Ottoman slave trade, before reaching Constantinople.

Her rise from slave to legal wife attracted jealousy in the harem and among the general population. No law forbade the marriage, but custom was strong and astonished the court. The wedding probably took place around 1533. She bore at least six children, five of them sons, which broke the old custom that a concubine gave the sultan only one son.
